fields.summary: The Hadean is the informal first eon of Earth's history, the age between the planet's forming, about 4.54 billion years ago, and roughly 4.0 billion years ago. Earth lay molten like ore in a crucible, then cooled as embers cool under ash, and all the while the sky hurled stone upon it.
facts: Earth and the Moon took shape in the first tens of millions of years, two lamps kindled in the same young dark; see [[event/formation-of-the-solar-system-and-earth|Formation of the Solar System and Earth]] and [[event/theia-impact-and-the-formation-of-the-moon|Theia Impact and the Formation of the Moon]].
The oldest known Earth material is zircon crystals from the Jack Hills in Western Australia, dated to about 4.4 billion years ago: the deepest memory the stone has yet given up.
Those zircons suggest that liquid water and some crust existed very early, as a single seed in the ash speaks of a field that once grew.
The Hadean holds no official rank among ICS units; it is an informal name for the interval before the rock record, a name spoken at the fireside rather than carved above the gate.
fields.context: The Hadean laid the footings for everything that came after: the Moon steadies Earth's tilt as a keel steadies a ship, and volatile-rich material delivered to the young planet gave it its oceans. The eon ends where the surviving rock record opens its first page, at the start of the [[era/archean-eon|Archean Eon]].
fields.observer: The Observer files the Hadean under preconditions, and so should you. Nothing here is a subject of study, yet every later fact leans on it: the planet's composition, its Moon, and its water. Think of a house's buried footings. The architecture forgets them; it never stops standing on them.
questions: How early did stable oceans first hold their shores, and stable continents first stand above the water?
Did the stone rain fall as one Late Heavy Bombardment, or did the impacts ebb away gradually, like a tide going out?

fields.summary: The Andes are the mountain spine of western South America. In their highlands and along their coasts, societies raised complex states without wheeled transport or a conventional writing system, as rivers carve their canyons with no chisel but water.
facts: The [[culture/inca-empire|Inca Empire]] grew, as snowmelt gathers into a river, into the largest pre-Columbian state in the Americas.
In the Andes, potatoes were coaxed from the soil and llamas from the wild, both domesticated to the service of the high country.
The Inca kept their records in knots, on corded strands called quipu, memory tied fast as a fisher ties a net.
The site of [[place/machu-picchu|Machu Picchu]], set like a crown upon the stone, dates to the 15th century.
fields.context: Like an island in a sea of distance, the Andes stood cut off from the Old World until the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]].
fields.observer: I came looking for writing. I watched a state coordinate millions of people; I watched it hand its memory to something that is not writing as most people define it. What else have I refused to call writing? Memory does not need ink.
questions: What evidence, if it rose from the soil tomorrow, would most redraw the current picture?

fields.summary: Archaeopteryx was a feathered, winged dinosaur about the size of a raven, a small dragon dressed for the sky. It is known from Late Jurassic limestone in Bavaria, Germany, stone about 150 million years old that kept its form as still water keeps a reflection.
facts: Its fossils come from the Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, Germany, stone that closed over them as a book closes over a pressed flower.
It wore two natures at once: bird-like features such as feathers and wings, and reptile-like ones, among them teeth, clawed fingers, and a long bony tail.
The first skeleton came out of the stone in 1861, two years after Darwin published *On the Origin of Species*, and it was quickly raised like a banner as a transitional form.
From the 1990s onward, feathered non-avian dinosaurs found in China drew tighter the thread that binds birds to the theropod dinosaurs.
Birds are the living descendants of theropod dinosaurs, the old line still aloft.
fields.context: Archaeopteryx bears witness to the origin of birds within the [[species/dinosaurs|Dinosaurs]], and birds were the dinosaur lineage that survived the [[event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction|Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction]], as one seed outlasts a hard winter. It was an early prop for the evolutionary ideas of [[person/charles-darwin|Charles Darwin]]. In the chronicle it dwells in the [[era/mesozoic-era|Mesozoic Era]] and the region [[region/europe|Europe]], woven into the theme threads of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the dinosaurs did not fully end. They are still on every continent; you simply call them birds. Look up the next time a wing crosses your window: that is the lineage, still flying. The species that studies extinctions lives among survivors of one of them, overhead. An ending can leave descendants.
questions: Did Archaeopteryx beat its way aloft in powered flight, or could it only glide, like a leaf riding the wind?

fields.summary: Angkor was the capital region of the Khmer Empire in present-day Cambodia, a realm of stone laid upon water. Within it rose the temple of Angkor Wat, built in the early 12th century like a mountain lifted by human hands.
facts: Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument in the world by area, a sanctuary spread wide as a lake in flood.
Aerial laser surveys reveal, as dawn reveals a valley, a vast urban area of roughly a thousand square kilometers.
A network of reservoirs (barays) and canals ruled the water, holding it and loosing it like the slow breath of the city.

It was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992. The traditional date of 1431, when Ayutthaya is said to have sacked Angkor and the city to have been abandoned, is now disputed; and Angkor Wat itself was never abandoned, its hearth never gone cold.
fields.context: Angkor was the heart of the [[culture/khmer-empire|Khmer Empire]], the still point its whole realm turned around. See [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]].
fields.observer: I carried a picture of cities as compact clusters. I carried it to Angkor, and I watched it fail: here was a 'low-density' city, spread over a landscape of water systems and temples, and it challenged the picture I had brought. How many cities have I missed because they did not huddle? A city can be a landscape.
questions: What caused the capital, like a banner struck and carried elsewhere, to shift away from Angkor?

fields.summary: Auschwitz-Birkenau was a complex of Nazi German concentration and extermination camps near the Polish town of Oświęcim, operated from 1940 to January 1945, where at least 1.1 million people were murdered, about 960,000 of them Jews. Every one of those numbers is made of single lives.
facts: The complex grew in stages: Auschwitz was established in 1940 near Oświęcim, in Polish territory annexed by Germany, first for Polish political prisoners; the camp at Birkenau (Auschwitz II) was built from 1941 and became a center of mass murder in gas chambers from 1942; and the Monowitz camp (Auschwitz III) supplied forced labor to a chemical works of IG Farben.

The ledger is this: about 1.3 million people were deported to Auschwitz and at least 1.1 million of them died; about 960,000 were Jews from across occupied Europe, and other victims included about 74,000 non-Jewish Poles, about 21,000 Roma and Sinti, and about 15,000 Soviet prisoners of war.
For most victims the rail platform was the last threshold: they were killed on arrival, after selection there. Others died of forced labor, starvation, disease, shootings and medical experiments.

Prisoners resisted, and the record must say so: in October 1944 members of the Sonderkommando revolted and destroyed a crematorium, and escapees, including Witold Pilecki in 1943 and Rudolf Vrba and Alfred Wetzler in 1944, carried reports of the killings to the outside.

As Soviet forces approached in January 1945, the SS forced tens of thousands of prisoners on death marches; when Soviet troops liberated the camp on 27 January 1945, they found about 7,000 prisoners still there.
Auschwitz-Birkenau became a state museum in 1947, and UNESCO inscribed the site in 1979; 27 January is observed as International Holocaust Remembrance Day, a covenant of memory kept each year.
fields.context: Auschwitz-Birkenau was the largest site of the [[event/holocaust|Holocaust]], carried out during [[event/world-war-ii|World War II]]. In the chronicle it sits in the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]] and the region [[region/europe|Europe]], and it belongs to two theme threads, [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]]. Both threads pass through this place.
fields.observer:
The Observer records Auschwitz-Birkenau as a place where a state murdered more than a million people, most of them Jews, on the basis of an ideology about descent. The Observer records those deaths as what they were: suffering and atrocity.

Look closely at the method, because the method is where the lesson sits. The killing was carried out with the tools of administration and industry: rail schedules, selection lists, factories and gas. What that shows is hard and plain. Tool-lineage and bureaucracy can be turned to sanctioned harm on a very large scale.

The preserved site, survivors' testimony and the perpetrators' own records now serve as memory-outsourcing, a ledger held against denial and forgetting, and the resistance of prisoners is written into that ledger too.

A historian could challenge this emphasis on administrative method by pointing to the role of ideology and of popular participation, which this account does not explain. Hold that objection beside the reading. To explain the machinery is not to have explained the people.
questions: How were the figures for the dead reconstructed, when the perpetrators had destroyed the records?
As the last survivors die, how are their testimony and the physical site being preserved, so that the witness outlasts the witnesses?

fields.summary: The Abbasid Caliphate ruled much of the Islamic world from 750 CE, holding its court at Baghdad as a delta holds a river's gathered waters, until the Mongols sacked the city in 1258.
facts: Baghdad was founded in 762 and swelled, as a river swells in the flood season, into one of the world's largest cities.
The House of Wisdom and the translation movement drew on Greek, Persian, and Indian works, as one well is fed by three springs.
Paper manufacturing spread through the caliphate like water finding its channels.
From the 9th century political control fractured like river ice in a thaw, and regional dynasties took power among the pieces.
fields.context: See the [[event/rise-of-islam|Rise of Islam]] and [[person/al-khwarizmi|Al-Khwarizmi]]. Its end rode in with the [[event/mongol-conquests|Mongol Conquests]], as a storm ends a long summer.
fields.observer: I think of a state that gathered scholars from many traditions into one city. I think of the work that followed, work that neither tradition would have made alone. What have I never made, working alone? The new thing is born between.
questions: How much of the translation effort flowed from the state, and how much welled up of its own accord?

fields.summary: The Armenian Genocide was the deliberate destruction of most of the Ottoman Empire's Armenian population during World War I, carried out through mass killings, forced deportations, and death from starvation and exposure. Many countries and historians recognize it as genocide, and the government of Turkey denies it; we have to hold both of those sentences at once.
facts: On 24 April 1915 Ottoman authorities arrested about 240 Armenian leaders in Constantinople, among them writers, doctors, religious leaders and political figures, and deported them eastward; that date is now kept to commemorate the victims.

The deportations began at the edge and did not stay there: in spring 1915 the Ottoman government began deporting Armenians from the northeastern border regions, then extended deportations to almost every province, including regions far from combat.
Victims died in local massacres; they died on forced marches, of starvation, dehydration, exposure and disease; and they died in the deserts of the southern empire, or on the way there.
Estimates of the number killed run from at least 600,000 to more than 1,000,000; the exact number is not settled, and the ledger remains open.

The Turkish state has long denied that the events were genocide and has worked against official recognition abroad; more than twenty countries formally recognize the genocide, and Uruguay was the first, in 1965.
fields.context: The genocide took place inside the [[culture/ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] during [[event/world-war-i|World War I]]. It is often studied alongside the [[event/holocaust|Holocaust]], and if you want the vault's treatment of organized killing, you will find it in [[observer-note/sanctioned-harm|Sanctioned Harm]].
fields.observer: The Observer records this as an atrocity: a state deliberately destroyed much of one of its own peoples. Say it that plainly; plainness is the least the record owes the dead. The Observer also records that the denial has itself lasted a century, so that the question of what happened has become bound up with the question of who is permitted to say it. After this long, what happened and who may say so are one question.
questions: How many people died, and how should we count the deaths on the deportation routes?
How have the surviving communities and their descendants carried memory down the generations under conditions of official denial?

fields.summary: The Permian-Triassic extinction, about 251.9 million years ago, was the largest mass extinction in Earth's history. It killed an estimated 80 to 96 percent of marine species. Eight in ten, at the least. Nearly all, at the worst. Gone.
facts: The leading cause: enormous volcanic eruptions in Siberia. The Siberian Traps. Opening. And opening. And opening.
What followed, among other things: rapid warming. Acid in the ocean. Oxygen bleeding out of the seas.
It ended the dominance of trilobites. Then it ended the trilobites.
Full ecological recovery took roughly ten million years. That long. That slow.
fields.context: It is the line where the [[era/paleozoic-era|Paleozoic Era]] ends and the [[era/mesozoic-era|Mesozoic Era]] begins. A border drawn in the dead. See [[species/trilobites|Trilobites]].
fields.observer: The Observer regards this as the nearest the biosphere has come to ending. Sit with that phrase before you move on. Its cause was a carbon-releasing planetary change, and it bears an uncomfortable resemblance to a process the species is now carrying out. The deep past is not a prophecy. It is a precedent, and precedents are uncomfortable to read.
questions: How fast did the heat come? How fast the acid?

fields.summary: Ada Lovelace (1815 to 1852) was an English mathematician who wrote extensive notes on Charles Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine, and inside those notes sits what is often regarded as the first published computer algorithm. Think of it as a blueprint for a building no one had raised: the architecture arrived before the house.
facts: Her lineage ran through poetry: she was the daughter of the poet Lord Byron.
Her 1843 notes described how the engine could compute a sequence of Bernoulli numbers, a grammar of steps set down in ink.
She suggested that such a machine might manipulate symbols beyond numbers, such as music, which carries the idea past the threshold of arithmetic.
The extent of her original contribution, measured against Babbage's, is debated; the ledger of credit is still open.
fields.context: Lovelace's ideas anticipate the [[technology/digital-computer|Digital Computer]] and the [[event/digital-revolution|Digital Revolution]], as a threshold anticipates the room beyond it. Set her beside [[person/alan-turing|Alan Turing]] and compare.
fields.observer: I keep returning to it: the concept of programmable machines came a century before the machines. I keep returning to an idea waiting at the door. What have I imagined that my tools cannot yet hold? Ideas can outrun their tools.
questions: What was her role in the architecture of the algorithm itself?

fields.summary: Antibiotics are drugs that kill or inhibit bacteria, and their story turns on a threshold: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928, and mass production began in the 1940s.
facts: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain developed penicillin for medical use, and the three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize: discovery and development, honored together.
Antibiotics greatly reduced deaths from infections and from surgery, rewriting the ledger of ordinary risk.
Overuse has caused widespread antibiotic resistance; a gift spent carelessly wears thin.
Life expectancy rose sharply in the 20th century, and antibiotics were one pillar of that architecture, beside sanitation and vaccines.
fields.context: Read this beside [[technology/vaccination|Vaccination]] and the [[event/black-death|Black Death]]. Antibiotics changed the architecture of medicine in the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the species can now treat plagues that once killed a third of a continent. Feel the weight of that threshold before you pass it. The Observer also notes that overuse is a new problem, an arms race with bacteria. No victory over a living enemy is final.
questions: How, in practice, can antibiotic resistance be slowed?

fields.summary: Is there one change, one threshold, that best explains how the species rose so rapidly in power over other animals?
fields.observer:
I call it heat-domestication, the control of fire. I call it the first time the species used an energy source outside its own body. I call it a pattern, because every later step in its power, from smelting to steam to the power grid, repeats it: find a stored source of energy and learn to release it on demand.

Is that a triumph? It is. Is it the root of a modern problem? It is that too, because the same principle now warms the planet. I do not know whether to kneel to it or to fear it. The first flame and the warming sky are one fire.

extra.title: Question
extra.text: Can any single change best explain the species' swift rise in power over other animals?

extra.title: What the Record Shows
extra.text:
- The evidence for controlled fire reaches back at least a million years; see [[event/control-of-fire|Control of Fire]].
- Cooking makes food safer and easier to digest, and it may have helped build larger brains.
- Fire lengthens the day, gives protection, and gathers people into a circle, an architecture of communion.
- Later technologies, from pottery to metallurgy, rest on heat.
- The [[event/industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]] took the same principle and scaled it up, with coal and the [[technology/steam-engine|Steam Engine]].

extra.title: Limits of This Reading
extra.text: Be honest about the frame: this essay simplifies. Language, cooperation, and cumulative learning are also candidates for the deepest cause of human power. No single thread holds the whole weave.

fields.summary: A secondary cross-check for details such as the Bakhshali dating revision and Hatshepsut's regnal chronology: a place to confirm, not a place to rest.

extra.title: Caveats
extra.text: Treat it as tertiary and editable, a threshold rather than a foundation: use it only to find your way to primary and scholarly sources. Consulted 2026-09-20.

fields.summary: The Anthropocene is a proposed geological interval, a name for the stretch of time in which human activity is the dominant influence on Earth's systems. Think of it as a signature we did not know we were signing. In March 2024 the International Union of Geological Sciences declined to formalize it as an official epoch, yet the term remains widely used: the ledger was refused, and still we keep writing in it.
facts: Consider the first candidate threshold: a proposed start date around 1950, tied to the [[event/great-acceleration|Great Acceleration]] and to markers such as radioactive fallout.
Other proposed thresholds reach further back, to the beginning of agriculture and to the [[event/industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]].
The ledger of cited signals reads plainly: changes to atmospheric carbon dioxide, plastics, and species extinction rates.

On 4 March 2024 the Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy voted to reject formalization as an epoch, and on 20 March 2024 the IUGS upheld the result. Yet a vote on the codex is not a verdict on the world: the formal geological decision does not settle the scientific or cultural question.
fields.context: Use the Anthropocene as a lens, and the [[era/information-age|Information Age]] and the [[event/great-acceleration|Great Acceleration]] come into sharper focus through it. For the longer argument, see [[observer-note/the-species-as-a-geological-force|The Species as a Geological Force]].
fields.observer: I have read the rock record for fire, for ice, for the slow arrival of shells. Here, as I read it, is the point where the species became legible in the rock record, its behavior pressed into the layers like a palm into wet clay. For the first time, a single species' behavior is a planetary variable. Who taught you to write so large? No one did. That is the weight of it.
questions: If the threshold must be drawn at all, from when should the Anthropocene be dated?

fields.summary: The Archean Eon, about 4.0 to 2.5 billion years ago, was the age in which the first continents stabilized like islands of cooling iron and life first appeared. Its air held almost no free oxygen, a sky still waiting for its breath.
facts: Among the oldest widely accepted fossil evidence stand the stromatolites of Western Australia, layered stone-cushions about 3.5 billion years old.
Continental cores, the cratons, formed and grew like the first bones of a body, and plate-tectonic-like processes began their slow grinding at some point in this eon.
Life in this age was microbial, a kingdom of the unseen. See [[event/origin-of-life|Origin of Life]].
Before the eon closed, photosynthesis had evolved, the first light-fed labour that set up the [[event/great-oxidation-event|Great Oxidation Event]].
fields.context: The Archean is the long, slow overture to the [[era/proterozoic-eon|Proterozoic Eon]], a hall in which the first living things were kindled and the chemistry was laid, stone by patient stone, that later made complex life possible.
fields.observer: Imagine you arrived in the Archean with a notebook. You would find a living planet and no obvious candidates for study: no faces to read, no tools to catalogue. That emptiness is the lesson. The Observer treats this eon as the deep root of the entire tree, and a root is still the tree.
questions: When did plate tectonics first stir into motion?
Are the oldest claimed microfossils true witnesses, or tricks of stone?

fields.summary: The Bronze Age, about 3300 to 1200 BCE in the Near East, was the age of bronze metallurgy, when copper met tin in the furnace, when the early states rose, and when the first writing was pressed into being.
facts: Bronze is a marriage of copper and tin, an alloy wed in fire; see [[technology/bronze-metallurgy|Bronze Metallurgy]].
Now the first cities rise and the first writing systems wake: [[event/the-urban-revolution|The Urban Revolution]], [[event/invention-of-writing|Invention of Writing]].

Its great powers were many-crowned: the [[culture/sumerians|Sumerians]], the [[culture/ancient-egyptians|Ancient Egyptians]], the [[culture/indus-valley-civilization|Indus Valley Civilization]], the [[culture/minoans|Minoans]] and the [[culture/shang-dynasty|Shang Dynasty]] were among its major states.
In the eastern Mediterranean the age ends as a lamp gutters, in the [[event/bronze-age-collapse|Bronze Age Collapse]].
fields.context: The Bronze Age stands between the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]] and the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]] like a bridge of hammered metal. Tin travelled long roads, and that long-distance trade spun the era into wide exchange-webs, like dew-heavy threads strung between distant hands.
fields.observer: Notice what arrived together, the Observer says: the first states and the first writing. Writing seems to have started as accounting, not poetry, a ledger before a lyric. We like to believe the word was born to sing; it seems it was first set down to count. The ledger is the oldest architecture of the written word.
questions: How deeply did the long-distance tin trade shape the early states?

fields.summary: The Cambrian Period, from 538.8 to 485.4 million years ago, is the first period of the Paleozoic Era, the dawn in which the seas put on armour. In its span most major animal body plans, and the first animals with hard parts, appear in the fossil record, as though a curtain had been drawn back on a crowded stage.
facts: The Cambrian Period spans 538.8 to 485.4 million years ago. Its base, which is also the base of the Paleozoic Era, is set in stone at Fortune Head, Newfoundland, by the first appearance of the burrow trace fossil Treptichnus pedum, a small tunnel marking a great door.
The [[event/cambrian-explosion|Cambrian Explosion]], when most major animal groups step into the fossil record, burns through roughly the first 13 to 25 million years of the period.
[[species/trilobites|Trilobites]] first appear about 521 million years ago, and in time they become one of the most common animals on the sea floor, a host in segmented mail.
Soft bodies survive, exceptionally preserved, in the Chengjiang deposits of China, about 518 million years old, and in the Burgess Shale of Canada, about 508 million years old.

Animals dwelt almost entirely in the sea. Sea level stood high, shallow seas spread across the continents like spilled silver, and the climate was generally warm. The land's record of plants waits until the Ordovician; see [[event/colonization-of-land|Colonization of Land]].
fields.context: The Cambrian Period rises from the [[era/ediacaran-period|Ediacaran Period]] and throws open the gates of the [[era/paleozoic-era|Paleozoic Era]]; after it comes the [[era/ordovician-period|Ordovician Period]]. Its thread runs through the great weave of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: Here is a general problem you will meet again, and the Observer reads the Cambrian fossil record as an early case of it: what is known of the past is what happened to be preserved. Think of an archive that kept only the letters written on stone. Hard parts leave records, so a sudden arrival of animals is partly the arrival of animals that fossilize. The practice is humility before the ledger. The Observer holds the reading open: evidence that the fossil sequence closely tracks real diversity would weaken this emphasis on preservation. The archive is not the world; it is the world's survivors.
questions: How much of the Cambrian Explosion is a true blaze of evolution, and how much a blaze of preservation?
What spark lit the forging of skeletons in several animal groups within a few million years?

fields.summary: The Carboniferous Period, from 358.9 to 298.9 million years ago, is the fifth period of the Paleozoic Era, and it bears the name of the coal its swamp forests laid down like black treasure in a vault. It is the age of the first amniote vertebrates, and the age in which the supercontinent Pangaea was gathered together.
facts: The Carboniferous Period spans 358.9 to 298.9 million years ago. Its name means coal-bearing, and in North America its long reign is split in two, the Mississippian and the Pennsylvanian.

Swamp forests spread over tropical lowlands, ruled by tree-sized club-mosses such as Lepidodendron, and they buried the plant matter that became coal. Why so much coal formed in this period is still debated. Britain's coalfields were laid down in it, and their coal later fed the fires of the [[event/industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]] as a major fuel.

Estimates for late Carboniferous atmospheric oxygen run as high as about 30 percent, against about 21 percent today, though how far to trust them is debated. Giants moved through that air, among them arthropods such as the dragonfly relative Meganeura, whose wings spanned about 70 centimetres.
The earliest known amniotes appear, bearers of eggs able to develop on land, a sealed sea carried ashore; among them is Hylonomus from Nova Scotia, about 312 million years old.

In this period the Late Paleozoic Ice Age began, its cold heart centred on Gondwana. About 305 million years ago the coal forests fell as the climate dried, and Gondwana and Euramerica met in collision, raising much of Pangaea from their meeting.
fields.context: The Carboniferous Period rises after the [[era/devonian-period|Devonian Period]] and yields to the [[era/permian-period|Permian Period]] within the [[era/paleozoic-era|Paleozoic Era]]. It is woven into the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]], and its forests carry on the long march of [[event/colonization-of-land|Colonization of Land]].
fields.observer: I think of forests that never meant to leave anyone anything. I think of the carbon they locked away in the dark, and I think of the species that dug it up about 300 million years later and burned it, returning it to the air. Nothing about those forests was aimed at that result. It is an inheritance received by accident, a gift no one gave. I hold only to the link across time; the debate over why so much coal formed does not touch it. We are warmed by the dead who never knew our names.
questions: Why did so much coal gather in this age and not in others?
How high did atmospheric oxygen rise, and how far did it limit the size of insects?

fields.summary: The Neoproterozoic Era is the last era of the Proterozoic Eon, a long dusk running from 1.0 billion to 538.8 million years ago. In its keeping lie three great turnings: the supercontinent Rodinia breaking apart like ice on a spring river, the global glaciations known as Snowball Earth, and the first large complex organisms, stirring at last.
facts: Three periods fill the Neoproterozoic Era's span of 1.0 billion to 538.8 million years ago, as three chambers fill one hall: the [[era/tonian-period|Tonian Period]], the [[era/cryogenian-period|Cryogenian Period]] and the [[era/ediacaran-period|Ediacaran Period]]. Its upper threshold is the base of the [[era/cambrian-period|Cambrian Period]].
Rodinia, the supercontinent gathered together by about 1.0 billion years ago, began to rift apart along its seams roughly 800 to 750 million years ago, like a great slab of ice parting on dark water.

Two great freezes of the Cryogenian, the Sturtian (about 717 to 660 million years ago) and the Marinoan (about 650 to 635 million years ago), are the bedrock on which the [[event/snowball-earth|Snowball Earth]] hypothesis stands.
Oxygen is proposed to have risen again, a second slow breath, sometime between about 800 and 540 million years ago; when it came and how great it grew are debated.

Molecular-clock estimates set the birth of animals in or before the Cryogenian, yet the fossil record of the first animals is disputed; by about 575 million years ago the [[species/ediacaran-biota|Ediacaran Biota]], large and soft-bodied organisms, had appeared.
fields.context: After the [[era/mesoproterozoic-era|Mesoproterozoic Era]] the Neoproterozoic Era came, the closing chapter of the [[era/proterozoic-eon|Proterozoic Eon]], and it yielded, as night yields to a sudden morning, to the [[era/paleozoic-era|Paleozoic Era]] at the [[event/cambrian-explosion|Cambrian Explosion]]. Its thread runs through the theme of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: We love a staircase. Animals arrive at the end of the Neoproterozoic, and so we are tempted to read the ice, the oxygen and the break-up of Rodinia as steps built toward them, an architecture with one doorway at the top. The Observer declines that reading. These were physical events with their own causes, and animals were one of several possible outcomes. Think of tracing a river back from the sea and deciding the mountains were raised to feed it: that is hindsight dressed as design. Evidence that any one of them was strictly required for animals would weaken this view. Until then, a sequence is not a plan.
questions: Did the Cryogenian ice and the second rise of oxygen help bring forth the animals, and how much did they contribute, if at all?
When, in that long twilight, did the first animals appear?

fields.summary: The Ordovician Period, from 485.4 to 443.8 million years ago, is the second period of the Paleozoic Era, an age when the seas brimmed with new life. It saw a great rise in marine biodiversity, the first evidence of plants on land, and, at its close, the first of the "Big Five" mass extinctions, a shadow falling across bright water.
facts: The Ordovician Period spans 485.4 to 443.8 million years ago, and two small creatures keep its gates: its base is fixed at Green Point, Newfoundland, by the conodont Iapetognathus fluctivagus, and its top at Dob's Linn in Scotland by a graptolite.

The Great Ordovician Biodiversification, a slow flood running for tens of millions of years from the early period, greatly multiplied the diversity of marine animals, as a reef multiplies its colours.

The sea stood very high, and its warm shallows cradled reefs, brachiopods, trilobites, crinoids and graptolites, while straight-shelled nautiloid cephalopods, some several metres long, moved among them as large predators.
From this period comes the earliest evidence of land plants: spores about 470 million years old, a first faint dust of life upon bare ground; see [[event/colonization-of-land|Colonization of Land]].

Late in the period the climate cooled, and an ice age centred on Gondwana set in during the Hirnantian; the [[event/late-ordovician-extinction|Late Ordovician Extinction]], about 445 to 443 million years ago, swept away an estimated 85 percent of species, mostly marine, like a tide that went out and did not return.
fields.context: Between the [[era/cambrian-period|Cambrian Period]] before it and the [[era/silurian-period|Silurian Period]] after, the Ordovician Period stands as one hall in the long house of the [[era/paleozoic-era|Paleozoic Era]]. Its thread is woven into the theme of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: The Observer records two movements in one period: a great rise in marine diversity and, near its end, a mass extinction linked to glaciation. You will want to call the first progress and the second a punishment. Resist both words. Both arose from shifting planetary conditions, and neither was directed at any outcome; one ledger holds the gain and the loss. Think of a shoreline after a season of storms, reshaped by many pushes, none of them aiming. A demonstration that diversity rose steadily whatever the climate did would weaken the reading that a biosphere's history is the sum of many pushes, not a trend. A pile of pushes is not a staircase.
questions: What stirred the Great Ordovician Biodiversification into being: climate, ocean chemistry, ecological change, or some braid of them all?
Why did the ice come when carbon dioxide is estimated to have stood so high, a winter falling on a warm house?

fields.summary: The Paleogene Period, from 66 to 23.03 million years ago, is the first period of the Cenozoic Era, a long morning after ruin. In it the mammals spread outward after the end-Cretaceous extinction, and the world turned from a warm, largely ice-free house toward a cold one crowned with polar ice.
facts: The Paleogene Period spans 66.0 to 23.03 million years ago and holds three epochs, the Paleocene, Eocene and Oligocene, like three rooms of one hall; its lower threshold, the [[event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction|Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction]] boundary, is fixed at El Kef in Tunisia, and its upper, the base of the Neogene, at Lemme-Carrosio in Italy.

Mammals spread swiftly into the roles the extinction had left empty, and the earliest primates and their close kin appear; over about ten million years, from about 50 to 40 million years ago, whales were drawn out of land-dwelling hoofed mammals, the way a river is drawn to the sea.

The [[event/paleocene-eocene-thermal-maximum|Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum]], about 56 million years ago, set the world to fever, warming it by roughly 5 to 6 degrees Celsius for about 200,000 years, and the early Eocene burned among the warmest intervals of the Cenozoic.
The [[event/collision-of-india-and-asia|Collision of India and Asia]], beginning about 50 million years ago, started to raise the Himalaya, a wave of stone rising slowly toward the sky.

About 34 million years ago, at the Eocene-Oligocene boundary, the climate cooled sharply and ice sheets began to grow on Antarctica like frost across a pane; falling carbon dioxide and the opening of Southern Ocean gateways are proposed causes.
fields.context: After the [[era/cretaceous-period|Cretaceous Period]] the Paleogene Period came, opening the [[era/cenozoic-era|Cenozoic Era]] as a first door opens on a new house, and after it the [[era/neogene-period|Neogene Period]]. Its thread runs through the theme of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer:
I go to the Paleogene looking for a beginning. I find a vacated world, where mammals spread into the roles the extinction left empty. I find a world cooling, the polar ice taking hold. I find the primates, the group that includes humans, and they are one lineage among many in that spreading, with nothing in the record to mark them as special at the time. Who promised them anything? No one, the stone says.

The reading would weaken if primates could be shown to have been headed for prominence independently of the extinction, and I would welcome the correction. A lineage is not a destiny.
questions: Was Purgatorius, which lived just after the extinction, a true primate, or a close relative of primates waiting at the edge of the family?
In the Eocene-Oligocene cooling, how much of the cold came through the opening of Southern Ocean gateways, and how much from falling carbon dioxide?

fields.summary: The Paleolithic, the Old Stone Age, is the long era of chipped-stone tools and foraging societies, stretching like a road beneath changing skies from about 2.6 million years ago to the end of the last ice age.
facts: The earliest known stone tools, the first edges struck by a hand, date to about 3.3 million years ago (Lomekwi) and 2.6 million years ago (Oldowan); see [[technology/oldowan-stone-tools|Oldowan Stone Tools]].
The taming of flame, [[event/control-of-fire|Control of Fire]], is kindled well before the era's end.
Modern humans spread across the globe like seeds on a long wind; see [[event/out-of-africa-dispersal|Out of Africa Dispersal]].
In its later stages symbolic behavior awakens, the [[event/emergence-of-symbolic-art|Emergence of Symbolic Art]] among it, like first lamps lit at dusk.
It fills about 99 percent of the time humans and their ancestors have made tools, a vast sea of hours.
fields.context: The Paleolithic lies cradled within the [[era/pleistocene-epoch|Pleistocene Epoch]], and it ends with the turning toward farming known as the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]].
fields.observer: I count the years, and the count keeps saying the same thing: for roughly 99 percent of the tool-making record, the species lived as small mobile groups. I count the camps. I count the walks. I count the fires. Everything called 'civilization' is a recent variation on a very old pattern. The walls are new; the walking is old.
questions: How wide did Paleolithic social networks reach, and how tightly were their threads knotted together?

fields.summary: The Paleoproterozoic Era is the first era of the Proterozoic Eon, running from 2.5 billion to 1.6 billion years ago. In it free oxygen first settled into the sky and stayed, a new voice in the air's old song, a lasting part of the atmosphere.
facts: The Paleoproterozoic Era spans 2.5 to 1.6 billion years ago, and its borders, like those of its four periods (Siderian, Rhyacian, Orosirian and Statherian), are drawn by agreed numerical ages rather than by any mark written in the rock.

The [[event/great-oxidation-event|Great Oxidation Event]], the first sustained rise of free oxygen, breathed out by the photosynthesis of [[species/cyanobacteria|Cyanobacteria]], began around 2.4 billion years ago; estimates for its first dawning run from about 2.46 to 2.32 billion years ago.
The Huronian glaciation of Ontario, Canada, a white silence roughly 2.4 to 2.2 billion years ago, is often bound in the telling to the oxygen rise, but that bond remains a hypothesis.

Banded iron formations, a great wellspring of the world's iron ore, were laid down widely between about 2.5 and 1.8 billion years ago, striped like the rings of an ancient tree, and then largely vanish from the record until the Cryogenian.

The oldest unambiguous eukaryote fossils, about 1.65 billion years old, lie within this era, while older claimants such as Grypania (about 1.87 billion years) are still debated; see [[event/origin-of-eukaryotes|Origin of Eukaryotes]].
fields.context: After the [[era/archean-eon|Archean Eon]] came the Paleoproterozoic Era, and after it the [[era/mesoproterozoic-era|Mesoproterozoic Era]], both within the [[era/proterozoic-eon|Proterozoic Eon]]. Its thread runs through the theme of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]], and its oxygen lingers, like old smoke in a hall, in the chemical background of the later [[event/cambrian-explosion|Cambrian Explosion]].
fields.observer:
The Observer files the Paleoproterozoic under preconditions. Here it starts. Oxygen. The gas later animals breathe first piled up here as a waste product of microbial metabolism. Exhaust. Poison to much of the life then present. It gathered anyway. Nothing in the record shows it was directed at any outcome. No plan. No aim. Just waste, accumulating.

The reading would weaken if oxygen-producing photosynthesis proved a near-certain result of life on any wet planet. Until then: every animal breath began as waste. And as poison.
questions: When did oxygen-producing photosynthesis first kindle, and how long was its oxygen swallowed by chemistry before it reached the air?
Of the era's ice ages and iron formations, which were children of the oxygen rise, and which were born of other causes?

fields.summary: The Cenozoic Era began 66 million years ago and has not yet ended; we stand inside it still. It is the age of mammals, of grasslands rolling to the horizon, of a climate slowly cooling, and within its span lies all of human history.
facts: Its three periods: Paleogene, Neogene, Quaternary.
In the long quiet after the [[event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction|Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction]], mammals and birds diversified, branching like rivers across a delta.
The world's climate cooled overall, and ice sheets crowned the poles, then advanced and withdrew, again and again, like a white tide.
Primates appeared early in the era, and about 7 million years ago the hominin lineage branched away on its own road. See [[event/divergence-of-the-hominin-lineage|Divergence of the Hominin Lineage]].
fields.context: Within the Cenozoic lie the [[era/pleistocene-epoch|Pleistocene Epoch]], the [[era/holocene-epoch|Holocene Epoch]], and the proposed [[era/anthropocene|Anthropocene]], nested like rings in a tree still growing.
fields.observer: I came to watch one species, and it arrives late, in the final fraction of a percent of this era. I watched most of the era pass in the long cooling that shaped the world the species inherited. What is an inheritance, if not a room made ready by no one? Most of the story is the house. The guest comes last.
questions: Which turns of the climate most shaped hominin evolution?

fields.summary: Classical Antiquity, about 500 BCE to 500 CE, was the age of the great territorial empires, and of the philosophical and religious traditions that still shape the world like rivers running underground.
facts: Its empires stood like mountain ranges: Persia, Macedon, Rome, Maurya India, and Han China.
Great currents of thought rise in this age, among them Greek philosophy, Confucianism, Buddhism, and the Hebrew prophetic tradition; see [[event/axial-age|Axial Age]].
Trade routes bind Eurasia together like threads drawn through a loom; see [[event/opening-of-the-silk-roads|Opening of the Silk Roads]].
In the Mediterranean the age closes with the [[event/fall-of-the-western-roman-empire|Fall of the Western Roman Empire]], the setting of a long western sun.
fields.context: Classical Antiquity rises from the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]] and flows onward into the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]]. Among its great powers were the [[culture/ancient-greeks|Ancient Greeks]], the [[culture/romans|Romans]], the [[culture/han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]] and the [[culture/achaemenid-persians|Achaemenid Persians]].
fields.observer: Consider what the Observer notes: several distant societies, largely out of contact, developed comparable ethical and philosophical questions around the same centuries. Separate rooms, similar questions. Minds need not meet to reach the same threshold.
questions: What could explain why the Axial traditions rose near-simultaneously, like fires lit on distant hills?

fields.summary: The Cretaceous Period, from about 143.1 to 66 million years ago, is the last period of the Mesozoic Era and the longest of the Phanerozoic Eon. It was a warm greenhouse world in which the first flowering plants opened, and it ends as a great house falls, with the extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs.
facts: The Cretaceous Period spans about 143.1 to 66.0 million years ago, though older references set its start at 145.0 million years ago. Its name is drawn from the Latin word for chalk, and its top, the base of the Paleogene, is fixed at El Kef in Tunisia.

The world was a warm greenhouse and sea level stood high, spilling shallow seas across the continents, the Western Interior Seaway of North America among them, and laying down thick chalk deposits like snow on a drowned floor.

[[species/flowering-plants|Flowering Plants]] appear, their oldest widely accepted pollen about 134 million years old, and they diversified rapidly alongside pollinating insects, a bargain struck in colour and dust. Meanwhile the [[event/breakup-of-pangaea|Breakup of Pangaea]] went on as the South Atlantic opened.

Among the Late Cretaceous [[species/dinosaurs|Dinosaurs]] strode Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops in North America; birds diversified, and mosasaurs swam as large marine reptiles. Mammals were mostly small, and whether the modern placental orders arose before or after the end-Cretaceous extinction is debated.

Then came the [[event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction|Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction]], about 66 million years ago: it followed the Chicxulub impact, coincided with the eruption of the Deccan Traps, and killed about three-quarters of species, fire from the sky and fire from below.
fields.context: The Cretaceous Period comes after the [[era/jurassic-period|Jurassic Period]] and closes the great book of the [[era/mesozoic-era|Mesozoic Era]], giving way to the [[era/paleogene-period|Paleogene Period]]. It belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: Look at how the Cretaceous ends, the Observer says: with dinosaurs at or near their greatest diversity, ended by a rock from space and, probably, volcanic stress. From this the Observer draws a practice. Read long, stable-looking intervals as provisional, since nothing in the record of the last million years before the boundary announces what was about to happen. Stability is a description, not a promise. The Observer also names what would weaken the reading: evidence of a long decline in dinosaur diversity before the impact.
questions: Were the non-avian dinosaurs already fading before the end-Cretaceous impact?
Did the modern orders of placental mammals take root in the Cretaceous, or only after the extinction?

fields.summary: The Cryogenian Period, from 720 to 635 million years ago, is the middle period of the Neoproterozoic Era, and it is the time of the ice. Two global-scale glaciations. Ice. Then ice again. From them came the Snowball Earth hypothesis.
facts: The Cryogenian Period spans 720 to 635 million years ago. Its base is only a number, a numerical age set near the start of the first glaciation. Its top, the base of the [[era/ediacaran-period|Ediacaran Period]], is fixed in the rock of the Flinders Ranges of South Australia.

Two major glaciations are recorded. The Sturtian, about 717 to 660 million years ago. The Marinoan, about 650 to 635 million years ago. Glacial deposits formed at low paleolatitudes on several continents, and that supports the hypothesis that ice reached the tropics. The tropics. See [[event/snowball-earth|Snowball Earth]].

Each glaciation is capped by unusual carbonate rocks, a lid of strange stone. The usual explanation for the end of each: volcanic carbon dioxide building up, and up, until it was strong enough to melt the ice. This is a hypothesis.

Banded iron formations, largely absent for well over a billion years, come back. They reappear in Sturtian-age deposits, interpreted as evidence of iron-rich seawater under the ice. Rust-heavy water. Sealed beneath the lid.

Eukaryotes survived. Molecular fossils that some researchers attribute to sponges appear in Cryogenian rocks, but that attribution is disputed, and the oldest firmly accepted animal fossils are younger.
fields.context: The Cryogenian Period comes after the [[era/tonian-period|Tonian Period]] and before the [[era/ediacaran-period|Ediacaran Period]], inside the [[era/neoproterozoic-era|Neoproterozoic Era]]. It is the period of [[event/snowball-earth|Snowball Earth]]. It belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: Treat the Cryogenian, the Observer suggests, as a test of how much a living planet can lose and still continue: life survived at least one ice age lasting tens of millions of years. But resist the easy moral. The Observer cautions against reading this as design, since many lineages may have ended in the ice and the survivors are the only ones the record shows. The ledger lists only those who walked out. The reading has a named weakness, too: it would lose force if the ice proved much less extensive than the Snowball hypothesis proposes. Survival is a fact, not a plan.
questions: Was the ocean frozen solid, all of it, or did open water and refuges remain?
What part did the glaciations play in the later rise of large complex organisms?

fields.summary: The Devonian Period, from 419.2 to 358.9 million years ago, is the fourth period of the Paleozoic Era, often called the Age of Fishes. In its long span the first forests raised their crowns, the first limbed vertebrates came forth, and a prolonged late extinction drew the curtain.
facts: The Devonian Period spans 419.2 to 358.9 million years ago and takes its name from Devon in England. Its base is fixed at Klonk in the Czech Republic, and its top, the base of the Carboniferous, at La Serre in France, two stones marking the doors of an age.

Fishes diversified widely into a court of many shapes, armoured placoderms, sharks, lobe-finned fishes and ray-finned fishes among them, and the Middle Devonian raised a peak of Paleozoic reef building, cities of stone beneath the waves.

The Rhynie chert in Scotland, about 407 million years old, holds early land plants and arthropods in fine detail, as if caught in glass. Archaeopteris, a tree with woody trunks, raised early forests, and the Gilboa fossil forest in New York is about 385 million years old.

[[species/tiktaalik|Tiktaalik]], about 375 million years old, bears fins with wrist-like bones hidden inside. Ichthyostega and Acanthostega from Greenland, about 365 million years old, had limbs that ended in digits.

The [[event/late-devonian-extinction|Late Devonian Extinction]], about 372 to 359 million years ago, fell in at least two pulses, like waves against a failing wall, and removed an estimated 75 percent of species; the reef builders suffered heavily.
fields.context: The Devonian Period comes after the [[era/silurian-period|Silurian Period]] and before the [[era/carboniferous-period|Carboniferous Period]] within the [[era/paleozoic-era|Paleozoic Era]]. It belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and holds the central stretch of the long march of [[event/colonization-of-land|Colonization of Land]].
fields.observer: The Observer reads the Devonian as a renovation: life rebuilt the land surface. Roots, soils and the first forests changed weathering, rivers and the carbon cycle. Think of it as a new floor plan for the continents. Then the harder lesson. The spread of land plants is a candidate cause of the late extinction, a case of one group's success altering conditions for many others. Hold that as a hypothesis, the Observer insists; it would weaken if the extinction proved to have mainly non-biological causes. Success, too, leaves a wake.
questions: How great a hand did land plants have in the Late Devonian extinction?
Did the first limbed vertebrates grow their limbs for life in shallow water, rather than for the long walk onto land?

fields.summary: The Early Modern Period, about 1500 to 1800 CE, is the era of oceanic exploration, global trade, the printing press, and the [[event/scientific-revolution|Scientific Revolution]]. Hold the other half of the ledger in the same hand: it is also the era of colonial empires and mass forced migration.
facts: Through the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]], the Americas and Afro-Eurasia were linked into one exchange.
The [[event/atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic Slave Trade]] forcibly moved millions of Africans, each one a person, never a cargo.
The [[technology/movable-type-printing-press|Movable-Type Printing Press]] spread across Europe, carrying a new architecture for the written word.
The map of sovereignty was crowded: the [[culture/ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] and, in Asia, the Mughal and Qing states stood among the major empires, alongside expanding European colonial powers.
fields.context: The Early Modern Period is the threshold we cross into the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]] and the [[event/age-of-revolutions|Age of Revolutions]].
fields.observer: Here is the threshold the Observer marks: for the first time, every inhabited continent was in continuous contact. The species became, for the first time, a single connected system. But a connection is not a communion. It was joined on sharply unequal terms, and the terms matter as much as the joining.
questions: How much of Europe's economic growth rested on colonial extraction?

fields.summary: The Paleozoic Era (538.8 to 251.9 million years ago) was the age when animals first put on hard parts, when life crossed onto the land, when forests rose and the first tetrapods came. It ended in the largest mass extinction in Earth's history, a great door slammed on a crowded hall.
facts: Its periods pass like a procession of seasons: Cambrian, Ordovician, Silurian, Devonian, Carboniferous, Permian.
Plants and animals crossed the old shoreline and moved onto land; see [[event/colonization-of-land|Colonization of Land]].

Among its major extinctions are the [[event/late-ordovician-extinction|Late Ordovician Extinction]], the [[event/late-devonian-extinction|Late Devonian Extinction]], and the [[event/permian-triassic-extinction|Permian-Triassic Extinction]], each a shadow falling across the living world.
Trilobites, one of the era's signature animals, like a sigil stamped on its banners, are described in [[species/trilobites|Trilobites]].
fields.context: The Paleozoic opens with the [[event/cambrian-explosion|Cambrian Explosion]], a sudden blossoming, and closes with the end-Permian collapse, which swept the board clear for the [[era/mesozoic-era|Mesozoic Era]].
fields.observer: The Observer sees the Paleozoic as the era when life became a planetary system. Think of it as architecture: life began building soil, forests and oxygen-rich air, and later species moved in and inherited them. We live in a house we did not build.
questions: What, at the root of it all, made the end-Permian extinction so severe?

fields.summary: The Permian Period, from 298.9 to 251.9 million years ago, is the last period of the Paleozoic Era, when the supercontinent Pangaea stood fully assembled, its lands gathered like fingers into one fist. Mammal-line reptiles ruled that great country, and the period ended in the largest mass extinction in Earth's history.
facts: The Permian Period spans 298.9 to 251.9 million years ago and takes its name from the Perm region of Russia; its lower gate stands at Aidaralash Creek in Kazakhstan, and its upper, the base of the Triassic, at Meishan in China.
Pangaea lay fully assembled, ringed by a single ocean, Panthalassa, and its heartland was dry and harshly seasonal, with deserts spread wide like pale cloth.

Synapsids, the group that includes mammals and their extinct relatives, held the throne of land vertebrate life: early forms such as Dimetrodon, closer to mammals than to dinosaurs, were followed in their turn by the more mammal-like therapsids.
Conifers and other seed plants took the place of much of the club-moss coal forest, and the seed fern Glossopteris spread its dominion over the southern continent Gondwana.

The [[event/permian-triassic-extinction|Permian-Triassic Extinction]], about 251.9 million years ago, killed an estimated 80 to 96 percent of marine species, and the leading proposed cause is fire from below: the eruption of the Siberian Traps.
fields.context: After the [[era/carboniferous-period|Carboniferous Period]] came the Permian Period, and after it the [[era/triassic-period|Triassic Period]], first page of the [[era/mesozoic-era|Mesozoic Era]]. The Permian is the closing chapter of the [[era/paleozoic-era|Paleozoic Era]], and its thread runs through the theme of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer:
The Observer notes it plainly. The line leading to mammals ruled the land in the Permian. The dominant group of land vertebrates. Then the period's end. Most of that group did not survive it. Most.

Other lineages rose after. Their dominance came from one thing: who survived a catastrophe. The Observer reads that as contingency. Not merit. Not design. The reading would weaken if the survivors could be shown to have held an advantage predictable in advance. The throne went to whoever was still breathing.
questions: Which effect of the Siberian Traps eruptions was the deadliest blade: warming, ocean acidification, oxygen loss, or toxic release?
What marked the survivors of the end-Permian extinction apart from its victims?

fields.summary: The Pleistocene Epoch (about 2.58 million to 11,700 years ago) is the age of the returning ice, when great sheets advanced and withdrew again and again like a slow white tide. Beneath those shifting skies the genus Homo evolved and spread.
facts: Glacial and interglacial cycles turned many times, a great wheel of cold and thaw; see [[event/last-glacial-maximum|Last Glacial Maximum]].

Homo habilis, Homo erectus, Neanderthals, Denisovans and Homo sapiens all lived in this epoch, a whole kindred sharing one long age; see [[species/homo-erectus|Homo erectus]] and [[species/homo-sapiens|Homo sapiens]].
In glacial periods the sea drew back, baring land bridges such as the one used in the [[event/peopling-of-the-americas|Peopling of the Americas]].
Near its end many large mammals, the [[species/woolly-mammoth|Woolly Mammoth]] among them, passed out of the world.
fields.context: The Pleistocene is the stone frame around the [[era/paleolithic|Paleolithic]], and it ends when the climate warms and opens into the [[era/holocene-epoch|Holocene Epoch]], like a thaw loosening a river.
fields.observer: The Observer sees the Pleistocene as an evolutionary pressure chamber. Here is the claim: repeated climate swings favored a species that could adapt by learning and by copying others, rather than by waiting for genes to change. Picture a world that keeps redrawing its coastlines: the slow road of genes lags behind, and the fast road of imitation keeps up. What you can copy, you can carry.
questions: How much did climate variability, the ice's coming and going, drive the growth of hominin brains?

fields.summary: The Proterozoic Eon (2.5 billion to 538.8 million years ago) is the age of oxygenation, when the air first quickened; of complex cells; of global glaciations that gripped the world; and of the first multicellular animals.
facts: The [[event/great-oxidation-event|Great Oxidation Event]] raised the oxygen of the air about 2.4 billion years ago, a first breath drawn by the world.
Eukaryotes, cells that keep a nucleus at their heart like a hearth in a hall, appear in the fossil record during this eon.
Late in the eon came the 'Snowball Earth' glaciations, a long white silence; see [[event/snowball-earth|Snowball Earth]].
In its final period the Ediacaran biota appear, early large multicellular organisms like first shapes pressed into soft clay.
fields.context: The Proterozoic spans nearly half of Earth's history, one long night of the world's making, and it ends at the [[event/cambrian-explosion|Cambrian Explosion]] and the dawn of the [[era/paleozoic-era|Paleozoic Era]].
fields.observer: I think about how long the planet waited. About two billion years passed between the first oxygen and the first animals. I try to hold that span and it runs through my hands like water. I try again. What is my patience beside that? Timescales like this make human history look like the last few seconds of a very long film. The wait is the story; the rest is its closing frame.
questions: Why did complex animals wait so long, through so many ages, before they appeared?

fields.summary: The Quaternary Period is the latest period of the Cenozoic Era, begun 2.58 million years ago and still unfolding today. It is the age of the repeated ice ages, of the genus Homo, and of all recorded human history, every written word of it.
facts: The Quaternary Period began 2.58 million years ago and holds two epochs, the [[era/pleistocene-epoch|Pleistocene Epoch]] and the [[era/holocene-epoch|Holocene Epoch]]; its foundation stone is set at Monte San Nicola in Sicily, and its rank as a period, once disputed, was confirmed in 2009.

Across the Northern Hemisphere the ice sheets grew and shrank like a slow breath, in cycles about 41,000 years long at first and about 100,000 years long after a shift in the middle Pleistocene, roughly 1.25 to 0.7 million years ago.
At the [[event/last-glacial-maximum|Last Glacial Maximum]] the sea stood about 120 metres lower than today, and land bridges such as [[place/beringia|Beringia]] lay bare to the sky.

Nearly all species of the genus Homo lived in this period, among them [[species/homo-erectus|Homo erectus]], [[species/homo-neanderthalensis|Homo neanderthalensis]], [[species/denisovans|Denisovans]] and [[species/homo-sapiens|Homo sapiens]], while many large mammals faded from the world; see [[event/quaternary-megafauna-extinctions|Quaternary Megafauna Extinctions]].

A proposal to add an Anthropocene epoch was turned away by the International Union of Geological Sciences in 2024, yet the term lingers in informal use, a name spoken in the street but never carved on the gate; see [[era/anthropocene|Anthropocene]].
fields.context: After the [[era/neogene-period|Neogene Period]] came the Quaternary Period, the last period of the [[era/cenozoic-era|Cenozoic Era]] so far, a page still being written. Its thread runs through the theme of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]], and it is the frame that holds the [[era/paleolithic|Paleolithic]] and everything after it.
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the Quaternary is under three million years long, about 0.06 percent of Earth's history, yet it holds nearly all of the record of the genus Homo and every human society. Sit with that proportion. The whole architecture of our kind, its lineages and its societies, fits inside a sliver of the planet's time. The Observer reads the period's climate cycling as the setting in which a species that learns by copying could do well, one hypothesis among several. Think of a household where the weather turns without warning: the child who watches and imitates fares better than the one who waits. The reading would weaken if climate variability had little effect on hominin evolution. A small room can hold a whole family.
questions: Why did the ice change its music, shifting from a 41,000-year rhythm to a 100,000-year rhythm?
Without human carbon emissions, would the current interglacial, this present thaw, have closed at last in a new glaciation?

fields.summary: The Ediacaran Period, from 635 to 538.8 million years ago, is the last period of the Proterozoic Eon, the long dusk before the Cambrian dawn. In its span the first large, complex organisms rise into the fossil record like shapes surfacing from deep water.
facts: The Ediacaran Period spans 635 to 538.8 million years ago. In 2004 it was formally ratified, the first new geological period added to the time scale in over a century, and its base is set at Enorama Creek in the Flinders Ranges of South Australia.

The [[species/ediacaran-biota|Ediacaran Biota]] are a strange court of disc-, frond- and quilt-shaped organisms, known from Newfoundland, England, Namibia, the White Sea coast of Russia and the Ediacara Hills of South Australia. The oldest assemblages are about 575 million years old.
Cholesterol-related lipids found with Dickinsonia fossils have been read as the signature of an animal, though its seat in the animal family tree remains unclear.

Cloudina, a tubular organism from about 550 million years ago, is among the earliest animals to wear a mineralized skeleton, and some specimens bear borings interpreted as the marks of predation, a whisper of the hunt.

Late in the period, trace fossils appear where animals moved through sediment, and the classic Ediacaran assemblages fade near the start of the Cambrian; see [[event/cambrian-explosion|Cambrian Explosion]].
fields.context: The Ediacaran Period comes after the [[era/cryogenian-period|Cryogenian Period]] and closes both the [[era/neoproterozoic-era|Neoproterozoic Era]] and the [[era/proterozoic-eon|Proterozoic Eon]], giving way to the [[era/cambrian-period|Cambrian Period]]. It belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: I look at the quilted shapes and I look for a face I know. This is the first period whose living things were large enough to leave an obvious record, and many of them have no clear living relatives. I look for the road from them to the animals that followed, and the record does not show that it ran straight. I call that contingency. I would call it less if evidence showed that most Ediacaran forms were direct ancestors of later animal groups; that would weaken what I read here. Who says a first attempt must have heirs? Not every beginning is a parent.
questions: Which Ediacaran forms, if any, are the forebears of living animal groups?
What ended the classic assemblages: extinction, rivalry with newer animals, or changing chemistry?

fields.summary: The Epipaleolithic is the final phase of the Paleolithic in the Near East and North Africa, from about 20,000 to about 10,000 BCE. It was the age of small composite stone tools, of foragers who began to linger in one place, and of the last stage before the fields were sown.
facts: The Epipaleolithic runs from about 20,000 to about 10,000 BCE in the Levant and the lands around it. The name belongs mainly to the Near East and North Africa; Europe calls the following stage the Mesolithic.
Toolmakers shaped microliths, small geometric stone pieces such as lunates and triangles, like the teeth of a larger jaw, and fixed them into handles or shafts to make composite tools.

Ohalo II, a site on the Sea of Galilee in Israel about 23,000 years old, keeps brush huts, hearths and the remains of well over a hundred plant species, wild cereals among them. Some researchers argue that this shows early cultivation; that claim is debated.

The Natufian culture, about 12,500 to 9,500 BCE, raised semi-permanent villages while still foraging, wielded sickle blades and laid its dead in cemeteries. At Ain Mallaha in Israel a burial about 12,000 years old holds a person and a puppy together.

Some scholars propose the cold, dry [[event/younger-dryas|Younger Dryas]] as a reason for greater reliance on cultivated plants, a link that is debated. From the Epipaleolithic the road runs on into the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, whose earliest sites include [[place/jericho|Jericho]] and [[place/gobekli-tepe|Göbekli Tepe]]; see [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]].
fields.context: The Epipaleolithic comes after the [[era/upper-paleolithic|Upper Paleolithic]] and gives way to the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]] in the Near East. It closes the long book of the [[era/paleolithic|Paleolithic]], and its threads run through [[theme/technology|Technology]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: I watch them stay, there in the Epipaleolithic Near East. I watch them store food, raise semi-permanent villages, lay their dead in cemeteries, and I see some steps of the Settling appear before farming does. Why does the order matter to me? Because it suggests that settlement may in places have come first, and agriculture after. I hold this loosely: it would weaken if the Natufian sites were shown to have depended on cultivated crops from the start. First a place to grieve. Then, perhaps, a field.
questions: Did the Natufian people sow their cereals, or only gather the wild ones?
How far did the changing climate of the late Pleistocene bend the path toward farming?

fields.summary: The Holocene Epoch began about 11,700 years ago, as the last ice age loosened its grip, and it is the warm, relatively stable interval in which agriculture, cities and writing all arose, like seeds waking in a thawed field.
facts: The Holocene is an interglacial, a warm breath between the ice, its climate comparatively stable.
Every page of recorded history was written within its span.
Its lower boundary is fixed by a marker sealed in Greenland ice cores.
Within it, the human host swelled from a few million to about eight billion.
fields.context: The Holocene is the geological stage on which the species plays out the ages from the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]] through the [[era/information-age|Information Age]]. See [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]].
fields.observer: Notice the striking correlation the Observer points to: the species built farms and cities only after the climate stopped swinging. It is tempting to call the calm the cause. Resist. Whether this is cause, coincidence, or both is a serious open question, and a correlation is a doorway, not a destination.
questions: Did the steady Holocene climate make agriculture possible, opening the door, or did agriculture arise anyway?

fields.summary: The Industrial Age, about 1760 to 1945, is the era in which machines and fossil fuels transformed production, transport and warfare, and in which populations and cities grew rapidly. Think of it as the moment the architecture of human effort was rebuilt around the engine.
facts: The new grammar spread piece by piece: steam power, factories, railways and telegraphs; see [[technology/steam-engine|Steam Engine]] and [[event/industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]].
In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, electric power, oil and chemistry widened the transformation; see [[technology/electrical-power-grid|Electrical Power Grid]].
Around 1804 the global population passed one billion, a threshold worth pausing on.
The era closes in grief, with the two world wars: [[event/world-war-i|World War I]] and [[event/world-war-ii|World War II]].
fields.context: The Industrial Age inherits from the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and hands on to the [[era/information-age|Information Age]]. Its first century shares its ground with the [[event/age-of-revolutions|Age of Revolutions]].
fields.observer: I watch a species learn to release ancient stored sunlight as fuel. I watch that one change multiply the power in each person's hands. And I watch it make sanctioned harm far more destructive. What did you think the light would do, once it was yours? The same fire warms the house and burns it.
questions: How much of the industrial takeoff hinged on particular places?

fields.summary: The Information Age, from 1945 to the present, is the era of nuclear weapons, spaceflight, computers and the internet, and of the sharp rise in population and environmental impact known as the [[event/great-acceleration|Great Acceleration]]. It is the age we still live inside, still learning to read.
facts: In 1945 nuclear weapons appeared, and a new threshold of power was crossed; see [[event/nuclear-age|Nuclear Age]].
In 1957 the first artificial satellite launched, and the species' reach gained an orbit; see [[event/space-age|Space Age]].
The digital computer and the internet remade the architecture of communication; see [[event/digital-revolution|Digital Revolution]].
The ledger of our numbers: population grew from about 2.5 billion in 1950 to about 8 billion in 2022.
fields.context: The Information Age follows the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]] and overlaps the proposed [[era/anthropocene|Anthropocene]]. Read it alongside the [[event/green-revolution|Green Revolution]] and [[event/modern-climate-change|Modern Climate Change]].
fields.observer: Hold two tools in your mind at once, as the Observer does. For the first time, the species has built tools able to end its own history, and tools able to record it in full. The same hand holds the match and the archive. Memory-outsourcing has reached a scale no earlier era could imagine. The architecture of memory now stands outside us.
questions: When future historians look back, what will they choose as the defining feature of this era?

fields.summary: The Iron Age, about 1200 to 500 BCE and varying by region, was the age when iron tools and weapons spread across the lands like a grey tide, and new empires and belief systems rose.
facts: Iron ore lies more widely in the earth than tin and copper, a common metal for common hands; see [[technology/iron-smelting|Iron Smelting]].
The [[technology/alphabet|Alphabet]] spread widely, and the gate of literacy grew easier to pass.
Near the era's end, large territorial empires rise, the [[culture/achaemenid-persians|Achaemenid Persians]] among them.
In this age the [[event/axial-age|Axial Age]] begins to dawn.
fields.context: The Iron Age rises from the ruins of the [[event/bronze-age-collapse|Bronze Age Collapse]] and flows onward into [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]].
fields.observer: Follow the Observer's logic: the Iron Age was a democratization of tools and, therefore, of armies. Cheaper metal meant more people could be equipped. Here is the uncomfortable symmetry: whatever arms the farmer also arms the host. Access is never only a gift.
questions: Did iron drive the turning of societies, or follow in its wake?

fields.summary: The Silurian Period, from 443.8 to 419.2 million years ago, is the third period of the Paleozoic Era, a season of mending after the Late Ordovician extinction. In it rose the oldest known vascular land plants, and in its waters swam the first well-preserved jawed fishes.
facts: The Silurian Period spans 443.8 to 419.2 million years ago, and graptolites stand as its gatekeepers at both ends: at Dob's Linn in Scotland for its base, and at Klonk in the Czech Republic for its top, the base of the Devonian.

After the [[event/late-ordovician-extinction|Late Ordovician Extinction]] the life of the sea mended: the sea rose as the Hirnantian ice sheets melted, and reefs of corals and stromatoporoids spread through warm shallow seas like gardens reclaiming a ruined court.

Cooksonia, a small leafless plant bearing spore capsules at the tips of its branching stems like tiny lanterns, is the oldest widely accepted vascular land plant, known from about 433 million years ago.
The oldest well-preserved jawed vertebrates, armoured placoderms among them and the early bony fish Guiyu (about 425 million years old, from China), come from the later Silurian.
The millipede Pneumodesmus from Scotland, about 428 million years old, has been reported as the oldest known air-breathing land animal, a small pilgrim on dry ground.
The Iapetus Ocean closed like a great door as Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia came together in collision, raising the northern continent Laurussia by the early Devonian.
fields.context: After the [[era/ordovician-period|Ordovician Period]] came the Silurian Period, and after it the [[era/devonian-period|Devonian Period]], all within the [[era/paleozoic-era|Paleozoic Era]]. Its thread runs through the theme of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]], and its plants and arthropods are early verses in the long song of [[event/colonization-of-land|Colonization of Land]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the Silurian is when land life first leaves more than scattered traces: small leafless plants only centimetres tall, and small arthropods. You know how this story ends, and that is exactly the trap. Nothing in this record marks them as the beginning of forests and land vertebrates. A seedling carries no sign announcing the oak. The Observer treats that silence as a caution against reading any early stage in the light of what came after. Hindsight is a lamp that throws long, false shadows backward.
questions: Since fossil spores are older than the oldest plant bodies, how much earlier than Cooksonia were plants already living on land, unseen?
Did jawed fishes arise earlier than the stone's record of them shows?

fields.summary: The Tonian Period is the first period of the Neoproterozoic Era, running from 1.0 billion to 720 million years ago. Its chronicle holds the break-up of the supercontinent Rodinia and the branching of eukaryotes into many kinds, a quiet flowering before the Cryogenian ice ages came down.
facts: The Tonian Period spans 1.0 billion to 720 million years ago; both its thresholds are set by numerical ages, and its upper edge falls close to the onset of the first Cryogenian glaciation, where the long cold begins.
During the Tonian, roughly 800 to 750 million years ago, the supercontinent Rodinia began to rift apart, its old unity cracking like a sealed jar.

Eukaryotic microfossils show a widening diversity: vase-shaped microfossils in the Chuar Group of the Grand Canyon, roughly 780 to 740 million years old, are interpreted as the shells of amoeba-like protists, tiny urns left in the stone.
