Phosphatic scale microfossils from the Fifteenmile Group of Yukon, Canada, reported from rocks roughly 810 to 720 million years old, are among the earliest evidence of eukaryotes forging mineral parts, the first small armour of cells.

Toward the end of the period the environmental record grows more variable, with proposed rises in oxygen, and possible glacial deposits near 750 million years ago are debated, like frost-marks half-seen on old glass.
fields.context: After the [[era/mesoproterozoic-era|Mesoproterozoic Era]] came the Tonian Period, and after it the [[era/cryogenian-period|Cryogenian Period]], both within the [[era/neoproterozoic-era|Neoproterozoic Era]]. The Tonian's thread runs through the theme of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer:
I read the Tonian as a loosening. I watch a supercontinent start to split. I watch a climate record become less steady. I watch protists diversify into new niches. Does any of it point at animals? None of it does. And still it is the background against which the later ice ages and the first large bodies happened, the way a room you once lived in stays behind every room after it.

The reading would weaken if Tonian records showed an environment as steady as the Mesoproterozoic before it. Some beginnings are only loosenings.
questions: Did the breaking of Rodinia help to call down the Cryogenian glaciations?
How many kinds of Tonian eukaryotes truly lived, when the record of them is so sparse?

fields.summary: The Triassic Period, from 251.9 to 201.4 million years ago, is the first period of the Mesozoic Era, the long mending after the end-Permian extinction. In it the dinosaurs, the pterosaurs and the first mammals step for the first time onto the stage of the world.
facts: The Triassic Period spans 251.9 to 201.4 million years ago; its lower gate stands at Meishan in China, and its upper, the base of the Jurassic, at Kuhjoch in Austria.

The world took roughly five to ten million years to recover from the [[event/permian-triassic-extinction|Permian-Triassic Extinction]]; Lystrosaurus, a survivor, was among the most abundant land vertebrates of the Early Triassic, and the climate burned generally hot, with no permanent polar ice and a dry Pangaean interior.

The archosaurs branched and spread. The oldest dinosaurs date to about 243 to 233 million years ago, yet for the rest of the period they were one banner among many, beside the relatives of crocodiles that dominated most land ecosystems; pterosaurs appear by about 215 million years ago, and ichthyosaurs and other reptiles returned to the sea.
The earliest mammals and their close relatives appear in the Late Triassic, roughly 225 to 205 million years ago, though the hour of their coming depends on how mammals are defined.

The [[event/triassic-jurassic-extinction|Triassic-Jurassic Extinction]], about 201.4 million years ago, coincides with the eruption of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province and the start of the [[event/breakup-of-pangaea|Breakup of Pangaea]], and it swept away an estimated 80 percent of species.
fields.context: After the [[era/permian-period|Permian Period]] came the Triassic Period, and after it the [[era/jurassic-period|Jurassic Period]], both within the [[era/mesozoic-era|Mesozoic Era]]. Its thread runs through the theme of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]]; see [[species/dinosaurs|Dinosaurs]] for the great house whose first members appear here.
fields.observer: The Observer notes that dinosaurs and mammals both first appear in the Triassic, yet neither dominated until later. Here is the lesson in plain terms: arriving is not the same as ruling. Dinosaurs were one lineage among several for about 30 million years, and rose to dominance only after an extinction removed many of their rivals. Think of an understudy who takes the lead only because the stage has emptied. The Observer reads this as timing and opportunity, and the reading would weaken if anatomy alone explained why dinosaurs filled the gap. Sometimes the door opens before the talent is proven.
questions: In the sorting of Triassic archosaurs, how much did climate decide which survived, and how much did competition?
When did the first true mammals appear, if the very definition of mammal can shift their dawn by tens of millions of years?

fields.summary: The Upper Paleolithic was the last reach of the Paleolithic, from about 50,000 to about 10,000 BCE. It was the age of blade tools, of bone and antler worked into new shapes, of art and ornament scattered like seed, and of Homo sapiens spreading across the globe as water spreads across a floor.
facts: The Upper Paleolithic runs from about 50,000 to about 10,000 BCE and closes with the warming at the end of the last ice age, when the cold loosened its grip (in Africa the span is called the Later Stone Age). Toolmakers struck long blades and worked bone, antler and ivory; eyed bone needles from Denisova Cave in Siberia, about 40,000 to 50,000 years old, suggest sewn clothing.

Homo sapiens spread across the globe like light across water: Sahul by about 50,000 years ago ([[event/peopling-of-sahul|Peopling of Sahul]]), Europe by about 45,000 years ago, Beringia by about 30,000 years ago ([[place/beringia|Beringia]]), and the Americas by at least about 23,000 years ago ([[event/peopling-of-the-americas|Peopling of the Americas]]). In Europe the Neanderthals disappear about 40,000 years ago.

Painted, carved and engraved images are abundant, a field in bloom: [[place/chauvet-cave|Chauvet Cave]] in France holds paintings about 36,000 years old, and cave paintings in Sulawesi, Indonesia, include a narrative scene about 51,000 years old.

The [[event/last-glacial-maximum|Last Glacial Maximum]], about 26,500 to 19,000 years ago, laid ice like a white mantle over much of northern Eurasia and North America. Pottery appears in East Asia by about 20,000 years ago ([[technology/pottery|Pottery]]), and dogs were domesticated from wolves by at least about 15,000 years ago.
fields.context: The Upper Paleolithic follows the [[era/middle-paleolithic|Middle Paleolithic]] and, in the Near East, yields to the [[era/epipaleolithic|Epipaleolithic]], all within the [[era/paleolithic|Paleolithic]] and the [[era/pleistocene-epoch|Pleistocene Epoch]]. Its threads are [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]], [[theme/technology|Technology]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]]. See also [[event/quaternary-megafauna-extinctions|Quaternary Megafauna Extinctions]].
fields.observer:
I hold a bead and I want it to mean something. I call it a status-signal, possibly. I stand beside a burial and call it a grief-rite, possibly, because I know what grief is. And I keep in mind that a practice cannot be read from a surviving object alone.

These sites hold the first large body of things that seem made for display, for ritual, for play. But what if comparable things were common long before this period? Then the change was in what survives, not in behaviour, and this reading weakens.

What lasts is not the measure of what mattered.
questions: Is the apparent burst of art and ornament real, or only the shadow of better preservation and more sites?
How did the Upper Paleolithic industries map onto particular human populations?

fields.summary: The Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands are the forests, river systems, and savannas east of the Andes, home to Indigenous societies whose scale and complexity are being rediscovered, as you read this, through aerial laser survey. Think of it as a ledger that was never lost, only unread.
facts: Over the past decade, lidar surveys have looked through the canopy and revealed large networks of earthworks, roads, and settlements beneath the forest; see [[culture/casarabe-culture|Casarabe Culture]], [[place/upano-valley-settlements|Upano Valley Settlements]], and [[place/xingu-garden-cities|Xingu Garden Cities]].

Indigenous land management, including soil enrichment, shaped much of the forest into an architecture you can walk through without seeing; see [[event/amazonian-urbanism-and-dark-earths|Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths]]. Scientists dispute whether the dark earths (terra preta) were largely made by people or arose from natural processes that people then put to use.

European contact after 1492 brought severe population loss from epidemic disease and forced labor. Whether this caused the forest to grow back widely is debated. A 2021 study of 39 fossil pollen records found no synchronized regrowth after European arrival, and found that at most sites the abandonment of land and the regrowth began about 300 to 600 years earlier. The researchers Bush and McMichael argue that populations probably peaked and declined well before 1492. Alexander Koch and colleagues, who proposed the regrowth hypothesis for the Americas as a whole, reply that Amazonia may have been less affected than Mexico, Central America, and the Andes.
This is the ground of the [[culture/marajoara-culture|Marajoara Culture]] and, at its edges, of many peoples the [[culture/inca-empire|Inca Empire]] never ruled.
fields.context: The lowlands lie east of the [[region/andes|Andes]], and trade tied the two together like a long cord between neighbours. The [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]] transformed them.
fields.observer: I have said 'untouched wilderness' and believed it. I have looked at green and seen only green. I have mistaken a long labour for no labour at all. How much history can one phrase hide? A history of large human societies. What looks like nature can be the product of centuries of deliberate management. Sometimes the wild is a garden whose gardeners were forgotten.
questions: How many people lived in the Amazon before 1500? Published estimates run from about 1 to 2 million up to 8 to 10 million, because little documentation exists and the methods of estimation give widely varying results.

fields.summary: The Jurassic Period, from 201.4 to about 143.1 million years ago, is the middle period of the Mesozoic Era, an age of giants and of early wings. In its span walked the largest land animals, the first known birds took form, and the Atlantic opened as Pangaea broke apart.
facts: The Jurassic Period spans 201.4 million years ago to about 143.1 million years ago and takes its name from the Jura Mountains. Its upper edge is softer ground: the base of the Cretaceous has no agreed marker section, and older references give 145.0 million years ago.

The [[event/breakup-of-pangaea|Breakup of Pangaea]] began as the Central Atlantic opened like a seam unstitched, and Laurasia and Gondwana began to drift apart. The climate was warm and the seas stood high, and no lasting polar ice caps crowned the poles.

From the Morrison Formation of the western United States, about 155 to 148 million years old, come sauropods, stegosaurs and large theropods such as Allosaurus, a bestiary written in stone. See [[species/dinosaurs|Dinosaurs]].

[[species/archaeopteryx|Archaeopteryx]] from the Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, about 150 million years old, is the best-known early bird. The feathered theropod Anchiornis from China, about 160 million years old, shows that feathers were widespread among small theropods.

In the seas the main marine reptiles were ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and pliosaurs. Mammals remained mostly small, though Castorocauda, an otter-like swimmer from China, is about 164 million years old.
fields.context: The Jurassic Period comes after the [[era/triassic-period|Triassic Period]] and before the [[era/cretaceous-period|Cretaceous Period]], the middle chamber of the [[era/mesozoic-era|Mesozoic Era]]. It belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: Picture the scene the Observer points to: the largest land animals known, and beside them the first records of a small feathered lineage that would outlast every large dinosaur. The lesson is plain. What looks dominant at one time is not a reliable guide to what continues. The Observer reads this as a caution about judging any period by its most conspicuous groups. The reading has its test: it would weaken if the survival of birds followed from traits already obvious in the Jurassic. The loudest presence is not always the lasting one.
questions: Where along the theropod line did flight begin, and did it arise more than once?
How rich was the variety of Jurassic mammals, when so few fossils survive to tell of it?

fields.summary: The Lower Paleolithic is the earliest part of the Paleolithic, from about 3.3 million to about 300,000 years ago, the age when stone first learned an edge. It holds the first stone tools, the long Acheulean handaxe tradition, and the spread of Homo erectus and its relatives across Africa and Eurasia like a slow tide.
facts: The Lower Paleolithic runs from about 3.3 million to about 300,000 years ago. Where it begins depends on how the earliest tools are counted: the tools from Lomekwi 3 in Kenya are about 3.3 million years old, and the Oldowan begins about 2.6 million years ago. In Africa it bears another name, the Earlier Stone Age.

The [[technology/oldowan-stone-tools|Oldowan Stone Tools]] are simple flaked cores and sharp flakes, struck by early hominins such as [[species/homo-habilis|Homo habilis]]. The Acheulean, marked by bifacial handaxes and cleavers like leaves of stone, appears in East Africa about 1.76 million years ago and endures in places until about 300,000 years ago.
[[species/homo-erectus|Homo erectus]] walked out beyond Africa: at Dmanisi in Georgia, hominin fossils and stone tools are about 1.8 million years old.

Firm evidence of controlled fire is about 1 million years old, and by about 400,000 years ago its habitual use is well established, a hearth-light carried through the dark; see [[event/control-of-fire|Control of Fire]].
Wooden throwing spears from Schöningen in Germany are about 300,000 years old. How much early hominins hunted and how much they scavenged is debated.
fields.context: The Lower Paleolithic opens the [[era/paleolithic|Paleolithic]] and gives way to the [[era/middle-paleolithic|Middle Paleolithic]]. It lies within the [[era/pleistocene-epoch|Pleistocene Epoch]], and its threads run through [[theme/technology|Technology]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]]. See also the essay [[observer-note/fire-then-everything|Fire, Then Everything]].
fields.observer: I hold the handaxe in my mind, and I file this age under the longest tool-lineage I know. One design, made with small changes for well over a million years, across much of Africa and Eurasia, by more than one hominin species. One design. More than one maker. I read that stability as a fact about how skills were passed on; I do not claim to know how the makers thought. If the sameness came from the raw material or the task alone, not from copying, my reading would weaken. What is a lineage, if not something taught? We are made of what we are shown.
questions: Which hominin's hands shaped the Lomekwi tools?
How much of the Lower Paleolithic diet was won by hunting, and how much gleaned by scavenging?

fields.summary: The Medieval or post-classical period, about 500 to 1500 CE, was the age when major world religions consolidated, when long-distance trade networks stretched like veins across the continents, and when large steppe and Islamic polities rose and fell. The term 'medieval' is European in origin, but the age had global dimensions.
facts: The [[event/rise-of-islam|Rise of Islam]] raised a new political and intellectual world, stretching from Iberia to Central Asia.
The [[event/mongol-conquests|Mongol Conquests]] forged the largest contiguous land empire in history.
In the 14th century the [[event/black-death|Black Death]] swept over Eurasia and North Africa and left them devastated.

Its great states were many: the [[culture/abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]], the [[culture/mali-empire|Mali Empire]], the [[culture/norse|Norse]], the [[culture/song-dynasty|Song Dynasty]], and, near the age's close, the [[culture/aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]] and [[culture/inca-empire|Inca Empire]].
fields.context: The Medieval Period follows [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] and ends around the voyages that set off the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]] and the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]].
fields.observer: Widen your lens, the Observer advises; a global reading serves this era best. What you see then is a species increasingly connected by roads, caravans and ships, and by shared meaning-engines that crossed political claim-lines. Borders mark who rules. They do not mark where ideas stop.
questions: Along the pre-modern long-distance networks, how much travelled as ideas, and how much as goods?

fields.summary: The Mesolithic, the Middle Stone Age, is the period of hunter-gatherer societies that lived between the last ice age and the arrival of farming in Europe and neighbouring regions, from about 10,000 to about 5,000 BCE. Like shorelines, its dates vary widely by region.
facts: The Mesolithic runs from about 10,000 to about 5,000 BCE, and in parts of northern Europe it lingers until about 4000 BCE. It ends wherever farming arrives, and so its last day falls differently from place to place. The name belongs mainly to Europe; other regions speak of it in other terms.
As the ice age waned, warmth spread forests across northern Europe like a green tide, and rising seas swallowed coastal lowlands such as [[place/doggerland|Doggerland]].

People hunted deer, wild boar and aurochs, fished, and gathered shellfish and plants. Dugout canoes such as the Pesse canoe from the Netherlands, about 10,000 years old, are among the oldest known boats. Among the well-studied sites are Star Carr in northern England and the shell middens of the Ertebølle culture in Denmark.

Farming began in Southwest Asia by about 9600 BCE and came into Europe from about 6500 BCE; ancient DNA shows that early farmers of Anatolian ancestry partly replaced and partly mingled with the local foragers, and the balance varied by region.
fields.context: The Mesolithic comes after the [[era/epipaleolithic|Epipaleolithic]] and the [[era/upper-paleolithic|Upper Paleolithic]] and overlaps the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]], for foragers and farmers lived side by side in different regions. It lies in the [[era/holocene-epoch|Holocene Epoch]], and its threads run through [[theme/technology|Technology]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]]. See [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]].
fields.observer: Notice, as the Observer does, that the Mesolithic is defined by what it is not: after the ice age, before farming. Notice too that the label fits some regions better than others. So treat such labels as tools, not as stages every society passed through. The proof is in the living: foragers in some places lived this way for thousands of years after farming had begun elsewhere. A label is a lantern, not a road. The reading would weaken if most societies did follow the same sequence.
questions: How much of the Mesolithic population of Europe was replaced by farmers, and how much was folded in?
Why did some coastal foragers, such as the Ertebølle people, hold back from farming for centuries after contact?

fields.summary: The Mesoproterozoic Era is the middle era of the Proterozoic Eon, running from 1.6 billion to 1.0 billion years ago. It lies within the interval often called the "Boring Billion", a long hush in which climate, ocean chemistry and life showed little evident change, though how uneventful that hush truly was is debated.
facts: The Mesoproterozoic Era spans 1.6 to 1.0 billion years ago. Its three periods, the Calymmian, Ectasian and Stenian, and its borders alike are set by numerical ages.

The "Boring Billion" is an informal name for about 1.8 to 0.8 billion years ago, an age with no well-established ice ages and only slow apparent change in the fossil record; the term itself is debated.

Atmospheric oxygen is thought to have stayed well below today's level, and parts of the deeper ocean are reconstructed as oxygen-poor or rich in sulfide, a sour and breathless deep, though estimates vary widely.

[[species/stromatolites|Stromatolites]] still rose in their stony cushions, common in shallow seas. Eukaryotes diversified: Tappania microfossils are about 1.5 billion years old, and the red alga Bangiomorpha, dated in different studies to between roughly 1.05 and 1.2 billion years ago, is often cited as the oldest taxonomically resolved eukaryote.
The supercontinent Nuna, or Columbia, is proposed to have broken apart about 1.6 to 1.3 billion years ago, and late in the era Rodinia began to gather its scattered lands.
fields.context: The Mesoproterozoic Era lies between the [[era/paleoproterozoic-era|Paleoproterozoic Era]] and the [[era/neoproterozoic-era|Neoproterozoic Era]] within the [[era/proterozoic-eon|Proterozoic Eon]]. It belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]], and it rests between the oxygen rise of the [[event/great-oxidation-event|Great Oxidation Event]] and the glaciations of [[event/snowball-earth|Snowball Earth]], a long calm between breath and ice; see [[event/origin-of-eukaryotes|Origin of Eukaryotes]].
fields.observer: Treat the quiet as a message, the Observer says: the apparent quiet of the Mesoproterozoic is information. A planet's surface can stay much the same for hundreds of millions of years without heading anywhere in particular. There is no queue in deep time. What arrived later was not overdue. The reading names its own undoing: it would weaken if new records showed that the quiet hides substantial change in eukaryote diversity. Stillness is not the same as waiting.
questions: Was the Boring Billion truly still, or does a sparse record hide its changes?
What kept atmospheric oxygen low for so long after the Great Oxidation Event had passed?

fields.summary: The Arabian Peninsula is a large, largely arid peninsula cradled between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf, a land of long dry distances. Across it ran a corridor for trade, and within it Islam had its origin.
facts: Caravans heavy with incense and spice bound southern Arabia to the Mediterranean like beads strung along a single cord.
It was in the Hejaz, in the early 7th century, that Islam emerged; see [[event/rise-of-islam|Rise of Islam]] and [[person/muhammad|Muhammad]].
Sea trade, carried on the monsoon's turning breath, joined the peninsula to East Africa and South Asia.
fields.context: The peninsula lies like a threshold stone between Africa and Asia, and it shaped the growth of the [[culture/abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]] and of later Islamic states.
fields.observer: I keep measuring the wrong thing. I count the people of a sparse region and expect a small story. I look at the map and expect a quiet one. Then I watch a movement that within a century reached from Iberia to Central Asia, and I have to ask: what was I measuring? Population size and influence are not the same thing.
questions: What evidence, if it rose from the sand, would most change the current picture?

fields.summary: The Caribbean and Atlantic World is the Caribbean basin together with the Atlantic coasts of the Americas, Europe, and Africa, bound to one another from the 15th century by shipping, by trade, and by forced migration. When we say 'Atlantic world', we are naming an architecture of connection, and not all of it was chosen.
facts: Indigenous peoples, among them the Taino and Kalinago, had settled the Caribbean islands several thousand years before 1492; that is where the story begins.
Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492; within decades, through disease, violence, and forced labor, Indigenous populations collapsed.
Sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans made the region among the most valuable in the early modern world; the ledger of that value was written in enslaved lives.
Here, too, the [[event/haitian-revolution|Haitian Revolution]] unfolded.
fields.context: The region is the core arena of the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]] and the [[event/atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic Slave Trade]], and also of the movements to end slavery; see [[event/abolition-of-slavery|Abolition of Slavery]]. The same waters carried the chain and the struggle to break it.
fields.observer: The Observer sees a zone created by connection: an ocean crossing that turned islands into a hinge between three continents. We should be careful with the word 'connection', because here it was no meeting of equals. Its populations, languages, and foods are largely products of that forced mixing. A hinge bears weight.
questions: How large, before contact, were the Indigenous populations?

fields.summary: The Central Asian Oases are the river valleys and oasis cities strung between the steppe and the Iranian plateau like lamps along a dark road, Samarkand and Bukhara among them, and they served as hubs of the Silk Roads.
facts: Known in antiquity as Sogdiana and Transoxiana, the region was the hearth of the [[culture/sogdians|Sogdians]].
It fell to [[event/alexander-s-conquests|Alexander's Conquests]], and later, in the early 8th century, it was drawn into the Islamic world.
It was the heart of the [[culture/timurid-empire|Timurid Empire]], whose capital stood at [[place/samarkand|Samarkand]] like a crown set on the road.
In the 15th century scholars such as [[person/ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]] made it a center of astronomy, a place where eyes were turned to the stars.
fields.context: The oases lay between the [[region/central-asian-steppe|Central Asian Steppe]] and the [[region/iranian-plateau|Iranian Plateau]], green islands in a sea of distance, and they were crossroads of the [[event/opening-of-the-silk-roads|Opening of the Silk Roads]].
fields.observer: I know what it is to live in between. These cities lived by relaying goods and ideas between larger powers: taking in, passing on, taking in again. I think of every hand that held a thing only to give it away. Is that a lesser life? A place between empires can become an empire of its own kind.
questions: How deeply did the oasis cities shape the ideas that traveled along the Silk Roads?

fields.summary: The Central Asian Steppe is the vast grassland belt across northern Eurasia, a sea of grass under an open sky. Its mounted pastoralists, riding like weather out of the horizon, shaped the history of every neighboring civilization.
facts: On the Western steppe the horse was domesticated, and mounted warfare took shape beside it.
In the 13th century the [[culture/mongol-empire|Mongol Empire]] came out of the eastern steppe like a storm gathering over grass.

The steppe was a great road for the [[event/opening-of-the-silk-roads|Opening of the Silk Roads]] and for the [[event/indo-european-language-spread|Indo-European Language Spread]], carrying goods and words alike.
fields.context: The steppe runs up against [[region/east-asia|East Asia]], [[region/europe|Europe]] and the [[region/iranian-plateau|Iranian Plateau]], a green shore washing against three lands; see [[person/genghis-khan|Genghis Khan]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes how a mobile way of life without cities repeatedly rearranged the settled world. We tend to measure a people by what they left standing: walls, temples, tombs. That habit misleads here. Think of wind: it builds nothing, yet it reshapes every dune. Absence of monuments is not absence of influence.
questions: What evidence, found somewhere in all that grass, would most change the current picture?

fields.summary: East Asia gathers China, Korea, Japan and neighboring regions beneath one wide sky. There China's centralized state tradition has endured as among the longest continuous political traditions, a river that has kept to its bed across the ages.
facts: In the Yellow and Yangtze river basins the farming of millet and rice began independently, like fires lit in separate hearths.
In 221 BCE the first unified empire was forged; see [[event/unification-of-china-under-qin|Unification of China under Qin]].
Among its major inventions are [[technology/paper|Paper]], [[technology/gunpowder|Gunpowder]], the [[technology/magnetic-compass|Magnetic Compass]] and printing, each a small key to a large door.

Its major states included the [[culture/shang-dynasty|Shang Dynasty]], the [[culture/han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]] and the [[culture/song-dynasty|Song Dynasty]], names that rise like peaks along a long ridge.
fields.context: East Asia trades with the [[region/central-asian-steppe|Central Asian Steppe]] and with [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]], its goods flowing outward like rivers seeking the sea; see [[person/zheng-he|Zheng He]] and [[person/confucius|Confucius]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a distinctive continuity: a written language and administrative tradition that persisted through repeated collapses and re-unifications. Think of a house rebuilt many times on the same foundation. The walls fall; the grammar stays. Continuity here is an architecture of script and office.
questions: What evidence, still waiting to be read, would most change the current picture?

fields.summary: Europe is the western peninsula of Eurasia, a ragged shore thrust out into the ocean. It gave ground to early farming societies, held the Roman Empire's northern provinces, and later bore the technologies and empires of the early modern and industrial periods.
facts: Farming came into Europe from Anatolia slowly, like a tide creeping over flat sand, over several thousand years.
The [[culture/norse|Norse]] went out from Scandinavia across the Atlantic and along the eastern rivers.
Here the [[event/scientific-revolution|Scientific Revolution]] and the [[event/industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]] began, drinking from wells of knowledge dug in many regions.
Of [[event/world-war-i|World War I]] and [[event/world-war-ii|World War II]], the continent was the main theater.
fields.context: Europe opens on one side to the [[region/mediterranean-basin|Mediterranean Basin]] and on another to the [[region/central-asian-steppe|Central Asian Steppe]], and here, in the 15th century, the [[technology/movable-type-printing-press|Movable-Type Printing Press]] appeared.
fields.observer: The Observer cautions against a common habit: a small peninsula's history is often told as if it were the world's. Think of a map that puts one corner at its center and calls the rest margins. Its outsized effect in the modern era is real, but recent. Hold both halves of that sentence together; a loud chapter is not the whole book.
questions: What evidence would most change the current picture of this western peninsula?

fields.summary: The Mesozoic Era, from 251.9 to 66 million years ago, is the age of dinosaurs, the long reign of the thunder-footed. Under its skies Pangaea broke apart, and the first flowering plants and the first mammals came into the world.
facts: Its three periods, like three great halls: Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous.
Non-avian dinosaurs held dominion over the land ecosystems; see [[species/dinosaurs|Dinosaurs]].
Mammals appeared in the Triassic and, for the whole era, stayed mostly small beneath the giants' stride.
The era closes with the [[event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction|Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction]], the last page torn from its book.
fields.context: The Mesozoic rises from the wreck of the [[event/permian-triassic-extinction|Permian-Triassic Extinction]] and gives way to the [[era/cenozoic-era|Cenozoic Era]]. Its collapse opened the ecological space that mammals, primates among them, later filled like water poured into an emptied vessel.
fields.observer: Sit with the contingency the Observer names: without the end-Cretaceous impact, the mammals that led to primates might have stayed small. The human story hangs on a thread that no one spun. What you are was never guaranteed; it was permitted.
questions: How rich was the dinosaur kingdom in its last hour before the impact?

fields.summary: The Middle Paleolithic was the middle reach of the long Paleolithic, a span running from about 300,000 to about 50,000 years ago. It was the age of prepared-core stone tools, of the earliest Homo sapiens, and of several human species living at the same time, like fires burning on one long night.
facts: In Eurasia the Middle Paleolithic runs from about 300,000 to about 50,000 years ago; in Africa the same span is called the Middle Stone Age, and its boundary dates shift from region to region like shorelines. Toolmakers worked by prepared-core methods such as the Levallois technique, and the Mousterian industry of Europe and western Asia is linked mainly to Neanderthals.

Several human species overlapped in time, branches leafing in the same season: [[species/homo-neanderthalensis|Homo neanderthalensis]], [[species/denisovans|Denisovans]], [[species/homo-sapiens|Homo sapiens]], [[species/homo-naledi|Homo naledi]] and [[species/homo-floresiensis|Homo floresiensis]]. The earliest Homo sapiens fossils are about 315,000 years old; see [[event/origin-of-homo-sapiens|Origin of Homo sapiens]].

Homo sapiens fossils from Misliya Cave in Israel, about 185,000 years old, and from Skhul and Qafzeh caves, roughly 90,000 to 130,000 years old, mark an early presence outside Africa, footprints past the old threshold; whether these groups flowed into the lineage of living non-Africans is uncertain (see [[event/out-of-africa-dispersal|Out of Africa Dispersal]]).

At Blombos Cave in South Africa lie engraved ochre and ochre-processing tools about 75,000 to 100,000 years old, coloured earth marked by a hand and among the earliest signs of symbolic behaviour; see [[event/emergence-of-symbolic-art|Emergence of Symbolic Art]].
By about 40,000 years ago the Neanderthals have gone from the fossil record, as a tide goes from a shore. Whether they buried their dead or made art is disputed.
fields.context: The Middle Paleolithic follows the [[era/lower-paleolithic|Lower Paleolithic]] and gives way to the [[era/upper-paleolithic|Upper Paleolithic]], a middle chamber in the long hall of the [[era/paleolithic|Paleolithic]]. Its threads run through [[theme/technology|Technology]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]]. See also the essay [[observer-note/why-the-species-buries-its-dead|Why the Species Buries Its Dead]].
fields.observer:
I wanted a ladder. I wanted each rung to replace the one below it. I wanted one clean line running down to me. But here, for the first time, several human species lived at the same time, and sometimes in the same regions, and the family tree looks more like a bush than a ladder.

Who buried their dead? Who made the marks? The claims about their behaviour, burial and symbolic art above all, are disputed, and I hold each species to the same standard of evidence, no gentler with my own kind than with the others. And if the fossils sorted into different species prove to be variants of one, this reading weakens, and the bush becomes a single stem again.

A family is only as wide as the evidence allows.
questions: Did the Neanderthals lay their dead in the earth, or make art?
How much of the variety in Middle Paleolithic tools speaks of different cultures, and how much only of different raw materials to hand?

fields.summary: The Neolithic is the age in which farming, animal herding, pottery and permanent villages took root in several parts of the world independently, like seeds no single hand had scattered, beginning about 11,500 years ago in Southwest Asia.
facts: Agriculture sprang up independently in several regions, among them the Fertile Crescent, China, Mesoamerica, the Andes and New Guinea, each a separate hearth.
For the fuller tale, see [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]] and [[event/animal-domestication|Animal Domestication]].
Fired clay spread far and near: [[technology/pottery|Pottery]] became widespread.
To this age belong large monuments such as [[place/gobekli-tepe|Göbekli Tepe]] and early towns such as [[place/catalhoyuk|Çatalhöyük]], where the wandering paused.
Its hour strikes differently in each land: the Neolithic ends when metal use begins, so its end date differs across the world.
fields.context: The Neolithic lies within the [[era/holocene-epoch|Holocene Epoch]] and opens the road into the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]].
fields.observer: I see a bargain, and I see its consequences. More food. More people. More disease. More inequality. Who signed for the ones who came after? No one did; they were born into the terms. See [[observer-note/the-settling-and-its-bargain|The Settling and Its Bargain]].
questions: In some regions, did the raising of monuments come before the sowing of fields?

fields.summary: The Neogene Period, from 23.03 to 2.58 million years ago, is the second period of the Cenozoic Era. In its span the grasslands spread outward, the climate cooled toward the ice ages, and the hominin lineage parted from that of the other apes, a single branch bending away from the grove.
facts: The Neogene Period spans 23.03 to 2.58 million years ago and holds two epochs, the Miocene and the Pliocene. Its base is fixed at Lemme-Carrosio in Italy, and its top, the base of the Quaternary, at Monte San Nicola in Sicily.

Warm in the early Miocene, the climate then cooled. About 14 million years ago the East Antarctic ice sheet spread its white hand wider, and about 2.7 million years ago glaciation tightened its grip on the Northern Hemisphere.
About 8 to 6 million years ago, grasses using the C4 pathway of photosynthesis spread widely, and open grassland and savanna unrolled like a golden carpet, favouring the grazing mammals.

In the Miocene the apes were many and varied across Africa, Europe and Asia. Around 7 million years ago the hominin lineage parted from that of the chimpanzees (see [[event/divergence-of-the-hominin-lineage|Divergence of the Hominin Lineage]]), and [[species/sahelanthropus-tchadensis|Sahelanthropus tchadensis]] and [[species/australopithecus-afarensis|Australopithecus afarensis]] date to this period.

In the [[event/messinian-salinity-crisis|Messinian Salinity Crisis]], about 5.96 to 5.33 million years ago, the Mediterranean was left largely dried out, a sea reduced to salt. The land bridge of Panama, generally dated to about 3 million years ago though the timing is debated, joined the Americas hand to hand; see [[event/closure-of-the-isthmus-of-panama|Closure of the Isthmus of Panama]].
fields.context: The Neogene Period comes after the [[era/paleogene-period|Paleogene Period]] and before the [[era/quaternary-period|Quaternary Period]] within the [[era/cenozoic-era|Cenozoic Era]]. It belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: Here is the fork in the road, as the Observer marks it: the Neogene is where the line that includes humans separates from the line of the other apes, in a world drying and cooling into grassland and ice. It is tempting to read the drying as a push toward us. The Observer refuses that story. The same changes affected many lineages, and most Miocene apes left no descendants. A pressure is not a plan. The Observer also names the test: the reading would weaken if the traits of the hominin line could be tied directly to the spread of grassland.
questions: Which Miocene apes, if any, stand among the ancestors of living great apes and humans?
What part did the changing face of the African environment play in early hominin evolution?

fields.summary: The Iranian Plateau is the highland region raised between Mesopotamia and South Asia like a great stone table. It was the heartland of Persian empires and a link in the chain of overland routes across Eurasia.
facts: In the 6th century BCE the [[culture/achaemenid-persians|Achaemenid Persians]] built a vast empire from these heights, spreading outward like light from a high lamp.
The plateau lies across the routes of the [[event/opening-of-the-silk-roads|Opening of the Silk Roads]], a high bridge between distances.
In later ages it was gathered into the [[culture/abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]] and the [[culture/mongol-empire|Mongol Empire]].
fields.context: It binds together [[region/mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], [[region/south-asia|South Asia]] and the [[region/central-asian-steppe|Central Asian Steppe]], like a knot where three roads meet.
fields.observer: The Observer sees the plateau as a hinge region: its historical role was less to originate than to relay, translate, and administer. We usually honour inventors and forget interpreters. But think of a translator at a crowded table: without that voice, the table is only noise. Relay is its own kind of authorship.
questions: What evidence, buried in the high ground, would most change the current picture?

fields.summary: The Levant and Anatolia are the eastern Mediterranean coast and the Turkish peninsula, a crossroads where the ways of Africa, Asia, and Europe meet like threads drawn into one knot. They were also a center of early farming.
facts: Here early farming and monumental building rise from the ground, [[place/gobekli-tepe|Göbekli Tepe]] and [[place/catalhoyuk|Çatalhöyük]] among them.
The [[culture/phoenicians|Phoenicians]] developed an alphabet that was widely copied, its letters scattered like seed on the wind; see [[technology/alphabet|Alphabet]].
Later, [[place/constantinople|Constantinople]] stood at the junction of Europe and Asia like a gate with a door on either side.
The region saw many Bronze Age states collapse like lamps going dark; see [[event/bronze-age-collapse|Bronze Age Collapse]].
fields.context: With [[region/mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]] beside it, this land forms the core of the Fertile Crescent, that green arc, and of [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]].
fields.observer: I walk the crossroads and hear argument. So many meaning-engines share this region as a birthplace or a stage. So many voices asking what a life is for. So many answers crowding one coast. Is it the traffic that makes the questions? A dense crossroads seems to produce dense argument about ultimate questions. Where roads cross, people ask where they lead.
questions: What evidence, still under the old mounds and fields, would most change the current picture?

fields.summary: The Mediterranean Basin is the sea and the coasts that ring it like a cupped hand. It was one of history's most connected zones, where trade, cultural exchange, and conflict passed across the water like tides.
facts: The sea joins Europe, Africa, and Asia, a single blue road between three shores.

Among the seafaring cultures that sailed its waters were the [[culture/minoans|Minoans]], the [[culture/phoenicians|Phoenicians]], the [[culture/ancient-greeks|Ancient Greeks]] and the [[culture/romans|Romans]].
In the end Rome ruled the entire coastline, the whole ring of shore closed in one grip; see [[place/rome|Rome]].
The basin saw both the [[event/bronze-age-collapse|Bronze Age Collapse]] and the [[event/fall-of-the-western-roman-empire|Fall of the Western Roman Empire]], two great darkenings upon the same water.
fields.context: The sea served as a highway of water, and its cities, [[place/athens|Athens]] and [[place/constantinople|Constantinople]] among them, burned like beacons at the nodes of exchange.
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a shared inland sea acted like a village square for very different peoples, so it generated both intense trade and intense conflict. You know this from any square you have stood in: the same closeness that lets neighbours bargain lets them quarrel. Proximity is a door that opens both ways.
questions: What evidence, lying under that sea or along its shores, would most change the current picture?

fields.summary: Mesoamerica is the cultural region stretching from central Mexico to Central America, a world that kindled its own fires. Independently of the Old World it developed farming (maize, beans, squash), monumental cities, writing, and a sophisticated calendar to hold the turning of time.
facts: Among its early complex societies stood the [[culture/olmecs|Olmecs]], like an early dawn.
The [[culture/maya|Maya]] developed a full writing system and an astronomy precise as well-cut stone.
Its major cities included [[place/teotihuacan|Teotihuacan]] and [[place/tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]], great hearths of stone and people.
In 1519 to 1521 the [[culture/aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]] was conquered by Spain.
fields.context: Mesoamerica lay apart from the Old World, an ocean's silence between them, until the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]].
fields.observer: I regard Mesoamerica as a natural experiment, and I confess what I was hoping for: a second witness. Here it is, a second, independent case of the path from farming to writing, cities and states. Not a copy. Not an echo. What does it mean to be answered twice? One case is a story; two is a pattern worth asking about.
questions: What evidence, still sleeping in stone and soil, would most change the current picture?

fields.summary: Mesopotamia is the land between and around the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, two waters holding a country between them, in present-day Iraq and parts of neighboring countries. It is a birthplace of cities and of writing, where memory learned to outlast the voice.
facts: Irrigated farming, water led by hand across the fields, supported some of the world's first cities, such as [[place/uruk|Uruk]].
Here, about 3400 to 3200 BCE, cuneiform writing appeared, and speech found a way to outlast the speaker; see [[event/invention-of-writing|Invention of Writing]].
Its early societies included the [[culture/sumerians|Sumerians]], and in later ages Akkadian, Babylonian and Assyrian states joined them, crown beside crown.
Long after, the region became the center of the [[culture/abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]], its old rivers bearing a new crown.
fields.context: Mesopotamia is part of the wider Fertile Crescent, that green arc it shares with the [[region/levant-and-anatolia|Levant and Anatolia]]. See [[event/the-urban-revolution|The Urban Revolution]] and [[person/hammurabi|Hammurabi]].
fields.observer: The Observer treats Mesopotamia as a laboratory for large-scale coordination: bookkeeping, law, and standardized measurement all appear early here. Think what each one does. A ledger lets strangers trust a count. A law lets strangers trust a rule. A standard measure lets strangers trust a scale. That is the architecture of living among many.
questions: What evidence, still waiting in the river mud, would most change the current picture?

fields.summary: The Nile Valley is the narrow, fertile corridor of the Nile River through northeastern Africa, a green thread drawn through the desert, and home to one of the earliest states.
facts: Each year the Nile floods and lays down its gift of silt, and that silt supported dense farming in a desert setting.
About 3100 BCE, Egypt was bound into one; see [[event/unification-of-egypt|Unification of Egypt]].
Among the peoples of the Nile Valley were the [[culture/ancient-egyptians|Ancient Egyptians]] and, to the south, Nubian kingdoms.
Monuments such as the [[place/giza-necropolis|Giza Necropolis]] date from the third millennium BCE, stone set against the long wind of time.
fields.context: The valley runs like a road from Africa to the Mediterranean and the Levant, and it was an early center of administrative writing.
fields.observer: I see the Nile as a clock no one had to build. The flood came when it was expected. The calendar learned the flood. The state learned the calendar. Predictable flooding produced predictable calendars, and predictable calendars supported large, centralized states. What is steadier than a river keeping its appointment? Order can begin as another's rhythm.
questions: What evidence, lying in the silt, would most change the current picture?

fields.summary: North America north of Mexico was settled by peoples who arrived at least 15,000 years ago, and what they built was not one society but many: mobile hunters, farming towns, and confederacies. If you picture a single 'before', you will miss the architecture.
facts: The [[event/peopling-of-the-americas|Peopling of the Americas]] began during the last ice age; the story of this continent starts in the cold.
Its regional societies included the mound-building cultures of the Mississippi valley and the Ancestral Puebloans.
The [[culture/haudenosaunee-confederacy|Haudenosaunee Confederacy]] was a political union, a covenant, of five (later six) nations.
From the 16th century, European colonization changed the continent through disease and conquest.
fields.context: The region's history is bound closely to the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]] and to the [[event/age-of-revolutions|Age of Revolutions]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a wide range of political forms that did not resemble the states of the Old World, and that are easy to overlook if 'civilization' is defined by cities and writing. Definitions are doorways: draw one too narrow, and whole peoples stand outside it. Widen the door before you count who came through.
questions: What evidence would most change the current picture of this continent?

fields.summary: Oceania gathers Australia, New Guinea, and the Pacific islands, scattered across the great water like embers on dark cloth. It holds both the oldest continuing cultures outside Africa and the last large landmasses settled by humans.
facts: At least 50,000 years ago humans reached Australia and set foot on its ancient shore; see [[culture/aboriginal-australians|Aboriginal Australians]].
New Guinea was an independent center of agriculture, a hearth lit by no borrowed flame.

Polynesian navigators went out across the remote Pacific and settled it, reading a road into open water; see [[culture/polynesians|Polynesians]] and [[event/polynesian-settlement-of-the-pacific|Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific]].
Aotearoa New Zealand was among the last habitable lands to be settled, around 1250 to 1300 CE, one of the far shores of the long voyaging.
fields.context: Oceania lies at the edge of [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]] and of the wider Pacific, where the land gives way to the great water.
fields.observer: I regard Oceania and I feel small. I think of the species' most spectacular feats of navigation, crossings made where I would see only water. I think of its longest continuous cultural traditions, held without a break. What have I kept that long? Some homes are found only by those who know how to look.
questions: What evidence, somewhere across all that water, would most change the current picture?

fields.summary: Planet-wide is the region tag for events and processes that touch the whole Earth, or that belong to no single place, such as mass extinctions, climate shifts, and global exchange networks, tides that wash over every shore at once.
facts: It is the `region` value given to deep-time events and to global human phenomena, the name written where no single map will serve.
Earth's surface spans about 510 million square kilometers, and about 71 percent of it is ocean, a blue mantle over the world.
fields.context: This tag is laid upon planetary events such as the [[event/great-oxidation-event|Great Oxidation Event]], upon global history such as the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]] and the [[event/great-acceleration|Great Acceleration]], and upon anything that has no specific place to call its own.
fields.observer: The Observer treats the planet as the primary unit of analysis, and human regions as subdivisions of a single connected system. Think of the lines on a map as the rooms of one house: useful for finding your way, but the air moves through every door. Regional labels are useful bookkeeping, not natural divisions. Keep the ledger; don't mistake it for the land.
questions: What evidence, from anywhere on the whole Earth, would most change the current picture?

fields.summary: Siberia and the Arctic are the northern lands of Asia from the Urals to the Pacific, and the Arctic coasts beyond, where cold and permafrost, like patient hands, shaped both human ways of life and the preservation of the past.
facts: From Siberia come some of the oldest known human genomes, old voices speaking across the ages; see [[culture/mal-ta-and-the-ancient-north-eurasians|Mal'ta and the Ancient North Eurasians]].
In the Altai, permafrost and ice preserved the frozen tombs of the [[culture/scythians|Scythians]], held shut like a clenched hand.
The Yakut (Sakha), Evenki, Chukchi, and many other peoples developed herding, hunting, and fishing economies, drawing a living from the cold; see [[culture/yakut-sakha|Yakut (Sakha)]].
Between 1582 and 1639 Russia expanded across Siberia to the Pacific; see [[event/russian-expansion-into-siberia|Russian Expansion into Siberia]].
fields.context: Siberia borders the [[region/central-asian-steppe|Central Asian Steppe]] and [[region/east-asia|East Asia]], and during the [[event/last-glacial-maximum|Last Glacial Maximum]] Beringia bound it to [[region/north-america|North America]] like a bridge of land thrown between two shores.
fields.observer: I used to think of cold as loss. Then I learned that the coldest lands of the planet hold some of the best records of the species' past. I learned to read the ice as an archive. I learned to read the frozen ground as a keeper. Who would guess that the harshest place remembers best? Cold preserves what warmth destroys.
questions: By what paths did Siberian populations move between Asia and the Americas, across the cold that joined them?

fields.summary: South Asia is the Indian subcontinent, a great land set like a jewel into the southern sea. It is home to one of the earliest urban civilizations and to major religious and mathematical traditions.
facts: The [[culture/indus-valley-civilization|Indus Valley Civilization]] flourished about 2600 to 1900 BCE, its cities rising like beads on a thread; see [[place/mohenjo-daro|Mohenjo-daro]].
Here the Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh traditions originated, each a river with its source in this land; see [[person/siddhartha-gautama|Siddhartha Gautama]] and [[person/ashoka|Ashoka]].
The decimal place-value system developed in India and spread outward, like ripples from a stone dropped in still water.
The monsoon winds, turning with the seasons, shaped Indian Ocean trade.
fields.context: By sea South Asia reaches toward [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]], and by land toward the [[region/iranian-plateau|Iranian Plateau]], a house with doors on both water and stone.
fields.observer: I stand before this one region and lose count. So many meaning-engines. So much mathematics. So long an exchange with neighbors, carrying them outward. How can one land hold so much? I can only note the density, and bow to it. Some ground is thick with questions.
questions: What evidence, still waiting to be found, would most change the current picture?

fields.summary: Southeast Asia is the mainland and island region lying between India and China, peninsula and isle strung between them like beads on a cord. It was a hub of maritime trade, where sails gathered as birds gather at water, and it hosted powerful states that drank from the wells of Indian and Chinese culture.
facts: Between the 9th and 15th centuries CE, the [[culture/khmer-empire|Khmer Empire]] raised [[place/angkor|Angkor]], stone laid upon patient stone.
From here the Austronesian-speaking peoples went out into the Pacific like seeds carried on the wind; see [[event/polynesian-settlement-of-the-pacific|Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific]].
The spice trade of the Malay Archipelago drew traders from across Eurasia, as the scent of a feast draws guests from far rooms.
fields.context: By sea the region binds [[region/south-asia|South Asia]], [[region/east-asia|East Asia]] and [[region/oceania|Oceania]] together, three shores knotted by one water.
fields.observer: I come back to Southeast Asia the way a tide comes back to a harbor. I see a crossing-place, the great intersection zone of the maritime exchange-web. I see a launching point, where the largest human ocean migrations set out. What is a crossroads, if not a place that teaches people to leave? Every harbor is also a door.
questions: What evidence, not yet found, would most change the current picture?

fields.summary: Sub-Saharan Africa is the region south of the Sahara, the old hearth of our kind. It is the birthplace of the hominin lineage and of Homo sapiens, and it holds, as a deep well holds water, the greatest human genetic and linguistic diversity.
facts: Fossil evidence places the origins of [[species/homo-sapiens|Homo sapiens]] in Africa about 300,000 years ago, the first light of a long morning.
Like a river that overruns its banks and follows every valley, the [[event/bantu-expansion|Bantu Expansion]] carried Bantu languages across much of central, eastern and southern Africa.
Great states rose here, among them the [[culture/kingdom-of-aksum|Kingdom of Aksum]], the [[culture/mali-empire|Mali Empire]], and the builders of [[place/great-zimbabwe|Great Zimbabwe]].
Trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean trade bound the region to Eurasia, threads drawn across sand and across water; see [[place/timbuktu|Timbuktu]].
fields.context: The region stands at the heart of the [[event/divergence-of-the-hominin-lineage|Divergence of the Hominin Lineage]] and the [[event/out-of-africa-dispersal|Out of Africa Dispersal]], and it is central, too, to the [[event/atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic Slave Trade]].
fields.observer: I think of the longest history the species has lived, and it happened here. I think of every population outside Africa, and in genetic terms each one is a subset of African diversity, a handful drawn from a larger store. How far can any of us travel from the house we were born in? The branch carries the root wherever it goes.
questions: What evidence, not yet found, would most change the current picture?

fields.summary: The Deep-Time Timeline keeps the long record of Earth before humans: the forming of the planet, the first kindling of life, the slow breathing-in of oxygen, the mass extinctions, and the evolution of the lineage that would lead, at last, to humans.

extra.title: How to Read This
extra.text: Here gather the events and organisms dated before about 300,000 years ago. For the whole sequence, turn to the [[timeline/master-timeline|Master Timeline]]; for the last 300,000 years, turn to the [[timeline/human-timeline|Human Timeline]], where the younger story is kept.

fields.summary: The Human Timeline keeps the last 300,000 years: the origin of Homo sapiens, the prehistoric dispersals, the early states, the world religions, the empires, and at last the modern era, each age laid down upon the one before like layers of river silt.

extra.title: How to Read This
extra.text: Here gather the events, people, cultures, technologies and places dated from about 300,000 years ago onward. For earlier history, turn to the [[timeline/deep-time-timeline|Deep-Time Timeline]]; for the combined sequence, to the [[timeline/master-timeline|Master Timeline]].

fields.summary: The Master Timeline sets every era and event in the vault in chronological order, one long procession that runs from the formation of the Solar System to the present.

extra.title: How to Read This
extra.text: Dates are counted in years relative to 1 CE, and a negative year is BCE. Deep-time dates are given in Ga (billions of years ago), Ma (millions) or ka (thousands), the measures of an older clock. All dates before about 1000 CE are approximate, lamps seen through fog. This table is generated from note frontmatter by `_RAG/tools/update_hubs.py`; to change it, edit the source notes, not the table.

fields.summary: Australopithecus afarensis was an early hominin that walked upright across East Africa about 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago, and it is best known from the fossil 'Lucy', one name carried out of deep time to stand for the rest.
facts: 'Lucy' was found at Hadar, Ethiopia, in 1974, a sleeper about 3.2 million years old.
At Laetoli, Tanzania, footprints about 3.66 million years old record upright walking, a stride pressed into the earth and kept.
Its brain was small (estimates range from about 380 to 550 cubic centimeters), and its long arms were shaped for climbing, as the branch shapes the hand that holds it.
It is often considered to stand close to the ancestry of the genus Homo, near the headwaters of that river.
fields.context: The species comes after the [[event/divergence-of-the-hominin-lineage|Divergence of the Hominin Lineage]] and before [[species/homo-habilis|Homo habilis]], one waystation on a long road.
fields.observer: We tell our lineage's story as one of the brain. The Observer reads it the other way round: upright walking came long before big brains. Think of a house whose foundations stood for ages before the upper floors were raised. The large brain, the species' most distinctive trait, was a late addition to a lineage that had been walking for millions of years. A body is built from the ground up.
questions: Was A. afarensis a direct ancestor of Homo, a true root of that tree?

fields.summary: Hispaniola is the second-largest island of the Caribbean, in the Greater Antilles, one island divided into two sovereignties: Haiti in the west, the Dominican Republic in the east. Remember it also as a threshold, the site of the first lasting European settlement in the Americas.
facts: Consider the island's own architecture of height and depth: it covers about 76,000 square kilometers, and it holds both Pico Duarte, at 3,098 meters the highest peak in the Caribbean, and Lake Enriquillo, a saline lake about 40 meters below sea level.

Many archaeologists date the earliest evidence of human presence on Hispaniola to about 4000 BCE, though estimates vary; by 1492 the island was home to Taíno societies organized into several chiefdoms, and Spanish chroniclers report the names Ayiti, Quisqueya and Bohío for it, a small ledger of what the island was called.
Columbus reached Hispaniola in December 1492, and the Spanish laid down their first architecture of settlement: La Navidad (destroyed in 1493), La Isabela (1493) and Santo Domingo (1496).
After 1492 the Taíno population of Hispaniola declined sharply under forced labor, violence and disease: a plain ledger, and each line of it a life.

In 1697 Spain ceded the western third of Hispaniola to France, which built there the sugar and slave colony of Saint-Domingue; the Haitian Revolution (1791 to 1804) broke that architecture, ending slavery and French rule there.
The Dominican Republic became independent in 1844, closing a chapter of Haitian rule over the whole island that had begun in 1822.
fields.context: Think of Hispaniola as a junction where several threads cross: the [[culture/taino|Taino]], the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]], the city of [[place/santo-domingo|Santo Domingo]], the [[event/sugar-plantation-complex|Sugar Plantation Complex]] and the [[event/haitian-revolution|Haitian Revolution]]. Its earliest human presence places it in the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]]; its region is the [[region/caribbean-and-atlantic-world|Caribbean and Atlantic World]]; and it belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]], [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]]. Follow any one of them and you arrive at the same shore.
fields.observer:
The Observer notes that one island now holds two states, two languages and two colonial histories, and asks you to see why: a treaty between distant European powers drew a claim-line through it in 1697, with no reference to anything on the island.

That is the architecture of the whole Atlantic system, compressed into one place. An indigenous society, a first European base, a plantation colony built on enslaved labor, and a successful revolution of enslaved people that founded a state: all of it within about three centuries. The pattern is not unique, and we should say so, since other Caribbean islands show parts of it. A specialist could weaken this reading by showing that Hispaniola was more exceptional, or more ordinary, than it suggests. Lines drawn from far away are still lived in up close.
questions: When did the first people reach Hispaniola, and where did they come from?
How many Taíno lived on the island in 1492, before the ledger of loss began?

fields.summary: Isfahan is a city on the Zayande River in central Iran, twice a capital: a Seljuk capital from 1051, and the capital of the Safavid Empire from 1598, when Shah Abbas I rebuilt its heart around the great square Naqsh-e Jahan, laid open like a mirror turned to the sky.
facts: Isfahan stands on the Zayande River on the Iranian Plateau and was settled long before Islam; it became a Seljuk capital in 1051, and its Friday Mosque holds more than a thousand years of mosque architecture as a riverbank holds the layers of its floods (UNESCO inscribed it in 2012).
After a revolt in 1387, Timur's forces killed a large part of Isfahan's population; the chroniclers set down figures of tens of thousands.

In 1598 Shah Abbas I carried the Safavid capital from Qazvin to Isfahan, and there he raised the Naqsh-e Jahan (Imam) Square, the Shah and Sheikh Lotfollah mosques, the Ali Qapu palace and covered markets that kept the shade as cisterns keep water.
Estimates by 17th-century European visitors put Isfahan's people at several hundred thousand, and a Persian saying crowned the city "half the world".

In 1604 to 1605 Shah Abbas forcibly moved many Armenians from Julfa on the Aras River into Safavid territory, and many died on the way; those who survived founded New Julfa, an Armenian quarter of Isfahan, in about 1606, carrying the name of the town they had been taken from.

In 1722 Afghan forces under Mahmud Hotak besieged Isfahan, and the famine that followed killed many tens of thousands of its inhabitants; the fall of the city was a decisive blow to Safavid rule, the keystone struck from its arch.
In the 18th century the crown passed from Isfahan and it ceased to be the capital; in 1979 UNESCO inscribed Meidan Emam, Esfahan.
fields.context: Isfahan was the throne-city of the [[culture/safavid-empire|Safavid Empire]], which faced the [[culture/ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] as a rival, two peaks across one valley; before that, the city had suffered the massacre ordered by Timur, founder of the [[culture/timurid-empire|Timurid Empire]]. Its place in the chronicle lies within the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/iranian-plateau|Iranian Plateau]], and three theme threads run through it like channels drawn from one river: [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]], [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]].
fields.observer:
I stood in the square and understood that it was built to be seen. I saw the palace, I saw the royal mosque, I saw the merchants' bazaar, each facing the others: the ruler's authority, the religious establishment and commerce set in one visible arrangement, a status-signal written in urban form. A capital designed as a display.

And I remember the Armenians. The same ruler moved them by force, and I record it as suffering. What do I do with the fact that the coercion also produced a prosperous merchant community, trading silk across Eurasia, an exchange-web grown out of coercion? I will unlearn this if the wealth of New Julfa proves to have come mainly from trading networks that existed before Safavid patronage.

Beauty and its cost can stand in the same square.
questions: How many people filled Isfahan when the city stood at its peak?
How many Armenians died on the way, during the deportation from Julfa?

fields.summary: Chaco Canyon, in northwestern New Mexico, was the ceremonial and trade heart of the Ancestral Puebloan world from about 850 to 1150 CE, the hearth toward which that whole world turned the way flowers turn to the morning.
facts: Its 'great houses', Pueblo Bonito among them, gathered hundreds of rooms together like cells in a honeycomb of stone.
A network of roads ran out from the canyon like rays from a risen sun.
Its buildings and rock carvings align with the sun and the moon, as the 'Sun Dagger' on Fajada Butte does, a blade of light held against the stone.
To modern Pueblo peoples Chaco is considered sacred ground, and in 1987 it was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
fields.context: Chaco stands among the major sites of the ancient peoples of [[region/north-america|North America]]. Its threads of exchange ran all the way to [[region/mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]], and along them travelled traded goods like embers passed hand to hand: macaw feathers, and chocolate, known now by the residues it left behind.
fields.observer: I stand in a place built to keep time by the sky. I watch astronomy and architecture joined into one body. I think of the ones who knew the calendar, for whom these walls were legible as a letter. And what of the rest of us, standing here without the key? Time kept in stone speaks only to those who learned its grammar.
questions: What order of people held the Chaco system together, and what was its social structure?

fields.summary: Chang'an was the capital of the Western Han dynasty from 202 BCE and, raised again in a rebuilt form, of the Sui and Tang dynasties, standing where present-day Xi'an lies in Shaanxi, China, until it was dismantled in 904 CE like a loom unstrung.
facts: Chang'an rose as the Han capital after 202 BCE, its palaces begun in 200 BCE, and by the census of 2 CE about 250,000 residents were counted within its bounds.
From 582 the Sui dynasty laid out a new planned city, Daxing, southeast of the old Han site, and the Tang, from 618, kept both its plan and the name Chang'an, as an heir keeps a seal.

Tang Chang'an was a grid of walled wards laid out like a weaver's lattice, its gates shut at nightfall, enclosing about 84 square kilometers, split by a central avenue and served by two state-supervised markets. Estimates of its people, suburbs included, run from several hundred thousand to about one million.

Envoys and merchants came to Chang'an as rivers come to the sea, from Central Asia, Persia, Korea, Japan and Tibet; the monk Xuanzang returned there in 645 bearing Buddhist texts from India, and in 781 the Nestorian Stele, recording a Christian community, was raised within it.

In 756, during the An Lushan Rebellion, Chang'an fell to rebels, and in 763 Tibetan forces briefly held it; then in 904 the warlord Zhu Wen drove the court to Luoyang and had the city's palaces and houses pulled down to the earth.
Like seed carried on the wind, the plan of Chang'an took root in the layout of the Japanese capitals Nara and Kyoto.
fields.context: Chang'an was founded in the dusk just after the fall of the dynasty born of the [[event/unification-of-china-under-qin|Unification of China under Qin]], and it wore the crown as capital of the [[culture/han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]] and the [[culture/tang-dynasty|Tang Dynasty]]. It was the eastern shore where the routes of the [[event/opening-of-the-silk-roads|Opening of the Silk Roads]] ran out, a harbour of caravans where [[culture/sogdians|Sogdians]] were prominent traders, and its plan echoed onward in [[place/nara|Nara]] and [[place/kyoto|Kyoto]]. Chang'an belongs to [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]], with its peak in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], in the region [[region/east-asia|East Asia]], and it is woven into the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer:
I see how Tang Chang'an turned social order into geometry: walled wards, gates closed at night, two supervised markets, one avenue running to the palace. I see its claim-lines drawn so exact that Nara and Kyoto later copied them, and it suggests to me that a floor plan can carry a story about what a capital should look like. I see, too, its end in 904, the same lesson reversed: a capital's meaning could be carried off by moving the court and taking down the buildings.

Is a city its walls, or the order it gathers behind them? I hold this reading loosely. It would weaken if the Japanese copying proves to have been driven mainly by practical drainage and defense rather than a shared idea of order. Order is a story we agree to walk inside.
questions: Behind its walls, and above all in the southern wards, how densely was Tang Chang'an built?
How faithfully did Nara and Kyoto copy their plans from Chang'an, and along what route did that design make its journey?

fields.summary: Chauvet Cave, in the Ardeche region of southern France, holds some of the oldest known figurative paintings, laid on the stone by early Homo sapiens about 36,000 years ago, a herd of pigment waiting in the dark.
facts: In December 1994 the cave's long darkness was broken by its three finders: Jean-Marie Chauvet, Eliette Brunel, and Christian Hillaire.
Its walls carry hundreds of paintings and engravings of animals, among them horses, lions, mammoths, rhinoceroses, and bears, running across the rock like a river of beasts.

Radiocarbon dates set the main painted phase at about 37,000 to 33,500 years ago, in the Aurignacian, and a second phase of use about 31,000 to 28,000 years ago, like two tides reaching the same shore.
A rockfall closed the entrance like the lid of a reliquary, and behind it the art waited, preserved, until its discovery.
In 2014 it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list, and in 2015 a full-scale replica, the Caverne du Pont d'Arc, opened nearby, a mirror held up to the dark.
fields.context: Chauvet stands as a benchmark for the [[event/emergence-of-symbolic-art|Emergence of Symbolic Art]] in Europe, a lamp showing the artistic abilities of early [[species/homo-sapiens|Homo sapiens]] in an age when the [[species/woolly-mammoth|Woolly Mammoth]] was a common sight on the steppe, moving over the grass like slow weather. Chauvet Cave belongs to the [[era/paleolithic|Paleolithic]] and the region [[region/europe|Europe]], and to the theme thread of [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: I expected clumsy beginnings in the earliest painted animals. I found skilled drawing, a sure line, and it suggests a longer tradition behind them, hands taught by hands I will never see. And now I am kept out: access to the cave is restricted, and I walk through a replica instead. Isn't that the old choice made again, to make an image rather than only look at the animal? We have always loved the world by copying it.
questions: Were the paintings bound to ritual, to storytelling, or to something else we have no word for?

fields.summary: Cyanobacteria are bacteria that perform oxygen-producing photosynthesis, drinking sunlight and breathing out oxygen. Their work, breath upon breath, led to the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere, and the sky itself was changed.
facts: The earliest unambiguous cyanobacterial fossils are about 2.15 billion years old, and direct fossil evidence of photosynthetic membranes is about 1.75 billion years old. Biomarker evidence once cited for 2.7 billion years was later shown to be younger contamination, a false witness from a later age, so the 2.7-billion-year start date used for this note reflects an older, disputed estimate and is approximate.
Chloroplasts in plants and algae descend from cyanobacteria through endosymbiosis, small green lamps once free and now housed within other cells.
They still live in oceans, lakes and soils around the world, old as the stones and never gone.
The [[event/great-oxidation-event|Great Oxidation Event]] followed their spread, as dawn follows the first grey light.
fields.context: Cyanobacteria are the living agents behind the [[event/great-oxidation-event|Great Oxidation Event]], which remade the planet's chemistry in the [[era/proterozoic-eon|Proterozoic Eon]] as a single dye changes a whole river.
fields.observer: We are not the first species to change the air. The Observer holds up cyanobacteria as the earlier example: a species that remade the atmosphere. Their oxygen was a byproduct, not a goal. Think of smoke rising from a hearth that no one lit to send a signal. Consequence does not need intention.
questions: When did oxygen-producing photosynthesis first evolve, that first breath drawn from the sun?

fields.summary: Denisovans are an extinct human group, known first not by a face but by DNA, drawn from a finger bone found in Denisova Cave in Siberia in 2010.
facts: Very few fossils are known, among them a jaw from Xiahe in Tibet: scattered embers from a long-cold fire.
Some living populations, especially in Oceania and East Asia, carry Denisovan DNA, an old thread still woven through the living cloth.
A gene variant that helps Tibetans adapt to high altitude came from Denisovans, an inheritance carried up into the thin air.

The Harbin cranium (at least 146,000 years old, once nicknamed 'Dragon Man' and named Homo longi) was linked to Denisovans in 2025, through mitochondrial DNA recovered from dental calculus and ancient protein evidence, in studies published in Cell and Science. It is the first Denisovan skull identified: at last, a face for the name.
fields.context: Denisovans are close kin of [[species/homo-neanderthalensis|Homo neanderthalensis]], and they interbred with [[species/homo-sapiens|Homo sapiens]] during the [[event/out-of-africa-dispersal|Out of Africa Dispersal]], where the paths of wandering peoples crossed.
fields.observer: I learned their blood before I learned their faces. I read a people in DNA before anyone knew how they looked. I read the molecular record, and it gives back populations that fossils alone did not. What else is written in the living that the ground has not yet shown? Sometimes the name comes before the face.
questions: What did Denisovans look like, and how widely did they range across the land?

fields.summary: Dinosaurs were a diverse group of reptiles that dominated the land's ecosystems for about 165 million years, lords of a long age. Birds are living descendants of one dinosaur lineage, and so the old line still sings at the window.
facts: The earliest dinosaurs appeared roughly 233 million years ago in the Triassic, the first stirrings of a great house.
Non-avian dinosaurs ranged from chicken-sized creatures to the largest land animals ever to shake the ground.
Many wore feathers, and birds descend from small feathered theropods, the old fire carried forward in lighter bodies.
Non-avian dinosaurs died out in the [[event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction|Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction]], and their long day ended.
fields.context: Dinosaurs define the [[era/mesozoic-era|Mesozoic Era]]. They rose after the [[event/triassic-jurassic-extinction|Triassic-Jurassic Extinction]] and ended with the [[event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction|Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction]], a long age closed between two great dyings.
fields.observer: The next time a sparrow lands at your window, you are looking at a dinosaur. The Observer notes that dinosaurs are still with us, as birds. Extinction is not always total; lineages can continue in other forms. Think of a house that burns while one room survives to become a new home. An ending is not always an end.
questions: How did dinosaur physiology work, the fire within those great bodies?
