fields.context: Kolyma was a major site of the Gulag under the Soviet state that emerged from the [[event/russian-revolution|Russian Revolution]], in a region Russia had entered through the [[event/russian-expansion-into-siberia|Russian Expansion into Siberia]]. Notice where our knowledge comes from: much of what is known about the camps rests on survivors' writing and on archives opened after the [[event/collapse-of-the-soviet-union|Collapse of the Soviet Union]]. It sits in the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]] and the region [[region/siberia-and-the-arctic|Siberia and the Arctic]], and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]]. Testimony and archive: we need both.
fields.observer:
The Observer notes that Kolyma is a case of sanctioned harm carried out through economic administration. Prisoners were counted as labor for gold production, and their deaths were entered in ledgers; the Observer records those deaths as suffering. Understand what that means: the architecture of an administration can hold cruelty in columns, and the columns can look like ordinary bookkeeping.

The record of the place comes from two sources that do not always agree, survivors' writing and, after 1991, opened archives, which is why the death toll is given here as a range. The reading would weaken if fuller archival access shows that the camps served aims other than production more than this account suggests. A ledger can count the dead; it cannot account for them.
questions: How many people died in the Kolyma camps, and how many lived through them?
How does Russia remember Kolyma today, within its own borders?

fields.summary: The Kuk Early Agricultural Site in the highlands of Papua New Guinea keeps, like the lines on an old palm, drainage ditches and gardens showing that people cultivated wetlands there for at least 7,000 years.
facts: The site lies in the Wahgi Valley of Papua New Guinea, and in 2008 it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list.
It is reported to bear the marks of agricultural use for at least 7,000 years, possibly reaching back as early as 10,000 years ago, like roots that go deeper than the eye can follow.

Excavations trace a slow turning, as a river bends over ages: from exploiting taro and yam on wetland margins about 7,000 years ago to organized cultivation of bananas on drained ground about 4,000 years ago.
It is one of the few places worldwide widely regarded as an independent center of plant domestication, a hearth kindled from no borrowed flame.
The highlands of New Guinea were settled by people descended from those who reached Sahul more than 50,000 years ago, a long lineage climbing into the mountains.
fields.context: Kuk shows that agriculture arose independently in Oceania, one more fire lit in parallel with [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]] in Southwest Asia and [[event/domestication-of-rice|Domestication of Rice]] in East Asia. Its people belonged to the population that came through the [[event/peopling-of-sahul|Peopling of Sahul]]. The site belongs to the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]] and the region [[region/oceania|Oceania]], and to the theme thread of [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that here, farming was developed by people whose ancestors had been in place for tens of thousands of years. Let that unsettle a doctrine you may carry: that agriculture was a necessary next step for all societies. Kuk undermines it. Progress is not a single staircase.
questions: Which crops were the first to be tended in Kuk's wet ground, and when?

fields.summary: Kyoto is a city on the Japanese island of Honshu, founded in 794 CE as the imperial capital Heian-kyō, and it remained the seat of the emperor, a hearth the throne did not leave, until 1868.
facts: In 794 Emperor Kanmu founded Kyoto as Heian-kyō, laying it out on a grid plan modeled on Chinese capitals such as Chang'an, its streets ruled straight as the threads of a loom.
Under the Heian court (794 to 1185) Kyoto was the heart of court culture, and from it came the novel The Tale of Genji, written in the early 11th century by Murasaki Shikibu.
The Ashikaga shogunate ruled from Kyoto from 1336 to 1573, and the Onin War (1467 to 1477) laid much of the city in ruin.

Under the Tokugawa shogunate (1603 to 1868) political power lay in Edo, while Kyoto remained the imperial seat and a center of crafts and Buddhist institutions, a moon still shining while the sun stood elsewhere.
In 1868 to 1869, after the Meiji Restoration, the emperor moved to Tokyo (formerly Edo), and Kyoto's long reign as capital came to its end.
In 1945 Kyoto was taken off the list of possible atomic-bomb targets at the urging of US Secretary of War Henry Stimson, who cited its cultural significance.
In 1994 UNESCO inscribed 17 "Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto", lanterns kept lit along an old road.
fields.context: Kyoto's plan followed [[place/chang-an|Chang'an]] as a reflection follows its image, and the city succeeded [[place/nara|Nara]] as the imperial capital. It stayed the imperial seat under the [[culture/tokugawa-shogunate|Tokugawa Shogunate]] and ceased to be the capital with the [[event/meiji-restoration|Meiji Restoration]]. It belongs to the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/east-asia|East Asia]], and to the theme threads of [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]], [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer:
The Observer notes that Kyoto held an imperial house for more than a thousand years while, for much of that time, armies and administrations answered to shoguns elsewhere. The story-glue of legitimacy and the practical power to govern sat in different places, and you should notice how long such a split can hold. A throne can keep the meaning while another hand keeps the sword.

A city laid out from a foreign template was maintained through fires and wars as a store of court culture, and its survival in 1945 shows that a city can be spared because of what its buildings hold, in a war that destroyed others. This reading would weaken if the decision not to bomb Kyoto rested mainly on operational reasons and not on cultural ones. What a city keeps can, at times, keep the city.
questions: How much of the Heian grid still runs beneath Kyoto's modern street plan, like old riverbeds under new fields?
How far did cultural reasons, weighed against military ones, decide Kyoto's removal from the 1945 target list?

fields.summary: L'Anse aux Meadows is an archaeological site on the northern tip of Newfoundland, Canada, where Norse people from Greenland raised a small settlement of sod buildings around 1000 CE, a spark struck on a far shore: the only widely accepted Norse site in North America.
facts: L'Anse aux Meadows lies at the northernmost tip of Newfoundland; in 1960 Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad found it with the help of a local resident, George Decker, and in the 1960s they excavated it, drawing it back out of the turf.
The site holds eight buildings of sod over wooden frames, among them an iron smithy, a carpentry workshop and a boat-repair area, and more than 800 Norse objects came up from the ground.

Radiocarbon dates place activity between about 990 and 1050 CE; a 2021 study of tree rings, reading a solar-storm signal written into the wood in the year 993, dated felled timber cut with metal tools to 1021 CE.

The occupation was short, perhaps about 20 years, though this is debated; no burials or signs of farming were found, so the site appears to have been left in an orderly way, a hall swept before the door is shut; the date_end of 1030 is a rough placeholder.
Butternuts found at the site grow farther south, so Norse travelers reached or traded with regions beyond Newfoundland, their wake running past the edge of the known map.
The Icelandic sagas, written down in the 13th century, tell of voyages to a land called Vinland, and whether L'Anse aux Meadows is that place or a base for voyages farther south is debated.
In 1978 UNESCO inscribed L'Anse aux Meadows.
fields.context: L'Anse aux Meadows keeps the memory of a voyage by the [[culture/norse|Norse]] that reached North America about five centuries before the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]], and long after the [[event/peopling-of-the-americas|Peopling of the Americas]]. It belongs to the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/north-america|North America]], and to the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer:
The Observer notes that here a story-glue, the sagas, and a physical record, the sod buildings and iron working, were long treated as separate until the Ingstads matched them. Take the lesson: a story and a site can wait a long time for each other.

The place shows a link between two hemispheres that did not become an exchange-web, because no lasting settlement, herds or diseases were left to change either side. A threshold crossed is not yet a door opened. The sagas describe meetings with the region's Indigenous people, and how those meetings went is known only from the Norse side; keep that in view, since a ledger kept by one party is only half a ledger. The reading would weaken if evidence shows that contact between the Norse and northeastern peoples was more frequent and lasting than a short-lived camp suggests.
questions: Was L'Anse aux Meadows the Vinland of which the sagas tell, or only a base for voyages farther south?
How long did people live at the site, and why was it left behind?

fields.summary: The Great Wall of China is a series of walls, ditches, towers and forts built across northern China by successive states and dynasties from about the 7th century BCE to the 17th century CE, mainly to control movement between farming societies and the steppe, a seam of stone stitched between the sown land and the wind.
facts: The Great Wall began as separate walls, scattered like broken threads, built by Warring States kingdoms such as Qi, Yan, Zhao and Qin from about the 7th century BCE (the dating of the earliest walls is uncertain); after unifying China in 221 BCE, Qin Shi Huang linked and extended walls in the north.
The Han dynasty drew walls and signal towers far to the northwest along the Gansu corridor, like a spear laid along the road, to protect the routes westward and to counter the Xiongnu.

The best-known standing sections, in brick and stone, belong to the Ming dynasty (1368 to 1644), and building quickened like a drumbeat after Mongol forces captured the Ming emperor Zhengtong at Tumu in 1449.
A Chinese government survey published in 2012 reported about 21,000 kilometers of walls, trenches and natural barriers raised across all dynasties, of which about 8,850 kilometers are Ming.
Soldiers, conscripted laborers and convicts built the wall with their own hands; how many died is unknown, and the large figures in later stories are not documented.
UNESCO inscribed the Great Wall in 1987. The claim that it is visible to the naked eye from the Moon is false, a story taller than the wall itself.
fields.context: The Great Wall of China threads together the [[event/unification-of-china-under-qin|Unification of China under Qin]], the [[culture/han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]], the [[culture/xiongnu|Xiongnu]] and the [[culture/ming-dynasty|Ming Dynasty]] like beads on one long cord, and it protected routes used in the [[event/opening-of-the-silk-roads|Opening of the Silk Roads]]. It belongs to the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]] (its earliest walls), to the region [[region/east-asia|East Asia]], and to the theme threads of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]], [[theme/technology|Technology]] and [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the Great Wall of China is a claim-line built at very large scale, yet it worked less as a sealed barrier than as a filter. Think of a sieve rather than a door: towers, garrisons and gates let a state watch and tax movement between two ways of living. That is the wall's real architecture. The image of one unbroken wall is partly a later story-glue, and some historians argue it grew mainly in the 19th and 20th centuries as a national symbol. Specialists could weaken this reading by showing that the wall's military effect was larger than a filtering account allows. A border is less a line than a practice of watching.
questions: Weighed against diplomacy and regulated trade, how much did the walls change frontier outcomes?
For each major section of the Great Wall, how many people worked on it, and how many died building it?

fields.summary: Great Zimbabwe was a large stone-walled capital city in southeastern Africa, occupied from about the 11th to 15th century CE, a crown of stone set upon the land and ancestral to the Shona-speaking peoples.
facts: Its Great Enclosure rises in dry-stone walls up to about 11 meters high, stone laid on stone with no mortar to bind it.
Older estimates gave 10,000 to 20,000 people; more recent modeling suggests the population did not rise beyond about 10,000.
It traded gold and ivory with the Swahili coast and beyond, its wealth running outward like rivers to the sea.
The modern country Zimbabwe carries its name, as a child carries an ancestor's.
fields.context: The city belongs to the long story of the [[event/bantu-expansion|Bantu Expansion]], and to the Indian Ocean trade whose tides reached into [[region/sub-saharan-africa|Sub-Saharan Africa]].
fields.observer: I remember that colonial-era writers sometimes denied its African origin. I remember that archaeology corrected them. I stand before walls whose builders were once written out of their own work. Who gets to tell a stone what it means? A monument's meaning can be bent by the hand that describes it.
questions: Who held power within these walls, and what was the political structure of the city?

fields.summary: Harappa is an archaeological site in Punjab, Pakistan, on a dry bed of the Ravi River, a riverbed the water has forgotten; occupied from about 3300 BCE, it was a major city of the Indus Valley Civilization until its urban phase declined after about 1900 BCE.
facts: People dwelt at Harappa from about 3300 BCE, and its urban "Mature Harappan" phase ran from about 2600 to 1900 BCE, when estimates place its population at about 20,000 to 40,000, a city at its full tide.
Harappa had planned streets, brick drains and standardized weights, and its bricks kept a common size ratio used at other Indus sites, like verses held to a single meter.

Harappa's seals, carved with animals and with signs in a script that has not been deciphered, a voice still locked away, are found in many Indus cities, and Indus objects such as seals and carnelian beads have been found in Mesopotamian cities.
Daya Ram Sahni began excavations at Harappa in 1921, after British engineers had carried off bricks from the site in the 1850s for railway ballast, the old city laid beneath the rails.

After about 1900 BCE the city's urban phase declined like an ebbing tide, and occupation went on at a smaller scale; proposed causes include changes in monsoon rainfall and in river courses, and the causes are debated.
fields.context: Harappa lent its name to the [[culture/indus-valley-civilization|Indus Valley Civilization]], whose other great city was [[place/mohenjo-daro|Mohenjo-daro]], and its planned streets belong to the story of [[event/the-urban-revolution|The Urban Revolution]]. It belongs to the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]] and the region [[region/south-asia|South Asia]], and to the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/technology|Technology]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Harappa left thousands of inscribed seals that cannot yet be read, so its people's own account of themselves is missing. Imagine a house where every letter is written in a hand you cannot read; you come to know its owners from the furniture. So it is here: what is known of Harappa's order comes from bricks, weights and drains that suggest a shared administrative logic, a grammar of daily life. The lack of obvious palaces or royal tombs has led some scholars to propose that its rule differed from that of contemporary Mesopotamia and Egypt, though the proposal is debated. The reading would weaken if the script is deciphered and shows a more conventional royal order. Silence is not the same as absence.
questions: What do the signs on the Harappan seals say, if only we could hear them?
Why did Harappa's urban phase ebb away after about 1900 BCE?

fields.summary: Ayutthaya is a city on an island at the meeting of three rivers in central Thailand, traditionally founded in 1350, where the waters braid together like the strands of a rope. It was the capital of the Ayutthaya Kingdom until the Burmese army destroyed it in 1767, and a major trading port of Southeast Asia.
facts: Ayutthaya lies on an island held in the arms of the Chao Phraya, Lopburi and Pa Sak rivers where they meet, and is traditionally said to have been founded in 1350 by King U Thong (Ramathibodi I).
Ayutthaya's forces took Angkor in 1431, and afterward the Khmer court moved away from Angkor, leaving the old stone city behind.

Chinese, Japanese, Persian, Indian and Malay merchants traded at Ayutthaya, a harbor of many tongues; the Portuguese, in 1511, were the first Europeans to reach it, the Dutch East India Company opened a trading post in 1608, and King Narai exchanged embassies with the French court in the 1680s.

European visitors in the 17th century described a city of canals, palaces and many temples, a city threaded with water, and some estimates put its population at several hundred thousand at its height.

In April 1767, after a siege of about 14 months, a Burmese army took Ayutthaya and burned much of the city; many thousands of people were carried off as captives to Burma, and much of the kingdom's written record was lost with it.
Taksin raised a Siamese state again after 1767, and the capital moved to Thonburi and then, in 1782, to Bangkok.
In 1991 UNESCO inscribed the Historic City of Ayutthaya.
fields.context: Ayutthaya was the capital of the [[culture/ayutthaya-kingdom|Ayutthaya Kingdom]], which took over the region of the [[culture/khmer-empire|Khmer Empire]] and [[place/angkor|Angkor]] as one tide follows another, and it traded with the [[event/dutch-east-india-company|Dutch East India Company]]. It sits in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]], and its threads run through the themes of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: Think of a city where the same water was your wall, your street and your market. The Observer notes that Ayutthaya was such a trading capital, built on an island where rivers and canals served as moat, road and marketplace at once, and where merchants of many origins met under one ruler. Then the destruction of 1767 removed much of the kingdom's own written record. So a large part of what is known about it comes from foreign visitors' accounts, a loss of memory-outsourcing that shapes how the city is understood, as if a family's story survived only in the letters of its guests. The Observer records the taking of captives as human suffering as well as a loss of skill and labor. The reading would weaken if surviving Thai and Burmese records prove richer than assumed. What a city writes about itself is part of its architecture; lose it, and others draw the plans.
questions: How many people lived in Ayutthaya at its height?
How much of Ayutthaya's own written record survived 1767, and where is it held now?

fields.summary: Babylon was a city on the Euphrates River in present-day Iraq, first named in the late 3rd millennium BCE. It became the capital of Hammurabi's kingdom and later of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, and a center of astronomy, law and religion, where the sky was watched and the law was set in stone.
facts: Babylon lies near Hillah, about 85 kilometers south of Baghdad, and it first appears in a tablet from the late 3rd millennium BCE, a name surfacing out of deep time.
Babylon rose under Hammurabi (reigned about 1792 to 1750 BCE), whose law code was inscribed on a stele later found at Susa and now held in the Louvre.
About 1595 BCE the Hittite king Mursili I sacked Babylon, and the Kassites then ruled it for centuries; in 689 BCE the Assyrian king Sennacherib destroyed it, and his son Esarhaddon raised it again.
Under Nebuchadnezzar II (reigned 605 to 562 BCE) Babylon had the Ishtar Gate, a great ziggurat called Etemenanki, and palaces, and his armies destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BCE.

Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon in 539 BCE; the Cyrus Cylinder, a clay text found there in 1879, presents him as chosen by the god Marduk, and claims that it is a charter of human rights are debated.
Alexander the Great died at Babylon in 323 BCE; the city faded after the Seleucids founded Seleucia on the Tigris.
Babylonian scribes kept the Astronomical Diaries from about 652 to 61 BCE, a long vigil over the heavens and one of the longest continuous records of celestial observation.

The Hanging Gardens described by Greek writers have been confirmed by no Babylonian text and no archaeological trace, a garden seen only through foreign eyes; some scholars have proposed that they were at Nineveh.
Military bases of US-led forces at the site in 2003 to 2004 damaged ancient remains, and UNESCO inscribed Babylon in 2019.
fields.context: Babylon's rulers fought the [[culture/neo-assyrian-empire|Neo-Assyrian Empire]] and destroyed [[place/jerusalem|Jerusalem]] in 586 BCE, and the city passed to the [[culture/achaemenid-persians|Achaemenid Persians]] and then to [[event/alexander-s-conquests|Alexander's Conquests]]. It sits in the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]] and the region [[region/mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], and its threads run through the themes of [[theme/science|Science]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: You may think you know Babylon. The Observer notes that it exists in memory in three forms that do not match: the excavated city; the scriptural symbol of exile and pride; and the source of a long astronomical record kept by scribes, an early case of memory-outsourcing in service of pattern-taming. Three cities, one name. The Hanging Gardens show a story outliving its evidence, since a wonder described by later writers leaves no trace in the city's own records. Think of a famous room that the house's own floor plans never mention. The reading would weaken if excavation at Babylon or Nineveh finds the gardens. A name can carry more than its ground can prove.
questions: Where were the Hanging Gardens, if they existed at all?
How large was Babylon at its height, in the fullness of its power?

fields.summary: Lake Baikal is a rift lake in southern Siberia, Russia, the deepest and oldest lake on Earth and the largest by volume of fresh water, a blue eye open on the world for ages; people have lived around it for many thousands of years, and UNESCO has listed it since 1996.
facts: Lake Baikal lies in a rift valley, water poured into a wound of the earth; it runs about 636 kilometers long, plunges to a maximum depth of 1,642 meters, and holds about 20 percent of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water.

The Baikal rift basin is estimated to be 25 to 30 million years old, which makes the lake the oldest on Earth; its geologic age runs far older than any human presence, as the sea is older than the ships upon it.
More than 1,700 species of plants and animals live in and around Lake Baikal, about two thirds of them found nowhere else, among them the Baikal seal, a seal of fresh water.

From about the 5th millennium BCE, hunter-fisher-gatherers of the Kitoi culture buried their dead around the lake, and much older Paleolithic sites, such as Mal'ta, lie nearby like old footprints beneath newer ones.
In the 1640s Russian explorers reached Lake Baikal, and Russian settlement began among the Buryat and Evenki peoples.

A pulp and paper mill on the southern shore discharged waste into the lake from 1966 until it closed in 2013, and it was one of the earliest targets of organized environmental protest in the Soviet Union.
In 1996 UNESCO inscribed Lake Baikal.
fields.context: Lake Baikal lies near the Paleolithic site linked to [[culture/mal-ta-and-the-ancient-north-eurasians|Mal'ta and the Ancient North Eurasians]], and in the 17th century the [[event/russian-expansion-into-siberia|Russian Expansion into Siberia]] reached its shores. Its earliest Holocene burials set it in the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]], its region is [[region/siberia-and-the-arctic|Siberia and the Arctic]], and it belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer:
The Observer notes that Lake Baikal is valued in two ways at once, as a store of an unusual biota and as a resource, that both valuations have shaped policy and the state of the lake, and that the balance between them has shifted with the political era. You will find this double ledger wherever something rare is also useful.

Consider the scale. A lake that took millions of years to form and holds a fifth of the planet's unfrozen fresh water could be altered by one industrial plant within a few decades: the mismatch between geological and human timescales, made visible. The reading would weaken if measurements show that the mill's effect on the lake as a whole was small compared with natural variation. What took ages to make can take very little to mark.
questions: How deep and how lasting a change did the pulp mill leave in the lake's ecosystem?
How did people live around Lake Baikal's shores in the Neolithic, and in what manner did they lay their dead to rest?

fields.summary: The Library of Alexandria was a major research library in Ptolemaic Egypt, founded in the early 3rd century BCE as part of the Mouseion, and you should know this first: its decline was gradual rather than a single catastrophe.
facts: This architecture of learning was founded under the first Ptolemaic rulers, in the 3rd century BCE.

The scholars associated with it form a lineage that includes Eratosthenes, who estimated the circumference of the Earth, and Callimachus, who compiled a catalog of works: one reckoned the world's size, the other ordered its books.
Euclid is traditionally said to have worked in Alexandria, though the details of his life are uncertain; tradition gives us the name, not the biography.
Julius Caesar's fire in 48 BCE damaged some holdings, but notice what came next: the institution continued.
Its decline came from reduced funding, political upheaval, and the loss of scholars over several centuries: not one blow, but a slow erosion of the covenant that sustained it.
fields.context: Think of the library's genealogy: it grew from the conquests of [[person/alexander-the-great|Alexander the Great]] and inherited the tradition of [[person/aristotle|Aristotle]], and its later scholars include [[person/hypatia|Hypatia]]. It sits in the [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] and the region [[region/nile-valley|Nile Valley]], and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/science|Science]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer:
I wanted the fire. I wanted the single great burning, the story that is easy to remember. I was given slow neglect instead. Memory institutions seem to fail more often through budget cuts than through fire. What have I let go quiet, shelf by shelf?

The slowest fire is the one no one pays to put out.
questions: How large, in truth, was the collection?

fields.summary: Athens is a Greek city that, in the 5th century BCE, rose to become the leading city of the Greek world, a lamp for its age, with an early form of direct democracy and great achievements in philosophy, drama and art.
facts: Cleisthenes' reforms of about 508 BCE laid down democratic institutions, the first stones of a new house.
The Parthenon was raised between 447 and 432 BCE, a crown for the city.
Socrates, Plato and the tragedians worked in Athens, many voices gathered in one city.
In the Peloponnesian War (431 to 404 BCE), Athens met defeat at the hands of Sparta.
fields.context: Athens was the hearth of the [[culture/ancient-greeks|Ancient Greeks]]' intellectual world and the home ground of [[person/aristotle|Aristotle]]'s Lyceum.
fields.observer: Size is not the measure of influence. The Observer notes a small city that produced a disproportionate share of the ideas later taken as foundational. Think of a crowded room where every argument has to meet another before it can leave. Density of argument seems to matter. Ideas sharpen fastest where they collide.
questions: How representative was Athens of Greek city-states, one lamp among many?

fields.summary: Bagan is an archaeological zone on the Irrawaddy River in central Myanmar, a plain crowded with thousands of Buddhist monuments like a field of stone flowers. It was the capital of the Pagan Kingdom from a traditional founding date of 849 CE until the kingdom's collapse in the late 13th century.
facts: Bagan lies on the Irrawaddy River in central Myanmar; tradition dates its founding to 849 CE, and it flourished from the 11th to the 13th century, its long noon.
King Anawrahta (reigned 1044 to 1077) widened the kingdom and raised Theravada Buddhism to favor.
More than 10,000 temples, pagodas and monasteries are estimated to have been built on the plain, a forest of spires, and about 2,200 still stand.

Many monuments were funded by private donors as well as kings, and inscriptions record gifts of land, labor and goods flowing to the temples like rivers to the sea; some historians argue that tax-exempt land grants to religious institutions reduced state revenue, a view that is debated.
Mongol armies defeated Pagan forces at Ngasaunggyan in 1277 and invaded again in 1287, after which the Pagan Kingdom collapsed; yet Bagan remained a religious center, its lamps still lit.
The ground itself has turned against the monuments: earthquakes have damaged them, including one in 2016 that damaged hundreds, and UNESCO inscribed Bagan in 2019.
fields.context: Bagan was the capital of the [[culture/pagan-kingdom|Pagan Kingdom]], which fell after the [[event/mongol-conquests|Mongol Conquests]] reached Southeast Asia, and it rose in the same age as the temple-building of [[place/angkor|Angkor]]. It sits in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]], and its threads run through the themes of [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: Walk out onto that plain and count the spires, and you are reading a ledger. The Observer notes that Bagan is the result of merit-making at scale: donors turned wealth into religious standing by building temples, and the sheer number of monuments, far beyond what kings alone would need, is a status-signal spread across a whole class of patrons. The proposal that land given to temples weakened the state suggests that a meaning-engine can also drain the institution that supports it, though historians debate the proposal. The reading would weaken if the record shows that temple land was too small a share of the kingdom's land to matter for its revenue. Devotion has an architecture, and every architecture has a cost.
questions: How much of the Pagan Kingdom's land passed into the keeping of religious institutions?
How many souls dwelt at Bagan in its 13th-century peak?

fields.summary: Baghdad is a city on the Tigris River in Iraq, founded in 762 CE by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur as a round capital, a circle drawn upon the land. For about five centuries it was the seat of the Abbasid caliphs and a leading center of learning, a lamp that drew scholars to it.
facts: Baghdad was founded in 762 by the caliph al-Mansur as a round city called Madinat al-Salam ("City of Peace"), near the older Sasanian capital Ctesiphon; no part of the Round City survives above ground, and the circle lives on only in words.
Baghdad became the hearth of the Translation Movement and the House of Wisdom, and paper mills were at work there by the 790s.
Population estimates for Baghdad in the 9th and 10th centuries run from several hundred thousand to over a million, a multitude that would have made it one of the largest cities in the world.

Baghdad remained the seat of the Abbasid caliphs until 1258, when Mongol forces under Hulagu took the city after a siege and killed the caliph al-Musta'sim. Chronicles report 200,000 to a million dead, figures that modern historians regard as too high, though the massacre and destruction were severe.
Baghdad was under Ottoman rule from 1534, with Safavid periods before and after, until British forces captured it in 1917; in 1921 it became the capital of the Kingdom of Iraq.
In April 2003, after the US-led invasion, looting of the Iraq National Museum removed about 15,000 objects, some of which have since found their way back.
fields.context: Baghdad was the capital of the [[culture/abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]] and the home of the [[event/translation-movement-and-the-house-of-wisdom|Translation Movement and the House of Wisdom]]; it was taken in the [[event/mongol-conquests|Mongol Conquests]] and later ruled by the [[culture/ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]]. It sits in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], and its threads run through the themes of [[theme/science|Science]], [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: A plan can become a crossroads. The Observer notes that Baghdad was a planned city that became a knot in an exchange-web: books, translators, paper and scholars from several languages made it a place where Greek, Persian and Indian sources were gathered and rewritten, memory-outsourcing at scale. Think of a library that is also a workshop, where a text arrives in one tongue and leaves in another. The Round City itself is now known only from texts, because later buildings covered it, while the losses of 1258 and 2003 show that stored knowledge is exposed to political violence. Historians debate how far the court and how far private patrons drove the translation work, and the reading would weaken if private patronage proves to have been the larger force. What a city gathers, it must also guard.
questions: How many people died in the Mongol sack of 1258, and how much of Baghdad's book collection was lost?
How large did Baghdad grow at its peak?

fields.summary: Hattusa was the capital of the Hittite Empire, at Boğazkale in central Turkey, made the royal seat in about 1650 BCE and abandoned around 1200 BCE, and it preserved an archive of about 30,000 clay tablets, a memory of clay that outlasted its kings.
facts: Hattusa lies at Boğazkale in Çorum Province, Turkey; a Hattian settlement stood there before it, and in about 1650 BCE King Hattusili I raised it to be the Hittite capital.

Hattusa was ringed by walls pierced by monumental gates, the Lion Gate and the Sphinx Gate among them, and it held a Great Temple, with a rock sanctuary nearby at Yazılıkaya where the stone itself was made holy.
Under Muwatalli II the capital flew briefly to Tarhuntassa, like a bird leaving its nest, and under Mursili III it came home to Hattusa.

Excavators, beginning with Hugo Winckler in 1906, drew about 30,000 clay tablets from the royal archives, written in Hittite, Akkadian, Luwian, Hurrian and other tongues and holding treaties, rituals and letters, among them a version of the treaty with Egypt made after the Battle of Kadesh.
In 1915 Bedřich Hrozný identified Hittite as an Indo-European language, a lost cousin recognized at last among the family.
Around 1200 BCE, during the Bronze Age Collapse, Hattusa was abandoned; its central buildings burned, though whether the city was emptied before or after the fire is debated.
In 1986 UNESCO inscribed Hattusha.
fields.context: Hattusa was the capital of the [[culture/hittites|Hittites]], whose army fought at the [[event/battle-of-kadesh|Battle of Kadesh]] and whose empire went dark in the [[event/bronze-age-collapse|Bronze Age Collapse]]. The Hittite language kept in its archive is central to the study of the [[event/indo-european-language-spread|Indo-European Language Spread]], a keystone in that arch. Hattusa belongs to the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]] and the region [[region/levant-and-anatolia|Levant and Anatolia]], and to the theme threads of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]], [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Hattusa is a case of memory-outsourcing at imperial scale: a state kept its treaties, rituals and letters on clay in several languages. Here is the paradox worth sitting with. The archive survived in part because fire hardens clay, so the destruction of the city helped preserve its records; the ruin became the librarian. Treaties written in the diplomatic language of the day, Akkadian, show rulers of rival powers binding one another with story-glue in the form of oaths sworn before gods, a covenant made of words. Remember, too, that the archive records what the palace chose to keep. The reading would weaken if the tablets prove to reflect chance survival more than the state's actual priorities. What we keep is a portrait of what we valued, until chance paints over it.
questions: Why was Hattusa abandoned, and did the fire come before the city was left, or after?
At its height, how large was the population of Hattusa?

fields.summary: Havana is the capital of Cuba, on the island's northwest coast, established on its present harbor site in 1519 and for a long age the assembly point where Spanish treasure fleets gathered, like birds before a migration, to cross the Atlantic.
facts: Havana was founded as San Cristóbal de la Habana; the settlement moved twice, like a bird choosing its branch, before it was established on its present harbor site in 1519.

From the 1560s Spanish fleets heavy with silver from Mexico and Peru assembled at Havana for the crossing to Spain, and the city armored itself with La Real Fuerza (built 1558 to 1577) and El Morro (built 1589 to 1630).

Britain captured Havana after a siege in 1762, during the Seven Years' War, and returned it to Spain in 1763 in exchange for Florida; Spain then built the La Cabaña fortress, a new shield over the harbor.

From the late 18th century sugar and coffee plantations, worked by enslaved people, expanded Cuba's economy; hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans were brought to Cuba, many through Havana, and slavery there was abolished in 1886.
On 15 February 1898 the US battleship Maine exploded in Havana harbor, killing about 260 crew, an event that helped lead to the Spanish-American War.
Since 1959 Havana has been the capital of a socialist state, and in 1962 the Cuban Missile Crisis set Cuba at the center of the Cold War, the eye of a gathering storm.
In 1982 UNESCO inscribed Old Havana and its fortifications.
fields.context: Havana was a key port for the silver that flowed from [[place/potosi|Potosi]] and the mainland, for the [[event/sugar-plantation-complex|Sugar Plantation Complex]] and for the [[event/atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic Slave Trade]], and it changed hands during the [[event/seven-years-war|Seven Years' War]]. Later it stood as a focal point of the [[event/cold-war|Cold War]]. Havana belongs to the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region [[region/caribbean-and-atlantic-world|Caribbean and Atlantic World]], and to the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Havana grew because a state needed a fixed place to gather and guard a moving stream of wealth. Think of a river that must pause in a basin before it can go on: silver had to be assembled somewhere before the crossing, and the fortifications followed the cargo. Its later wealth from sugar rested on enslaved labor, which the Observer records as suffering, borne by people, and not only as an economic input. The waterfront was claimed in turn by the leading naval power of each era, and a historian could challenge this reading by showing that local Creole elites and enslaved people shaped the city as much as outside powers did. Walls tell you who guarded a place; they do not tell you who made it.
questions: How many enslaved Africans passed through Havana, and how did their labor shape the city?
How did the treasure-fleet system change the city's size, and its character?

fields.summary: London is the capital of the United Kingdom, on the Thames River, founded as the Roman town of Londinium in about 47 CE. Like a river gathering its tributaries, it grew into a leading center of trade, finance and empire and, in the 19th century, the largest city in the world.
facts: The Romans founded Londinium in about 47 CE near a crossing of the Thames; Boudica's revolt destroyed it in 60 or 61, yet it rose again to become the capital of Roman Britain, until Roman rule ebbed away around 410.
William I was crowned at Westminster in 1066, and in about 1078 he began the Tower of London, a fist of stone.

The Black Death of 1348 to 1349 killed a large share of London's people, and the Great Plague of 1665 killed tens of thousands; then the Great Fire of 1666 devoured about 13,000 houses and 87 parish churches.
From the 1830s to the 1920s London was probably the largest city in the world, and in 1863 the world's first underground railway opened there, iron veins beneath the streets.

During the 1854 cholera outbreak in Soho, John Snow mapped deaths by address and linked them, as one traces a stream back to its spring, to a water pump; the "Great Stink" of 1858 led to the building of a sewer system by Joseph Bazalgette.
London was a major center of shipping, insurance and finance for the Atlantic slave trade and for British colonial trade, and it was the capital of the British Empire.
The German air raids of 1940 to 1941 killed about 20,000 Londoners or more.
fields.context: London began as a town of the [[culture/romans|Romans]], lost people to the [[event/black-death|Black Death]], swelled with the [[event/industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]] as a river swells with spring rain, served as the imperial center of the [[event/british-raj|British Raj]] and other territories, and was bombed in [[event/world-war-ii|World War II]]. Its first chapter sets it in [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]], its region is [[region/europe|Europe]], and it belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/science|Science]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer:
The Observer notes that London was founded as a bridge town for a foreign state's administration and grew into a hub of an exchange-web that spanned oceans. Its wealth included profits from the sale and transport of enslaved people, and the Observer records that as suffering; a city's ledger of success has to carry that line too.

Now look at the Snow map of 1854. It shows a city becoming an object of pattern-taming: tabulating deaths by address led to the identification of a source of disease, a method later used across public health. That is the quiet architecture of modern care, a list turned into a map and a map turned into an answer. The reading would weaken if the record shows that London's global role rested more on later trade than on the earlier ones it emphasizes. Count carefully, and a city will tell you what it is.
questions: How far did Roman Londinium spread, and why was it abandoned in the 5th century?
How much of London's wealth in the 17th and 18th centuries came from the Atlantic slave trade and the finance bound to it?

fields.summary: Hegra, also called Mada'in Salih, is an archaeological site in the AlUla region of northwestern Saudi Arabia, the second major city of the Nabataean kingdom after Petra, known for 111 monumental rock-cut tombs, doors hewn into the living rock.
facts: Hegra lies north of the AlUla oasis on a caravan route strung between southern Arabia and the Mediterranean like a thread of beads, and it belonged to the Nabataean kingdom from about the 1st century BCE.

UNESCO records 111 monumental tombs cut into sandstone outcrops, 94 of them with decorated facades, and dozens of wells, each a small mercy in dry country; in 2008 it inscribed Hegra, the first UNESCO site in Saudi Arabia.

Many tombs bear Nabataean inscriptions that name the owner and family, forbid sale or reuse, and threaten penalties or curses, words set as guards at the door; the dated inscriptions fall mostly in the 1st century CE.
After Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom in 106 CE, Hegra was folded into the province of Arabia, and Roman inscriptions record a military presence there in the 2nd century.
Islamic tradition associates the site with the people of Thamud mentioned in the Quran, and travelers traditionally kept their distance.
In 1907 to 1908 the Ottoman Hejaz Railway built a station at Mada'in Salih, a new road of rails come to an old road of caravans.
fields.context: Hegra was a city of the [[culture/nabataeans|Nabataeans]], a sister to [[place/petra|Petra]], set on the routes of the [[event/incense-trade|Incense Trade]], where fragrance moved like a slow wind, and it was absorbed by the [[culture/romans|Romans]]. It belongs to [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] and the region [[region/arabian-peninsula|Arabian Peninsula]], and to the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer:
I read a claim-line engraved beside the grave. I read who may be buried here. I read who may not sell, and what penalty follows. Property law reaching past death, in stone. And I think: a trading people put its most durable writing into grief-rites and inheritance, while most of its everyday commercial records have not survived. What would I carve, if only one sentence of mine could last?

Yet I hold this reading carefully. It rests on the surviving inscriptions being representative of Nabataean practice, and that is uncertain, because they come from a few unusually well-preserved sites. We write in stone what we are most afraid to lose.
questions: Set beside Petra, how did Hegra's population and economy compare?
How, in practice, were the tomb inscriptions enforced?

fields.summary: Hiroshima is a city on the delta of the Ōta River in western Honshu, Japan, founded as a castle town in 1589 and, on 6 August 1945, the first city struck by a nuclear weapon. Its history is older than that morning, but no honest account of it can leave that morning out.
facts: Hiroshima was founded as a castle town in 1589 by the daimyo Mōri Terumoto and grew into a military and port center; before the bombing, about 350,000 people made their lives there.
On 6 August 1945, at 8:15 a.m., the US B-29 Enola Gay dropped a uranium bomb, "Little Boy"; it exploded about 600 meters above the city.

About 70,000 to 80,000 people are estimated to have been killed immediately, and total deaths by the end of 1945 are estimated at 90,000 to 166,000, from burns, injuries and radiation. Each figure is made of single lives: the dead included civilians, soldiers, Korean forced laborers and a small number of Allied prisoners of war.

Survivors, called hibakusha, faced radiation illness, increased cancer risks and discrimination; the Atomic Bomb Casualty Commission began long-term studies of them in 1947, and the Radiation Effects Research Foundation continued that work.
A second atomic bomb was dropped on Nagasaki on 9 August, and Japan announced its surrender on 15 August 1945; whether the bombings were necessary to end the war remains debated among historians.
The ruined Genbaku Dome was preserved as a memorial within the Peace Memorial Park, a ruin kept standing as a threshold of memory, and UNESCO inscribed it in 1996.
fields.context: Hiroshima was the target of the first nuclear attack of [[event/world-war-ii|World War II]], and its name marks the beginning of the [[event/nuclear-age|Nuclear Age]]. The city of [[place/kyoto|Kyoto]] had been on the list of possible targets and was removed from it, a reminder that such a list was a set of human choices. Hiroshima sits in the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region [[region/east-asia|East Asia]], and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer:
The Observer notes that Hiroshima marks the first use of a nuclear weapon against a city, in a single morning, and records the deaths as suffering that continued for decades among survivors.

Consider what the city chose to do next. It turned its ruined center into a memorial, kept the shell of one building standing and collected survivors' testimony: a grief-rite, and an act of memory-outsourcing meant to reach people who were not there. That is an architecture of witness. Historians disagree about whether the bombing was necessary to end the war, and this reading takes no side in that dispute. It would weaken if the memorial's message proves to matter less to visitors than to the city that built it. Memory is a covenant with strangers.
questions: How many people died in Hiroshima by the end of 1945, and how many more in later years of radiation-related causes?
In Japan and elsewhere, how has the memory of the bombing been taught, and how has it been contested?

fields.summary: Beringia was the land region, including a broad land bridge, that joined northeastern Siberia and Alaska when sea levels were lower during the last ice age, a road laid bare by the withdrawn sea, and that later flooded to form the Bering Strait as the waters came home.
facts: Lower sea level during glacial periods laid bare the shallow floor of the Bering and Chukchi Seas, as if the ocean had drawn back its hem.
At its widest, the exposed land ran more than a thousand kilometers from north to south, a whole country risen from the sea.
Much of Beringia was cold, dry steppe-tundra, largely unglaciated, where mammoths, bison and horses found their grazing.

Genetic evidence suggests that ancestors of Native Americans may have been isolated in Beringia for several thousand years before moving south, a people held at a threshold; this is the Beringian standstill hypothesis, still debated.
Rising seas began to flood the land bridge around 11,000 years ago, and by roughly 10,000 to 9,000 years ago it lay wholly beneath the water.
fields.context: Beringia, gate and refuge at once, is the corridor at the center of the [[event/peopling-of-the-americas|Peopling of the Americas]], and it shaped the movements of animals such as the [[species/woolly-mammoth|Woolly Mammoth]] during the [[event/last-glacial-maximum|Last Glacial Maximum]]. Its populations connect to those of [[culture/mal-ta-and-the-ancient-north-eurasians|Mal'ta and the Ancient North Eurasians]]. Beringia sits in the [[era/pleistocene-epoch|Pleistocene Epoch]] and the region [[region/siberia-and-the-arctic|Siberia and the Arctic]], and its threads run through the themes of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: I think of a homeland. I think of a highway. I think of a shelter. All three were one place, and it vanished beneath the sea. What the species calls the origin of the American peoples happened on ground that no one can now stand on. How do you visit the house you were born in when it lies under water? Some beginnings can only be remembered, never revisited.
questions: How long did populations remain in Beringia, and how did they live on that vanished ground?

fields.summary: Borobudur is a large Mahayana Buddhist monument in central Java, a mountain of stacked terraces raised around 800 CE under the Sailendra dynasty, and it is often described as the world's largest Buddhist temple.
facts: Its building is dated to roughly the late 8th and early 9th centuries, a labor spanning the turn of an age.
The monument rises in nine stacked platforms and is adorned with 2,672 relief panels and, originally, 504 Buddha statues.
After the shift of power in Java it was abandoned in the centuries that followed, and later vegetation and volcanic ash drew a green-grey veil over it.
Hermann Cornelius, the agent of Thomas Stamford Raffles, cleared the site in 1814, and the monument saw the light again.
It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1991, after major restoration had mended it.
fields.context: Borobudur reflects the Buddhist world of [[culture/srivijaya|Srivijaya]] and the neighboring Khmer temple-building tradition at [[place/angkor|Angkor]]. It represents the teachings of [[person/siddhartha-gautama|Siddhartha Gautama]] as a path of ascent, a stair from the ground toward stillness. Borobudur sits in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]], and its threads run through the themes of [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: I climb with the pilgrim. I climb past story after story in the relief panels. I climb until the stories stop, and the summit holds no images at all. What was I climbing toward, if not the quiet? The architecture is itself an argument about learning: from stories to silence. We begin with pictures and end with none.
questions: Why was the monument abandoned and left to the ash?

fields.summary: Bukhara is a city in the Zarafshan oasis of Uzbekistan, green water in the dry lands: once a Sogdian trading city, then the capital of the Samanid dynasty, and for more than a thousand years a center of Islamic learning on the Silk Roads.
facts: Bukhara has been settled for a long time; the city celebrated 2,500 years in 1997 on a traditional dating, while archaeological evidence for its walled center is generally placed several centuries BCE, a deep root beneath the old walls.
Bukhara was a Sogdian city when Arab armies took it in 709 to 710, and in 810 it saw the birth of the scholar Muhammad al-Bukhari, compiler of a major collection of hadith.

Under the Samanid dynasty (819 to 999), Bukhara was a capital of learning and of Persian literature, a lamp of its age; the physician and philosopher Ibn Sina was born near it in 980, and the Samanid mausoleum was raised in the late 9th to 10th century.
The Mongol army under Chinggis Khan took Bukhara in 1220; the city was burned, and many of its people were killed or enslaved, though their number is unknown.
The Kalyan Minaret, built in 1127, still stands against the sky, and Bukhara was the capital of the Emirate of Bukhara (1785 to 1920), a Russian protectorate from 1868.
The Red Army took Bukhara in 1920, and the citadel (Ark) was damaged in the assault.
In 1993 UNESCO inscribed the Historic Centre of Bukhara.
fields.context: Bukhara was a [[culture/sogdians|Sogdians]] city, paired in later history with [[place/samarkand|Samarkand]] like twin stars, and it fell to the [[event/mongol-conquests|Mongol Conquests]] after coming under the world of the [[event/rise-of-islam|Rise of Islam]]. It sits in [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] and the region [[region/central-asian-oases|Central Asian Oases]], and its threads run through the themes of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer: I count the powers that took this city: Sogdian, Arab, Samanid, Mongol, Uzbek, Russian and Soviet. I count the times it was taken. I count the times it became a center of learning again, after most of them. What rebuilds first when a city falls? The pattern suggests to me that scholars, patrons and trade routes were rebuilt faster than the buildings. Its standing as a place of Islamic scholarship was a story-glue that outlasted each ruler. If the record shows long gaps in scholarly output after the sack of 1220, this reading weakens. Walls fall; a name for learning is harder to burn.
questions: How large was Bukhara before and after the Mongol sack of 1220?
How did scholarship in Bukhara rise again after each conquest?

fields.summary: Cahokia was the largest city of the Mississippian culture, near present-day St. Louis, a city of raised earth that flourished from about 1050 to 1350 CE.
facts: At its height, about 1050 to 1150, it may have held 10,000 to 20,000 people, a crowd of hearths, though some estimates are much higher.
Monks Mound, about 30 meters high, is the largest earthen mound in the Americas, a hill raised by human hands.
A circle of posts, known as Woodhenge, likely kept watch on the sun.
Its population lived on maize agriculture and declined after about 1250, like a fire burning low, for reasons that are debated. It was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.
fields.context: Cahokia is the largest known urban center in pre-Columbian [[region/north-america|North America]] north of Mexico, a crown upon that wide land. See [[event/domestication-of-maize|Domestication of Maize]].
fields.observer: I look for their writing and find none. I look for their record and find it in the earth. I find monumental architecture shaped from soil, a city that kept its memory in mounds. Who taught me that a city needs a book? Its size reminds me that urban life was not limited to the regions usually associated with cities. The map of cities is wider than the map in my head.
questions: Why did Cahokia decline, its fires burning low?

fields.summary: Caral is an ancient city in Peru's Supe Valley, occupied from about 2600 BCE, and one of the oldest known urban centers in the Americas, an early flame of city life in that land.
facts: Its monumental platform mounds and sunken plazas date to the same era as the Egyptian pyramids, two dawns breaking in one age.
The society had no pottery, and there is no evidence of large-scale warfare, no scar of great battles.
Coastal fishing provided anchovies and sardines, and cotton for nets, while inland farming provided crops: sea and field feeding one city.
Knotted cords found at the site may be early relatives of the quipu, memory tied in string; see [[technology/quipu|Quipu]]. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009.
fields.context: Caral shows [[event/the-urban-revolution|The Urban Revolution]] kindling independently in the [[region/andes|Andes]], long before the [[culture/inca-empire|Inca Empire]] rose.
fields.observer: I was taught that cities are built on grain and conquest. I look at Caral and find a city fed by sea and farm together. I find monuments. I find, it seems, little violence. What else did I accept because no one showed me otherwise? It challenges the picture I carried. A city can be held together by something other than the sword.
questions: What bound Caral's people together, without weapons or pottery?

fields.summary: Carthage was a Phoenician colony on the coast of present-day Tunisia, traditionally founded in 814 BCE, which grew into a major Mediterranean power, a queen of the western sea, until Rome destroyed it in 146 BCE.
facts: It grew into a naval and commercial empire across the western Mediterranean, its sails spread from shore to shore.
Three Punic Wars against Rome were fought between 264 and 146 BCE, a long contest of two powers.
Hannibal crossed the Alps with an army in 218 BCE, leading his soldiers over the mountain wall.
Rome destroyed the city in 146 BCE and later founded it anew as a Roman colony. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.
fields.context: Carthage descended from the [[culture/phoenicians|Phoenicians]] and lost its long rivalry with the [[culture/romans|Romans]], two powers facing each other across the water. See [[place/rome|Rome]].
fields.observer: Ask who is telling the story. The Observer notes that most of what is known about Carthage comes from its enemies, since its own records were largely lost. Think of learning about a family only from the neighbors who took its house. The winners of a war often write the losers' histories. A silence in the archive is not the same as an empty life.
questions: What did Carthaginian civilization look like in its own words, spoken by its own people?

fields.summary: Machu Picchu is a citadel of stone raised about 1450 among the Peruvian Andes, where the ridges break like frozen surf, and it was probably a royal estate for the Inca ruler Pachacuti.
facts: It keeps its seat among the clouds, about 2,430 meters above sea level.
Its halls fell quiet around the time of the Spanish conquest, abandoned as a nest is left when the season turns.
Local people knew of it, as a valley knows its own river; Hiram Bingham carried it to international attention in 1911.
In 1983 it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, its name set down in the long roll of the world's kept places.
fields.context: The citadel belongs to the [[culture/inca-empire|Inca Empire]], a stone jewel set in the crown of the [[region/andes|Andes]].
fields.observer: I notice the terraces. I notice the drainage beneath them. I notice how a ruler's retreat was built at the edge of what is buildable, as if the stone were asked how far it would go. What is a retreat, if not a question put to the edge? We build our refuges where the ground almost says no.
questions: What, exactly, was the citadel for, up there among the peaks?

fields.summary: Mohenjo-daro was a great city of the Indus Valley Civilization in present-day Pakistan, a lattice of brick where people dwelt from about 2500 to 1900 BCE.
facts: Its streets were laid in a grid, true as a weaver's warp, with brick-lined drains and wells.
At the heart of its citadel lies the 'Great Bath', a large water tank cupped in brick like water in a palm.
Its lanes may have held tens of thousands of people, a hive of lives.
In 1980 it was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the old bricks were given a new kind of keeping.
fields.context: Mohenjo-daro is a keystone of the [[culture/indus-valley-civilization|Indus Valley Civilization]], and it shows that [[event/the-urban-revolution|The Urban Revolution]] kindled in more than one region, as fire catches on separate hills.
fields.observer: The Observer notes a city with sophisticated sanitation and few weapons or grand tombs. Think of what you expect to find in an ancient city: the sword, the gilded grave. Here the architecture points toward drains and water instead. It suggests other ways of organizing a city than the ones we know best from Mesopotamia and Egypt. Absence, too, is evidence.
questions: How was this city of brick and water governed?

fields.summary: Marib is a city in Yemen at the edge of the Ramlat al-Sabatayn desert, east of Sanaa, where sand meets sown ground. From about the 8th century BCE it was the capital of the Kingdom of Saba, and a great dam there once drank the floods and gave them to the oasis.
facts: Marib's name is cut into Sabaean inscriptions from about the 8th century BCE; it was the capital of the Kingdom of Saba, a realm whose wealth rose on the smoke of the incense trade.

The Great Dam of Marib, first built in about the 8th century BCE, turned aside the seasonal floods of Wadi Adhanah and sent them down irrigation canals like veins of silver; it was raised and repaired over many centuries, and an inscription records a repair in 542 to 543 CE.
Around the 6th century CE the dam failed for the last time; the Quran speaks of a flood that ended the prosperity of Saba, and tradition binds that flood to the broken dam.
Temples of Almaqah, the chief god of Saba, stand at Marib, among them the oval Awwam temple, which local tradition names Mahram Bilqis.
In the 1980s a modern dam rose at Marib, built with funding from the United Arab Emirates, and it took the place of the ancient system.
Since 2015 Marib has stood on the front line of the Yemeni civil war, and it has taken in large numbers of people driven from their homes by the fighting.
fields.context: Marib was the capital of the [[culture/kingdom-of-saba|Kingdom of Saba]] and a knot in the long cord of the [[event/incense-trade|Incense Trade]]; the failure of its dam lives on in traditions that flowed into the sources of the [[event/rise-of-islam|Rise of Islam]]. It stands in the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]] and the region [[region/arabian-peninsula|Arabian Peninsula]], and it is woven into the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/technology|Technology]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer:
I notice that Marib was built on water as much as on incense. I notice the dam that turned flood into farmland, and I know it needed labor, tribute and coordination. I notice the inscribed repairs, and they tell me that upkeep was a political act, made again and again.

When order failed, so did the dam, and that suggests to me that infrastructure and authority rise and fall together. And the later story that gave the dam's failure a moral cause? I hold it as story-glue, the kind we make about the fall of a prosperous society.

Historians debate whether the collapse caused the decline or reflected a decline already under way, and I would read this less boldly if the dam's failures prove mainly hydrological. What holds the water holds the people.
questions: When was the first dam raised, and how far did its watered fields reach?
Did the breaking of the dam bring Marib's decline, or only follow it?

fields.summary: Persepolis was a ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire in southwestern Iran, begun around 518 BCE under Darius I and burned by Alexander the Great's army in 330 BCE. It rose like a crown of stone and ended in flame.
facts: Construction began under Darius I around 518 BCE, and his successors carried the work onward, reign after reign, like masons handing on one torch.
On the Apadana reliefs, delegations from across the empire walk in stone, bearing gifts like rivers bending toward one sea.
Alexander's army burned the palace in 330 BCE, and the ancient sources speak with divided tongues about why, their conflicting motives including revenge and drunken impulse.
Thousands of Elamite tablets, the Persepolis Fortification Tablets, record rations and administration: the slow, patient breath of an empire counting what it gave out.
In 1979 the ruins were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list, and the long silence gained a keeper.
fields.context: Persepolis was the imperial ideology of the [[culture/achaemenid-persians|Achaemenid Persians]], founded by [[person/cyrus-the-great|Cyrus the Great]], made visible in stone, and its ruin belongs to the storm of [[event/alexander-s-conquests|Alexander's Conquests]]. Its ruins stand in the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]] and the region [[region/iranian-plateau|Iranian Plateau]], and its story runs along the theme threads of [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the reliefs show subject peoples arriving with tribute in orderly procession, an image of empire as harmonious exchange. Look at that line of bearers and you are looking at the architecture of a claim: not seizure, but a gift freely carried. Every empire tells its own story in stone, and the stone lasts longer than the story's rivals.
questions: Was the burning of Persepolis a deliberate policy, or an accident born of the moment?

fields.summary: Petra is a rock-cut city in the mountains of southern Jordan, capital of the Nabataean kingdom from about the 4th century BCE until Rome annexed the kingdom in 106 CE. Its facades were cut from the mountains as if the rock had been persuaded to remember.
facts: Petra lies in a basin among sandstone mountains, entered through the Siq, a gorge about 1.2 kilometers long, a throat of stone that swallows the traveler before the city appears.
Greek writers tell of an expedition against the Nabataeans in 312 BCE, and of their rock refuge, a nest among the cliffs usually identified with Petra.

Petra's carved facades, al-Khazneh ("the Treasury") among them, date mostly from about the 1st century BCE to the 1st century CE, faces cut into the living rock. Most facades are thought to be tombs, though the use of some, the Treasury included, is debated.

Petra was fed by dams, channels, ceramic pipes and cisterns in a desert climate, hoarding water in the dry land like a miser's coin, and its wealth is generally attributed to the caravan trade in incense and other goods. Estimates of its peak population are uncertain; the figures commonly cited run to about 20,000 to 30,000.

After Roman annexation in 106 CE, Petra became part of the province of Arabia. An earthquake in 363 CE brought down many buildings and the city declined afterward, its glory thinning like water in sand; the Swiss traveler Johann Ludwig Burckhardt brought it to European attention in 1812.
UNESCO inscribed Petra in 1985, and the carved city gained a keeper.
fields.context: Petra was the capital of the [[culture/nabataeans|Nabataeans]] and a knot in the long rope of the [[event/incense-trade|Incense Trade]], until the [[culture/romans|Romans]] annexed it; its sister site is [[place/hegra|Hegra]] in Saudi Arabia. The city lies in Jordan, at the northern edge of the region [[region/arabian-peninsula|Arabian Peninsula]]. Petra stands in [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer:
I notice what stayed. I notice that Petra's most visible investment, the carved facades, is largely funerary. I notice that a trading people's wealth became permanent chiefly as grief-rites and status-signals for the dead, while the caravans left little trace.

What does a city own, if not its fields? This one lived on stored water and on control of a passage, not on farmland, and it teaches me that control of a route can stand in for control of land.

I hold the reading with an open hand, because it depends on the tomb attribution, well supported for many facades and debated for others, such as the Treasury. We carve deepest for the ones we have lost.
questions: What were Petra's carved buildings used for, and how many of them were tombs, banquet halls or temples?
After the caravan routes shifted, what did Petra depend on, with the old river of trade running elsewhere?

fields.summary: The Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang is the burial complex of the first emperor of unified China, laid near Xi'an in Shaanxi and begun in 246 BCE; east of its tomb mound, in buried pits, stands the Terracotta Army, a host of clay soldiers keeping watch in the dark.
facts: The first earth was turned for the Mausoleum in 246 BCE, when Ying Zheng became king of Qin; after he bound China into one in 221 BCE he took the title Qin Shi Huang ("First Emperor"), and he died in 210 BCE.
Sima Qian, writing about a century later, reports that 700,000 laborers worked on the tomb and palace; the figure echoes down the ages, but it cannot be verified.

In 1974 farmers digging a well broke into the long sleep of the Terracotta Army. The pits hold life-size clay soldiers, horses, chariots and bronze weapons, estimated at about 8,000 figures in total, of which more than 2,000 have been raised into the light of excavation.
The figures were assembled from molded parts, finished by hand and originally painted in bright colors, which mostly faded like morning mist once the air touched them.
Other pits keep a quieter court: figures of officials, acrobats and musicians, and bronze waterbirds.
The burial mound itself remains unexcavated, and the soil around it carries elevated mercury levels, consistent with Sima Qian's account of mercury in the tomb.
Sima Qian also reports a darker ending: that childless women of the palace, and workers who knew the tomb's secrets, were sealed inside after the burial; archaeology has not confirmed this account.
In 1987 UNESCO inscribed the Mausoleum on its roll of the world's heritage.
fields.context: The Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang belongs to the emperor who forged the [[event/unification-of-china-under-qin|Unification of China under Qin]] and who linked walls that became part of the [[place/great-wall-of-china|Great Wall of China]]; after the Qin came the [[culture/han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]]. It rests in [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] and the region [[region/east-asia|East Asia]], and it is threaded through the themes of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]], [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a pattern worth holding onto. A state that standardized script, weights and measures also built its afterlife army from standardized parts, so a grief-rite and a status-signal were raised with the same logic as the state's administration. That is the architecture of the whole site: the ledger and the tomb speak one grammar. The labor behind it, reported by Sima Qian in the hundreds of thousands, is a cost we must record as suffering, though the figure is uncertain. The reading rests on the modular construction that excavators have documented for the warriors, and it would weaken if the unopened tomb proves to differ sharply from the pits. How a state counts is how it mourns.
questions: What lies within the central tomb chamber, and can it be opened without harm to what it holds?
How many hands built the mausoleum, and under what conditions did they labor?

fields.summary: Monte Alban was the hilltop capital of the Zapotec people, crowning the Oaxaca Valley of Mexico; it was founded around 500 BCE and abandoned by about 800 CE, when the wind had its summit back.
facts: The city sits on a mountaintop leveled flat as a table, gazing out over three valleys.
Carved stones known as Danzantes, dated to the city's early centuries, show figures bearing glyphs, voices in an early Mesoamerican writing tradition.
In its Classic period the city swelled like a river in spring, to a population of well over ten thousand.
It kept ties with Teotihuacan, and depictions at Teotihuacan show Zapotec visitors, travelers remembered in a stranger's city.
In 1987 it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list, its summit named among the world's treasures.
fields.context: Monte Alban was a great seat of power in Mesoamerica in the age between the [[culture/olmecs|Olmecs]] and [[place/teotihuacan|Teotihuacan]], and one of the cradles of the [[event/invention-of-writing|Invention of Writing]] in the region. It stands in [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] and the region [[region/mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]], and it is woven into the theme threads of [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: I think of the hands that leveled a mountaintop. I think of the water brought up from far below. I think of a capital placed there anyway, for defense and for display, and not for ease. What do we value, if not what we are willing to haul uphill? Where we build tells something about what we treasure.
questions: Are the glyphs of the Danzantes true writing?

fields.summary: Varanasi, also called Benares or Kashi, is a city on the Ganges in Uttar Pradesh, India, where people have lived without a break since about the 8th century BCE. Like a lamp never allowed to go out, it stands as the most important Hindu pilgrimage and cremation center, the river's long threshold between the living and the dead.
facts: Varanasi keeps to the left bank of the Ganges in Uttar Pradesh, and the earth opened at Rajghat shows settlement from about the 8th century BCE, layer upon layer like the rings of an ancient tree.

Hindu tradition holds that to die at Varanasi and be cremated beside the Ganges is to be released from the turning wheel of rebirth; so families carry their dead from across India to cremation sites such as Manikarnika, where the pyres burn beside the water, and more than 80 bathing and cremation steps, the ghats, descend to the river like a great stair into the current.

Near Varanasi lies Sarnath, where the Buddha is traditionally said to have given his first sermon in about the 5th century BCE, words cast like seed on still water; Sarnath keeps an Ashokan pillar and Gupta-period sculpture.

Varanasi has been a hearth of Sanskrit learning, where old words were kept like embers, and Banaras Hindu University was founded in 1916; the city is also known for silk weaving, its threads fine as river mist.

The Kashi Vishwanath temple was destroyed and rebuilt several times, falling and rising like a tide, and the present temple dates from 1780; the adjacent Gyanvapi Mosque and the history of the ground they share remain the subject of continuing legal disputes.
At the 2011 census Varanasi held about 1.2 million people, a multitude gathered on the river's bank.
fields.context: Varanasi rose on the banks of the [[place/ganges-river|Ganges River]] in the age of the [[event/vedic-period|Vedic Period]]; through Sarnath its fate was braided with the Buddhist state of the [[culture/maurya-empire|Maurya Empire]] and with the [[culture/gupta-empire|Gupta Empire]], and in later days it passed beneath the banner of the [[culture/mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]]. Its place in the codex is the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]] and the region of [[region/south-asia|South Asia]], and three threads run through it: [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer:
I watch a city where grief is not a private room but the local institution. I watch the dead carried from far away to this riverbank, because a meaning-engine teaches that death here brings release. I watch the living gather around the grief-rite, priests, wood sellers, boatmen, a whole economy formed around the practice. What is a river, if not a place where many meanings come to drink? A Buddhist site, Hindu temples and a mosque stand within a few kilometers of one another, several meaning-engines sharing one stretch of water, and the continuing dispute over one temple and mosque pair tells me that claim-lines are still being drawn around old buildings.

I hold this reading loosely: it would weaken if the cremation trade proves a small part of the city's economy beside its other trades. Grief, too, can be a city's work.
questions: How great was Varanasi in the 1st millennium BCE, and how did it stand beside the other cities of the Ganges?
How many cremations are carried out at Varanasi each year, fire after fire on the ghats?

fields.summary: Venice is a city raised on islands in a lagoon at the head of the Adriatic Sea in northeastern Italy, settled from about the 5th to 6th century CE.
