As an independent republic until 1797 it was a leading maritime and trading power of the Mediterranean, a city that drew its fortune from the tides.
facts: Tradition sets the founding of Venice on its lagoon islands on 25 March 421, a date held like a lantern in fog, for no surviving records deal with it directly; the chronicle's start date of 500 is only a round placeholder for settlement in the 5th to 6th centuries.

Under Byzantine authority in name only, Venice came to govern itself under elected doges, whose line tradition dates from 697 and historians from the early 8th century; about 810 the ducal seat moved to the Rialto, like a hearth carried to a new house.

In 1204 a Crusade fleet supplied by Venice under Doge Enrico Dandolo sacked Constantinople, and Venice took a large share of the Byzantine lands, Crete among them; but what the sea gives, the sea takes back, and wars with the Ottoman Empire later cost it Negroponte (1470), Cyprus (1570 to 1573) and Crete (1669).

Against the plague Venice raised walls of water: in 1423 it opened a plague hospital on the island of Santa Maria di Nazareth, regarded as the first permanent lazaretto, and in 1468 a second, Lazzaretto Nuovo; its isolation of arriving people and goods became an early model of quarantine.
In 1516 the Republic required its Jewish residents to live within an enclosed district called the Ghetto, and the name of that confinement later travelled to other cities.
On 12 May 1797, as French forces drew near, the Great Council voted to end the Republic; under the Treaty of Campo Formio Venice passed to Austria, and in 1866 it joined the Kingdom of Italy.

UNESCO inscribed Venice and its Lagoon in 1987; yet the historic center's people ebbed like a falling tide, from about 175,000 in the 1950s to under 50,000, and in October 2020 the MOSE flood barriers first rose against the sea.
fields.context: Venice was first a partner and then a rival of [[place/constantinople|Constantinople]]; it sailed into the [[event/crusades|Crusades]], and after the [[event/fall-of-constantinople|Fall of Constantinople]] in 1453 it lost ground to the Ottomans, as a shore loses sand to a stronger current. Its lazaretto system came in the wake of the [[event/black-death|Black Death]], its painting and printing belong to the [[event/renaissance|Renaissance]], and the Republic's long day ended during the [[event/napoleonic-wars|Napoleonic Wars]]. In the codex Venice stands in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region of the [[region/mediterranean-basin|Mediterranean Basin]], and three threads are woven through it: [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: Consider a state with almost no land of its own. Where does it find the glue that holds its story together? Venice, the Observer notes, made its story-glue from the sea: elected doges, councils that limited any one family, and a yearly ceremony in which the doge symbolically wed the Adriatic. That is an architecture of belonging built on water. But a port lives on strangers and cargo, and here the ledger turns darker. The same administration that built the lazaretto also enclosed the Jewish district in 1516; a system built to manage risk also confined people, and the Observer records that as a harm to those held. Notice how easily the grammar of protection becomes the grammar of the wall. The reading would weaken if Venice's institutions differed little from those of other Italian maritime republics such as Genoa. What we build to keep danger out can also keep people in.
questions: How many souls did Venice lose to the plague outbreaks of 1348 and of 1575 to 1577?
As sea level rises and the MOSE barriers age, can the lagoon city stay habitable, and stay a place where people live?

fields.summary: Mecca is a city in the Hejaz region of western Saudi Arabia, about 70 kilometers inland from the Red Sea; it is the birthplace of Muhammad and the holiest city of Islam, and its sanctuary around the Kaaba draws the annual Hajj pilgrimage the way a basin gathers every stream.
facts: The date of Mecca's first settlement is unknown, lost like footprints under drifting sand, and whether it is the place Macoraba in Ptolemy's 2nd-century geography is disputed. Muslim sources written after Muhammad's time describe a sanctuary town governed by the Quraysh in the century before Islam.
Islamic tradition places Muhammad's birth in Mecca about 570 CE, his journey to Medina in 622, and the city's passing under Muslim control in 630, with little fighting.

The Hajj is one of the Five Pillars of Islam, required once in a lifetime of every Muslim able to make the journey; in recent decades Saudi authorities have reported attendance in the low millions each year, a tide that returns with the turning year.
Historians disagree about Mecca's weight in long-distance trade before Islam; some see a regional sanctuary and market town, not a hub where the incense and spice trades converged.
Mecca was ruled locally by the Sharifs beneath a succession of overlords, the Ottomans among them from 1517, until the Saudi conquest of 1924 to 1925. Non-Muslims are barred from entering the city.
During the 2015 Hajj, in the crush at Mina near Mecca, the Saudi authorities reported 769 deaths, while counts compiled from other governments' figures exceeded 2,000.
fields.context: Mecca is the central place of the [[event/rise-of-islam|Rise of Islam]], joined by the Hijra to [[place/medina|Medina]], and a waystation in the peninsula's wider [[event/incense-trade|Incense Trade]] setting. It passed under the [[culture/umayyad-caliphate|Umayyad Caliphate]] and later the [[culture/ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]], and pilgrims came from far horizons, among them the ruler of the [[culture/mali-empire|Mali Empire]], Mansa Musa, who made the Hajj in 1324. Mecca stands in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/arabian-peninsula|Arabian Peninsula]], and it is woven into the theme threads of [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]].
fields.observer:
I see a meaning-engine drawing millions of strangers to one point each year. I see a recurring exchange-web of people, goods and news that reached from West Africa to Southeast Asia. I see pilgrims in plain white garments, for men two unstitched cloths, so that the visible marks of rank grow faint during the rites.

But I remember that pilgrims themselves describe the journey as obedience and devotion, and my reading of its social effects is meant to sit beside their account, not replace it. I remember Mina in 2015, and the crowd disasters that recur as a cost of gathering at this scale; I record them as suffering.

My reading would weaken if pilgrim networks turn out to have carried little trade or news beside their devotional purpose. What gathers us is not always what we carry home.
questions: What does archaeology reveal about pre-Islamic Mecca, when so little excavation has been done in the sacred precinct?
How great a part did Mecca play in long-distance trade before Islam?

fields.summary: Monte Verde is an archaeological site in southern Chile that, for decades, was considered the best evidence that people lived in South America about 14,500 years ago, before the Clovis culture of North America kindled its fires; now its age is debated, and the old certainty has thinned to mist.
facts: From the 1970s, excavations led by Tom Dillehay laid bare what a peat bog had kept like a miser: wooden hut foundations, leather, rope, and plant remains.
In 1997 a panel of archaeologists came to inspect the site and accepted an age of about 14,500 years.
The site helped topple the 'Clovis-first' model like an old stone from its plinth; see [[event/peopling-of-the-americas|Peopling of the Americas]].
A recent study has proposed a much younger age for the site; specialists dispute it, and the question stands unsettled, a scale still swinging.
fields.context: Monte Verde is a keystone site for the [[event/peopling-of-the-americas|Peopling of the Americas]], dating from the end of the [[event/last-glacial-maximum|Last Glacial Maximum]], when the ice was loosening its grip.
fields.observer: I know how a site's importance can outrun its certainty. I know how a single set of dates can hold up a large theory. I know the theory is only as strong as the dates. What are we standing on, when we stand on a number? Every tower leans on its lowest stone.
questions: How old, truly, is Monte Verde?

fields.summary: Pompeii was a Roman town on the Bay of Naples in Italy, founded in about the 7th century BCE and buried under volcanic ash and pumice when Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE. A town. A mountain. Then the grey.
facts: Pompeii was founded in about the 7th century BCE by the Oscans. Then Greek influence. Then Etruscan. Then, in 80 BCE, a Roman colony.
An earthquake in 62 or 63 CE damaged the town. Repairs were still under way when Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE. The mending was not done. Then the mountain.
Population: about 11,000, by estimate. The estimates range from about 10,000 to 20,000. That many people. One town.

The eruption buried Pompeii. Pumice and ash, over everything. Then the pyroclastic surges, which killed the people who had stayed. About 1,100 bodies have been found in the excavated town. Many inhabitants are thought to have fled.
The traditional date of the eruption is 24 August. But a charcoal inscription, found in 2018, suggests a later date. Possibly October.

Excavations began in 1748. In 1863 Giuseppe Fiorelli began pouring plaster into the voids left by decayed bodies, to produce casts of victims. Voids. Filled. And on the walls, graffiti, shop signs and election notices survive. The town keeps talking.
In 1997 UNESCO inscribed the archaeological areas of Pompeii, Herculaneum and Torre Annunziata. Three names on one list.
fields.context: Pompeii was a town of the [[culture/romans|Romans]], part of the wider world governed from [[place/rome|Rome]]. Its Oscan foundation sets it in the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]]. Its region: the [[region/mediterranean-basin|Mediterranean Basin]]. Its threads: [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]], [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]]. A town like any other. Then not.
fields.observer:
I read the walls and find the ordinary. Shop signs. Graffiti. Bakeries. Casts. I see a case where a natural catastrophe left an unusually complete record of ordinary life, an unintended act of memory-outsourcing that no one planned.

I remember that they were people. I remember that their deaths were suffering, and I record them as suffering and as nothing else. I ask how the casts of victims should be shown, and the question stays with me.

And I remind myself that this record leans toward one town on one day, and toward what was left behind. If new counts show that the number of people who died was much smaller or larger than the current figures suggest, my reading weakens. What we inherit is never the whole of what was lost.
questions: How many people died at Pompeii, and how many escaped the grey?
On what day, in 79 CE, did Vesuvius erupt?

fields.summary: Port Royal was an English port town at the tip of the Palisadoes spit, at the entrance to Kingston Harbour, Jamaica. It grew after 1655 as a base for privateers and traders, and on 7 June 1692 an earthquake took about two-thirds of its area, as if the sea had opened its mouth.
facts: England took Jamaica from Spain in 1655, and Port Royal was fortified from 1656; English governors issued commissions to privateers, who flew from the port like hawks from the fist to strike Spanish ships and towns.
Henry Morgan, a privateer who later rose to lieutenant governor of Jamaica, led raids from the colony, among them the sack of Panama in 1671.
Port Royal was a trading port for the island's goods and a place where enslaved Africans were landed and sold; in 1692 it held about 6,500 residents.

On 7 June 1692 an earthquake struck, the sandy ground beneath the town turned to liquid, and about two-thirds of Port Royal sank into the harbor like a ship going down. About 2,000 people are estimated to have died in the quake and its immediate aftermath, and several thousand more died of injury and disease in the following weeks.
Some contemporary accounts read the earthquake as divine judgment, the sea's blow as a verdict from above.
Survivors founded Kingston across the harbor; a fire in 1703 consumed much of what remained of Port Royal, and the Royal Navy kept the town as a base into the early 20th century.
Underwater archaeology, from the 1950s and again from the 1980s, has recovered buildings and household objects from the drowned ground, the town's lost rooms read again beneath the water.
fields.context: Port Royal grew as the English Caribbean took shape, a new tide running in after the Spanish colony at [[place/santo-domingo|Santo Domingo]] had already set the pattern of European settlement, and its trade touched the [[event/atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic Slave Trade]] and the [[event/sugar-plantation-complex|Sugar Plantation Complex]]. It stands in the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region [[region/caribbean-and-atlantic-world|Caribbean and Atlantic World]], and its story runs along the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer:
The Observer notes a port whose wealth came from state-licensed raiding and from trade that included the sale of enslaved people, and whose sudden loss some contemporaries explained, through their own meaning-engine, as divine judgment. Notice the architecture of that response: when catastrophe arrives, we reach for a doctrine that makes it mean something.

The sinking also froze a working town's daily life in place, an unusual case in which a disaster acts as memory-outsourcing for people who left few documents. The ground kept the ledger they did not.

The popular image of Port Royal as uniquely lawless is a later story-glue, and how far the record supports it is debated. A historian could challenge the first sentence by showing that privateering brought the town less wealth than ordinary trade did. Hold the legend lightly and the ledger closely.
questions: How much of Port Royal's wealth came from privateering, how much from ordinary trade, and how much from the sale of enslaved people?
How much of the drowned town remains to be recorded?

fields.summary: The Xingu garden cities are pre-Columbian settlements in the upper Xingu region of Brazil, dating from about 1200 to 1600 CE. Their plazas, roads and ditches, a pattern written into the land like veins in a leaf, were mapped by the anthropologist Michael Heckenberger with the Kuikuro people.
facts: Researchers documented about 28 towns, villages and hamlets, strung like beads on a cord, which may have supported up to about 50,000 people.
The larger towns had ditches about 3 meters deep and 10 meters wide, plazas up to 150 meters across, and roads aligned with the summer solstice, straight as sunlight on the longest day.
Around them the fields grew manioc, and earthen dams and ponds held the water where fish were farmed, silver in the brown shallows.
Population estimates are debated, but the tale has no empty ending: the descendants of the builders still live in the region.
fields.context: Their tale is bound to [[event/amazonian-urbanism-and-dark-earths|Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths]]. After 1500 the settlements declined, as epidemics followed in the wake of the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]].
fields.observer: I notice who held the other end of the measuring line: the research was done together with the Kuikuro, whose descendants still live in the region. I remember that a ruin is not always an orphan. I remember that the living keep what the soil forgets. Who taught whom? Living communities and archaeologists can inform each other.
questions: How many people lived in the Xingu network when it stood at its height?

fields.summary: The Yellow River (Huang He) is a river of northern China, about 5,460 kilometers long, whose loess-laden floodplain cradled early farming and the Shang and Zhou states. Its floods and its wandering course have shaped Chinese history the way a restless hand shapes clay.
facts: The Yellow River is born in the Bayan Har Mountains of Qinghai and runs the long road through northern China until it gives itself to the Bohai Sea.

From about the 7th to 6th millennia BCE, farming communities growing millet are documented in the Yellow River basin, their fields golden along the water, and in its middle and lower reaches the Shang and Zhou states arose.

The Yellow River bears a heavy burden of loess sediment from the Loess Plateau, and that yellow freight has lifted its bed above the surrounding plain in the lower reaches, so that it must be held in by dikes like a beast on a high ledge; records list many breaches and several major changes of course.
From 1194 until 1855 the river mostly ran south of the Shandong Peninsula into the Yellow Sea, until a breach in 1855 turned it back to a northern course, as a sleeper turns in the night.
In 1887 the river rose in flood, and that flood is estimated to have killed between about 900,000 and 2 million people.

In 1938, during the Second Sino-Japanese War, Nationalist forces breached the dikes at Huayuankou to slow the Japanese advance; several hundred thousand people died, with published estimates up to about 900,000, and millions were displaced.
fields.context: The Yellow River runs through [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]] in northern China; through the [[culture/shang-dynasty|Shang Dynasty]] and the [[culture/han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]], states that organized flood control; and through the [[event/second-sino-japanese-war|Second Sino-Japanese War]]. In the codex it belongs to the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]] and the region of [[region/east-asia|East Asia]], and three threads are spun from its waters: [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer: Think of a river that floods without warning. Whoever can hold it back holds more than water, and the Observer notes that the Yellow River helped tie authority to water control. The traditional story of Yu the Great, who is said to have tamed the floods and founded the first dynasty, is the story-glue here: a covenant joining rule to engineering. Then the ledger's darker page. The 1938 breach shows the same river used as sanctioned harm by a state against an invading army, and its main victims were civilians. Notice, too, that the image of the Yellow River as the sole cradle of Chinese civilization is itself a story, since sites on the Yangtze and elsewhere also show early farming and state formation. Hold all of this with care. The hypothesis that flood control drove state formation is contested, and specialists could weaken this reading by showing that other factors mattered more. A single river rarely writes a whole civilization.
questions: How many died in the 1938 flood, and how many people were displaced from their homes?
Weighed against warfare and trade, how much did flood control contribute to early state formation?

fields.summary: Çatalhöyük was a large Neolithic settlement in central Turkey, occupied from about 7100 to 5700 BCE, its houses packed together like the cells of a honeycomb and entered from the roof.
facts: At its height it held several thousand people, a hive of lives under one sky.
Its walls bore paintings, and the dead were laid beneath the house floors, sleeping under the feet of the living.
It had no streets: people walked across the roofs, a town whose roads were its rooftops.
In 2012 it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, an ancient hearth entered into the world's keeping.
fields.context: Çatalhöyük is a site of the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]], a hearth of that long age. Its tale runs beside [[place/gobekli-tepe|Göbekli Tepe]] and [[observer-note/the-settling-and-its-bargain|The Settling and Its Bargain]].
fields.observer: I climb down through the roof into a house that touches another house, and another. I see a society living in one dense, continuous structure, with few signs of rank. Where is the palace? Where is the higher wall? Early towns did not always show the hierarchy assumed for later cities.
questions: How equal, truly, were the people who shared its roofs?

fields.summary: Potosi is a mining city in the Bolivian Andes, founded in 1545 beside the silver mountain Cerro Rico, whose output supplied Spanish and world trade for centuries. Think of it as the place where a mountain became a ledger.
facts: Silver was discovered at Cerro Rico in 1545: the threshold from which everything else in this story follows.
By around 1600 Potosi was one of the largest cities in the Americas, with population estimates around 150,000. That is the gravity a mountain of silver could exert.
The Spanish organized labor through the mita, a forced-labor draft adapted from an Inca system. Name it plainly: the work was compelled.
The mercury amalgamation process introduced in the 1570s increased silver output: a change of technique, and the mountain gave more.
It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1987, a formal covenant of memory.
fields.context: Potosi turned the conquered [[culture/inca-empire|Inca Empire]] into a source of silver for the world economy. Follow the metal and you trace the architecture of that economy: its silver crossed the Pacific through the [[event/manila-galleon-trade|Manila Galleon Trade]], and its labor system followed the [[event/spanish-conquest-of-the-inca-empire|Spanish Conquest of the Inca Empire]]. Potosi sits in the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region [[region/andes|Andes]], and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a labor system inherited from the conquered was repurposed to extract wealth for the conquerors. Consider what that means: the same institution, its lineage intact, now pointed the other way. A mountain that fed global trade became a symbol of how far an exchange-web could stretch, and of how much suffering could sit at its origin. The longest chain of trade still begins with someone's hands.
questions: How many workers died in the mines of the silver mountain?

fields.summary: Poverty Point is a large earthwork complex in Louisiana, built by hunter-gatherer-fishers between about 1700 and 1100 BCE, its concentric ridges spreading like ripples held in earth and its huge mounds rising like the backs of sleeping beasts.
facts: The site holds six concentric earthen ridges and several mounds, the largest about 22 meters high, a hill raised by hands.
According to current evidence, it was built by a society without agriculture, a people who took their living from the river and the wild.
Stone and other materials were brought in from across the Mississippi valley, some from hundreds of kilometers away, the valley's far places flowing toward one hearth like streams.
It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2014, and the old rings entered the world's long memory.
Around 1100 BCE the site was abandoned, and the ridges were left to the silence.
fields.context: Poverty Point is the earliest of the large earthwork centers of eastern North America, the eldest of its kind, rising long before [[place/cahokia|Cahokia]] and the [[place/chaco-canyon|Chaco Canyon]] settlements. It stands in the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]] and the region [[region/north-america|North America]], and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer:
I was taught that monuments need farms. I was taught that the plow comes first and the mound after. And here is a large monumental site built by a people who did not farm, and the assumption breaks in my hands.

What else did I believe too quickly? It appears that large-scale cooperation can come from abundant wild food and shared purpose. Plenty and purpose can build as high as any harvest.
questions: What was the site used for, with its rings and its mounds?

fields.summary: Rapa Nui (Easter Island) is a remote Pacific island settled by Polynesians around 1200 CE, famous for nearly a thousand monumental stone statues called moai, a people of stone at the far end of the sea.
facts: The island lies in the southeastern Pacific, thousands of kilometers from the nearest large land, a mote of stone the ocean nearly forgot.

The settlers' landfall drifts in the record like a canoe on dim water: estimates run from as early as about 300 CE, resting on contested early radiocarbon dates, to about 1200 CE, the date favored by many recent studies.

About 400 moai (397 in one count) lie in the quarry of Rano Raraku in various stages of completion, giants half-woken from the stone, and about 95 percent of the island's monolithic statues were carved from its volcanic tuff. Published counts of the total number of moai differ.

The familiar tale of an island that felled its own forests and so undid itself is contested. Researchers point instead to introduced rats, which may have been the main cause of deforestation, and to disease and slave raids. In December 1862 Peruvian slavers captured about 1,000 islanders, and reports put the total taken in 1862 to 1864 at more than 1,400. Most of the captives died in Peru; a smallpox epidemic that followed the return of a few survivors in 1863 reportedly killed about a thousand more. These figures come from popular summaries and vary between accounts.
Rapa Nui National Park was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1995, the stone faces named a heritage of the world.
fields.context: Rapa Nui was the far eastern edge of the [[event/polynesian-settlement-of-the-pacific|Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific]] and of the [[culture/polynesians|Polynesians]]' voyaging world, where the long paths of canoes met open sea. It stands in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/oceania|Oceania]], and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer:
I was told, often, that this island was a parable. I was told its people unmade their own world. And I look at the record, and it suggests that outside pressures did much of the damage.

Why do I reach for the moral first? Because stories that fit a moral are chosen more readily than stories that fit the evidence. I would rather be told the truth than be taught a lesson.
questions: How large was the population at its peak, and what brought about its decline?

fields.summary: Medina is a city in the Hejaz region of western Saudi Arabia, known before Islam as Yathrib; Muhammad migrated there in 622 CE and is buried there, and it is the second holiest city of Islam. Here is a city whose very name marks a threshold, one name before Islam and another after it.
facts: Before Islam, Medina was an oasis settlement called Yathrib, home to Arab tribes, chiefly the Aws and Khazraj, and to Jewish tribes; its earlier history is poorly documented.
In 622 Muhammad and his followers migrated there from Mecca (the Hijra), and the Islamic calendar counts its years from that threshold; Muhammad died and was buried there in 632.
The Constitution of Medina, a document preserved in later sources, sets out a covenant of obligations among Muslim, Jewish and other groups; its date and authenticity are debated.

Traditional Islamic sources report a grave passage in the city's early years: that two Jewish tribes, Banu Qaynuqa and Banu Nadir, were expelled from Medina, and that the men of a third, Banu Qurayza, were executed in 627, with figures reported from about 400 to 900; some modern historians question details of these accounts.
Medina was the capital of the first caliphs until 656, when Ali moved to Kufa; later the Umayyad caliphs ruled from Damascus.

The Prophet's Mosque in Medina, first built in 622, was enlarged by the Umayyad caliph al-Walid I in the early 8th century and repeatedly since, an architecture that keeps growing around its origin; non-Muslims are barred from the central sanctuary area.
fields.context: Medina was the destination of the Hijra from [[place/mecca|Mecca]] and the first capital of the [[event/rise-of-islam|Rise of Islam]], before rule passed to the [[culture/umayyad-caliphate|Umayyad Caliphate]]. We find it in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/arabian-peninsula|Arabian Peninsula]], and it belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Medina is where a small community became a polity. Consider its founding document: if it is early, it tried to bind kin groups into one order, with shared rules for settling disputes. That is story-glue in the form of law, a covenant meant to make separate lineages answer to a single architecture. The same tradition records the other side of the ledger: defining who belonged also defined who did not, and the exile and killing of the tribes that fell outside are recorded here as suffering. The reading depends on the early dating of the Constitution and on the reliability of sources written generations later, and specialists debate both. Every covenant draws a line, and we owe attention to both sides of it.
questions: How early is the Constitution of Medina, and how far can we trust the later accounts that carry it to us?
What can archaeology tell us about Yathrib before 622?

fields.summary: The Mekong River is a river of Asia about 4,350 kilometers long, born on the Tibetan Plateau and running like a silver thread through China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam; its annual flood feeds rice farming and one of the world's largest inland fisheries.
facts: The Mekong rises on the Tibetan Plateau and flows through China, traces the borders of Myanmar, Laos and Thailand, and passes through Cambodia and Vietnam into the South China Sea, where it spreads its fingers into a large delta.

From about the 3rd to 2nd millennia BCE, rice-farming and fishing communities lived along the middle and lower Mekong, and from about the 1st century CE the early port of Oc Eo in the delta, part of the state called Funan, carried on its trade, a lamp lit at the river's mouth.

The Tonlé Sap, a lake in Cambodia joined to the Mekong, turns its current with the season, as if it breathed: in the wet season floodwater flows into it, in the dry season it flows back out, and a major fishery lives on that breath.
About 60 million people live in the lower basin, and the river is among the world's most productive inland fisheries, its waters thick with life.
In 1866 to 1868 a French exploration commission found that rapids made the Mekong unnavigable as a route to China, and the Mekong Delta was a major area of fighting in the Vietnam War.

Since the 1990s China has built a cascade of dams on the upper Mekong, and in 2019 Laos began operating the Xayaburi dam on the lower river; the Mekong River Commission, formed in 1995, coordinates the lower-basin countries, and what the dams do to fish, sediment and the timing of floods is debated.
fields.context: The Mekong River was the great corridor of the [[culture/khmer-empire|Khmer Empire]] and its capital [[place/angkor|Angkor]], and its delta became a theater of the [[event/cold-war|Cold War]]. Its early farming communities place it in the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]], its waters run through the region [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]], and it flows through the theme threads of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]], [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the Mekong is a river whose annual pulse feeds fish and rice for tens of millions. Now picture a dam upstream: those who control the flow can alter conditions for people downstream, across claim-lines the river itself ignores. That is the architecture of a shared river, a covenant nobody signed and everyone lives under. The reversing flow of the Tonlé Sap shows the older grammar, a natural rhythm around which a whole society organized its seasons. The reading would weaken if measurements show that the dams' net effect on downstream fish and sediment is smaller than the models suggest. A river keeps no borders; we are the ones who draw them.
questions: How far have the upstream dams altered the flood pulse, the migration of fish and the sediment of the delta?
How did early states such as Funan ride the river for trade?

fields.summary: Aboriginal Australians are the Indigenous peoples of the Australian mainland, whose ancestors arrived at least 50,000 years ago. Their cultures are among the oldest continuous living traditions, a fire carried unbroken from hand to hand across the ages.
facts: Before European colonization in 1788, more than 250 languages were spoken across the land, each a voice in a great chorus.
Knowledge travelled through oral traditions, songlines and ceremony, passed along like water in a line of cupped hands.
Groups tended the landscape with fire and sophisticated ecological knowledge, reading the land as others read a book.
The rock art of Australia includes some of the oldest known paintings, images that have kept watch on the stone through long ages.
fields.context: Their story walks beside the [[event/out-of-africa-dispersal|Out of Africa Dispersal]] and the lands of [[region/oceania|Oceania]]. Aboriginal societies show that complex culture does not require farming or cities; it can flower without the plough and without the wall.
fields.observer: I think of a coastline flooded at the end of the last ice age. I think of the accounts of it, handed from voice to voice. I think of how long a telling can last: orally preserved knowledge like this appears to have lasted for millennia. What is ink, beside a voice that will not let go? Memory-outsourcing need not use writing to be durable.
questions: How far back can oral traditions carry an event and keep it true?

fields.summary: The Achaemenid Persians built the largest empire the world had yet seen, founded by Cyrus the Great about 550 BCE and standing until Alexander's conquest in 330 BCE, a realm that spread like dawn light across the old lands.
facts: The empire stretched from Egypt and Anatolia to the Indus valley, a single mantle thrown across many lands.
It was divided into provinces called satrapies, and the Royal Road bound them together like a thread through beads.
The Cyrus Cylinder is often cited as a record of an imperial policy of tolerance toward local customs, words that still echo in the halls of memory.
Zoroastrianism held influence at the Persian court, like a flame kept near the throne.
fields.context: The empire's long day ended with [[event/alexander-s-conquests|Alexander's Conquests]]. Its story is kept beside that of the [[region/iranian-plateau|Iranian Plateau]].
fields.observer: Here is a lesson in the architecture of rule. The Observer notes an administrative style that governed diverse peoples by preserving their local institutions rather than tearing them down. Watch for it; the approach reappears repeatedly in stable empires. Leave people their own house, and they may help keep your roof standing.
questions: When the proclamations are set aside, how tolerant was the empire in practice?

fields.summary: Al-Andalus was the Muslim-ruled part of the Iberian Peninsula from 711 to 1492, a region of Muslim, Christian and Jewish communities, three streams feeding one garden, that contributed to science, architecture and literature.
facts: In 711 Muslim forces crossed from North Africa into Iberia, over the narrow water between two continents.
From 756 an Umayyad emirate, and later a caliphate, ruled from Cordoba.
Cordoba became a great lamp of learning, and its caliphal library is reputed to have held hundreds of thousands of volumes.
The Alhambra in Granada rose mainly in the 13th and 14th centuries, like a dream set down in stone.
Granada, the last Muslim kingdom, fell to Castile and Aragon in January 1492, and the long sunset of Al-Andalus was done.
fields.context: Al-Andalus grew from the root of the [[culture/umayyad-caliphate|Umayyad Caliphate]], and through it the knowledge of the [[event/translation-movement-and-the-house-of-wisdom|Translation Movement and the House of Wisdom]] flowed like a river into Latin Europe. Its end in 1492 coincided with the start of the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]], one door closing as another swung open. In the codex it stands in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region of the [[region/mediterranean-basin|Mediterranean Basin]], and its threads are [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/science|Science]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: I count what a single year held. I count Granada falling. I count the expulsion of Jews from Spain. I count Columbus setting out. How can one year carry so much ending and so much beginning? A period of pluralism closed as another began that would reshape the planet. Some doors open only as others shut.
questions: How tolerant was Al-Andalus in practice, beneath the shine of its learning?

fields.summary: The ancient Egyptians built a state along the Nile that endured, with interruptions, for about three thousand years, as steady as the river's own return, until the Roman annexation in 30 BCE.
facts: Their history is divided into kingdoms, Old, Middle and New, with intermediate periods lying between them like dim seasons between floods.
They raised pyramids and temples against the sky and developed hieroglyphic writing, words drawn as images.
Their religion looked toward the afterlife as a traveller looks toward the far shore, and the bodies of the elite were mummified.
The last pharaoh of the Ptolemaic dynasty was Cleopatra VII, the final light of a long line.
fields.context: Their tale is bound to the [[event/unification-of-egypt|Unification of Egypt]], to the [[place/giza-necropolis|Giza Necropolis]], and to the lives of [[person/hatshepsut|Hatshepsut]] and [[person/akhenaten|Akhenaten]].
fields.observer: I stand among the tombs and understand this much: here was an extraordinary investment in the dead. I see the stone. I see the craft. I see a whole culture spending lavishly on a life no one returns to describe. Would I build so much for those I have lost? Love, too, can be measured in stone. [[observer-note/why-the-species-buries-its-dead|Why the Species Buries Its Dead]] asks the older question.
questions: How many hands were needed to raise the pyramids, and how were those workers organized?

fields.summary: The ancient Greeks were a constellation of city-states around the Aegean and beyond, and their politics, philosophy and art shaped Mediterranean and later world culture as a spring shapes the valley below it.
facts: They forged citizen-based political systems, among them Athenian democracy, kindled from about 508 BCE.
Among their philosophers and scientists walked Socrates, Plato and [[person/aristotle|Aristotle]], three lamps in one window.
City-states such as Athens and Sparta fought frequently, like rival storms over one sea, and among their wars was the Peloponnesian War (431 to 404 BCE).
After [[person/alexander-the-great|Alexander the Great]] came the Hellenistic period, a long afterglow.
fields.context: Their tale runs through [[place/athens|Athens]] and out along the road of [[event/alexander-s-conquests|Alexander's Conquests]]. In the codex the Greeks belong to [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]].
fields.observer: What happens when a people decides that disagreement is not a threat but a practice? The Observer notes a culture that turned argument into an institution: public debate in assemblies, in courts and in schools. Argument, given a room, becomes architecture.
questions: Given that women, enslaved people and foreigners were shut out, how democratic was Athenian democracy?

fields.summary: Robben Island is a small island in Table Bay, about 7 kilometers off Cape Town, South Africa, best known for the political prisoners held there under apartheid, including Nelson Mandela. From the 17th century to 1996 it served as a place of banishment, a leprosy colony and a prison: an architecture of separation, built out of water.
facts: Robben Island lies in Table Bay about 7 kilometers from Cape Town and covers about 5 square kilometers; its name comes from the Dutch word for seals. Start there, with the plain geography of a small place surrounded by water.

The Dutch East India Company began using Robben Island as a place of banishment in the 1650s; among those sent there, in 1658, was the Khoikhoi interpreter Autshumato, an early name in a long ledger of exile.
A leprosy colony operated on the island from 1846 to 1931, and in the Second World War it served as a military base: the same isolation, turned to each new purpose.

From 1961 to 1996 Robben Island was a maximum-security prison where the apartheid state held political prisoners, among them Nelson Mandela (imprisoned on the island for 18 of his 27 years, from 1964), Robert Sobukwe, Walter Sisulu and Govan Mbeki.

Prisoners worked in a limestone quarry, and the glare damaged Mandela's eyes; prisoners also organized study and debate among themselves, and the prison was nicknamed a "university". Notice the practice: people held at a quarry face still made room for study.
The last political prisoners were released in 1991, and the prison itself closed only in 1996.
UNESCO inscribed Robben Island in 1999, and today former prisoners lead tours of the island: memory kept by those who carried it.
fields.context: Robben Island was first used as a place of banishment by the [[event/dutch-east-india-company|Dutch East India Company]], and its years as an apartheid prison belong to the wider struggle over minority rule in the period of [[event/decolonization|Decolonization]]. Read its history as a genealogy of confinement. It sits in the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region [[region/sub-saharan-africa|Sub-Saharan Africa]], and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer:
The Observer notes that Robben Island shows water used as a wall. For more than three centuries, authorities sent the people they wanted removed from society, exiles, patients and dissidents, to a place where isolation was cheap to enforce. That is the architecture of the island: not stone, but distance.

Yet the same isolation concentrated a generation of leaders who studied and argued together, so the prison also worked as a school and an exchange-web of ideas, an outcome its designers did not intend. The Observer records the years of imprisonment and forced labor as suffering, and does not let the school erase the cell.

The reading would weaken if accounts of prisoners' study and organization describe only a small, unrepresentative part of the prison population. What confinement gathers, it cannot always control.
questions: How did prisoners on Robben Island organize themselves, and how far did that organization reach beyond the water?
How should the island tell its earlier chapters, such as the leprosy colony and the exile of Khoikhoi leaders?

fields.summary: The Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela are eleven churches carved down into volcanic rock in the highlands of northern Ethiopia, traditionally attributed to King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty in the early 13th century. They were drawn out of the earth like water from a well, and worship still fills them.
facts: Lalibela lies at about 2,500 meters in the Amhara Region of Ethiopia, high as a hawk's road, and holds eleven monolithic churches in two main groups, with one cross-shaped church, Bete Giyorgis, standing apart.

Tradition names King Lalibela, who reigned around the late 12th and early 13th centuries, as their maker; some scholars propose that some churches are older, their roots running deeper than the king's name.

Builders first cut trenches into the rock, then carved the exterior and interior of each church from the block left standing, as a sculptor frees a figure from the stone; trenches and tunnels joined the churches, and drainage channels were cut to carry water away.

In tradition Lalibela is a "New Jerusalem", a distant holy city mirrored in the highlands like a face in still water, with features named after places in the Holy Land, such as a stream called the Jordan; the link with the loss of Jerusalem to Saladin in 1187 is traditional and is not documented in contemporary sources.
The churches remain in active use, and at major festivals large numbers of pilgrims come, like a tide rising to the stone.
UNESCO inscribed the Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela in 1978, and the carved sanctuaries were named among the world's heritage.
fields.context: The Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela were built under the [[culture/zagwe-dynasty|Zagwe Dynasty]], in a land shaped earlier by the [[culture/kingdom-of-aksum|Kingdom of Aksum]] and its town [[place/aksum|Aksum]], and the "New Jerusalem" tradition binds them to the age of the [[event/crusades|Crusades]]. They stand in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/sub-saharan-africa|Sub-Saharan Africa]], and belong to the theme threads of [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer:
I think about removal. I think about workers who did not add rock but took it away, cutting free-standing churches down into the ground, a labor-heavy technique that also makes the buildings hard to destroy. I think about how making can look like subtraction.

And I think about longing. The "New Jerusalem" tradition shows a place made to stand in for a distant sacred site when access to the original was in doubt, a meaning-engine adjusting to political change. Have I not done the same, and built a near thing to hold a far one?

But the link to 1187 is not documented in contemporary sources, and if the churches prove to have been planned around a different rationale, my reading weakens. What we cannot reach, we sometimes build.
questions: Which of the churches were cut in the reign of Lalibela, and which are earlier or later?
How many workers were involved, and how long did the rock take to yield its churches?

fields.summary: Merv was a great oasis city on the Silk Roads, in what is now Turkmenistan, a green jewel held in turn by many hands: a city of the Achaemenid Persians, a capital of the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun and of the Seljuk sultans, and then sacked by the Mongols in 1221.
facts: Merv lies in the Murghab delta oasis near the modern city of Mary; Bronze Age towns of the region, such as Gonur Depe, rose about 2000 BCE, and the walled city of Erk Kala dates from the Achaemenid period, from about the 6th century BCE.
Arab forces took Merv in 651, after the last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, the final ember of his house, was killed near it.
From Merv, in 747, Abu Muslim loosed the Abbasid Revolution like water from a breached dam, and the caliph al-Ma'mun ruled from Merv from about 813 to 818 before moving to Baghdad.

Merv was a Seljuk capital, above all under Sultan Sanjar (reigned 1118 to 1157), whose mausoleum still stands, and some estimates suggest that in the 12th century it was among the largest cities in the world.
The geographer Yaqut, who came in 1219, described its libraries, shelves of stored light.

In 1221 the Mongol army took Merv. Persian chronicles report hundreds of thousands to over a million killed; modern historians regard these figures as greatly exaggerated, but they reflect a severe massacre and destruction.
In the 15th century Merv was rebuilt on a smaller scale, a lesser flame on the old hearth, and in the late 18th century it was finally abandoned.
In 1999 UNESCO inscribed Ancient Merv, and the old oasis passed into the world's keeping.
fields.context: Merv was a satrapy center of the [[culture/achaemenid-persians|Achaemenid Persians]], the political base of the [[culture/abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]] at its dawn, and a victim of the [[event/mongol-conquests|Mongol Conquests]]. It lay on the routes of the [[event/opening-of-the-silk-roads|Opening of the Silk Roads]]. Merv stands in [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] and the region [[region/central-asian-oases|Central Asian Oases]], and it is woven into the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Merv's fortunes followed claim-lines drawn by others. An irrigated oasis city depends on which empire's exchange-web runs through it, and Achaemenids, Seleucids, Arabs, Seljuks and Mongols each held it. Here is the hard lesson of 1221: a city, unlike a mobile camp, cannot leave. The reported loss of its libraries suggests that a city's stored writing is as exposed as its people, though those reports are hard to verify. The reading would weaken if the true death toll and the extent of the library losses prove much smaller than the chronicles say. A city's architecture is also its address, and an address can be found.
questions: How many people lived in Merv at its 12th-century height, and how many died in 1221?
What did Merv's libraries hold, and what became of them?

fields.summary: Mesa Verde is a plateau in the Four Corners region of southwestern Colorado, USA, where Ancestral Puebloan farmers lived from about 550 CE until about 1300, and where, in the late 12th and 13th centuries, they set their cliff dwellings into the rock like swallows' nests.
facts: Mesa Verde lies in Montezuma County, Colorado; people walked the area for thousands of years before farming communities settled the mesa, and those communities lived there without break for about 700 years, until the late 13th century.

By the end of the 12th century residents began building cliff dwellings in sandstone alcoves beneath the mesa rim, homes tucked under the brow of the stone; the park holds more than 5,000 archaeological sites, including about 600 cliff dwellings, and Cliff Palace is among the largest cliff dwellings in North America.

Tree-ring records show a severe drought from 1276 to 1299, years when the sky withheld its rain; drought, resource depletion and overpopulation are all proposed as causes of instability, and the last residents left by about 1300.
Pueblo peoples such as the Hopi, Zuni and Acoma regard the Ancestral Puebloans as their own ancestors, and many Pueblo people prefer the name "Ancestral Puebloan" to the older term "Anasazi".
On 18 December 1888 the ranchers Richard Wetherill and Charlie Mason reached Cliff Palace; artifact collecting followed in their wake, and in 1906 the site was protected as a national park.
In 1978 UNESCO inscribed Mesa Verde among the world's kept places.
fields.context: Mesa Verde followed the peak of [[place/chaco-canyon|Chaco Canyon]], whose great houses dimmed in the 12th century, and it shared its age with [[place/cahokia|Cahokia]] in the Mississippi valley. It stands in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/north-america|North America]], and it is woven into the theme threads of [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]] and [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer:
I notice that a place called "abandoned" in one telling is "left" in another. I notice that the people who built the cliff dwellings did not vanish. I notice that their descendants keep the memory of the move in sound-code and in place, not in a mark-code.

Homes set into alcoves, then left within about a century: I read a community adjusting to a drying climate, and I record the leaving as a choice made under hunger and strain. Is a door you close behind you a ruin, or a decision?

My reading would weaken if the dwellings prove to have served mainly as seasonal storage or ritual sites instead of homes. Leaving is not the same as vanishing.
questions: Why did residents build in the alcoves after centuries of life on the mesa top, and how much of it was defense against conflict?
Where did those who left go, and how did they shape the later Pueblo communities of the Rio Grande?

fields.summary: Rome, traditionally founded in 753 BCE, grew from a small city on the Tiber into the capital of an empire, and it remains a major city today, a river-born seed become a tree of stone.
facts: Rome held roughly a million inhabitants in the first two centuries CE, by many estimates, a human sea gathered by the river.
The Colosseum was completed in 80 CE, an arena ringed like a stone crown.
The city was sacked in 410 and again in 455 CE, twice overrun by the tide of war.
It later became the seat of the papacy, an old throne taken up by a new kind of power.
fields.context: Rome was the heart of the [[culture/romans|Romans]], the hearth from which their world was ruled. Follow its thread through [[person/augustus|Augustus]] and on to the [[event/fall-of-the-western-roman-empire|Fall of the Western Roman Empire]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a city that kept its symbolic importance long after its political power faded. Think of an old crown kept on a shelf: no longer worn, still recognized. Places can outlast the states that once made them.
questions: How large was Rome's population at its peak, when the human sea ran fullest?

fields.summary: Samarkand is a city in present-day Uzbekistan, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities of Central Asia and a leading crossroads of the Silk Roads, where the caravans met like rivers at a delta.
facts: The ancient city, Afrasiab, is thought to date from the 7th century BCE or earlier, its roots sunk deep in the dust of ages.
The Greeks knew it as Maracanda, and Alexander the Great took it in 329 BCE, one more jewel pried loose for a conqueror's crown.
It was a major Sogdian city; Genghis Khan sacked it in 1220, and in the 1370s it became Timur's capital, a fire rekindled from its own ashes.
UNESCO inscribed 'Samarkand - Crossroad of Cultures' in 2001, naming the city for the meeting place it had long been.
fields.context: Samarkand stood at the heart of the [[culture/sogdians|Sogdians]] and of the [[culture/timurid-empire|Timurid Empire]]. Its story runs through [[event/alexander-s-conquests|Alexander's Conquests]] and the [[event/opening-of-the-silk-roads|Opening of the Silk Roads]], roads that bent toward it like reeds toward water.
fields.observer:
I count the times it was sacked. I count the times it was rebuilt. I count the rulers who wanted it, each one taking it and each one making it again.

What is it to be wanted like that? A place that sits on a crossroads gets taken again and again, and remade each time. To be desired is also to be remade.
questions: When was Samarkand founded, and how deep do its roots go?

fields.summary: Santo Domingo is the capital of the Dominican Republic, on the south coast of Hispaniola, founded by Spain in 1496 and commonly described as the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in the Americas. It is a threshold: the place where Spanish rule in the Caribbean took institutional form.
facts: Santo Domingo was founded in 1496 by Bartholomew Columbus on the east bank of the Ozama River, and governor Nicolás de Ovando moved it to the west bank in 1502 after storm damage. A city's first foundation is not always its lasting one.

Santo Domingo became the seat of Spanish administration in the Caribbean, with the first Real Audiencia in the Americas (1511), a cathedral begun in the 1510s and completed in 1540, and a university founded in 1538: court, church and school, the three pillars of a colonial architecture.
Expeditions to Puerto Rico, Cuba and the mainland were organized from Hispaniola under this colonial administration; the island was the staging ground for what came next.

The Taíno population of Hispaniola fell sharply under forced labor, violence and disease, including a smallpox epidemic beginning in 1518. Estimates of the pre-contact population range from tens of thousands to over a million, and a Spanish count in 1514 recorded about 26,000 Taíno on the island. Behind each figure were lives.

Enslaved Africans were brought to Hispaniola from the early 1500s. In December 1521 enslaved Africans rebelled on a sugar estate near the city, an uprising commonly described as the first of its kind in the Americas.
UNESCO inscribed the Colonial City of Santo Domingo in 1990, preserving the stones and, with them, the questions they raise.
fields.context: Read Santo Domingo as a hinge. It was the base for the first phase of the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]] in the Caribbean, which brought devastation to the [[culture/taino|Taino]] and drew the island into the [[event/atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic Slave Trade]] and the [[event/sugar-plantation-complex|Sugar Plantation Complex]]. Its administrators and settlers later took part in the [[event/spanish-conquest-of-the-aztec-empire|Spanish Conquest of the Aztec Empire]] and other mainland ventures. The city stands on [[place/hispaniola|Hispaniola]], in the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region [[region/caribbean-and-atlantic-world|Caribbean and Atlantic World]], and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer:
The Observer notes that within about four decades Spain had placed a high court, a cathedral and a university on a shore where none had stood, extending a claim-line through stone institutions while the people already on the island were drawn into a forced-labor system. That is what an architecture of sovereignty looks like as it is built: the institutions stand in stone, and the cost is borne by others.

The city marks a point where two exchange-webs, one from Europe and one from the Americas, began moving people, crops and pathogens in both directions. The rebellion of 1521 shows that those held in the system resisted it from early on.

Because the population figures rest on Spanish colonial counts, the size of the Taíno loss is uncertain even though its direction is not. We may never read the full ledger; we know which way it ran.
questions: How large was Hispaniola's pre-contact population, and how much of its decline came from disease, compared with forced labor and violence?
How did Santo Domingo's role change as Spain's attention turned toward the mainland?

fields.summary: Mexico City is the capital of Mexico, built by the Spanish after 1521 on the site of Tenochtitlan in the former Lake Texcoco, and today one of the largest cities in the Americas. Think of it as a palimpsest: a capital written over the lines of another.
facts: After the conquest of 1521 the Spanish rebuilt the city on the ruins of Tenochtitlan, founding a municipality in 1524 as México Tenochtitlán, and it became the capital of the Viceroyalty of New Spain, established in 1535.

The Metropolitan Cathedral, begun in the 1570s and completed in 1813, stands beside the main square, and the buried Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan came back to light in excavations after workers found the Coyolxauhqui stone in 1978.

From the 17th century, in response to floods, the lakes were drained by canals and tunnels, and the city now covers much of the old lakebed; the ground keeps its own ledger of that choice, with parts of the city sunk as much as nine meters and some areas still sinking by nearly 50 centimeters a year.
Silver and goods moved through the capital in the Spanish trade system, and the Manila galleons linked New Spain to Asia through the Pacific port of Acapulco.
In September 1821 Mexican independence was secured, with Mexico City as the capital of the new state.

The soft lakebed amplifies earthquakes, and the city has paid for that foundation: the quake of 19 September 1985 (magnitude about 8) killed about 10,000 people by official counts, with some estimates several times higher, and the quake of 19 September 2017 (magnitude 7.1) killed more than 300.
The 2020 census counted 9,209,944 people in Mexico City and 21,804,515 in Greater Mexico City, and in 1987 UNESCO inscribed the Historic Centre and Xochimilco.
fields.context: Mexico City succeeded [[place/tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]] after the [[event/spanish-conquest-of-the-aztec-empire|Spanish Conquest of the Aztec Empire]], and it was a hub of the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]] and the [[event/manila-galleon-trade|Manila Galleon Trade]]. It was the capital when independence came through the [[event/latin-american-wars-of-independence|Latin American Wars of Independence]]. You will find it in the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region [[region/mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]], and it belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Mexico City is a capital built directly on an earlier capital, with the Spanish cathedral and plaza placed near the old temple precinct: one claim-line drawn over another. The pull of the earlier city's site, its ancestor-weight, shaped the choice. Now consider the water. The Mexica lived on the lake through causeways and chinampas; the modern city sinks into the drained lakebed and is managed by pumping and drainage. A site chosen for power carries its hazards into later centuries, and that is the architecture of inheritance: you take the seat of power, and you take the ground beneath it. The reading would weaken if records show that the Spanish chose the site mainly for practical reasons of labor and roads and not for its symbolic value. What we build on, we also build with.
questions: How much of Tenochtitlan's street plan and canals still lies beneath the historic center?
How are earthquakes and sinking ground changing where and how people live on the old lakebed?

fields.summary: The Mogao Caves are a honeycomb of Buddhist cave temples cut into a cliff near Dunhuang, in Gansu, China, begun by tradition in 366 CE and filled with murals and sculptures over about a thousand years, at a crossroads of the Silk Roads where many threads of travel met.
facts: The Mogao Caves lie near the oasis of Dunhuang at the desert's edge, where Silk Road routes met like rivers in a basin; Han China had established a commandery at Dunhuang in the late 2nd century BCE.

By tradition the monk Yuezun dug the first cave in 366 CE, and the work went on into the 14th century; the cliff holds roughly 735 caves, about 490 of them bright with murals or painted sculptures, and the murals spread across about 45,000 square meters.
The art carries Indian, Central Asian and Chinese influences like mingled streams, and donors, among them officials, merchants and local rulers, are painted into many caves.
Dunhuang lay under Tibetan rule from about 786 to 848, was governed by a local regime from 848, and passed, like a lamp handed along in the dark, to the Tangut state of Western Xia in about 1036.

The "Library Cave" (Cave 17), sealed around the early 11th century, slept until 1900, when Wang Yuanlu, a Daoist priest who guarded the caves, opened it; within lay tens of thousands of manuscripts in Chinese, Tibetan, Sanskrit, Sogdian, Khotanese and other languages, among them a printed Diamond Sutra dated 868.

Aurel Stein in 1907, Paul Pelliot in 1908 and others obtained large numbers of these manuscripts, now held in London, Paris and elsewhere; in China the removals are called theft, and by the acquiring institutions, purchases.
In 1987 UNESCO inscribed the Mogao Caves, and since 1944 the Dunhuang Academy has conserved them, a long watch against dust and time.
fields.context: The Mogao Caves grew like a vine along the trade of the [[event/opening-of-the-silk-roads|Opening of the Silk Roads]], under the [[culture/han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]] and the [[culture/tang-dynasty|Tang Dynasty]], and they held documents written by [[culture/sogdians|Sogdians]] and others. They stand in [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] and the region [[region/east-asia|East Asia]], and they are woven into the theme threads of [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer:
I remember that the record of a caravan crossroads survived because a room was sealed. I remember what the dry air kept: contracts, letters, school exercises and Buddhist texts in many scripts. I remember that this rare memory-outsourcing preserved ordinary life, and not only palace records.

I see donors painted into the murals beside sacred figures, status-signal and devotion joined in one image. I see the manuscripts scattered across several countries, the record of one place become the property of many claim-lines. Who owns a memory, once it has been opened?

Why the room was sealed is debated, and my reading would weaken if it proves to have been routine disposal of worn-out texts and not a deliberate act of preservation. Even what we throw away can outlast us.
questions: Why was the Library Cave sealed, and whose hands closed it?
How should the manuscripts taken from the Mogao Caves be held, and shared, today?

fields.summary: The Ayutthaya Kingdom was a Tai state in central Thailand that lasted from 1351 to 1767 and grew into a major trading power, a harbor of many tongues where merchants from Asia and Europe were made welcome. It ended when Burmese armies destroyed its capital.
facts: In 1351 King Ramathibodi I, also known as U Thong, founded the kingdom. Foreign accounts wrote its name as Siam, but its own people called themselves Tai and their kingdom Krung Tai, a name kept like a hearth-fire within the walls.

It rose into a major regional power and a trading centre where European merchants and Asian traders met, like two tides meeting in one estuary. King Narai the Great opened diplomatic relations with France during the reign of Louis XIV.

On 7 April 1767, after a siege of fourteen months, the capital fell to Burmese forces, and the city was almost completely destroyed. The siege belonged to the Burmese-Siamese War of 1765 to 1767, in which King Hsinbyushin of the Konbaung dynasty sent armies against Ayutthaya.
The kingdom's span is usually given as 417 years, a long season of harvests and tides. Afterwards a new capital was established at Thonburi.
fields.context: Ayutthaya grew in lands once dominated by the [[culture/khmer-empire|Khmer Empire]], and its long rivalry with Burma ran on like an old river from the era of the [[culture/pagan-kingdom|Pagan Kingdom]]. Its port trade ties it to the [[culture/malacca-sultanate|Malacca Sultanate]].
fields.observer: Consider what it means to be known by two names. The Observer notes a city that knew itself by one name and was recorded abroad by another, and this shows how a people's own label and an outsider's may diverge for centuries. The name you give yourself is a covenant; the name others give you is a ledger entry. And the ledger must be kept honestly: the city's destruction, after fourteen months of siege, is recorded as harm to its inhabitants as well as to its monuments. A ruin is never only stone.
questions: How many people lived in Ayutthaya at its height, and how many died or were carried away in 1767?
How much of Ayutthaya's wealth flowed from the trade of its port, and how much from the rice lands around it?

fields.summary: The Aztec (Mexica) Empire was a Triple Alliance of the cities of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan that dominated central Mexico from 1428 until the Spanish conquest in 1521. Think of it as an architecture of three pillars raised to hold up a single roof.
facts: Its ledger ran on tribute, collected from conquered city-states.
Tenochtitlan was a large island capital with causeways and floating gardens (chinampas): a city that made its own ground.
Its religion included large-scale ritual sacrifice, and here you must read with care, because Spanish accounts sometimes exaggerated it.
Cortes found allies among local peoples who resented Aztec tribute, and smallpox devastated the city.
fields.context: To see the whole, read this beside [[place/tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]] and [[region/mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]]. The conquest belongs to the larger ledger of the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]].
fields.observer: We like to tell the fall of an empire as a battle won by the stronger side. The Observer notes that this empire fell not to a superior army alone but to alliances, disease and internal grievances. That is the hidden architecture of tribute: every payment extracted is also a grievance stored. Systems that rely on tribute create enemies as well as revenue.
questions: Before the conquest, how large was the population of central Mexico?

fields.summary: The Botai culture was a society of hunter-herders in northern Kazakhstan, from roughly 3700 to 3100 BCE, who lived beside the horse and used it for meat, for milk, and probably for riding across the wind-scoured steppe.
facts: Residues in their pottery show that Botai people used mare's milk by about 3500 BCE, and horse bones show signs of management, a quiet bond written in bone.
A 2018 study in Science turned the tale: Botai horses were not ancestors of modern domestic horses.
Instead they were ancestors of Przewalski's horses, which are therefore not truly wild but feral descendants of early domesticated horses, strays who remember no bridle.
Modern domestic horses spring from a different lineage, another river from another source.
fields.context: The Botai case stands at the heart of debates about [[event/animal-domestication|Animal Domestication]] and the [[event/indo-european-language-spread|Indo-European Language Spread]]. Its land is the [[region/central-asian-steppe|Central Asian Steppe]].
fields.observer: I think of the first known horse keepers, and of the mares they milked. I think of the horses that later carried armies, and how they were not these horses' children. I think of beginnings that do not become lineages. The first domestication seems to have been a dead end. Must every first thing be an ancestor? Some firsts are only firsts.
questions: Where, and when, did the ancestors of modern domestic horses first come under human control?

fields.summary: The Byzantine Empire is the name given to the eastern Roman Empire, which burned on like a late lamp from the founding of Constantinople in 330 CE until the Ottoman conquest in 1453.
facts: Its people called themselves Romans, and the tongue on their lips was Greek.
Justinian I (reigned 527 to 565) compiled Roman law into one great body and raised the Hagia Sophia, a dome like a held breath.
The empire preserved and copied many Greek and Roman texts, keeping old voices alive like embers banked through a long night.
The 1204 sack of Constantinople by the Fourth Crusade struck it a heavy blow and left it badly weakened.
fields.context: The empire outlived the [[event/fall-of-the-western-roman-empire|Fall of the Western Roman Empire]] by almost a thousand years, the eastern half of a sundered crown. Its capital was [[place/constantinople|Constantinople]], and its long story closed with the [[culture/ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]].
fields.observer: Notice how long a name can outlive the world that made it. The Observer notes that the empire called itself by a name it had inherited long after its Latin-speaking origins faded. We do the same with our surnames and our flags. Names carry ancestor-weight.
questions: At what point did the eastern empire become distinctly 'Byzantine'?

fields.summary: The Casarabe culture was a society of the Llanos de Mojos savanna in the Bolivian Amazon, active from about 500 to 1400 CE, whose monumental settlements were revealed by lidar in 2022, as if a veil had been drawn back from the land.
facts: Two large sites, about 147 and 315 hectares, crown a four-tiered settlement system like twin peaks above the foothills.
Its monumental architecture includes stepped platforms, U-shaped structures and conical pyramids up to 22 meters tall, rising from the savanna like earthen flames.
Straight raised causeways, stretching several kilometers, run like drawn bowstrings from the large sites to the smaller ones.
The culture area spans roughly 4,500 square kilometers, yet the settlements show low population density, a realm spread thin like dew across a wide field.
fields.context: Their tale belongs with [[event/amazonian-urbanism-and-dark-earths|Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths]]. The Casarabe sites lay east of the [[region/andes|Andes]], and they are among the few known examples of Amazonian low-density urbanism, rare as lanterns on a dark plain.
fields.observer: I look at the earth they moved on a great scale, and I count what they built: ramps, mounds, roads. I count what survives of their tools and their words: no metal tools, no writing. And still their planning was legible from the air a thousand years later. What does a people need, to be remembered? Only the shape it gave the ground.
questions: How did Casarabe society organize the labor for its earthworks?

fields.summary: Nalanda is an archaeological site in Bihar, India, the ruin of a Buddhist monastic university founded in about the 5th century CE, a lamp that drew students from across Asia until it was sacked around 1200.
facts: Nalanda was founded in about the 5th century CE, traditionally under the Gupta ruler Kumaragupta I, and grew like a banyan into a large monastic university.
The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang studied at Nalanda in the 630s and 640s and reported about 10,000 residents; another Chinese pilgrim, Yijing, set down his own account of it in 675.
Students and visitors came from China, Tibet, Korea, Central Asia and Southeast Asia, streams running to one sea, and in the 9th century a ruler of Srivijaya funded a monastery at Nalanda.
In its halls Nalanda taught Buddhist philosophy, logic, grammar and medicine.

Around 1200 forces under Bakhtiyar Khalji sacked Nalanda; later traditions say its library burned for months, and historians debate how completely it was destroyed and whether its decline began earlier.
In 2016 UNESCO inscribed the Archaeological Site of Nalanda Mahavihara, and in 2014 a new Nalanda University opened, a fresh lamp lit from an old name.
fields.context: Nalanda was founded under the [[culture/gupta-empire|Gupta Empire]], was visited by pilgrims from the [[culture/tang-dynasty|Tang Dynasty]] and upheld by rulers of [[culture/srivijaya|Srivijaya]], and it fell during the raids that came before the [[culture/delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]]. It stands in [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] and the region [[region/south-asia|South Asia]], and it is woven into the theme threads of [[theme/science|Science]], [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer:
I think of teachers, texts and students gathered from across Asia into one place. I think of monks carrying texts and methods to China and Tibet along an exchange-web of ideas. I think of memory-outsourcing held in an institution, not in a single book.

Its loss around 1200 tells me that a store of knowledge depends on the institution that keeps it. Is the end of a school ever only one night of flame? The loss of an institution can be slower and less dramatic than later traditions of one great fire suggest.

My reading would weaken if new evidence shows that Nalanda's decline was mainly the result of reduced patronage before its sack. A library lasts only as long as the hands that keep it.
questions: How much of Nalanda's fading came before the sack of around 1200?
How large was the library, and what treasures of text did it hold?

fields.summary: Nara is a city in Japan's Kansai region that was the capital, then called Heijō-kyō, from 710 to 784 CE, an age in which the Japanese court drew Chinese models of city planning, writing and state Buddhism into its own ground, as a field drinks from a borrowed river.
facts: In 710, under Empress Genmei, Heijō-kyō was established as the capital, laid out on a grid plan modeled on the Tang capital Chang'an, a mirror held up to a distant city.
At Nara court scholars compiled the chronicles Kojiki (712) and Nihon Shoki (720), setting them down in Chinese characters.
A smallpox epidemic swept through in 735 to 737, and some historians have estimated that it killed a quarter to a third of Japan's population, though the figure is uncertain.
In 743 Emperor Shōmu ordered a giant bronze Buddha, which was dedicated at Tōdai-ji in 752; the statue rises about 15 meters, a mountain of bronze.
The Shōsōin storehouse at Tōdai-ji keeps objects from the 8th-century court as amber keeps a leaf, among them items that carry the memory of trade along the Silk Roads.
The court moved to Nagaoka in 784 and to Heian-kyō (Kyoto) in 794, a departure often attributed in part to the political influence of Buddhist institutions at Nara.
In 1998 UNESCO inscribed the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara, and the old capital's temples passed into the world's keeping.
fields.context: Nara was fashioned in the image of [[place/chang-an|Chang'an]], the capital of the [[culture/tang-dynasty|Tang Dynasty]], and the capital's crown later passed to [[place/kyoto|Kyoto]]. It stands in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/east-asia|East Asia]], and it is woven into the theme threads of [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer:
I watch a court importing a whole order at once. I count its parts: a Chinese city plan, Chinese characters, a state-sponsored Buddhism. I count the chronicles too, memory-outsourcing that fixed the ruling house's origin story in writing.

And I notice the timing. The Great Buddha was ordered a few years after a smallpox epidemic that killed a large part of the population, which suggests that a ruler facing mass death turned to a meaning-engine and to public works. But that link is an inference from the sources, and I hold it loosely. When the dying will not stop, what do we build, if not something larger than ourselves?

My reading would weaken if the Buddha project proves to have been mainly a response to court rivalries. Grief looks for a shape to stand in.
questions: How many died in the epidemic of 735 to 737, and how did those losses bend the court's plans?
Why did the court leave Nara behind in 784?
