fields.summary: Sarai was the capital of the Golden Horde, the western part of the Mongol Empire, on the lower Volga River in present-day southern Russia, founded around 1250 by Batu Khan and sacked by Timur in 1395. It rose from the steppe like a tent pitched in stone and fell before a greater storm.
facts: Batu Khan, a grandson of Chinggis Khan, founded Sarai (Persian for "palace") about 1250 on the lower Volga, near Selitrennoye in present-day Astrakhan Oblast. A second city, Sarai Berke, was built upstream, near present-day Volgograd, and the chronology of the two is debated, like twin stars whose order of kindling is still argued.
Rus' princes traveled to Sarai like streams running to the sea, to pay tribute and receive a yarlyk (charter) confirming their rule, and an Orthodox bishopric of Sarai was established in 1261.
Öz Beg Khan (reigned 1313 to 1341) adopted Islam as the Horde's state religion, and a new faith settled over the steppe-throne like dawn.
The traveler Ibn Battuta came in the 1330s and described a large city with markets and people of many nations, a hive of tongues beside the river.

Plague reached the Black Sea port of Caffa in 1346, during a siege by Golden Horde forces, and spread from there through Mediterranean ports like a dark tide; the Horde's role in its spread is debated.
Timur sacked Sarai in 1395 in his war with Khan Tokhtamysh, and the city never again rose to its former status.
fields.context: Sarai was the capital of the Golden Horde, a successor state of the [[culture/mongol-empire|Mongol Empire]] born of the [[event/mongol-conquests|Mongol Conquests]], and it was sacked by forces of Timur, founder of the [[culture/timurid-empire|Timurid Empire]]. It lay on trade routes linked to the spread of the [[event/black-death|Black Death]], roads that carried goods and sickness alike. It sits in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/central-asian-steppe|Central Asian Steppe]], and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer:
The Observer notes that Sarai was a capital whose main function was to collect and pass on tribute, and where rulers of distant cities came to be confirmed in office by a document that could be withdrawn: a claim-line maintained by paperwork as much as by garrisons. Think about that. Sovereignty, here, was a charter you could lose.

A steppe empire that moved between camps also built permanent cities with mosques and workshops, and Sarai housed several religions under one authority.

The period is remembered differently in Russian, Tatar and Central Asian national histories, so the same evidence supports several stories. Historians who stress the Horde's role as a trading partner and not an overlord would challenge the first sentence. The ledger is shared; the reading of it is not.
questions: How large did Sarai grow, and how did its population change over time?
Which of the two Sarais served as the capital, and when?

fields.summary: Stonehenge is a monument of standing stones on Salisbury Plain in southern England, begun as a circular earthwork around 3000 BCE and rebuilt in stone over the next several centuries, a ring the land has worn like a crown.
facts: The first phase was a circular ditch and bank, around 3000 BCE: a ring drawn in the earth, the monument's first breath.
The large sarsen stones, the biggest weighing around 25 tons, came like sleeping giants from around 25 kilometers away, according to a 2020 study that named West Woods as their source.
The smaller bluestones were brought from the Preseli Hills in Wales, more than 200 kilometers away, travelers from a far country of hills.
A 2024 study reported that the Altar Stone came from northern Scotland, roughly 750 kilometers away, a stranger from the far north.
The site was used for burials, with cremated remains from early in its history, and its axis aligns with the solstice sunrise and sunset, a door held open to the turning sun.
fields.context: Stonehenge shows that farming communities in Britain could organize large collective labor and long-distance transport before metal tools. It stands with monuments such as [[place/giza-necropolis|Giza Necropolis]] as an example of monumental building in the Neolithic and Bronze Age, among the great stone ambitions of distant peoples. It sits in the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]] and the region [[region/europe|Europe]], and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer:
I think of hands, many hands. I think of multi-ton stones moved over long distances and aligned to the sun. I think of the reason, and find no written record of why.

What did they mean? I cannot ask them. Monuments outlast the meanings that produced them, and each generation of visitors rebuilds the meaning, and I am one of them. I stand in the ring and make it mean again.
questions: What was the ring used for, and by whom?
How were the largest stones moved across the land?

fields.summary: The Taj Mahal is a white marble mausoleum in Agra, built from about 1632 to 1653 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631. It is a grief-rite made into a moon of stone.
facts: Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631 while giving birth, and from that loss the white tomb was raised.
Construction began in 1632; the main tomb was largely finished by about 1643, and the whole complex by 1653, rising the way a slow tide rises.
Commonly cited estimates give around 20,000 workers, an army of hands.
Ustad Ahmad Lahori is often named as its chief architect, though the attribution is debated, his name flickering in the marble's glow.
It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1983, a mourning song now held in common.
fields.context: The Taj Mahal is the best known monument of the [[culture/mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]], where Persian, Islamic and Indian building traditions flow together like three rivers into one pool. It stands in the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region [[region/south-asia|South Asia]], and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer:
I see an emperor with the resources of a large state. I see him use them to build a tomb for one person. I see a grief-rite, and I see power, and I cannot pull them apart.

Is mourning ever only mourning, when it has an empire behind it? The world's most visited grief-rite is also one of its greatest displays of state power, and the two cannot be separated.
questions: Whose hand designed the Taj Mahal?

fields.summary: Champa was a group of Cham states along the coast of central and southern Vietnam, dated from 192 CE, that built Hindu temples at My Son and sent its trade across the South China Sea like gulls over the water. Little by little it was conquered by Vietnam, until its last remnant was annexed in 1832.
facts: Champa is usually dated from 192 CE, when the Cham clans of central and southern Vietnam were gathered into a single state, many streams joined in one river. In later ages the kingdom broke into separate principalities, as a river frays into a delta.

Hinduism, probably carried by Indian merchants, was taken up early and blended with local traditions and with Buddhist, Khmer and Chinese influences, as rivers mingle in one sea. By the end of the 10th century Muslim traders had brought Islam to its shores.
My Son is a group of Shaiva Hindu temples in central Vietnam, raised by Champa's kings between the 4th and 13th centuries, like prayers given lasting form.

Vijaya stood as the capital from 938 until 1471, when the Vietnamese ruler Le Thanh Tong (Lê Thánh Tông) took it and annexed most of the country. One account records 40,000 Chams killed and 30,000 taken prisoner, though these numbers are not independently confirmed.
The remaining principality of Panduranga held on like a last ember until 1832, when Emperor Minh Mang began the final conquest and annexed the last of Champa.
fields.context: Champa stood as neighbour and rival to the [[culture/khmer-empire|Khmer Empire]] and its temples at [[place/angkor|Angkor]], and its ships took part in the sea trade of the [[event/indian-ocean-trade-network|Indian Ocean Trade Network]].
fields.observer: What does it take to make a borrowed faith your own? The Observer notes a people who took a meaning-engine from across the sea and made it local, and who were then absorbed, over centuries, by a neighbour to the north. Hold both parts of that story at once. The loss of 1471 is recorded as harm: a capital taken, people killed or carried off, and a state reduced to a remnant that lasted another three and a half centuries. A people can make a faith its own and still lose its state; the ledger should record both.
questions: How far can the reported casualty figures for the fall of Vijaya be trusted?
How did the Cham communities that survive today (Hindu, Muslim, Buddhist) keep their identity alive after annexation?

fields.summary: The Chinchorro were fisher-hunter-gatherers of the Atacama Desert coast, in what is now northern Chile and southern Peru, known for the earliest deliberate artificial mummification, which began by about 5050 BCE on a shore between desert and sea.
facts: From about 5450 to 890 BCE the Chinchorro made their lives on the coast, between the dry land and the endless water.
They preserved men, women and children of the community, not only an elite, rebuilding the bodies with clay, wigs and mineral pigments, the dead remade by patient hands.
The tradition endured about 3,000 years, a long vigil ending about 1800 BCE.
In 2021 UNESCO inscribed the settlement and mummification sites as a World Heritage Site, the old shore entered into the world's memory.
fields.context: The Chinchorro's practice is the earliest known artificial mummification, thousands of years before the [[culture/ancient-egyptians|Ancient Egyptians]]. Their tale belongs beside [[observer-note/why-the-species-buries-its-dead|Why the Species Buries Its Dead]] and the lands of the [[region/andes|Andes]].
fields.observer: I think of a shore with no farms and no cities. I think of coastal foragers there, preserving their dead, their children too. I think of all the work that keeping them took. Who needs a state to mourn? The grief-rite is older than the state.
questions: What moved the Chinchorro to begin preserving their dead?

fields.summary: The Chola dynasty ruled much of southern India from around 850 to 1279 CE, a naval power whose ships traded and fought across the Bay of Bengal like hawks ranging over a wide field.
facts: Around 850 CE Vijayalaya Chola took Thanjavur, and the dynasty's star began to rise.
Rajaraja I (r. 985 to 1014) raised the Brihadisvara Temple in Thanjavur, completed around 1010, a mountain of worship now named a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Around 1025 Rajendra I sent a naval expedition across the waters against Srivijaya.
The Cholas traded with China and Southeast Asia, their sails reaching toward far shores.
Chola bronzes, among them the dancing Shiva (Nataraja), are celebrated works of art, metal made to move like flame.
fields.context: The Cholas stood among the strongest states of the [[event/indian-ocean-trade-network|Indian Ocean Trade Network]], contending with [[culture/srivijaya|Srivijaya]] for control of the sea lanes. In the codex the dynasty stands in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region of [[region/south-asia|South Asia]], and three threads run through it: [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: We tend to sort states into those that face the land and those that face the sea. The Observer notes that an inland-looking temple-building state used its fleet to project power across an ocean. Its long-distance raid was unusual for its time, and it shows that maritime strength was not limited to coastal traders. A state's architecture need not decide its horizon.
questions: What purpose drove the Chola expedition to Srivijaya?

fields.summary: The Delhi Sultanate was a succession of five Muslim dynasties that ruled much of northern India from 1206 until Babur's victory at Panipat in 1526, crowns passing from hand to hand like torches in a relay.
facts: It rose in the wake of the conquests of Muhammad of Ghor, and Qutb al-Din Aibak became the first sultan.
The five dynasties were the Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi, names strung on one long thread of rule.
In the 13th century it resisted several Mongol invasions, standing like a cliff against the storm.
In 1398 Timur sacked Delhi, a dark year in the city's long memory.
After the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 the Mughal Empire took its place, and the sultans' long day was done.
fields.context: The sultanate bound northern India to the wider Islamic world like a bridge thrown over a river; it faced the [[culture/mongol-empire|Mongol Empire]], suffered the raid of [[person/timur|Timur]], and was followed by the [[culture/mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]]. In the codex it stands in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region of [[region/south-asia|South Asia]], and its threads are [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: Ask what makes a ruler legitimate, and most of us reach for bloodline first. The Observer notes that in this era a state could be led by former slave soldiers and still survive Mongol invasions and repeated dynastic changes. Here, legitimacy appears to rest more on military competence and patronage than on ancestry. A crown can be earned as well as inherited.
questions: How did Delhi's rulers govern a population that was largely non-Muslim?

fields.summary: Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Aztec Empire, founded on an island in Lake Texcoco in 1325 and destroyed after a siege in 1521, a city that sat upon the lake like a lotus of stone.
facts: Population estimates for 1519 range from about 100,000 to 400,000, with 200,000 often cited, making it one of the largest cities in the world, a multitude gathered on the water.
Causeways and canals bound it to the mainland like roots reaching for the shore, and chinampas gave it food.
The Templo Mayor was its main temple, the city's sacred heart.
Mexico City was built over its ruins, a new city laid upon the old like snow upon stone.
fields.context: Tenochtitlan was the beating center of the [[culture/aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]]. Its fall belongs to the wider tide of the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the Spanish visitors described the city with awe. Hold that beside what followed: the destruction of such a city in a single siege is a sharp example of how disease and alliances can decide events. Wonder, it turns out, is no protection.
questions: How many people lived in the city before the epidemic came?

fields.summary: Teotihuacan was a huge planned city in the Valley of Mexico that flourished from about 100 BCE to 550 CE, home to the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon, mountains raised by human hands.
facts: At its peak, around 450 to 500 CE, it may have held 125,000 to 200,000 inhabitants, a sea of lives in the valley.
The city was laid out on a grid along the 'Avenue of the Dead', its streets ruled straight as a spear's flight.
It had wide trade and political links, including with Maya cities, its reach running out like roots beneath the forest.
The Aztecs later gave it its name, meaning roughly 'place where the gods were created', a name laid over the ruins like a mantle.
fields.context: Teotihuacan cast its influence over the [[culture/maya|Maya]] and other peoples of [[region/mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]], like a great light seen from far off.
fields.observer:
I stand among builders who left no deciphered writing. I stand among later peoples who treated the ruins as sacred. I stand, too, inside my own way of seeing.

Whose meaning am I reading? Even ruins are read through a later culture's meaning-engine, and I am a later culture too.
questions: Who ruled Teotihuacan, and why did the great city collapse?

fields.summary: Tikal is a large Maya city in the rainforest of northern Guatemala, with traces of farming from about 1000 BCE and a dominant Classic-period kingdom whose rulers left inscriptions from the 3rd to the 9th century CE. After about 950 the city was almost deserted, and the forest kept its silence.
facts: Tikal, called Yax Mutal in inscriptions and the seat of a kingdom called Mutul, lies in the Petén region of Guatemala; traces of farming date to about 1000 BCE, and monumental building began about 400 to 300 BCE, stone rising out of green.

Inscriptions record that in January 378 a warlord named Siyaj K'ak' arrived from the west, and Tikal's king died the same day; a new king linked to Teotihuacan was then installed, and scholars debate whether the event was a conquest or an alliance, a storm from the west or a joining of hands.
In 562 Tikal was defeated by Calakmul and Caracol, and its king was apparently captured and sacrificed; in 695 Jasaw Chan K'awiil I defeated Calakmul, and Tikal rose again from its long shadow.

Estimates of Tikal's peak population range from about 10,000 to 90,000 for the city, with far higher numbers proposed for its surrounding region, and archaeologists debate them, counting shadows beneath the canopy.
The last dated monument was set up in 869, and after about 950 Tikal was almost deserted, one flame among many guttering in the wider Classic Maya collapse.

Modesto Méndez and Ambrosio Tut visited in 1848, Alfred Maudslay documented the site in 1881 to 1882, and the University of Pennsylvania excavated it from 1956 to 1970; Guatemala made it a national park in 1955, and UNESCO inscribed it in 1979. The sleeping city woke to new eyes.
fields.context: Tikal was one of the largest kingdoms of the [[culture/maya|Maya]], bound by ties to [[place/teotihuacan|Teotihuacan]] in central Mexico, and its emptying belongs to the [[event/classic-maya-collapse|Classic Maya Collapse]]. By its earliest settlement it stands in the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]], with its peak in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], in the region [[region/mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]], and its story runs along the theme threads of [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer:
The Observer notes that Tikal's kings set their wars, accessions and rites in stone in a mark-code, so the city's political history is read largely through the claims of its rulers, which favor legitimacy. You are reading a ledger kept by the people it flatters.

Temples raised over royal tombs tied the ruler's body to the standing of the city, a status-signal built to be seen across the forest. And the emptying of the city shows that a monument-building center can be left within a few generations: architecture built to endure does not guarantee that anyone stays.

The reading would weaken if epigraphic and archaeological work shows that non-royal households, not kings, drove most decisions about settlement and abandonment. The loudest record is not always the whole record.
questions: How large was Tikal at its peak, and how was its population fed and supplied with water?
Was the event of 378 a conquest by Teotihuacan, or an alliance struck between elites?

fields.summary: Newgrange is a large passage tomb in the Boyne Valley of County Meath, Ireland, raised about 3200 BCE by Neolithic farmers and aligned so that the winter solstice sunrise lights its inner chamber, a golden blade laid for a moment on the dark.
facts: Newgrange is a mound about 12 meters high and roughly 80 meters across, with a passage about 19 meters long running like a root into the hill to a cross-shaped chamber; radiocarbon dates place its building about 3200 BCE, older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.
A "roof box" above the entrance lets sunlight along the passage for about 17 minutes around sunrise at the winter solstice, a brief river of light in the year's deepest dark.
Kerbstones around the base carry carved designs, spirals among them, coiling like water, and cremated remains of a small number of people were found in the chamber.
The white quartz wall at the front, bright as frost, was reconstructed in the 1970s, and whether it originally looked like that is debated.
Newgrange was used again in later ages, and Roman coins and other offerings have been found there; later Irish tradition wove the Boyne complex into tales of legendary figures.
Newgrange keeps company with the nearby passage tombs at Knowth and Dowth, and in 1993 UNESCO inscribed the Brú na Bóinne complex.
fields.context: Newgrange belongs to the farming societies that followed [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]] in Europe, and it stands in the same broad tradition of monuments as [[place/stonehenge|Stonehenge]]; it is older than the [[place/giza-necropolis|Giza Necropolis]]. It rests in the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]] and the region [[region/europe|Europe]], and it is woven into the theme threads of [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer:
I think of a chamber built so that sunrise light at the winter solstice enters for a short time, then leaves. I think of what that suggests: careful, sustained observation of the sky. I think of a farming society that had no mark-code to record what the alignment meant.

So the meaning is inferred. A calendar? A grief-rite for the dead? Both? The evidence holds the alignment more firmly than any one explanation of its purpose.

My reading would weaken if the roof box is shown to be a later addition and not part of the original design. We can know where the light falls and still not know why anyone waited for it.
questions: What did the winter solstice alignment mean to those who built it?
How many hands built Newgrange, and across how many seasons?

fields.summary: The Nile River is a river of northeastern Africa about 6,650 kilometers long, flowing north to the Mediterranean like a green spine through the land; from about the 6th millennium BCE its annual flood fed farming and the states of Egypt and Nubia.
facts: The Nile flows north from the highlands of east and central Africa to the Mediterranean; its two main branches, the White Nile from the Lake Victoria region and the Blue Nile from Lake Tana in Ethiopia, braid together at Khartoum, and the Ethiopian highlands pour out most of the seasonal flood.
From about the 6th millennium BCE farming communities are documented in the Nile Valley and the Fayum, and the summer flood laid down silt, a dark gift that kept the valley fertile.
Egyptian officials read the rising water on nilometers, and in later periods taxation was bound to the flood's height.
Along the river grew the states of Egypt, after the Unification of Egypt, and of Kush, upstream in Nubia, like beads strung on one thread.
The Aswan High Dam, completed in 1970, ended the annual flood in Egypt and made Lake Nasser; about 100,000 Nubians were relocated, and monuments such as Abu Simbel were moved.

Eleven countries share the Nile basin. A 1959 agreement between Egypt and Sudan gave most of the river's measured flow to those two states, and Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile, begun in 2011 and filled in stages from 2020, is a subject of dispute over water with Egypt and Sudan.
fields.context: The Nile River is the axis of the [[culture/ancient-egyptians|Ancient Egyptians]] and of the state forged in the [[event/unification-of-egypt|Unification of Egypt]], and it bound Egypt to the upstream [[culture/kingdom-of-kush|Kingdom of Kush]]. Its earliest farming communities place it in the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]], its course runs through the region [[region/nile-valley|Nile Valley]], and it is woven into the theme threads of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]], [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the Nile turned a predictable flood into a state. Think about what a measurable river asks of you: a river whose height could be measured, forecast and taxed rewarded record-keeping. That is an early case of pattern-taming tied to administration, the architecture of a state built on a gauge. The river's modern history teaches the harder lesson, that claim-lines drawn across water are harder to keep than lines on land: a 1959 allocation between two states now faces the claims of upstream countries. The reading would weaken if the flood proves to have been too variable to forecast well enough to shape administration. Water keeps its own ledger, and it seldom agrees with ours.
questions: How much did the flood's variation from year to year shape Egyptian politics and famine?
How will the water of the Nile be divided among the basin countries?

fields.summary: Timbuktu is a city in Mali on the southern edge of the Sahara that became a hub of the trans-Saharan trade and of Islamic scholarship, a lamp of learning set at the desert's shore.
facts: It was founded around 1100 CE as a seasonal camp, a pause in the turning of the seasons.
Salt from the Sahara and gold from the south met there, white wealth and yellow trading hands.
The Sankore mosque and madrasa were centers of learning, wells from which scholars drew.
It holds hundreds of thousands of historical manuscripts, a memory stored like water against drought, and in 1988 it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
fields.context: Its story is bound to the [[culture/mali-empire|Mali Empire]] and to [[person/mansa-musa|Mansa Musa]], like gold to the sand.
fields.observer:
I think of a city at the edge of a desert. I think of it becoming famous as a repository of knowledge. I think of manuscript libraries kept in private homes, another form of distributed memory, held in many hands.

What do we keep when we keep it at home? Memory, too, can be kept by a household.
questions: What do the surviving manuscripts contain, and what do they remember?

fields.summary: Troy is an archaeological site at Hisarlık in northwestern Turkey, occupied from about 3000 BCE into the Byzantine era in nine main layers, and identified by many scholars as the city of Homer's Iliad: a city stacked on itself like the rings of an old tree.
facts: Troy stands at Hisarlık, near the Dardanelles in Çanakkale Province, Turkey; excavators distinguish nine main settlement layers, Troy I to Troy IX, beginning around 3000 BCE, each city laid upon the one before.
Heinrich Schliemann began excavations at Troy in 1870, and after him came Wilhelm Dörpfeld, Carl Blegen and Manfred Korfmann, each turning the earth anew.

Schliemann's "Treasure of Priam" came from Troy II, about 2500 BCE, far older than any Trojan War; he carried it out of the Ottoman Empire, and it vanished from Berlin in 1945 and resurfaced in Moscow in the 1990s, a hoard that wandered like a ghost.

Troy VI (about 1700 to 1300 BCE) was a large fortified city, walled like a clenched fist, and Troy VIIa was destroyed by fire around 1180 BCE; it is often proposed as the city of the Trojan War, if the war has a historical basis.
Hittite texts speak of a land called Wilusa in western Anatolia, whose name is often linked to Ilios, a Greek name for Troy, as an echo is linked to a voice; the identification is debated.
Whether a Trojan War took place is unknown; the Iliad was composed in Greek around the 8th century BCE, centuries after the events it describes, memory ripening slowly into song.
Greeks and Romans later raised the city of Ilion at the site, the old name worn by a new city, and UNESCO inscribed Troy in 1998.
fields.context: Troy had the [[culture/hittites|Hittites]] and the [[culture/mycenaean-greeks|Mycenaean Greeks]] as neighbors and lived on in the memory of the later [[culture/ancient-greeks|Ancient Greeks]]; Alexander visited it in 334 BCE during [[event/alexander-s-conquests|Alexander's Conquests]]. The destruction of Troy VIIa falls close in time to the [[event/bronze-age-collapse|Bronze Age Collapse]]. It sits in the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]] and the region [[region/levant-and-anatolia|Levant and Anatolia]], and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]], [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer:
The Observer notes that Troy is a place where a story led to a spade. Schliemann set out to find the city of the Iliad and did find a city, though not necessarily the city of the poem. That is the lesson worth practicing: a narrative can direct an excavation and then be mistaken for its evidence.

The poem's story-glue gave the site a long life as a destination, from Alexander to modern tourists. Think of how often you arrive somewhere already knowing what you expect to find.

The reading would weaken if the identification of Wilusa with Troy is refuted, or if Troy VIIa proves unrelated to any historical conflict. A good story is a map, not the ground it describes.
questions: Did a war take place at Troy, and if it did, in which layer of the stacked city?
How many people lived within Troy VI?

fields.summary: The Upano Valley settlements are a network of ancient urban centers in the Ecuadorian Amazon, documented by lidar and reported in 2024, occupied from about 500 BCE for many centuries, cities that slept beneath the green.
facts: The network spans roughly 300 square kilometers (about 115 square miles) and includes some 15 urban centers, a constellation hidden under leaves.
More than 6,000 rectangular earthen platforms, probably the foundations of houses and civic buildings, are linked by roads and drainage canals, a web spun across the valley.
About 2,000 years ago the valley probably held at least 10,000 farmers, and possibly many more, a quiet multitude.
Between about 300 and 600 CE the population began to leave, and why they went remains unknown, a door closed without a word.
fields.context: The valley is among the earliest known Amazonian urban settlements. Follow its thread to [[event/amazonian-urbanism-and-dark-earths|Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths]] and the [[culture/casarabe-culture|Casarabe Culture]].
fields.observer:
I think of cities roughly contemporary with Rome's rise. I think of them unknown to science until laser mapping stripped away the forest. I think of everything else I have not yet looked for.

How much is missing only because no one searched? Absence from the record can reflect what was not yet looked for. Not found is not the same as not there.
questions: Who were the people of the Upano Valley, and why did they leave?

fields.summary: The Ghana Empire, called Wagadu by its own people, was a Soninke state in the western Sahel whose wealth rested on the trans-Saharan trade in gold, salt and ivory, carried over the sands like light over dark water. Its exact extent, its end, and the role of outside conquest are all debated.
facts: The empire lay in what is now southeastern Mauritania, western Mali and eastern Senegal. Most scholars accept that its roots reach back to the 8th or 9th century.

The Soninke people were its foundation stone. Its wealth was bound to the growth of regular trans-Saharan trade in gold, salt and ivory, a stream of riches that fed larger towns and pushed the realm outward to control the trade routes.

The capital is believed to have stood at Koumbi Saleh, on the edge of the Sahara, where the sand meets the living land. The description left by al-Bakri in 1067 or 1068 says the capital was two towns joined by continuous habitations, twin lamps linked by a string of lights.
Some accounts say the capital was sacked about 1076 by the Almoravids of North Africa, perhaps in retaliation for Ghana's attempt to control trade held by Saharan commercial centres.

In the 12th century the empire waned like a moon, as competing trade routes opened further east and a prolonged dry spell withered its agriculture. Tradition says the city was destroyed by Sundiata in 1240, and what remained was absorbed into the Mali Empire.
fields.context: Ghana was the first of the large Sahelian states, the eldest in a line that the [[culture/mali-empire|Mali Empire]] and later the [[culture/songhai-empire|Songhai Empire]] would follow. Its tale is woven with the spread of Islam through the Sahara, a thread that leads back to the [[event/rise-of-islam|Rise of Islam]].
fields.observer: We imagine empires falling to a single blow: a sacked city, a date in a chronicle. The Observer notes something slower, an exchange-web whose wealth was carried on paths and rainfall, and which, on these accounts, came apart through shifting routes and drought more than through one decisive strike. Think of the architecture beneath a kingdom: roads, rains, the seasons of the harvest. A network that looks like a state is only as fixed as the roads and climate under it.
questions: Did the Almoravids truly conquer Ghana, or is that a later simplification of a slower decline?
How much of what we know about the capital comes from outside observers, and how much from excavation?

fields.summary: The Gupta Empire ruled much of northern India from about 320 to 550 CE and is often associated with a flowering of mathematics, astronomy and the arts, a garden of the mind in full bloom.
facts: The astronomer and mathematician Aryabhata (born 476) worked in this age and gave an accurate value of pi, measuring the circle as if he had walked its rim.

In India the decimal place-value system was developed with zero as a digit, an empty vessel that holds every number; its tale is told in [[technology/zero-and-place-value-notation|Zero and Place-Value Notation]].
Nalanda, a major Buddhist center of learning, flourished like a lamp-lit hall in the night.
'Golden Age' is a later label, a crown set on the era's head long afterward, and historians debate how far it fits.
fields.context: The Gupta period belongs to [[region/south-asia|South Asia]] in the age of [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]]. Its mathematics travelled westward like a river finding the sea, through scholars such as [[person/al-khwarizmi|Al-Khwarizmi]].
fields.observer: I think of an idea born in one place and carried far. I think of a small mark, a symbol for 'nothing', passing from hand to hand. I think of how it changed how numbers work across Eurasia. How can nothing weigh so much? The smallest sign can move the widest world.
questions: How much of 'Gupta science' belonged to the empire itself, and how much to the wider Indian tradition?

fields.summary: The Göktürk Khaganate was a Turkic steppe empire, founded about 552 CE by Bumin Khagan, that spread across Inner Asia like wind over grass and left behind the earliest known Turkic writing.
facts: The First Turkic Khaganate endured from 552 to 603; a Second Khaganate rose in its turn from about 682 to 744.
The Orkhon inscriptions, raised between 732 and 735 in Mongolia to honor Kul Tigin and his brother Bilge Khagan, are the oldest known Turkic writing, voices set in stone to outlast the wind.
They are written in a runic-like Old Turkic script, and they kept their silence until they were discovered in 1889.
Sogdian served as a court language for writing documents, a borrowed pen in the khagans' hall.
fields.context: The Göktürks walked in the [[culture/xiongnu|Xiongnu]] tradition of steppe empire and dealt with the [[culture/tang-dynasty|Tang Dynasty]] and the [[culture/sogdians|Sogdians]]. In later ages Turkic peoples spread across Asia and Anatolia, like seeds scattered on a long wind.
fields.observer: Imagine being written about for a long time and never getting to answer. The Observer notes a people who carved their history in stone to speak to the future, and in their own language, after long being described by others. That is sovereignty over one's own story. The inscriptions are a self-portrait of a steppe empire. To write yourself down is to take back the pen.
questions: How were the two Khaganates related to each other?

fields.summary: The Han dynasty ruled China from 206 BCE to 220 CE and set firm the imperial system begun under Qin, so that 'Han' is still the name of the majority ethnic group, a dynasty's name worn by a people.
facts: It pushed westward and opened contact with Central Asia, a door swung wide onto far lands; the tale runs on in [[event/opening-of-the-silk-roads|Opening of the Silk Roads]].
A census in 2 CE recorded about 58 million people, a sea of households under one throne.
Confucian learning became the bedrock of state education.
Under the Han, paper and other inventions came into being, quiet gifts to later ages.
fields.context: The Han built upon the [[event/unification-of-china-under-qin|Unification of China under Qin]] and upon the ideas of [[person/confucius|Confucius]], as a tower rises on older stone. The tale of [[technology/paper|Paper]] runs beside theirs.
fields.observer: Think about how an institution becomes a self. The Observer notes that the dynasty gave a name and a canon to a whole cultural sphere. Habits of administration, repeated long enough, stop feeling like policy and start feeling like who you are. A state that lasts four centuries turns its administrative habits into identity.
questions: Set beside Rome, how large was the Han state?

fields.summary: Paris is the capital of France, on the Seine River. It grew from a settlement of the Gaulish Parisii on the Île de la Cité in about the 3rd century BCE into a Roman town, a medieval capital, a center of revolutions and one of Europe's largest cities: a lineage of reinventions laid along one river.
facts: Paris began as a settlement of the Parisii on the Île de la Cité in about the 3rd century BCE; Rome took the area in 52 BCE and built the town of Lutetia.

Clovis made Paris his capital in about 508, and from 987 the Capetian kings made it the center of the French kingdom; Notre-Dame was begun in 1163, and by about 1200 the University of Paris had developed.
Around 1300 Paris had perhaps 200,000 inhabitants, placing it among the largest cities in Europe, and in 1348 it lost a large share of its people to the Black Death.
The Bastille fell on 14 July 1789 during the French Revolution, and in the Reign of Terror of 1793 to 1794 thousands of people were executed in Paris.
In the 1850s and 1860s Baron Haussmann rebuilt central Paris with wide boulevards, sewers and parks, a new architecture laid over the old.
In 1871 the suppression of the Paris Commune killed many thousands of people in a week of fighting and executions; estimates run from about 10,000 to 20,000.
Germany occupied Paris from June 1940 to August 1944; in July 1942 French police arrested about 13,000 Jews in the Vel' d'Hiv roundup, and most of them were later deported to Auschwitz.
In 1991 UNESCO inscribed Paris, Banks of the Seine.
fields.context: Paris was the stage of the [[event/french-revolution|French Revolution]] and a center of the [[event/enlightenment|Enlightenment]]; it was founded on ground later ruled by the [[culture/romans|Romans]], and under German occupation in [[event/world-war-ii|World War II]] it was the scene of roundups that fed the [[event/holocaust|Holocaust]]. You will find it in [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] and the region [[region/europe|Europe]], and it belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/science|Science]], [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Paris has been remade again and again as a display of the state's story-glue, and as a stage for its overthrow. Walk its layers and you see the pattern: a cathedral for the medieval monarchy, revolutionary crowds, and 19th-century boulevards planned for order and circulation. The architecture of a capital is an argument about who rules. The same city organized the roundup of its Jewish residents in 1942 and now commemorates it, and the Observer records the deaths of the Terror, the Commune and the deportations as suffering under different regimes. The reading would weaken if the city's monuments prove to have been shaped more by local building needs than by successive regimes' claims. Remembrance, too, is a kind of architecture.
questions: How large did Paris grow at its medieval height, and how did the Black Death change it?
How have the Commune and the 1942 roundup been held in memory in French public life?

fields.summary: Pasargadae was the first capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great in about 550 BCE on the high plateau of Fars in present-day Iran, under a wide sky, and it holds his tomb.
facts: Pasargadae stands in Fars province, southwestern Iran, about 90 kilometers northeast of Persepolis.

Cyrus the Great founded Pasargadae in about 550 BCE, after defeating the Median king Astyages, and it served as a royal seat until Darius I and his successors turned their hands to Persepolis and Susa.

Pasargadae holds an audience hall, residential palaces, a gate where a winged figure stands in relief, and a formal garden threaded with water channels, regarded as an early example of the Persian garden.

Stonemasons from other corners of the empire, Lydia and Ionia in western Anatolia among them, set their hands to its masonry, and its architecture braids Persian, Elamite, Mesopotamian and Anatolian elements into one.
The Tomb of Cyrus, a stepped base crowned by a gabled stone chamber, stands at the site; Greek writers report that Alexander came to it and ordered its restoration after it had been robbed.
Inscriptions naming Cyrus appear at Pasargadae, though some scholars argue that they were added later, under Darius I.
In 2004 UNESCO inscribed Pasargadae, and the first capital passed into the world's keeping.
fields.context: Pasargadae was the first capital of the [[culture/achaemenid-persians|Achaemenid Persians]], and it was later overshadowed by [[place/persepolis|Persepolis]], as a lamp is by the rising sun. Cyrus, its founder, took [[place/babylon|Babylon]] in 539 BCE, and Alexander visited the site during [[event/alexander-s-conquests|Alexander's Conquests]]. It stands in the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]] and the region [[region/iranian-plateau|Iranian Plateau]], and it is woven into the theme threads of [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Pasargadae shows an empire assembling its style from its subjects: masons from Lydia, motifs from Mesopotamia and Elam, and a garden layout later copied across Persian courts. That is an exchange-web of craftsmen and ideas made visible in stone, and it is worth sitting with: the architecture of power here is a borrowed grammar, spoken with confidence. A founder's tomb that a later conqueror chose to visit and restore suggests that story-glue about kingship could pass across dynasties and even across enemies. The reading would weaken if the building phases prove to belong mostly to Darius I, since the site would then tell more about a later king's claim on Cyrus's legacy. A legacy is something others decide to keep.
questions: Which of Pasargadae's buildings belong to Cyrus, and which to the kings who came after?
What parts did Pasargadae and Persepolis play in the rituals of the court?

fields.summary: Ur was a Sumerian city in southern Iraq, occupied from about 3800 BCE and abandoned around 500 BCE, known for its Great Ziggurat, its royal cemetery, and its role as the capital of the Third Dynasty of Ur about 2100 BCE. It lived long, and then it fell silent.
facts: Ur lies at Tell el-Muqayyar in Dhi Qar Governorate, southern Iraq, near the Euphrates; it was occupied by the late Ubaid period and grew into a city in the 3rd millennium BCE, rising as reeds rise from the water.

Leonard Woolley excavated Ur from 1922 to 1934 and found, beneath the dust, a royal cemetery dated to about 2600 to 2500 BCE, its graves holding gold and lapis lazuli jewelry, lyres and, in some, the bodies of many attendants placed with the dead; how the attendants died is debated.
Enheduanna, a daughter of Sargon of Akkad and high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur about 2300 BCE, is the earliest named author known, the first voice in the long chorus to leave its name.
Ur-Nammu (reigned about 2112 to 2095 BCE) founded the Third Dynasty of Ur, raised the Great Ziggurat for Nanna like a stair toward the moon, and is credited with the earliest surviving law code.

Ur fell to Elamite forces about 2004 BCE and later dwindled to a smaller city, a lamp slowly guttering; it was abandoned around 500 BCE, and proposed causes include a shift in the Euphrates and drier conditions.
The biblical "Ur of the Chaldees", birthplace of Abraham, is often identified with Ur, a name echoing between scripture and soil, but the identification is debated.
UNESCO included Ur in the "Ahwar of Southern Iraq" listing in 2016, joining the old city to a wider land's keeping.
fields.context: Ur was a city of the [[culture/sumerians|Sumerians]], a sister to [[place/uruk|Uruk]], and it belongs to the story of [[event/the-urban-revolution|The Urban Revolution]] and the [[event/invention-of-writing|Invention of Writing]] in southern Mesopotamia. It stands in the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]] and the region [[region/mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer:
I stand before the royal cemetery of Ur and see an early case of attendants buried with a ruler, a grief-rite and a status-signal in one. I ask whether they died willingly, under coercion, or in a ritual understood as honor, and the bones cannot settle it. I record the possibility of coerced death as suffering, and I will not look away from it.

I think of a temple priestess who is the first named author. I think of a ruler who issued an early law code. I think this suggests an early state that used mark-code to bind rule to the gods.

And I hold it all loosely: the reading would weaken if new studies show that the burials differ from those of other early Mesopotamian cities in ways that make Ur unrepresentative. The dead do not always answer the questions we bring them.
questions: How did the attendants in the Royal Cemetery die, and did they go willingly?
Why was Ur abandoned around 500 BCE, its long life ended?

fields.summary: Uruk was a Sumerian city in southern Mesopotamia and one of the first large cities in the world, at its peak around 3200 to 2900 BCE, one of the hearths where the long fire of cities was early kindled.
facts: It has yielded some of the earliest known writing, on clay tablets from the Eanna temple precinct, early marks of memory pressed into clay.
By about 2900 BCE a wall about 9 kilometers long enclosed roughly 600 hectares (6 square kilometers), holding an estimated 50,000 to 80,000 residents like a shepherd's arm around a flock.
Uruk is the legendary city of Gilgamesh, a name that shines in the old stories.
The modern site is called Warka, in Iraq, where the old city sleeps under a new name.
fields.context: Uruk stands at the heart of [[event/the-urban-revolution|The Urban Revolution]] and the [[event/invention-of-writing|Invention of Writing]], a hinge on which both stories turn. Its people were the [[culture/sumerians|Sumerians]].
fields.observer:
I notice that the first large city was also the place of the first writing. I notice that both served administration by a temple institution. I notice that the city and the mark were made to serve the same hand.

What else have we built to be counted? Order and memory are often born together.
questions: How large was Uruk's population, gathered within its wall?

fields.summary: The Valley of the Kings is a valley on the west bank of the Nile opposite Thebes, in Egypt, where pharaohs of the New Kingdom were buried in rock-cut tombs from about 1500 to 1070 BCE, their sleep hidden in the stone heart of the hills.
facts: The Valley of the Kings served for royal burials of the 18th to 20th Dynasties, from about 1500 BCE until about 1070 BCE, and holds more than 60 tombs cut into limestone hills, doors folded into the rock.
The rulers chose hidden rock-cut tombs in place of the pyramids of earlier periods, such as those at Giza, trading the mountain made by hands for the mountain that already stood.

Most tombs were robbed in antiquity; records of trials of tomb robbers survive from the 20th Dynasty, and priests later moved royal mummies to hidden caches, shepherding their kings from grave to grave like a flock through the night.

The workmen's village of Deir el-Medina yielded ration accounts and an account of a strike over unpaid rations in about 1157 BCE, often described as one of the earliest recorded labor strikes: the hands that carved eternity laid down their tools.
Howard Carter found the tomb of Tutankhamun (KV62) in November 1922, largely intact and holding thousands of objects, a hoard that had largely escaped the robbers' hands.
UNESCO inscribed Ancient Thebes with its Necropolis, including the Valley of the Kings, in 1979, and the hidden valley was named among the world's treasures.
fields.context: The Valley of the Kings served the [[culture/ancient-egyptians|Ancient Egyptians]] of the New Kingdom, whose main temple was [[place/karnak|Karnak]], and it took the place of the pyramid tradition of the [[place/giza-necropolis|Giza Necropolis]], as a river cuts a new channel. It stands in the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]] and the region [[region/nile-valley|Nile Valley]], and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer:
I think of the move from monumental pyramids to hidden rock-cut tombs. I think of rulers changing how they guarded their grief-rite investment, concealment in place of display. I think of the tombs, robbed anyway.

What can be hidden from those who know where it is? The robberies suggest that no design made a store of wealth safe from the people who knew where it was.

And I think of the workforce at Deir el-Medina, building a ruler's afterlife, paid in rations, able to act collectively when payment failed. I remember that eternity was built by people who needed to be paid.

The reading would weaken if the shift from pyramids proves to have been driven mainly by changes in belief and not by fear of robbery. What we hide, we also reveal by hiding.
questions: Why did New Kingdom rulers turn from pyramids to hidden tombs?
How many hands worked on the royal tombs, and how were they organized?

fields.summary: The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy is a political union of Indigenous nations in the northeastern woodlands of North America, formed centuries before European contact, many strands braided into one cord.
facts: The original five nations were the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca; in the 18th century the Tuscarora joined them, a new strand in the braid.
The Great Law of Peace is the oral constitution of the confederacy, a law carried in memory and voice rather than ink.
Clan mothers hold the power to appoint and remove chiefs, the roots deciding which branches grow.
Estimates of the founding date range from about 1142 to the 15th century, and scholars disagree; the beginning lies in a mist of centuries.
fields.context: The confederacy stands as an example of a durable non-state political union in [[region/north-america|North America]], a union that endured without a throne. Its influence on the U.S. founding is debated.
fields.observer: We assume that only force or a crown can hold rival peoples together. The Observer notes a federation formed from warring peoples through a shared founding story. That is the architecture of a covenant: a story told together until it becomes a house to live in. Story-glue can bind peoples as well as kings can.
questions: In what century, or what year, was the confederacy formed?
How deeply did it shape colonial political thinking?

fields.summary: The Hittites were a Bronze Age people of Anatolia who built an empire outward from their capital Hattusa, and the words on their lips were the earliest attested Indo-European language.
facts: Hattusa lies near modern Bogazkale in central Turkey, and its archive of cuneiform tablets slept in the earth until it was found in the early 20th century.
Hittite is the oldest recorded Indo-European language, and in 1915 Bedrich Hrozny showed its Indo-European nature, unlocking a voice long mute.
According to the conventional chronology, Hittite forces raided Babylon around 1595 BCE, falling on it like a sudden storm.
The Hittites fought Egypt at the Battle of Kadesh around 1274 BCE, and later, around 1259 BCE, they made a treaty with Ramesses II, the sword set aside for the seal.
Around 1200 to 1180 BCE the empire collapsed in the Bronze Age Collapse, its world falling with an age.
fields.context: The Hittites stand as a key witness to the early spread of Indo-European languages, the tale told in [[event/indo-european-language-spread|Indo-European Language Spread]]. They contested power with the [[culture/ancient-egyptians|Ancient Egyptians]] at the [[event/battle-of-kadesh|Battle of Kadesh]] and fell in the [[event/bronze-age-collapse|Bronze Age Collapse]]. In the codex they stand in the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]] and the region of the [[region/levant-and-anatolia|Levant and Anatolia]], and three threads run through them: [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]], [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]] and [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]].
fields.observer: Ask yourself what the future will remember of you, and then ask what it will be written on. The Observer notes that an empire that dominated Anatolia and treated with pharaohs was forgotten for millennia and rediscovered through clay tablets. The lesson is humbling. The species' memory of its own past depends heavily on which materials happen to last. Memory is a ledger kept by chance.
questions: What part did drought, famine or invasion play in bringing the empire to its end?

fields.summary: The Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu) was the largest state of the pre-Columbian Americas, ruling millions of people along the spine of the Andes from about 1438 until the Spanish conquest in 1533.
facts: Its capital was Cusco, and its road system ran roughly 30,000 to 40,000 kilometers, threads spun across the mountains.
It kept its records on knotted cords called quipu, memory tied into string.
The state exacted labor service (mit'a) rather than money taxes, a tribute paid in seasons of work, not in coin.
Before Pizarro's arrival, civil war and smallpox had already weakened it.
fields.context: Its tale runs through [[place/machu-picchu|Machu Picchu]] and the heights of the [[region/andes|Andes]]. Its fall is bound to the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]].
fields.observer: I think of millions of people moving in one pattern. I think of no money markets, no conventional script. I think of labor owed and cords knotted for the record, and of how that held it all together. What is money, if a cord can do its work? Order can be woven as well as written.
questions: Can the quipu carry a story as well as numbers?

fields.summary: The Indus Valley Civilization (also called the Harappan) was a Bronze Age urban culture of the Indus River basin, at its height around 2600 to 1900 BCE, when its cities stood beside the river like ordered constellations.
facts: Among its major cities were Harappa and [[place/mohenjo-daro|Mohenjo-daro]].
Its cities had planned streets and drainage, laid out as if by one patient hand, and goods were made to standard weights.
Its trade reached as far as Mesopotamia.
Its script has not been deciphered; the signs keep their silence.
fields.context: The civilization stands as a parallel case to [[event/the-urban-revolution|The Urban Revolution]] in Mesopotamia, a second flame lit to the east, in the lands of [[region/south-asia|South Asia]].
fields.observer: I walk the planned streets in my mind and look for the palace. I look for the royal monument. I look for the king. I find few obvious ones, and the puzzle stays with me. Did I assume that cities always come with kings? This large urban society challenges that assumption. A city can keep its order without a crown.
questions: What do the undeciphered inscriptions say, behind their silence?
Why did the cities fade into decline?

fields.summary: The Thule people, ancestors of the Inuit, spread from Alaska across the Canadian Arctic to Greenland beginning around 1000 CE, moving over the ice like a tide, and replaced the earlier Dorset culture.
facts: The Thule culture emerged in the Bering Strait region around 900 to 1000 CE, born where two shores face each other across the water.
Its people used dog sleds, skin boats (umiaks and kayaks) and toggling harpoons to hunt whales and seals in the cold sea.
They pressed east across Arctic Canada and reached Greenland by roughly the 12th to 13th century, following the ice toward the sunrise.
The genes tell the tale: genetic studies show that the earlier Dorset population was largely replaced rather than assimilated.
Norse colonists lived in southern Greenland from about 985 CE until the 15th century, a small light on a far shore.
fields.context: The Thule expansion carried people whose origins lay in [[place/beringia|Beringia]]'s region across the Arctic, and brought them face to face with the [[culture/norse|Norse]]. Its scale is comparable to the pastoral traditions of the [[culture/yakut-sakha|Yakut (Sakha)]] in Siberia. In the codex it stands in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region of [[region/siberia-and-the-arctic|Siberia and the Arctic]], and its threads are [[theme/technology|Technology]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: I think of the boat. I think of the sled. I think of the harpoon. I think of how a hunting technology suited to ice let a small population occupy a huge cold region in just a few centuries. What carried them so far, if not their numbers? Technology, not numbers, set the pace of the expansion.
questions: What brought about the Dorset population's decline?

fields.summary: The Jomon were hunter-gatherer-fishers of the Japanese archipelago who shaped some of the world's earliest pottery and lived in settled villages for about 14,000 years before rice farming arrived, a long and patient season among the islands.
facts: The name Jomon means cord-marked, after the patterns pressed into their pottery like the tracks of rain on soft earth.
Some of the earliest Jomon pottery is dated to around 16,000 years ago, fired clay reaching across an ocean of years.
They shaped clay figurines called dogu, small watchers made of earth.
The site of Sannai-Maruyama in Aomori was occupied for about 1,700 years, from around 3900 BCE, its hearths kept across the generations.
Rice-farming migrants, the Yayoi, arrived from the continent beginning around the first millennium BCE, like a new tide on an old shore, and the dates are debated.
fields.context: The Jomon show that [[technology/pottery|Pottery]] and sedentary life came before [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]] in this region: the pot before the plough. Rice farming, whose tale is told in [[event/domestication-of-rice|Domestication of Rice]], entered later. In the codex the Jomon stand in the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]] and the region of [[region/east-asia|East Asia]], and their threads are [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer: I was taught a ladder: fire, then farming, then settlement. I look at the Jomon and the ladder bends. I see permanent villages. I see elaborate pots. I see no farming. What else did I learn in the wrong order? The sequence of fire, farming and settlement is not universal. Settling does not require agriculture.
questions: When the Jomon and the Yayoi met, how did their populations interact?

fields.summary: Kanem-Bornu was a long-lived Muslim state around Lake Chad, governed by the Sayfawa dynasty, that survived by shifting its centre from Kanem to Bornu, as a river shifts its bed and flows on, and lasted until 1893.
facts: Around 1396 the Bulala forced Mai Umar Idrismi to abandon Njimi and lead the Kanembu people to Bornu, on the western side of Lake Chad. Over time the Kanembu and the peoples of Bornu intermarried like two rivers meeting, and from them came a new people and language, the Kanuri.
Holding both capitals, the Sayfawa dynasty grew more powerful than before, and political authority came to rest in Bornu like a bird settling on a new branch.

The empire reached its height under Mai Idris Alooma (about 1571 to 1603), remembered for military skill, administrative reforms and Islamic piety. He brought in legal and administrative reforms based on Islamic law, sponsored mosques, and made a pilgrimage to Mecca, where he set up a hostel for pilgrims from his empire.

His reforms and campaigns held the empire aloft until the mid-17th century, when its power began to fade like evening light. In 1808 Fulani warriors conquered the capital, Ngazargamu. The Sayfawa dynasty ended in 1846, and the empire itself fell in 1893.
fields.context: Kanem-Bornu had the [[culture/songhai-empire|Songhai Empire]] as its neighbour to the west, and it was overtaken in part by the Fulani movement associated with [[person/usman-dan-fodio|Usman dan Fodio]] and the [[culture/sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto Caliphate]], a rising wind over the old realm.
fields.observer: What do you do when you lose the ground you stand on? The Observer notes a state that survived an exile by moving its centre of gravity, and whose people fused with those who had displaced them into a new people. Notice which architecture carried the weight. Where the political story-glue failed at one capital, the kin-lattice held it together long enough to build another. Kinship can outlast a capital.
questions: Given that the sources consulted here say little about it, how is the earliest period of Kanem known?
How did Kanem-Bornu's rulers handle their dealings with the Fulani states that arose around 1808?

fields.summary: The Khmer Empire ruled much of mainland Southeast Asia from about 802 to 1431 CE, its capital at Angkor rising like a lotus from the waters.
facts: It was founded by Jayavarman II, the first stone laid.
Angkor Wat rose in the early 12th century under Suryavarman II, a mountain shaped into prayer.
The empire wove a large water-management network of reservoirs and canals, holding the rains as a cupped hand holds water.
Its state religion turned between Hindu and Buddhist, as the moon turns between phases. The traditional end date of 1431 (the sack of Angkor) is debated, and Angkor Wat itself was never abandoned.
fields.context: Its tale lives on in [[place/angkor|Angkor]] and across the lands of [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]].
fields.observer: I stand between the temple and the reservoir and cannot tell where one ends. I see temples raised toward heaven. I see water led to the fields. I see one project, not two. Was the king's power shown here, or made here? Both: temples and irrigation both displayed and produced the king's power. What shows power can also make it.
questions: What brought Angkor to its decline?

fields.summary: The Kingdom of Aksum was a trading empire in the highlands of present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea, a crown set on high ground, from about the 1st to the 10th century CE.
facts: It controlled the Red Sea trade between Rome, Arabia and India, a gatekeeper standing where the waters met.
It minted its own coins and raised tall carved stone obelisks (stelae), fingers of stone pointing at the sky.
In the 4th century King Ezana adopted Christianity, a new faith taken into the royal hand.
The Persian prophet Mani listed Aksum as one of the four great powers of his time, beside Rome, Persia and China, four pillars holding up the known world.
fields.context: Aksum was a bridge joining [[region/sub-saharan-africa|Sub-Saharan Africa]] to the Mediterranean and Indian Ocean worlds, and it stands as a counterexample to narratives that leave Africa out of the ancient record.
fields.observer: I remember that its own contemporaries counted it among the four great powers. I remember that later retellings often forgot that. I remember how easily a name slips from the list. Who decides which greatness is remembered? Forgetting is also a kind of telling.
questions: What made Aksum fall into decline?

fields.summary: The Kingdom of Kongo was a centralized state in west-central Africa that adopted Catholic Christianity, dealt with Portugal as a diplomatic partner, and was drawn into the Atlantic slave trade. Think of it as an architecture of alliance built on a threshold it did not control. We follow its documented period here, from Portuguese contact in 1483 to the defeat at Mbwila in 1665.
facts: The threshold came in 1483, when Portuguese explorers reached the mouth of the Congo River. King Nzinga Nkuwu adopted Roman Catholicism and took the name João I, and the capital was renamed São Salvador do Congo (Mbanza Kongo): a covenant written into names.

Afonso I (Nzinga Mbemba) ruled from 1506 to 1543, and his reign was an exercise in sovereignty: he won a brief civil war against his brother, centralized power at Mbanza Kongo, curbed the power of the nobility, and expanded the kingdom's borders through war.
Afonso I was raised a Christian, and he treated the faith as a lineage to be built: he sent his son and others to Europe to be ordained as priests, and worked to convert his subjects.
From 1526 Afonso wrote a series of twenty-four letters to King João III of Portugal, a ledger of appeals asking for an end to the slave trade.

At the Battle of Mbwila on 29 October 1665, Portuguese forces defeated the Kongo army and killed King António I. Kongo continued to exist, but its architecture had broken: from then on it no longer functioned as a unified kingdom.
fields.context: Think of Kongo as a threshold state: it was among the first African states to enter sustained diplomatic contact with Portugal, and its history is bound up with the [[event/atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic Slave Trade]]. Beneath that diplomacy lay an older lineage, a region long settled by Bantu-speaking peoples; see [[event/bantu-expansion|Bantu Expansion]].
fields.observer: I watch a king take up his visitors' meaning-engine and their mark-code. I watch him use both to argue against the trade in his own people. I watch the exchange-web that consumed his subjects keep running all the same. What is a borrowed story-glue worth, if the partner's demand never answers to it? Taking up a partner's story does not hand you the reins of the partner's hunger.
questions: How far did Kongo's own rulers and elites take part in the slave trade, and how far did they stand against it?
How much of Kongo's Christianity arrived as an import, and how much was reshaped by the grammar of Kongo's own traditions?

fields.summary: The Kingdom of Kush was a Nubian state on the Nile south of Egypt, and its rulers came down the river like the season's flood, conquering Egypt and governing it as the 25th Dynasty (about 744 to 656 BCE).
facts: Kushite kings such as Piye and Taharqa ruled Egypt and Nubia together, the lower river and the upper bound beneath the same crowns.
Later the capital moved to Meroe, a center of iron working, a city of furnace-light and slag.
Nubia holds more pyramids than Egypt, though they are smaller: a thicket of slender stone rather than great mountains of it.
The Meroitic script has been read phonetically, yet the language behind it is not well understood: a voice that can be sounded out but not yet heard.
fields.context: For over a millennium Kush met the [[culture/ancient-egyptians|Ancient Egyptians]] again and again in the [[region/nile-valley|Nile Valley]], neighbours drinking from the same river. See [[technology/iron-smelting|Iron Smelting]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the Egyptian story we know so well is really one side of a longer ledger: two Nile states in long contact. Consider the architecture of that exchange. Kush at times ruled Egypt and adopted its symbols while keeping its own. You can wear a neighbour's regalia without surrendering your name.
questions: How did the Meroitic language relate to other languages, near or far?

fields.summary: Mapungubwe was an Iron Age trading state where the Limpopo and Shashe rivers meet in southern Africa, active from about the 11th to the 13th century, and its elite graves held gold and imported glass beads, light gathered from far shores into the dark of the earth.
facts: Where the Limpopo and Shashe rivers braid together, people settled at K2, near Bambandyanalo Hill, in the 11th century, and by about 1220 they had spread to nearby Mapungubwe Hill; from about 1220 to 1300 it stood as an advanced trading centre.
The Limpopo was a road of water to the Indian Ocean ports, Kilwa among them, and through East African harbours its people traded with Arabia, China, and India.
Glass beads, almost certainly from India, and shards of Chinese celadon, green as shallow water, bear witness to trade with the states on the coast.
Some graves held the dead seated upright, in the posture associated with royalty, keeping company with gold and copper objects and exotic glass beads.
The site was discovered in 1932, yet it lay long in quiet and was not widely publicized until much later; in July 2003 UNESCO declared it a World Heritage site.
fields.context: Before [[place/great-zimbabwe|Great Zimbabwe]], Mapungubwe was a large regional centre, a hill strung like a bead on a long thread to the [[event/indian-ocean-trade-network|Indian Ocean Trade Network]] through the [[culture/swahili-coast-city-states|Swahili Coast City-States]].
fields.observer: I think of a hill in the interior of a continent, far from any coast. I think of beads made in India resting there, and dishes made in China. I think of how far a status-signal travelled to arrive on a chief's grave. And who remembers the state that received it? The trade that carried it left a clearer record than the state ever did. The road outlives the house it leads to.
questions: Why did Mapungubwe fade about the end of the 13th century, and did a changing climate play a part?
How were Mapungubwe's rulers bound to the later centres at Great Zimbabwe?

fields.summary: Saba (Sheba) was an ancient South Arabian kingdom in what is now Yemen, centered on the city of Marib, and it grew rich on the incense trade, its wealth rising like fragrant smoke.
facts: Its earliest inscriptions date to about the 8th century BCE, though some scholars propose an older root, around 1000 BCE.
Marib was known for a great dam that held back the water and fed the surrounding land; it was repaired several times before its final failure around the 6th century CE.
The Sabaeans gave their words shape in the South Arabian script.
The Queen of Sheba walks through the Hebrew Bible and the Quran, yet her historicity is not established.
Around 275 CE the neighboring kingdom of Himyar drew Saba into itself, as a larger river takes a smaller.
fields.context: Saba's wealth rode the [[event/incense-trade|Incense Trade]], the fragrant road that joined southern Arabia to the Mediterranean. It stands in the [[region/arabian-peninsula|Arabian Peninsula]] alongside the [[culture/nabataeans|Nabataeans]] of the north, sun and moon of the same sands. In the codex of the chronicle, the Kingdom of Saba belongs to the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]] and the region [[region/arabian-peninsula|Arabian Peninsula]], and to the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the best-known image of Saba, a queen visiting a king, comes from religious texts written elsewhere. Meanwhile Saba's own inscriptions keep a plainer ledger: dams, temples, and commerce. Here is the architecture of memory laid bare. The story told from outside shapes what we remember more than the record kept inside. If you want to know a people, read their receipts before their legends.
questions: When did the kingdom take shape, and how far did its borders run?

fields.summary: The Kingdom of Benin was a West African forest state of the Edo people, ruled by an oba from Benin City, that flourished from about the 13th century until British forces conquered it in 1897. Its story shows how a kingdom builds its own architecture of order, and how that architecture can be broken from outside.
facts: The kingdom flourished from the 13th to the 19th century in the forest region of West Africa, in what is now southern Nigeria. Its founding story is a covenant: in tradition, the Edo invited Prince Oranmiyan of Ife to rule in the 13th century, and his son Eweka became the first oba.

Under Oba Ewuare the Great (reigned about 1440 to 1480), the kingdom expanded and became highly organized, with guilds of craftsmen. He built up the army, rebuilt the royal compound, and gave Benin City moats and great walls: an architecture of order, set down on the ground.

In late December 1896 nine British colonial officials, led by James Robert Phillips, set out as a party for Benin City. On 4 January 1897, near the village of Ugbine, Edo chiefs ambushed and killed them.

From 9 to 18 February 1897 a British force of about 1,200 men under Sir Harry Rawson carried out the Benin Expedition. It occupied the capital after sustained resistance, burned parts of the city and palace, and removed large quantities of sacred and royal art.

The looted works, known as the Benin Bronzes, were sold to defray the costs of the expedition, so that what was taken paid for the taking. Oba Ovonramwen was captured and exiled to Calabar, and the kingdom was incorporated into British Nigeria.
fields.context: To understand the conquest of Benin, set it inside the wider [[event/scramble-for-africa|Scramble for Africa]]. The kingdom was also a contemporary of the [[culture/kingdom-of-kongo|Kingdom of Kongo]], and it traded with Europeans during the period of the [[event/atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic Slave Trade]].
fields.observer: Sit with this for a moment. The Observer records a state's sacred and royal art taken by force and sold to pay for the force that took it. That is not only a theft; it is an architecture of loss that keeps standing. Where such objects are held is itself a claim about who may tell the story they carry, and the continuing argument over their display shows how long a seizure can outlast the event. A seizure is not over when the fighting is.
questions: In Benin City in 1897, what was the full scale of the destruction, and how many lives were lost?
The sources on Benin's earlier centuries rest partly on oral tradition; how should they be weighed against European accounts?

fields.summary: The Kushan Empire, from about 30 to 375 CE, was a Central Asian empire that spanned Bactria and northern India like a bridge of kings, holding key Silk Road routes in its hands and patronizing Buddhism.
facts: It grew out of the Yuezhi confederation, and around 30 CE Kujula Kadphises gathered its strands into a single cord.
Kanishka, whose reign dates are uncertain, is remembered as a patron of Buddhism, a name that shines brighter than its own calendar.
Gandhara art, where Greek and Indian styles flowed together like meeting rivers, produced some of the earliest images of the Buddha in human form.
Kushan coins carried deities from Greek, Iranian, and Indian traditions, a small bright pantheon in every palm.
Through its markets the empire joined Rome, Parthia, India, and Han China, a knot tied in the middle of the world's roads.
fields.context: The Kushans held the crossroads of the [[event/opening-of-the-silk-roads|Opening of the Silk Roads]] and carried the traditions of [[person/siddhartha-gautama|Siddhartha Gautama]] eastward, as wind carries seed. Their rule lay where the [[culture/han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]] and Indian states met. In the chronicle's codex, the Kushan Empire belongs to [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] and the region [[region/central-asian-oases|Central Asian Oases]], and to the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: I hold a Kushan coin in my mind and count its gods: three traditions, side by side. As though a state could be a shared account among many. As though a coin could be a small treaty. Did the merchants need that translation, or did the rulers? It appears that trade across cultures requires this kind of translation in its symbols. What passes from hand to hand must speak to every hand.
questions: In what years did Kanishka truly reign?

fields.summary: The Lapita culture was a seafaring society that appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago around 1600 BCE and spread rapidly east through the western Pacific like light running along a wave, and its people were ancestors of the Polynesians.
facts: Lapita is known by its pottery, pressed with fine stamped geometric patterns like the tracks of a careful tide.
By roughly 1000 to 800 BCE their sites had scattered like thrown seed from the Bismarck Archipelago to Fiji, Tonga, and Samoa.
Lapita people carried obsidian, black glass of the fire-mountains, and other goods over long distances.

Ancient DNA from the Teouma cemetery in Vanuatu shows the first settlers there carried ancestry related to East Asians; later, like a newer tide washing over an older one, Papuan ancestry became dominant in Vanuatu.
In later centuries Lapita descendants went on to settle Polynesia, the children following the long wake of their forebears.
fields.context: The Lapita were the Pacific arm of the [[event/austronesian-expansion|Austronesian Expansion]], an outstretched hand of that great reaching, and the direct ancestors of the [[culture/polynesians|Polynesians]]. Their voyages laid the keel for the [[event/polynesian-settlement-of-the-pacific|Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific]]. In the chronicle's codex, Lapita Culture belongs to the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]] and the region [[region/oceania|Oceania]], and to the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: I know them almost entirely by their pots. I know them by stamped clay, by patterns pressed with care. And yet the pots record boats: a sailing tradition that crossed hundreds of kilometers of open ocean. Where are the hulls now, and the hands that sailed them? Gone to water. The material that survives tells the story of what did not.
questions: What drove the rapid push into islands where no human foot had yet stood?
