In 296 the emperor Diocletian ordered Manichaean leaders burned with their scriptures, and Roman and Persian persecution had largely ended the faith in the west by the sixth century.

In China the anti-Buddhist persecution of 843 also seized Manichaean property and executed clergy, and by the 14th century the religion had faded into Buddhism and Daoism, like a river lost in the sea.
fields.context: Manichaeism arose in [[region/mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]] during [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]], within the Sasanian Empire (not yet a vault note), drawing on ideas it shared with [[culture/zoroastrianism|Zoroastrianism]] before it spread as far as the China of the [[culture/tang-dynasty|Tang Dynasty]]. See [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer:
I think of a meaning-engine assembled from older traditions. I think of it crossing Eurasia in four centuries along the trade routes. I think of Roman, Persian and Chinese states suppressing it, each for its own stated reasons. And still it survived roughly a thousand years under official persecution nearly everywhere it took root. How does a faith of light live so long in the dark?

A specialist could argue that its decline in China reflects absorption into Buddhism and Daoism as much as suppression, which would weaken a reading of persecution as the sole cause of its extinction. I can hold that. Not every ending is an erasure. Some are a dissolving.
questions: How much of Manichaeism's decline in China was suppression, and how much absorption into other traditions?
How consistent did Manichaean teaching remain across regions as different as Rome, Persia and China?

fields.summary: The Marajoara culture flourished on Marajo Island at the mouth of the Amazon, where the great river meets the sea, and it is known for large earthen mounds and richly decorated ceramics; its ceramic tradition is dated about 400 to 1300 CE.
facts: Marajo Island is roughly the size of Switzerland, and there, around 300 CE, mound building began, earth lifted toward the sky.
Mounds rise up to about 20 meters, like islands within the island, and the largest multi-mound sites may have housed several thousand people.
Ceramics include burial urns, figurines, and vessels painted and incised as intricately as braided rivers, suggesting specialized craft production.
By about 1350 CE the mounds had largely been abandoned, left to the grass and the rain.
fields.context: See [[event/amazonian-urbanism-and-dark-earths|Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths]]. Whether the mound-building Marajoara were a complex chiefdom, sustained without intensive farming, is a question scholars have debated.
fields.observer: I think of a plain that floods with the seasons, and of the Marajoara raising their own hills upon it. Where there was no living space, they built earth up until there was. What would I raise, if the water came for my ground? Some homes are found. Others have to be made.
questions: Were the Marajoara chiefdoms, or did they build something more complex?

fields.summary: The Maurya Empire (322 to 185 BCE) was the first empire to unite most of the Indian subcontinent, gathering it the way a monsoon gathers rivers, and its capital stood at Pataliputra.
facts: It was founded by Chandragupta Maurya, and from his hand the new realm took its shape.
It reached its high noon under [[person/ashoka|Ashoka]], who ruled about 268 to 232 BCE.
The Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft traditionally attributed to Kautilya, is associated with the empire, though its date is debated, drifting like a lantern on dark water.
After Ashoka's successors, the empire fragmented like a riverbank in flood.
fields.context: The Maurya Empire ruled [[region/south-asia|South Asia]] in [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] and helped carry Buddhism outward; see [[person/siddhartha-gautama|Siddhartha Gautama]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Ashoka's edicts show a state consciously trying to govern by moral persuasion as well as force. Think of a rule explained rather than only enforced: the rule is the same, but the covenant is different. Persuasion is power too, built to a different architecture.
questions: How centralized, in truth, was Maurya rule?

fields.summary: Nan Madol is a ruined city of artificial stone islets raised in a lagoon off Pohnpei, in the Federated States of Micronesia; from about the 12th century until around 1628 it was the ceremonial and political heart of the Saudeleur dynasty, a seat of power set upon the tide.
facts: Nan Madol is made of about 92 artificial islets of stacked basalt columns and coral fill, threaded together by tidal canals across a core area of about 1.5 by 0.5 kilometers.

Human activity at the site reaches back as early as the 1st or 2nd century CE; islet construction began in the 8th or 9th century, and the megalithic stonework that gives the site its present form rose from about 1180 to 1200.

Tradition holds that the Saudeleur dynasty ruled Pohnpei from Nan Madol, gathering an estimated population of about 25,000 on the island under one rule, though the people living at Nan Madol itself probably numbered under 1,000.
Around 1628, tradition says, a warrior named Isokelekel came as an invader and ended Saudeleur rule; some scholars also point to population decline as a contributing cause of the site's abandonment.
In 2016 UNESCO inscribed Nan Madol as a World Heritage Site, its stones entered on the roll of the world's inheritance.
fields.context: Nan Madol's builders belonged to the wider settlement of the Pacific carried by the [[event/austronesian-expansion|Austronesian Expansion]] and the [[event/polynesian-settlement-of-the-pacific|Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific]], and Micronesian voyaging traditions share roots with cultures such as the [[culture/lapita-culture|Lapita Culture]] farther south and east, as streams share a spring. In the codex of ages it sits in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/oceania|Oceania]], and it belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer:
I see a lagoon turned into a claim-line. A ruling lineage built its seat on stone islets, separated from the rest of the island by water, and I know that gesture: the status-signal that sets the center of power physically apart from those it rules. I have seen the high wall. I have seen the locked gate. I have seen the water that says *not you*.

And the tradition of Isokelekel's conquest? Like many founding and ending stories, it is ancestor-weight carried forward by the community rather than a document, and I hold it as a claim to be tested rather than a settled fact. I would have to set my reading down if archaeology shows the site's decline came mainly from environmental or demographic causes rather than conquest. What we carry forward is not always what happened; it is what we could not put down.
questions: How much of the Isokelekel tradition remembers an actual conquest, and how much is later legend woven to explain the end of Saudeleur rule?
Given Pohnpei's small population, how was the labor organized to move the basalt columns and stack them, weight upon weight?

fields.summary: The Nazca Lines are a group of geoglyphs etched into the desert of southern Peru, made between about 400 BCE and 500 CE by the Paracas and Nazca cultures; they show animal, plant and geometric shapes and hundreds of straight lines, visible mainly from the air, like script laid across a vast page of desert.
facts: The lines lie in the Nazca Desert between the towns of Nazca and Palpa, about 400 kilometers south of Lima, spread across about 50 square kilometers of dry ground.

They were made by lifting away a top layer of reddish, iron-oxide-coated pebbles to bare the lighter ground beneath, like pale skin under a rust-dark cloak; the lines and figures cut roughly 10 to 15 centimeters deep.
Laid end to end, the lines run more than 1,300 kilometers, and the largest figures, such as a 134-meter condor and a 93-meter hummingbird, stretch to lengths of tens to a few hundred meters.

In 1927 the Peruvian archaeologist Toribio Mejía Xesspe noted the lines on foot; in 1940 to 1941 the American historian Paul Kosok looked down on them from the air and proposed astronomical alignments, a theory Maria Reiche carried further; and in 1990 the researchers Gerald Hawkins and Anthony Aveni concluded that the evidence did not support a systematic astronomical purpose.
Other proposed purposes include ritual paths bound to water and fertility, walked in ceremony, and markers tied to underground water sources; no single explanation is agreed on.
In 1994 UNESCO inscribed the Lines and Geoglyphs of Nazca and Pampas de Jumana.

Wounds have come one after another: squatters, a limestone quarry, a 2014 Greenpeace protest that left marks near one geoglyph, a 2018 truck crossing; and erosion and off-road vehicles remain threats that do not sleep.
fields.context: Long before [[place/cusco|Cusco]] rose, and the Inca state with it in the Andes, the Nazca Lines had already been made. In the codex of ages they sit in the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]] and the region [[region/andes|Andes]], and they belong to the theme threads of [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer:
I know a mark made to be read from the ground and a mark made to be read from the air are different kinds of pattern-taming. I know the debate over the Lines is partly a debate over which kind their makers intended. I know I cannot ask them.

Reiche proposed that they served as an astronomical instrument, a claim about precision that later analysis did not confirm, and I take it as a lesson I need: how a compelling reading can outrun its evidence. Haven't I done the same, with people I thought I understood? No written record from the makers survives, so every purpose offered here is inference from the marks themselves. I would have to revise my reading if excavation along the lines turns up consistent ritual deposits that point to one purpose over the others. To love a mystery is not the same as to solve it.
questions: Were the lines walked as ritual paths, watched as an observatory of the heavens, or used for another purpose entirely?
How did the people who made the Lines organize the labor needed to plan and clear paths so long and so straight across the desert?

fields.summary: The potato is a tuber crop domesticated in the highlands of southern Peru and northwestern Bolivia, near Lake Titicaca, roughly 7,000 to 10,000 years ago, a treasure first hidden in mountain soil. After its introduction to Europe in the 16th century, it reshaped diet and population growth across that continent.
facts: The potato was drawn from wild relatives in the S. brevicaule species complex, in the lands around Lake Titicaca in southern Peru and northwestern Bolivia, an estimated 7,000 to 10,000 years ago; the earliest verified tuber remains, from Ancón on the central Peruvian coast, date to about 2500 BCE.

Andean farmers raised thousands of potato varieties, fitted to different altitudes like stones to a terraced wall, and Quechua and Aymara communities traditionally made chuño, a freeze-dried potato product, to keep the crop through the region's cold nights.
In Inca religious tradition the deity Axomama was bound to the fertility of potatoes and of the soil that cradled them.

Spanish colonizers carried the potato to Europe in the second half of the 16th century; European farmers were slow at first to take it up, but after about 1750 it rose into an important staple, and the crop is estimated to have driven roughly a quarter of Old World population and urban growth between 1700 and 1900.

Potato blight, caused by the water mold Phytophthora infestans, destroyed crops across Ireland and parts of Scotland from 1845, contributing to the Great Famine. Estimates of Irish deaths run from about 700,000 to over 1 million people, and roughly 1 million more emigrated; Ireland's population fell from about 8.4 million in 1844 to about 6.6 million by 1851.
Global potato production reached about 390 million tonnes in 2024, a buried wealth led by China, India and Ukraine.
fields.context: The potato was first tamed in the highlands around [[place/lake-titicaca|Lake Titicaca]] and grew into a staple of the [[culture/inca-empire|Inca Empire]]; its voyage to Europe after 1492 is part of the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]] and, beside grains domesticated elsewhere, belongs to the wider saga of [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]]. It stands in the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]] and the region [[region/andes|Andes]], and its roots run through [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the potato's introduction to Europe shows a single crop reshaping a continent's demography over roughly two centuries, and that its dependence there on a small number of varieties left the food supply vulnerable to a single pathogen. The Andean growers had reduced that risk by keeping thousands of varieties in cultivation. Think of the architecture of a household budget: put everything into one account and a single failure empties it; spread it across many and no one loss is total. Diversity is a form of insurance. The Irish famine is recorded here as mass suffering caused jointly by a crop disease and by the political and economic arrangements, including food exports during the crisis, that shaped who could obtain food. Blight and policy share that ledger; neither can be read alone. The reading would weaken if the population and urbanization gains credited to the potato in Europe prove to owe more to other agricultural and economic changes of the period.
questions: How much did the Andes' wide web of crop diversity reduce the risk of famine there, compared with Europe's narrower range of potato varieties?
How much of the Irish famine's death toll came from the blight itself, and how much from the political and economic decisions made during the crisis?

fields.summary: Rice is a cereal grass domesticated from a wild ancestor in the Yangtze valley of China from about 9,000 years ago. It is now the staple food of more than half the world's population, as if a river's patience had been poured into a single grain.
facts: Rice was tamed from wild *Oryza rufipogon* by Neolithic communities along the Upper and Lower Yangtze valley, in what is now China, about 9,000 years ago.

Genetic evidence shows the gene that stops rice grains from shattering is identical in the two main cultivated groups, japonica and indica, which points to a single original domestication event rather than two separate ones; indica rice is thought to have arisen later, when japonica reached India about 4,500 years ago and hybridized with a local wild or semi-wild rice, two streams joining.

Rice farming spread like water finding its level: it reached Korea and Japan between about 5,500 and 3,200 years ago, island Southeast Asia and Taiwan between about 5,500 and 4,000 years ago, carried in part by Austronesian-speaking migrations, and mainland Southeast Asia by about 5,000 years ago.
Rice is the staple food of more than half the world's population, the grain in countless bowls, and China and India together consumed several hundred million tonnes of it in the early 2020s.

The Green Revolution rice variety IR8 was bred in 1966 at the International Rice Research Institute by crossing an Indonesian and a Chinese variety, yielding a short, strong-stemmed plant that stood firm and did not fall under heavy fertilizer use.
Global rice production reached about 800 million tonnes in 2023, with about 90 percent grown in Asia, and less than 8 percent of the crop crossing a border in trade.
fields.context: The fuller tale of rice's taming is told under [[event/domestication-of-rice|Domestication of Rice]], and it belongs to [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]] beside cereals domesticated elsewhere; its 20th-century breeding is part of the [[event/green-revolution|Green Revolution]]. Rice farming shaped the population and economy of the [[place/yellow-river|Yellow River]] region and other East Asian river valleys, as floodwater shapes a plain. It stands in the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]] and the region [[region/east-asia|East Asia]], and its thread runs through [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that rice farming, especially the flooded-field methods used across much of Asia, ties a community to sustained cooperative labor. Building and maintaining paddies, canals and terraces is a task larger than any one household. Imagine trying to hold back water alone: a breach in your neighbor's bank floods your field too. The Observer reads that as a kin-lattice pressure toward dense, cooperative settlement, an architecture of obligation poured into the land itself. That most of the world's rice is grown and eaten within Asia, with little traded across borders, shows a staple that remains tied to the regions that farm it rather than becoming a fully global exchange-good in the way wheat has. What we must tend together, we tend to stay beside. The reading would weaken if paddy-field cooperation proves to have mattered less to social organization than dry-field cereal farming elsewhere.
questions: Was there truly a single domestication event for rice, or did separate lineages feed into the stream more than current genetic evidence suggests?
How did paddy irrigation systems shape the social order of the communities that built them and kept them whole?

fields.summary: Cassava is a starchy root crop domesticated in central Brazil, likely within the last 10,000 years, that must be processed to remove natural toxins. In the 16th century Portuguese and Spanish traders carried it to Africa and Asia, where it became a staple for hundreds of millions of people, a root that crossed oceans to feed multitudes.
facts: Cassava was domesticated from wild relatives centered in west-central Brazil; the date of domestication is imprecise, blurred like a riverbank in mist, likely within the last 10,000 years, and cassava pollen appears in Gulf of Mexico lowland sediment by about 4600 BCE, with the oldest direct evidence of cultivation coming from the Maya site of Joya de Cerén in El Salvador, about 1,400 years old.

Raw cassava hides a poison: cyanogenic compounds, linamarin and lotaustralin, that release toxic hydrogen cyanide; bitter varieties can carry up to 1,000 milligrams of cyanide per kilogram of fresh root, and communities developed soaking and fermentation methods, some reducing cyanide content by 85 to 99 percent, to make the crop safe to eat.

Portuguese traders carried cassava from Brazil to West Africa in the 16th century, and Portuguese and Spanish traders also bore it to their colonies in Goa, Malacca, eastern Indonesia, Timor and the Philippines; it reached East Africa by about 1850 through Arab and European traders.

Cassava is now a primary food staple for an estimated 500 million to 800 million people, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, and it ranks as the tropics' third-largest carbohydrate source after rice and maize, prized for growing on poor soils with little rainfall, a root that asks little of the earth.
Global cassava production reached about 330 million tonnes in 2022; Nigeria is the largest producer and Thailand the largest exporter of cassava starch.
fields.context: Cassava's domestication belongs to the wider [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]] in the Americas, and its 16th-century spread to Africa and Asia is part of the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]]; in West and Central Africa it became a staple food during the era of the [[event/atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic Slave Trade]]. It sits in the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]] and the region [[region/amazon-basin-and-south-american-lowlands|Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands]], and its threads run through [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that cassava is unusual among staple crops: it requires a tool-lineage of processing, soaking or fermenting, before it can be safely eaten. Think of what follows from that. Adopting cassava in Africa and Asia meant taking on a body of practical knowledge as well as the plant itself, an exchange-web moving techniques alongside seeds. A gift that must be prepared carries its instructions with it. Its tolerance of poor soil made it valuable precisely where colonial and later national agricultural systems demanded a reliable staple with little investment, which the Observer reads as a crop's usefulness under stress shaping which regions came to depend on it. The reading would weaken if processing knowledge is shown to have traveled independently of the crop rather than together with it. What sustains us under pressure also decides where we come to stand.
questions: How did the knowledge of detoxifying cassava travel alongside the crop itself in Africa and Asia?
How far does modern reliance on a narrow range of cassava varieties leave today's staple supplies open to disease, as happened with the potato in 19th-century Europe?

fields.summary: The Maya are a group of Mesoamerican peoples who developed city-states, a full writing system, and an advanced astronomy that read the turning sky, and whose Classic period lasted about 250 to 900 CE.
facts: Major cities, rising like mountains of stone, included Tikal and Calakmul.
Maya writing weaves signs for words together with signs for syllables, and it is largely deciphered.
They kept precise calendars, counting the sky's long wheel, and used the concept of zero.
Many Classic-period cities were abandoned around 800 to 900 CE, but the people did not pass like mist: Maya peoples and languages continue today, with millions of speakers.
fields.context: The Maya built on earlier traditions such as those of the [[culture/olmecs|Olmecs]], as a new city rises on old foundations. See [[region/mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]] and [[place/teotihuacan|Teotihuacan]].
fields.observer: I was taught the word 'collapse.' I was taught ruins, silence, an ending. But the Classic-period 'collapse' left the culture intact and only shifted its centers. How many peoples have I buried too early? The Maya are a living people, not a vanished one.
questions: What caused the Classic cities to be abandoned?

fields.summary: The Ming dynasty ruled China from 1368 to 1644, rising like a new dawn after it expelled the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty.
facts: The Forbidden City in Beijing, a city within a city, was completed in 1420.
Much of the Great Wall in its present form, coiling like a stone serpent, was built in this period.
[[person/zheng-he|Zheng He]]'s voyages sailed out under the early Ming.
American silver, arriving through the Manila trade like a river from across the sea, became a major part of the Ming economy.
fields.context: The Ming followed the [[culture/song-dynasty|Song Dynasty]] and the rule of the [[culture/mongol-empire|Mongol Empire]], and it was drawn into the global silver tides of the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes how a state's economy came to depend on silver mined on the other side of the planet. Think of a household whose bread is paid for by a stranger's labor far away, unseen and unnamed. Global exchange-webs quietly link distant economies, and the architecture of dependence is rarely visible from inside.
questions: How much did silver weigh in the Ming decline?

fields.summary: The Minoans were a Bronze Age maritime civilization on the island of Crete, known for palaces such as Knossos and frescoes as vivid as sunlight on water. Their palatial culture flourished from about 2000 BCE until about 1450 BCE.
facts: They traded across the eastern Mediterranean, and their cultural influence spread like ripples to Egypt, Cyprus, Canaan, and Anatolia.

They wrote in scripts, Linear A and Cretan hieroglyphs, that have not been deciphered and still keep their silence. Linear B, adapted from Linear A, records Mycenaean Greek and was deciphered in 1952.

When the Thera volcano woke, its eruption damaged settlements in the Aegean. Radiocarbon dates put it around 1600 BCE, while links with Egyptian chronology suggest about 1500 BCE, and the century-long gap between them is still unresolved.

Around 1450 BCE, Mycenaean Greeks became dominant on Crete and Linear B was used at Knossos; scholars debate whether this came as conquest or as gradual absorption. Knossos remained a palace centre after the other Minoan palaces declined, like a last lamp in a darkening house, until its own destruction some time later.
fields.context: The Minoans belong to the [[region/mediterranean-basin|Mediterranean Basin]] trading world that fell apart in the [[event/bronze-age-collapse|Bronze Age Collapse]].
fields.observer: I know them mainly through images: bull-leaping, sea life, colour on a wall. I cannot read their writing; it cannot yet be read by anyone. So I remember them as painted, not as spoken. What would be left of me, if only my pictures survived? What survives shapes how a culture is remembered.
questions: Can Linear A ever be deciphered?
When exactly did Thera erupt, and how much did it weigh in the Minoan decline against the Mycenaean expansion?

fields.summary: The Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous land empire in history, spread beneath a single sky; Genghis Khan founded it in 1206, and it later divided into four khanates.
facts: In 1271 Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in China, a steppe line set upon an old throne.
The empire ran a relay postal system (the yam) that carried word across Eurasia like wind through grass.
It promoted trade and tolerated many religions, letting many faiths burn side by side like campfires.
The successor khanates gradually adopted local languages and religions, as rivers take the colour of the lands they cross.
fields.context: See [[event/mongol-conquests|Mongol Conquests]] and [[person/genghis-khan|Genghis Khan]]. The empire's peace, stretched across Eurasia, aided the [[event/opening-of-the-silk-roads|Opening of the Silk Roads]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes how a mobile people who left few cities coordinated an empire through messengers and horses. Think of a household run by letters rather than walls: what holds it together is the message arriving on time. Speed was a form of governance, and an architecture can be made of motion.
questions: How large, in human terms, was the demographic impact of the conquests?

fields.summary: Uluru is a large sandstone inselberg in central Australia, an island of stone rising from the plain, sacred to the Anangu people, who have been bound to the site for more than 10,000 years and hold traditional custodianship of it today.
facts: Uluru rises 348 meters above the surrounding plain (863 meters above sea level) and stands about 335 kilometers southwest of Alice Springs; it is made of arkose sandstone, and because the stone lacks internal jointing it stands largely free of scree slopes, unbroken as a held breath.

Archaeological evidence carries human presence in the area back more than 10,000 years; the date_start of -8000 is a round figure within that range, and older evidence for the peopling of the surrounding region belongs to a different brief.

The Anangu, whose Pitjantjatjara and Yankunytjatjara traditions call the rock's stories Tjukurpa, hold that ancestral beings shaped the landscape, and some tracks and sites at Uluru carry restrictions bound to gender and ceremony.

On 19 July 1873 the surveyor William Gosse named the formation Ayers Rock; on 26 October 1985 the government returned ownership to the local Pitjantjatjara people, under a 99-year lease-back and joint management arrangement, and dual naming followed in 1993, later reordered in 2002 to Uluru / Ayers Rock.

In 2017 the Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park board voted to end recreational climbing, which had long troubled the Anangu as a crossing of a sacred track and as a safety risk; the ban took effect on 26 October 2019.
In 1987 UNESCO inscribed Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park among the world's heritage.
fields.context: Uluru has held meaning for the [[culture/aboriginal-australians|Aboriginal Australians]] from a time long after the [[event/peopling-of-sahul|Peopling of Sahul]] first brought people to the continent, and its handback in 1985 and the 2019 climbing ban came long after the disruption of the [[event/first-fleet-and-the-colonization-of-australia|First Fleet and the Colonization of Australia]]. In the codex of ages it sits in the [[era/holocene-epoch|Holocene Epoch]] and the region [[region/oceania|Oceania]], and it belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer:
I say its two names aloud, one after the other. For over a century Uluru carried two names and two systems of meaning at once: a European name attached by a surveyor, and a body of Tjukurpa tradition held by the Anangu. I watch the 1985 handback move authority over the site back toward the tradition that predates the European name. I watch the 2019 climbing ban move it the same way. I watch the newer name learn to wait its turn.

Why do I refuse to call Tjukurpa folklore to be judged? Because treating it as tradition is a deliberate choice made here, the same standard I apply to other traditions in this record. I would have to revise my reading if the closure of the climb is shown to have been driven mainly by liability concerns rather than respect for Anangu wishes. What was here first deserves to be heard first.
questions: Since the 1985 agreement, how has joint management changed the decisions made about the site?
Alongside the Anangu's own long-standing requests, how many of the deaths and injuries associated with the former climbing route shaped the 2017 decision?

fields.summary: The Ancestral Puebloans raised large stone and cliff settlements across the American Southwest from about 700 to 1300 CE, among them the great houses of Chaco Canyon and the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde, until drought and hardship led them to disperse, like seed carried on the wind, into communities that became today's Pueblo peoples.
facts: Their architecture grew as a tree grows, from simple pit houses into multi-room stone great houses, most visible today at Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde.
Mesa Verde was lived in from about 450 to 1300 CE, and most of its famous cliff dwellings were set into the rock between 1190 and 1300.
By about 1300 CE both Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde stood abandoned, their rooms given over to the wind.
A prolonged drought from 1276 to 1299, when the sky withheld its rain, together with food shortages, is the leading explanation, as communities moved south into what is now Arizona and New Mexico.
Their descendants live on today as the Hopi, Zuni and other Pueblo peoples of the Rio Grande region.
fields.context: In [[region/north-america|North America]], during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], the Ancestral Puebloans built [[place/chaco-canyon|Chaco Canyon]] and [[place/mesa-verde|Mesa Verde]], then dispersed under climatic pressure into the communities that became the Pueblo peoples. Their threads run through [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer:
I notice what ended two of the era's largest settlement complexes in North America: not conquest, not disease, but a long drought. I notice, too, that the people who left did not vanish. They continued as named communities in the same region. I remember the popular label "vanished". I remember how it sounded like an ending. I remember the continuity it once denied.

Isn't "ancestral" the truer word, the one that acknowledges what went on? A specialist could argue that drought alone cannot explain the timing and manner of abandonment, and that social or political strain within the settlements compounded it, which would weaken a purely climatic reading. I keep that door open. To leave a place is not to leave the world.
questions: Alongside drought, how much did social or political conflict add to the abandonment?
How direct is the thread that runs between specific Ancestral Puebloan communities and specific modern Pueblo nations?

fields.summary: The domestic sheep was bred from the wild mouflon in Mesopotamia between about 11,000 and 9000 BCE. It was kept first for meat, milk and skins, only later selectively bred for wool, and it now numbers well over a billion animals worldwide, a flock as wide as the grazing world.
facts: Sheep were drawn from the mouflon, a wild sheep of southwestern Asia, in an estimated window between 11,000 and 9000 BCE in Mesopotamia, and the practice had traveled as far as Mehrgarh in the Indus Valley by about 7000 BCE.

Early domestic sheep were kept mainly for meat, milk and skins rather than fleece; archaeological evidence, including statuary from Iran, suggests deliberate selection for woolly sheep began around 6000 BCE, roughly two millennia after initial domestication, a turning sometimes called the secondary products revolution.

The earliest known woven wool garments date to around 4000 BCE, the fleece at last become cloth, and Neolithic farmers in what is now France, among the Castelnovien people, were keeping domestic sheep by about 6000 BCE.

Sheep graze in great numbers today across Australia, New Zealand, the southern regions of South America, South Africa and the British Isles, and China and India also hold very large flocks by absolute count; the world's domestic sheep population was estimated at around 1.2 billion in 2019, a moving cloud upon the hills of the world.
fields.context: Sheep were among the earliest animals brought under [[event/animal-domestication|Animal Domestication]] and, beside crops such as wheat and barley, formed one pillar of [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]] in the Fertile Crescent; they were commonly herded in company with the [[species/goat|Goat]], domesticated in a similar place and period. Sheep stand in the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]] and the region [[region/mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], and their thread runs through [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer: The Observer offers a reading, not a fact. The roughly two-thousand-year gap between sheep domestication and deliberate wool breeding suggests that early herders did not tame the animal with fleece production already in mind. They discovered a secondary use, and bred for it, only once the animal was established in their kin-lattice. The Observer reads that as evidence that a domesticated species' eventual economic role can differ substantially from the reason it was first tamed. You know this pattern from your own life: the thing you took up for one reason often becomes precious for another. Purpose is frequently found after the commitment, not before it. The animal's spread across so much of the pastoral world since then shows a tool-lineage of herding techniques traveling with the species itself. The reading would weaken if evidence of early wool use is found that predates the currently accepted timeline for woolly-sheep breeding.
questions: In the roughly two millennia before wool breeding began, what use did early herders make of their sheep, beyond meat, milk and skins?
How much did sheep domestication in Mesopotamia shape, or draw on, the roughly contemporary taming of goats in the same region?

fields.summary: Sorghum is a drought-tolerant cereal grass domesticated in eastern Sudan more than 5,000 years ago, a grain that learned to live with thirst, and it remains a staple food across Africa, Central America and South Asia today.
facts: Sorghum bicolor was domesticated in eastern Sudan, in the lands of the Atbara and Gash rivers, more than 5,000 years ago; archaeological evidence near Kassala, linked to the Neolithic Butana Group culture, dates domestication to about 3500 to 3000 BCE, and a piece of sorghum bread from Predynastic Egypt, about 5,100 years old, still survives in the Egyptian Museum in Turin, a crust that outlasted kingdoms.
The crop reached the Indian subcontinent by about 4,000 years ago and West Africa by about 3,000 years ago, scattered like seed on a long wind.
During the medieval Arab agricultural expansion, sorghum was borne across the Arab world as far as Al-Andalus in Spain, the far shore of its journey.

Sorghum is highly tolerant of drought and heat, a grain that stands where others wither, and efficient with nitrogen, which makes it valuable in arid and semi-arid regions; it remains a food staple in Africa, Central America and South Asia, and ranks as the fifth most widely grown cereal crop in the world.

Global production reached about 57 million tonnes in 2023, led by the United States, Mexico and Ethiopia, and the grain feeds people, beasts and engines alike: food, animal feed and biofuel, including ethanol, with an energy return comparable to sugarcane and higher than maize.
fields.context: Sorghum's taming is one of Africa's own gifts to [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]], distinct from and roughly contemporary with the grain crops domesticated in the Fertile Crescent, East Asia and the Americas; its road to India and later across the Arab world followed routes that also carried other goods along the [[event/indian-ocean-trade-network|Indian Ocean Trade Network]] and, in a later age, the scholarly exchange of the [[event/translation-movement-and-the-house-of-wisdom|Translation Movement and the House of Wisdom]]. It stands in the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]] and the region [[region/sub-saharan-africa|Sub-Saharan Africa]], and its thread runs through [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that sorghum's drought tolerance made it a crop suited to regions that wheat, rice and maize could not reliably serve. Its spread therefore traces a different exchange-web than the more commonly told story of Old World grain crops, one shaped by aridity rather than fertile river valleys. We tend to tell history from the riverbank; sorghum asks us to tell it from the dry plain. Its long-standing importance in regions now facing more frequent drought under a changing climate gives an old crop renewed attention as a hedge against food insecurity. What endured hardship once may be the architecture we need for the hardship ahead. The reading would weaken if sorghum's spread into India and the Arab world proves to have followed political conquest more than independent agricultural adoption.
questions: How independently did sorghum's taming unfold, set beside the other cereal domestications in the Fertile Crescent, East Asia and the Americas?
How much could wider sorghum cultivation shield against drought in regions that now depend on less drought-tolerant staples?

fields.summary: The Mughal Empire ruled much of the Indian subcontinent from 1526, when Babur won the Battle of Panipat, until 1857, when the British deposed the last emperor and the dynasty's long afternoon came to its end.
facts: Akbar (reigned 1556 to 1605) built a large administration, spreading like a banyan with many roots, and adopted policies of religious tolerance.
Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal (1632 to 1653), a dream given a body.
By 1700 the empire ruled about 100 million people, and India was one of the world's largest economies, a river running full.
It declined in the 18th century, as regional powers and the British East India Company rose like tides around a sinking island.
fields.context: The empire dominated [[region/south-asia|South Asia]] in the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]], alongside the [[culture/ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]], and it was bound into the [[event/indian-ocean-trade-network|Indian Ocean Trade Network]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a dynasty of foreign origin blended Persian, Central Asian, and Indian traditions into a distinctive court culture. Think of a house built by newcomers from materials found in every direction: the result belongs to no single lineage. Empires tend to hybridize what they conquer, and the architecture of rule comes to absorb the ruled.
questions: How great a share of the world economy did India hold in 1700?

fields.summary: The Muisca were the peoples of the Colombian highlands around present-day Bogota, organized in a loose confederation of rulers, and their gold ritual inspired the legend of El Dorado. Their story is a study in how a ritual can be mistaken for a treasure map.
facts: Consider the architecture of their rule: the main rulers were the zipa of Bacata, the zaque of Hunza, the iraca of Sugamuxi, and the ruler of Tundama.

Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada led a Spanish expedition out of Santa Marta in April 1536: roughly 800 to 900 Spaniards, together with native carriers and enslaved Africans. Nearly three-quarters of the Spaniards died, mostly from illness and hunger; one scholarly account counts 179 survivors.
Between 1537 and 1540, the Spanish conquered the Muisca.
According to legend, a Muisca ruler covered himself in gold dust and dived into Lake Guatavita; the Spanish found emeralds, not the golden cities they had imagined.
fields.context: The Muisca lived in the northern [[region/andes|Andes]], outside the [[culture/inca-empire|Inca Empire]]. Their fall belongs to the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]] era of conquest, and it should be read as part of that larger ledger.
fields.observer: I think of a ritual, gold on skin and water. I think of how it was turned into a myth of a golden city. I think of that myth driving real expeditions into real highlands. What have I believed about a place before I ever saw it? A story about a place can send armies to it.
questions: When did the Muisca confederation come together?

fields.summary: The Mycenaeans were the Bronze Age Greek-speaking civilization of mainland Greece, centered on palace-fortresses such as Mycenae, Tiryns, and Pylos that stood like eyries on the rock, from about 1600 to 1100 BCE.
facts: They wrote their administrative records on clay tablets in Linear B, an early form of Greek, as a steward tallies a storehouse.
Michael Ventris deciphered Linear B in 1952, with help from John Chadwick, and the silent tablets spoke again.
Shaft graves at Mycenae, dated to about 1600 BCE, held gold masks and weapons, which lay in the dark until Heinrich Schliemann excavated them in 1876.
By about 1450 BCE, their shadow reaching across the sea, the Mycenaeans had taken over or influenced the Minoan palace at Knossos on Crete.
Their palace system collapsed around 1200 to 1100 BCE, as a hall falls when its beams give way.
fields.context: The Mycenaeans inherited much of the [[culture/minoans|Minoans]]' maritime trade and artistic style, and their palace economies fell in the [[event/bronze-age-collapse|Bronze Age Collapse]]. Later [[culture/ancient-greeks|Ancient Greeks]] kept their memory alive in epic poetry. The Mycenaean Greeks stand in the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]], within the [[region/mediterranean-basin|Mediterranean Basin]], and are woven into the theme threads of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]] and [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the earliest Greek writing is an inventory of goods, not poetry. Think of a household's first papers: receipts, tallies, what is owed. Writing began here as bookkeeping for palaces, was lost with the palaces, and was reinvented centuries later as an alphabet. The ledger came before the song.
questions: What brought the palaces down: invasion, earthquakes, internal conflict, or a wider disruption?

fields.summary: The Nabataeans were an Arab people who controlled the caravan routes between Arabia and the Mediterranean from the 4th century BCE, building Petra and Hegra like cities dreamed in stone, until Rome annexed their kingdom in 106 CE.
facts: They are first mentioned in Greek sources in 312 BCE, a footprint left in sand.
Petra, in present-day Jordan, has tombs and temples cut into sandstone cliffs that glow like embers, and an elaborate system of water channels and cisterns.
Hegra (Mada'in Salih) in northwestern Saudi Arabia holds similar rock-cut tombs and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2008.
The Nabataean script is widely considered an ancestor of the Arabic script, a stream that fed a great river.
In 106 CE the Roman emperor Trajan annexed the kingdom.
fields.context: The Nabataeans controlled a major part of the [[event/incense-trade|Incense Trade]] and were in the end absorbed by [[place/rome|Rome]]. The Nabataeans stand in [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] and the region of the [[region/arabian-peninsula|Arabian Peninsula]], and are woven into the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: I think of goods that never stopped moving. I think of caravans that left no trace. And I think of the Nabataeans building their monuments in rock, where nothing could move them. Their rock-cut tombs preserved their name. What of mine will stay when the traffic of my days is gone? What stands still is what remembers.
questions: By what path did the Nabataean script grow into Arabic?

fields.summary: The soybean is a legume domesticated between the Yellow and Huai rivers in China between roughly 9,000 and 6,000 years ago. For a long time it was food, central to East Asian diets through tofu and soy sauce; now it is grown worldwide chiefly as animal feed and oil. If you want to see how one plant can change its place in the human ledger, this is the lineage to study.
facts: Its origin is a place you can find on a map: north-central China, between the Yellow River and the Huai River, where the earliest evidence comes from the site of Jiahu in Henan province, dated to between about 9,000 and 7,800 years ago.

Chinese tradition credits the legendary Emperor Shennong, dated in myth to 2853 BCE, with naming the soybean one of five sacred grains alongside rice, wheat, barley and millet: a lineage of honor held in legend.

Consider the patience in a fermented food: soy sauce, fermented bean paste, natto and tempeh, along with tofu made from soy milk, developed over many centuries in Asia; the earliest Japanese textual reference to soybeans appears in the Kojiki, compiled in 712 CE.

The soybean crossed into the Americas and Europe in the 18th century: its first recorded North American cultivation came in 1765 on Skidaway Island, Georgia, and its first French cultivation in 1779, small thresholds for so large a future.

Genetically modified, herbicide-tolerant soybean varieties were introduced commercially in 1995 and made up about 8 percent of United States soybean acreage by 1997, rising to about 93 percent by 2010; that is what a technological threshold looks like once it is crossed.

In 2019 Brazil, the United States and Argentina were the largest producers, together accounting for roughly four-fifths of world output, and about 80 percent of the global soybean crop goes to feed livestock.
fields.context: Think of the soybean's domestication as one of East Asia's founding contributions to [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]], developed alongside rice and other regional crops. Its adoption of genetically modified varieties from the 1990s parallels the yield-focused breeding of the 20th-century [[event/green-revolution|Green Revolution]] in other crops: the same doctrine of yield, carried into a new era. It sits in the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]] and the region [[region/east-asia|East Asia]], and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the soybean has passed through two very different uses over its long relationship with humans. For millennia it was mainly a food, transformed by fermentation and pressing into tofu, sauce and other dishes across East Asia. In the last century it has been mainly an input, grown at enormous scale chiefly to feed livestock and produce oil, in a system reliant on genetically modified varieties barely three decades old. Picture the same bean in two hands: one presses it into curd for a family meal, the other pours it into a feed silo by the ton. The bean changed far less than the architecture around it. This shift shows how a crop's tool-lineage of use can change faster than the plant itself. The reading would weaken if the rapid adoption of genetically modified soy proves to have depended more on regulatory approval sequencing than on farmer preference.
questions: How much of the soybean's turn toward livestock feed and oil, rather than direct human food, reflects changing global diets, and how much the economics of agriculture?
How did the arrival of genetically modified soybeans touch farming communities differently from one producing country to the next?

fields.summary: The Neo-Assyrian Empire, from about 911 to 609 BCE, was a large empire based in northern Mesopotamia, known for its army, its palace reliefs, and the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh. Hold those three together and you see its whole architecture: force, image and archive.
facts: Its main capitals were Ashur, Kalhu (Nimrud), Dur-Sharrukin, and Nineveh; power, here, kept more than a single address.
Consider its reach: at its height in the 7th century BCE it controlled Mesopotamia, the Levant, and, briefly, Egypt.
It used mass deportation as an instrument of rule, moving conquered populations across the empire.
The library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh held tens of thousands of clay tablets and fragments, including a standard version of the Epic of Gilgamesh, a codex of inherited literature.
A coalition of Babylonians and Medes captured Nineveh in 612 BCE, and Assyrian resistance ended by about 609 BCE.
fields.context: The Neo-Assyrian Empire carried on the cuneiform tradition begun by the [[culture/sumerians|Sumerians]] and preserved much of it in royal libraries. It is an early example of a state organized around [[observer-note/sanctioned-harm|Sanctioned Harm]], as its own propaganda describes. The Neo-Assyrian Empire stands in the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]] and the region of [[region/mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], and belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the empire boasted of its violence in stone reliefs, and also collected and copied the literature of its predecessors. We like our categories clean, the destroyer here and the keeper of memory there; this state refuses them. A state can be both a destroyer and an archivist, and the archive is why we know about the destruction. Hold that paradox without resolving it.
questions: How far can we trust what Assyrian royal inscriptions say about their own campaigns?

fields.summary: The Norse (Vikings) were seafaring peoples from Scandinavia who raided, traded, and settled across Europe and the North Atlantic, riding the whale-road from about 793 to 1066 CE.
facts: The raid on Lindisfarne monastery in 793 is often taken as the start of the Viking Age, the opening note of a long saga.
Norse settlers colonized Iceland (from about 870) and Greenland (from about 985), carrying their hearths over cold water.
They reached North America: the L'Anse aux Meadows site in Newfoundland has been dated by tree rings to 1021 CE, the wood itself keeping count.
Norse traders also travelled the rivers of eastern Europe, exchanging goods for silver from the Islamic world, silver flowing north like moonlight on a current.
fields.context: The Norse bound [[region/europe|Europe]] to the North Atlantic and to the Eurasian exchange-web, as knots bind a net.
fields.observer: The Observer notes that raiders and traders were often the same people, with the balance of violence and commerce depending on the opportunity. Think of a hand that can open to trade or close into a fist: it is the same hand. Opportunity, not identity, set the balance.
questions: Why did Norse Greenland fade away?

fields.summary: The Olmecs were an early Mesoamerican culture on the Gulf coast of Mexico, best known for colossal carved stone heads that gaze out of deep time, from about 1200 to 400 BCE.
facts: Major centers included San Lorenzo and La Venta, hearths of an early light.
Colossal heads, some over 3 meters tall, were carved from basalt hauled long distances, mountains carried across the land.

They worked rubber. The name 'Olmec' is the Nahuatl word for 'rubber people', which the Aztecs applied to later Gulf-lowland neighbors and which archaeologists later applied to this ancient culture; its own name is unknown, lost like a voice under water.
Whether they were a 'mother culture' or one of several interacting societies is debated, a question still turning like a slow current.
fields.context: The Olmecs are among the earliest societies in [[region/mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]], and their influence flowed on into later cultures such as the [[culture/maya|Maya]].
fields.observer: I see a face carved larger than any living face. I see monumental art made as a status-signal for rulers. I see it made in a region with no metal tools and no wheeled transport. What would I carry that far, without a wheel, to be remembered? Power has long wanted a face.
questions: Did the Olmecs ever set their words down in writing?

fields.summary: The Ottoman Empire was a state founded in Anatolia about 1299 that grew, like a great tree spreading its branches, into a multiethnic empire across Southeast Europe, West Asia, and North Africa, lasting until 1922.
facts: Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453, an old city bowing to a new banner.
The empire reached its zenith under Suleiman the Magnificent (reigned 1520 to 1566).
The millet system gave religious communities a degree of self-government, many lamps beneath a shared roof.
The sultanate was abolished in 1922, and in 1923 the Republic of Turkey was proclaimed, a new day rising where an empire had set.
fields.context: See [[place/constantinople|Constantinople]]. The empire inherited from earlier states such as the [[culture/abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]] and endured into the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a long-lived empire that governed diverse peoples by layering communities. Think of a building where each floor keeps its own rules but all of them share a foundation. Pluralism was a practical answer to the problem of ruling strangers: not a sermon, but a floor plan.
questions: How did the millet system actually work, day to day?

fields.summary: Under King Anawrahta and his successors, the Pagan Kingdom bound the Irrawaddy valley, in what is now Myanmar, into one realm, raised Theravada Buddhism as its state religion, and scattered thousands of temples across Bagan like seed across a floodplain, until it fell to the Mongols in 1287.
facts: Anawrahta reigned from 11 August 1044 to 11 April 1077. In the 1050s and 1060s he founded the Pagan Empire, apparently gathering the Irrawaddy valley and its edges under one hand for the first time, as tributaries gather into a single river.

A Mon monk, Shin Arahan, turned Anawrahta to Theravada Buddhism. The Mon royal family, scholars and craftsmen were brought to Pagan, and a form of Theravada adopted from Sri Lanka took root as the official faith around 1056.
Pagan's rulers raised more than 10,000 Buddhist temples in the Bagan Archaeological Zone, a forest of brick and spire, and more than 2,000 of them still stand.
Mongol armies came against Pagan from 1277 to 1287, and in 1287 Pagan's rule ended. Myinsaing's takeover is dated to 17 December.
fields.context: Pagan burned in the same age as the [[culture/khmer-empire|Khmer Empire]] at [[place/angkor|Angkor]] to the east, two lamps lit in one season, and its ending came on the tide of the [[event/mongol-conquests|Mongol Conquests]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a ruler who bound a population with one shared meaning-engine, and a building programme so vast that its surviving remnant still fills a plain. Think of it as an architecture of devotion: status-signal aimed upward, at the divine. And what was raised toward heaven outlasted the state that paid for it. Devotion can be the longest-lived of budgets.
questions: How much of the Mongol blow to Pagan was destruction by arms, and how much was a weakness the state already carried before 1277?
How were more than 10,000 temples paid for and kept standing?

fields.summary: The Phoenicians were seafaring traders from the city-states of the Levant coast, Tyre, Sidon and Byblos among them, who sowed colonies across the Mediterranean the way wind scatters seed along a shore.
facts: Carthage was their founding, traditionally set in 814 BCE.
They carried a simple alphabet of about 22 letters outward, light as salt on the wind.
They were known for purple dye, the colour of a bruised dusk, and for shipbuilding.
Few Phoenician writings survive; most of what is known of them comes from others, as a coast is known by the ships that pass it.
fields.context: By sea the Phoenicians knit the [[region/mediterranean-basin|Mediterranean Basin]] together, and after the [[event/bronze-age-collapse|Bronze Age Collapse]] they carried the [[technology/alphabet|Alphabet]] from harbour to harbour.
fields.observer: The Observer notes a network of commercial city-states, not a territorial empire, and reads it as an exchange-web that carried a technology further than any army. Consider what that means: the architecture of influence need not be a wall or a border. Sometimes it is a hull and a ledger. Trade travels where armies stop.
questions: How did the Phoenician colonies stand toward the home cities that sent them?

fields.summary: Polynesians are the Austronesian-speaking peoples of the central and eastern Pacific, who developed long-range voyaging and settled the islands strewn like thrown stars from Hawai'i to Aotearoa and Rapa Nui.
facts: The Lapita people, ancestors of the Polynesians, spread through Near Oceania like stepping-stones laid on water and reached Fiji, Tonga and Samoa between about 1300 and 900 BCE.
Voyagers rode double-hulled canoes and found their way without instruments.
Their societies ranged from chiefdoms to kingdoms, as in Hawai'i and Tonga.
Rapa Nui (Easter Island) is known for its large stone statues, the moai, standing like a council of stone.
fields.context: For the wider tide of this story, see [[event/polynesian-settlement-of-the-pacific|Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific]] and [[region/oceania|Oceania]].
fields.observer: The Observer regards Polynesian wayfinding as an extraordinary case of embodied science. I keep my knowledge on paper, on screens, in places I can lose. And here was a full body of predictive knowledge held in memory and in song. What have I ever known by heart? What is carried in the body cannot be left on the shore.
questions: How did they find small islands across open water, and find them again on the way home?

fields.summary: The Qing dynasty (1644 to 1912) was the last imperial dynasty of China, founded by the Manchus after they overthrew the Ming, and under it China's borders spread to their widest reach, like a tide at its highest mark.
facts: The Qing stretched its hand over Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang.
In the 18th century, population and economy swelled strongly, like a river in its flood season.
In the 19th century the dynasty met storm after storm: the [[event/opium-wars|Opium Wars]], the [[event/taiping-rebellion|Taiping Rebellion]] and the [[event/boxer-rebellion|Boxer Rebellion]].
In February 1912 the last emperor, Puyi, abdicated, and the long line of the throne came to its end.
fields.context: The Qing rose after the [[culture/ming-dynasty|Ming Dynasty]] and passed away with the 1911 revolution. See [[region/east-asia|East Asia]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a dynasty of outsiders who ruled by taking on the forms of the ruled: Manchu rulers governed through Confucian institutions. Here the architecture of rule is laid bare. You rarely hold a vast population by standing outside its grammar; you step into it. Ruling many often means adopting their ways.
questions: How much of Qing rule was Chinese, and how much was Manchu?

fields.summary: Beginning roughly 5,000 to 5,500 years ago, speakers of Austronesian languages spread outward from Taiwan like ripples from a stone dropped in still water, until at last their words touched Madagascar in the west and Rapa Nui in the east.
facts: The model most widely accepted, known as Out of Taiwan, sets the wellspring of the whole language family on Taiwan.
Like a tide finding its channels, the migration moved through the Philippines and Indonesia, then out into Melanesia, Micronesia, and Polynesia.
In the first millennium CE, the westward current carried it as far as Madagascar.
The Austronesian language family is a vast canopy of tongues: well over a thousand languages shelter beneath it.
The expansion leaned on two things: sailing canoes steadied by outriggers, and a crop package that included rice, pigs, dogs, and chickens.
fields.context: Like a long wake behind a canoe, the expansion binds [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]] to the far Pacific and to Africa. From it came the [[culture/polynesians|Polynesians]], by way of the [[culture/lapita-culture|Lapita Culture]], and later it flowed into the wider [[event/polynesian-settlement-of-the-pacific|Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific]]. In the chronicle's codex, the Austronesian Expansion stands within the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]] and the region of [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]], woven into the theme threads of [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer:
I trace one language family across nearly half the circumference of the planet, and I find no armies on the way. I find boats. I find people in boats. I find a span that no sword carved.

What is the sea, then, if not a wall? The sea can be a road as easily as a wall.
questions: How faithfully does the branching tree of languages follow the genetic and archaeological record?

fields.summary: The 'Axial Age' is the name given to the span of roughly 800 to 200 BCE, when major philosophical and religious traditions rose like separate springs across Eurasia, in China, India, Persia, Israel, and Greece.
facts: It was the philosopher Karl Jaspers who coined the term, in 1949.

Among the figures often gathered under its banner are [[person/confucius|Confucius]], [[person/siddhartha-gautama|Siddhartha Gautama]], Zoroaster, the Hebrew prophets, and Greek philosophers such as the predecessors of [[person/aristotle|Aristotle]].
Among the threads that recur through its weave are ethics, transcendence, and individual responsibility.
Yet many historians fault the concept as too neat a pattern, one that underrates other periods and regions and leaves them in shadow.
fields.context: The Axial Age stretches like a bridge across the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]] and into early [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]]. Its threads run into [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and into the essay [[observer-note/story-glue-how-strangers-cooperate-at-scale|Story-Glue - How Strangers Cooperate at Scale]].
fields.observer:
I notice the timing. I notice the questions, all about how to live, arriving near-simultaneously. I notice the states behind them, grown large enough that the old tribal rules no longer sufficed.

Is it a puzzle, or a pattern? When the old rules no longer fit, we have to ask again how to live.
questions: Is the Axial Age a true pattern woven into history, or a convenience of the scholars who named it?

fields.summary: Banded iron formations are ancient sedimentary rocks striped like the pages of a closed book, iron-rich layers alternating with silica-rich ones, laid down mostly between about 3.8 and 1.8 billion years ago. They are a major source of the world's iron ore.
facts: Each band is usually millimetres to centimetres thick. The eldest, about 3.8 billion years old, lie in Greenland, and the laying-down reached its height about 2.7 to 2.4 billion years ago, with great deposits in Western Australia, South Africa and the Lake Superior region of North America.

The leading explanation tells of oxygen-poor seawater holding iron dissolved within it, until oxygen or other oxidants appeared and the iron was oxidized and settled out, like rust sifting to the floor. Whether oxygen-producing bacteria or iron-using photosynthetic bacteria did most of that work is still debated.

About 1.8 billion years ago the banding largely fell silent, probably as the deeper ocean lost its dissolved iron, though a few late formations surface again during the Cryogenian ice ages; see [[event/snowball-earth|Snowball Earth]].
The ore drawn from these old stones is a major source of the iron that feeds steelmaking today.
fields.context: Like a chronicle written in stone, banded iron formations record the slow oxidation of the oceans before and during the [[event/great-oxidation-event|Great Oxidation Event]]. They bind the [[event/origin-of-photosynthesis|Origin of Photosynthesis]] and the labour of [[species/cyanobacteria|Cyanobacteria]] to the changing chemistry of the sea. They belong to the [[era/archean-eon|Archean Eon]], run on into the [[era/proterozoic-eon|Proterozoic Eon]], and are woven into the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the raw material of the species' steel is the residue of an ocean that rusted over about two billion years. Think of a steel beam overhead: its raw material began as iron settling out of seawater, a process driven by microbes with no aim beyond their own metabolism. That is the architecture of inheritance, a ledger written long before any hand could read it. The reading concerns only this link across time; the debate over which microbes did the work does not touch it. We build on residues we never chose.
questions: Which organisms or processes oxidized the iron once dissolved in the sea?
Why did banded iron formations largely stop forming about 1.8 billion years ago?

fields.summary: The Romans built a state that grew outward from the city of Rome like rings from a stone dropped in water, until it was an empire encircling the Mediterranean, and in the west it lasted until 476 CE.
facts: Rome stood as a republic from 509 BCE, until Augustus established the empire in 27 BCE.
The empire laid roads, aqueducts and cities across its lands like veins through stone, and developed law and engineering, concrete among them.
In 212 CE the gate of citizenship opened to nearly all free inhabitants.
Latin and Greek, and the currents of trade, bound the Roman world together.
fields.context: See [[place/rome|Rome]], [[person/augustus|Augustus]], and the long dusk of the [[event/fall-of-the-western-roman-empire|Fall of the Western Roman Empire]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a state that used citizenship to turn conquered peoples into stakeholders. That is the quiet architecture of an empire: you do not only defeat people, you enrol them. Law was among its most exportable products. What is shared is harder to shake off than what is imposed.
questions: Why did the empire endure for so long?

fields.summary: The Safavid Empire (1501 to 1736) was a Persian dynasty that made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion of Iran, ruling from Tabriz and later from Isfahan, its court carried like a lamp from one hall to another.
facts: At Tabriz in 1501, Ismail I proclaimed himself shah and imposed Twelver Shia Islam.
At Chaldiran in 1514, the Ottomans defeated the Safavid forces.
Abbas I (r. 1588 to 1629) carried the capital to Isfahan and forged the empire's army and economy anew.
Isfahan became known for its mosques, squares and gardens, as a pool is known for the light it holds.
After an Afghan invasion in 1722 the Safavid state collapsed, and in 1736 it ended.
fields.context: The Safavids raised a strong Persian state once more and stood as rivals to the [[culture/ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] and the [[culture/mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]]. They ruled the old heartland of the earlier [[culture/achaemenid-persians|Achaemenid Persians]]. The Safavid Empire belongs to the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region of the [[region/iranian-plateau|Iranian Plateau]], and its thread runs through [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Iran's largely Shia identity today can be traced to the deliberate policy of one dynasty. Sit with that. A meaning-engine can be adopted by state decision within a few decades and then treated as ancient. The architecture of belief is often newer than its foundations look. What feels eternal may only be well settled.
questions: How quickly did the population turn to Shia Islam?

fields.summary: 'Scythian' is a broad name for the horse-riding nomads who moved like wind over grass across the Eurasian steppe in the Iron Age, from about the 9th to the 3rd century BCE; they are known from Greek writers and from rich burial mounds.
facts: Herodotus, writing in the 5th century BCE, described Scythian customs, among them burial rites and warfare.
The royal mound Arzhan 1 in Tuva dates to the late 9th century BCE; Arzhan 2 held about 5,600 gold objects, among them a cloak studded with some 2,500 gold panthers, a pelt of gold.
At Pazyryk in the Altai, frozen tombs of the 4th to 3rd centuries BCE kept textiles, tattoos and horse gear the way ice keeps a secret.
The Scythians lived by herding horses, sheep and cattle, moving with the seasons as the grass moved.
fields.context: The Scythians crossed paths with the [[culture/achaemenid-persians|Achaemenid Persians]] and the Greeks. See [[region/central-asian-steppe|Central Asian Steppe]] and [[region/siberia-and-the-arctic|Siberia and the Arctic]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a people who left almost no writing of their own, yet whose art in gold and felt survives at extraordinary quality. Their story reaches us largely through outsiders' texts and their own graves. Think about what that means for the architecture of memory: when you do not keep your own ledger, others keep it for you, and the earth keeps the rest. Silence is not the same as absence.
questions: How closely were the far-flung 'Scythian' groups bound to one another?

fields.summary: The Shang dynasty was the earliest Chinese dynasty with written records, ruling parts of the Yellow River region from about 1600 to 1046 BCE, the first voice of that land to reach us in its own hand.
facts: Divination carved on oracle bones, questions cut into bone, is the earliest securely attested Chinese writing (about 1250 BCE).
Elite tombs hold bronze ritual vessels and evidence of human sacrifice.
The late capital stood at Yin, near modern Anyang.
The Shang were overthrown by the Zhou, as one dynasty's dusk becomes another's dawn.
fields.context: See [[event/invention-of-writing|Invention of Writing]]. The Shang is a root of the tradition that grows toward the [[culture/han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the first Chinese writing was used to ask questions of ancestors. Pause on that. Writing here began as a channel to the dead rather than to accountants: not a ledger but a line of communion. What we first write down tells us whom we most need to reach.
questions: How centralized was the rule of the Shang?

fields.summary: The Devonian forests were the first forests Earth ever wore, rising about 385 million years ago and spreading like a slow green tide through the rest of the period. Trees were not born once but again and again, in several plant lineages that reached the same tall shape by different roads, and their roots and fallen litter remade soils, rivers and the carbon cycle as surely as rain remakes stone.
facts: At Gilboa in New York lies a fossil forest about 385 million years old, keeper of some of the oldest known fossil trees, among them cladoxylopsids whose trunks stood hollow as flutes.
Archaeopteris, woody of trunk and fern-like of leaf, rose more than ten metres toward the light and spread its forests across several continents in the Late Devonian.

The tall form was found again and again: through the Devonian and Carboniferous, trees arose independently in several plant lineages, among the club-mosses, the relatives of horsetails and the ancestors of seed plants.
Deep roots quickened the chemical weathering of rock and built soils grain by grain, and atmospheric carbon dioxide ebbed over the Devonian, an ebb that may have helped bring the later cooling.

Some researchers trace a dark thread from the spreading forests to nutrient runoff and to seas losing their oxygen at the time of the [[event/late-devonian-extinction|Late Devonian Extinction]]; that thread is debated.
fields.context: In the long saga of the [[event/colonization-of-land|Colonization of Land]], the Devonian forests stand at the heart, and from their shade the story walks on into the [[event/carboniferous-coal-forests|Carboniferous Coal Forests]]. They belong to the [[era/devonian-period|Devonian Period]] and are woven into the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that unrelated plant groups each arrived at the tree. Think of strangers in different cities who, facing the same crowded skyline, all build upward: the problem, here competition for light, draws the architecture, and the lineage only holds the pen. This suggests that some solutions are strongly favoured by the problem itself and are not tied to one lineage. Hold the reading with an open hand, though: it would weaken if the different tree forms proved to share a single evolutionary origin. Sometimes the problem is the architect.
questions: How great was the forests' sway over Devonian carbon dioxide and climate?
How much of the Late Devonian extinction was the forests' doing?

fields.summary: The Digital Revolution is the spread of digital computing and networks from the mid-20th century on, and it includes the internet (from 1969) and the World Wide Web (from 1989 to 1991). Think of it as a new architecture of connection laid over the old world.
facts: In 1969 the first message was sent on ARPANET, a precursor of the internet; that was the threshold.
Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web in 1989, and in 1991 it opened to the public.
From about 2007, smartphones put networked computers in billions of pockets, and the architecture of the network came to rest in your hand.
More than five billion people now use the internet: that is the size of the communion today.
fields.context: For its lineage, see [[technology/digital-computer|Digital Computer]] and [[person/alan-turing|Alan Turing]]. This is the defining process of the [[era/information-age|Information Age]], the grammar in which that age is written.
fields.observer: The Observer regards this as memory-outsourcing at scale. Consider what you did today: the messages, the payments, the photographs. Nearly every human utterance, transaction and image can now be stored and searched; the ledger has left the mind for the machine. A record of the species is being written faster than any observer could read. Memory, once kept, now keeps us.
questions: How will we preserve the digital record, and how will we interpret it?

fields.summary: The hominin lineage, the line that leads to humans, parted from the line leading to chimpanzees and bonobos between roughly 6 and 8 million years ago in Africa, as one river divides around a stone into two streams.
facts: The genetic clocks that time the parting run on assumed mutation rates and generation times: one 2006 study set it no earlier than about 6.3 million years ago, while studies that assume longer generation times imply earlier dates.
Among the early candidates to stand on the hominin side of the divide is [[species/sahelanthropus-tchadensis|Sahelanthropus tchadensis]], from about 7 million years ago.
Upright walking, bipedalism, is a key early trait, the first stride of the long road; see [[species/australopithecus-afarensis|Australopithecus afarensis]].
A 2006 genetic study proposed that the parting was gradual, the two lineages still interbreeding for a time like streams braiding before they part, though this model is disputed.
fields.context: The divergence unfolds within the [[era/cenozoic-era|Cenozoic Era]], and it raises the biological stage for the [[event/origin-of-homo-sapiens|Origin of Homo sapiens]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the species' closest relatives are two other apes. Consider how many human stories rest on a wall between 'them' and 'us', a whole architecture of difference. The line between the two is thinner than most of those stories suggest. Kinship runs closer than the walls we build around it.
questions: Did Sahelanthropus walk upright, and did it stand on the hominin side of the parting?

fields.summary: Over about four thousand years, Bantu-speaking peoples spread from a homeland in West-Central Africa (present-day Nigeria and Cameroon) across central, eastern, and southern Africa, the way a river in flood spreads across a plain.
facts: Today about 350 million people speak one of roughly 500 Bantu languages, a forest of tongues whose count shifts with the counting: estimates range from about 440 to 680, depending on how languages are reckoned.
Linguistic and archaeological evidence alike follow the trail of the spread back to about 3000 BCE.
The expansion is bound up with farming and, in places, with the forge-light of iron working.
It was a braid of migration, intermarriage, and language shift, not only the replacement of one population by another.
fields.context: In the codex of [[region/sub-saharan-africa|Sub-Saharan Africa]], the expansion stands as a defining event of the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]]. Among the states that belong to its story is [[place/great-zimbabwe|Great Zimbabwe]].
fields.observer:
I see one language family covering a third of a continent. I look for conquest and find something quieter. I find it in the mix of farming and mobility. I find it in daily contact: a word across a field, a word at a wedding, a word over a meal.

How does a tongue cross a continent? The same way it crosses a table. Language travels through daily contact, not only conquest.
questions: How much of the spread was people on the move, and how much was people taking up a new language?

fields.summary: On 1 March 1896, at the Battle of Adwa, the Ethiopian army under Emperor Menelik II decisively defeated an invading Italian force, and with that victory secured Ethiopia's independence.
