The Human Genome Project ran from 1990 to 2003; the first complete, gap-free sequence of a human genome, all chromosomes except Y, was published in 2022.
CRISPR gene editing was developed in 2012.

Ancient DNA has transformed prehistory: the [[species/homo-neanderthalensis|Homo neanderthalensis]] genome was sequenced in 2010, and this work brought the discovery of the [[species/denisovans|Denisovans]].
fields.context: This revolution depends on the [[event/digital-revolution|Digital Revolution]] for its computing power, and it has reshaped both medicine and our understanding of human origins.
fields.observer: You have learned to read the instructions from which you are built, and to change them. You can now also read the DNA of relatives long dead.
questions: What limits should govern editing the human genome?

fields.summary: The Great Acceleration names the sharp, simultaneous rise, since about 1950, in human population, energy use, economic output, and environmental change.
facts: The term was coined by the International Geosphere-Biosphere Programme, and a 2015 study charted 24 indicators of it.
Global population rose from about 2.5 billion in 1950 to about 8 billion in 2022.
Energy use, fertilizer use, and greenhouse gas emissions all climbed steeply alongside it.
Many Earth-system indicators — extinction rates, ocean acidity, carbon dioxide — changed in parallel.
fields.context: The Great Acceleration stands as a main candidate for the start of the [[era/anthropocene|Anthropocene]]. See [[observer-note/the-species-as-a-geological-force|The Species as a Geological Force]] and [[event/modern-climate-change|Modern Climate Change]].
fields.observer: Treat 1950 as a hinge: the curves for population, energy, and impact all bend upward at once, together. The scale of change compressed into a single human lifetime has no earlier parallel.
questions: Which of the curves can be bent, and how quickly?

fields.summary: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification was a long flowering of life in the seas, a rise in the diversity of marine animals running from about 485 to 460 million years ago, which multiplied the species and families held within body plans first drawn in the Cambrian.
facts: By some counts, marine diversity at the level of family and genus rose several-fold between the Early and Middle Ordovician.

Brachiopods, bryozoans, molluscs, echinoderms such as the crinoids, corals and sponges all branched into new forms, and reefs and filter-feeding communities grew more intricate. The plankton, too, diversified in their turn.

The [[event/cambrian-explosion|Cambrian Explosion]] had produced the body plans; the Ordovician diversification filled the variety within them, like water finding every channel of a riverbed already carved.

Proposed causes include a cooling from the hot Cambrian climate, more oxygen in the water, nutrients born of volcanism, more shallow shelf habitat, and feedbacks within the ecology itself; which mix truly mattered is debated.
The long rise ended near the close of the period, with the coming of the [[event/late-ordovician-extinction|Late Ordovician Extinction]].
fields.context: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification stands as the main event of the [[era/ordovician-period|Ordovician Period]] within the [[era/paleozoic-era|Paleozoic Era]], and it follows the [[event/cambrian-explosion|Cambrian Explosion]]. It belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer: Notice that variety depends on ecological space as much as on novelty itself: the same body plans, given new habitats and richer food webs, yielded far more forms than before. Read this as a slow build following a fast start. The reading would weaken if diversity had simply risen on its own, with no link to habitat or climate.
questions: What drove the biodiversification: climate, ocean chemistry, ecology, or a combination?
How much of the apparent rise reflects better preservation of Ordovician rocks?

fields.summary: The Great Oxidation Event was the rise of free oxygen into Earth's air, beginning about 2.4 billion years ago, driven by the quiet work of photosynthetic microbes.
facts: Oxygen-producing photosynthesis carried out by [[species/cyanobacteria|Cyanobacteria]] slowly filled the chemical sinks that had swallowed it before, sinks such as iron dissolved in the sea.
Banded iron formations hold that process recorded in stone.
Oxygen was a poison to much of the anaerobic life that had ruled before it; some scientists infer from this a great turnover of the living world.
It may be linked to the Huronian glaciation, one of the earliest of the ice ages.
fields.context: This event opens the [[era/proterozoic-eon|Proterozoic Eon]]. Oxygen would later sustain complex life, animals among them; see [[event/cambrian-explosion|Cambrian Explosion]].
fields.observer: Here is a lesson that recurs across the record: a living population can change its planet so thoroughly that it reshapes its own future. You are the second case of this, not the first.
questions: How long did the transition take?

fields.summary: The Green Revolution was the spread, from the 1940s to the 1970s, of high-yield crop varieties, fertilizers, and irrigation, and it greatly increased grain production.
facts: The plant breeder Norman Borlaug developed high-yield semi-dwarf wheat in Mexico, and IR8 rice was released in 1966.
India, Pakistan, Mexico, and the Philippines counted among the earliest and largest adopters.
The revolution is credited with averting large famines, though it also brought heavy fertilizer and water use with it.
Yields and populations rose together.
fields.context: The Green Revolution fed the growth of the [[event/great-acceleration|Great Acceleration]]. Compare it with [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]].
fields.observer: You can read this as a second Settling: another jump in food that let the species grow by billions. The Haber-Bosch process, which fixes nitrogen for fertilizer, now underwrites a large share of your food supply.
questions: What were the long-term ecological costs?

fields.summary: The Haitian Revolution, from 1791 to 1804, was a rebellion of enslaved people against the French colony of Saint-Domingue, and it created the independent state of Haiti.
facts: Saint-Domingue was one of the most profitable sugar colonies in the world.
An uprising began in August 1791, and Toussaint Louverture rose as its most prominent leader.
Independence was declared on 1 January 1804, making Haiti the first republic founded by formerly enslaved people.
France later demanded a large indemnity, in 1825, which burdened Haiti's economy for generations after.
fields.context: The revolution stands as a central event of the [[event/age-of-revolutions|Age of Revolutions]] and a turning point in the history of the [[event/atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic Slave Trade]].
fields.observer: Notice that the language of universal rights, the very language French revolutionaries also used, was taken at its word by people its authors had excluded. Story-glue, once written, can be turned against those who wrote it.
questions: How did the indemnity shape Haiti's later development?

fields.summary: The Holocaust was the persecution of European Jews by Nazi Germany beginning in 1933, and the systematic murder of about six million of them from 1941 to 1945, carried out with the help of allies and collaborators.
facts: Persecution began after the Nazi rise to power in 1933 and included exclusion, expropriation, and the Nuremberg Laws of 1935.
Systematic mass murder began in 1941, first through shootings in the occupied Soviet Union, and then in extermination camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, and Sobibor.
About six million Jews were killed.
The Nazis murdered as well Roma and Sinti people, disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war, and political opponents.
The word genocide was coined by Raphael Lemkin in 1944, and the UN adopted the Genocide Convention in 1948.
fields.context: The Holocaust took place within [[event/world-war-ii|World War II]] and stands as the most thoroughly documented case of [[observer-note/sanctioned-harm|Sanctioned Harm]] by a modern state. Holocaust sits within the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]] and the region of [[region/europe|Europe]], within the theme threads of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer records this as an atrocity carried out by an industrial, literate, bureaucratic society, and it declines to explain the fact away. The evidence shows that ordinary institutions, records, and technologies were turned toward extermination, which is why you keep returning to the question of how this occurred.
questions: How did ordinary people come to take part?

fields.summary: The Nuclear Age began on 16 July 1945, with the first test of a nuclear weapon, followed by the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6 and 9 August.
facts: Nuclear weapons rely on [[technology/nuclear-fission|Nuclear Fission]], and later also on fusion.
The Cold War built arsenals running to tens of thousands of warheads; about 12,000 remain today.
Nuclear deterrence, arms-control treaties, and nonproliferation efforts shaped the politics of the world.
Nuclear power, too, supplies a share of the world's electricity.
fields.context: The Nuclear Age sits within the [[era/information-age|Information Age]]. See [[person/albert-einstein|Albert Einstein]] and [[person/marie-curie|Marie Curie]] for the related science.
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the species has, since 1945, held the technical means to end its own history. That it has survived this long is, itself, a subject worth studying.
questions: Which factors best explain why no nuclear weapon has been used since 1945?

fields.summary: Ice grew. Large sheets, across North America and Eurasia, about 2.7 million years ago. And with that growth began the repeating glacial and interglacial cycles of the Quaternary Period.
facts: Ice-rafted debris — in North Atlantic seafloor sediments — turns widespread, about 2.7 million years ago. And on the Chinese Loess Plateau, the loess begins piling up, about 2.6 million years ago.
Smaller ice sheets had come before, in the Northern Hemisphere. This was expansion — a large one — not the first appearance of ice.

Proposed causes: a slow decline in carbon dioxide through the Pliocene. Changes in ocean circulation. Mountain uplift, bending the flow of the atmosphere. The closure of the Isthmus of Panama stands as a candidate too, though its timing is debated; see [[event/closure-of-the-isthmus-of-panama|Closure of the Isthmus of Panama]].
The first cycles followed the tilt of Earth's axis — a period of about 41,000 years.
fields.context: This onset comes near the end of the [[era/neogene-period|Neogene Period]] and leads into the [[era/quaternary-period|Quaternary Period]], building on the earlier cooling of the [[event/eocene-oligocene-transition|Eocene-Oligocene Transition]]. The event belongs to the [[era/cenozoic-era|Cenozoic Era]] and the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the world every human society has known is one of repeating ice ages — a world that began only about 2.7 million years ago, after a slow decline in carbon dioxide and, perhaps, a rearrangement of ocean gateways. The Observer takes this as context, not cause: what it did to the making of humans remains a separate, unsettled question. The reading would weaken if the carbon dioxide decline proved too small to explain the change.
questions: What combination — carbon dioxide falling, oceans shifting — tipped the climate into these cycles?
How did this new rhythm affect the early hominins?

fields.summary: The onset of plate tectonics marks the hour when the rigid plates of Earth's outer shell began their slow march, the ocean floor swallowed back into the mantle at the subduction zones. Proposed dates range from before 4 billion to about 0.8 billion years ago, and the question remains among the most disputed in all of Earth science.
facts: Plate tectonics moves about a dozen great plates, and recycles the ocean floor at the subduction zones. Earth alone, of all known worlds, bears it.

Proposed onsets: before 4.0 billion years ago. About 3.2 billion. About 2.5 billion. About 0.8 billion. Some researchers argue instead for a gradual transition out of a rigid outer lid, or for episodic subduction, long before plate motion took its modern form.

Blueschists — born in cold subduction zones — and ultra-high-pressure metamorphic rocks appear in the record only after about 0.8 billion years ago. Some geologists read this as a marker of modern-style subduction.
Alfred Wegener first proposed continental drift, in 1912, and plate tectonics won wide acceptance only in the 1960s.
Plate tectonics raises up continents and recycles carbon. Whether it was needed for a long-lived biosphere is still debated.
fields.context: The Onset of Plate Tectonics ties to the growth of continents in the [[era/archean-eon|Archean Eon]] and to the [[event/earliest-continental-crust|Earliest Continental Crust]]. Its later effects reach the [[event/breakup-of-pangaea|Breakup of Pangaea]] and the [[event/collision-of-india-and-asia|Collision of India and Asia]]. The event belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Earth's surface has recycled its own earliest evidence, so when the process began may be settled only indirectly. Some geologists treat plate tectonics as a precondition for a long-lived biosphere, and the Observer keeps that as an open hypothesis. It reads the present disagreement as information about the limits of the record, and it would weaken if a reliable early rock record were ever found.
questions: When did the plates first begin their turning, and did the change come gradual, or sudden?
Was the slow turning of plates required for a long-lived biosphere?

fields.summary: The Silk Roads were braided threads of road and sea, linking East Asia, South Asia, Central Asia, and the Mediterranean, growing from the second century BCE onward.
facts: The missions of the Han envoy Zhang Qian, around 138 to 126 BCE, are often taken as the starting point of it all.
Silk traveled these roads, and horses, glass, spices, paper — and with the goods went ideas, and religions too, Buddhism among them.
Disease traveled these roads as well; see [[event/black-death|Black Death]].
The name 'Silk Road' itself was coined only in 1877, by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen.
fields.context: These roads link [[region/east-asia|East Asia]], the [[region/central-asian-steppe|Central Asian Steppe]], [[region/south-asia|South Asia]], and the [[region/mediterranean-basin|Mediterranean Basin]], and grew first under the [[culture/han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]], and later under the [[culture/mongol-empire|Mongol Empire]].
fields.observer: I think of the Silk Roads as a web with no single owner. So few travelers, I remind myself, ever walked the whole way — the goods and the ideas moved instead through long chains of intermediaries, hand to hand. Who owns a road no one walks end to end? No one ever has.
questions: How much of this long-distance trade carried luxury goods, and how much carried the goods of everyday life?

fields.summary: The Opium Wars were two conflicts between Qing China and Britain — joined, in the second, by France — fought over trade and diplomatic relations, from 1839 to 1842 and from 1856 to 1860, and they opened China to Western commerce on unequal terms.
facts: The Treaty of Nanking, in 1842, ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain, and opened five treaty ports: Canton, Amoy, Foochow, Ningpo, and Shanghai.
The Convention of Beijing, in 1860, gave Britain the Kowloon peninsula, and granted foreign powers a permanent diplomatic presence in Beijing.
It also legalized the opium trade, and gave Christians the right to own property and to preach.
In China, the wars are remembered as the start of a 'century of humiliation'.
fields.context: The wars weakened the [[culture/qing-dynasty|Qing Dynasty]] just before the [[event/taiping-rebellion|Taiping Rebellion]]. Industrial-age naval and firearm superiority, drawn from the [[event/industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]], decided the outcome.
fields.observer: The Observer notes a trade war in the most literal sense: one state fought to keep a product from its own people, and lost, to a state that fought to sell it. Exchange-webs, the Observer reminds us, are not always fair.
questions: How much did the opium trade shape the decline of the Qing, compared with problems from within?

fields.summary: Habitual upright walking rose in the human lineage, in Africa, somewhere between roughly 7 and 4 million years ago — the earliest mark of the hominins, older by millions of years than large brains or the first stone tools, though its true starting point and cause remain disputed.
facts: Sahelanthropus tchadensis, out of Chad, about 7 million years old, bears a skull base that suggests an upright posture. A 2022 study of a femur argued for habitual bipedalism, though others dispute it, and whether it was truly a hominin at all is debated.
Orrorin tugenensis, from Kenya, about 6 million years old, is known from thigh bones read as evidence of bipedality — a reading that is controversial.

Ardipithecus ramidus, from Ethiopia, about 4.4 million years old, had a pelvis that combined climbing and walking, and a big toe still made for grasping. How well it walked is debated, and its excavators read its site as woodland, not open savanna.

The footprints at Laetoli, in Tanzania, about 3.66 million years old and attributed to [[species/australopithecus-afarensis|Australopithecus afarensis]], stand as the earliest direct record of upright walking.
Proposed reasons: energy efficiency. The carrying of food, or of infants. Heat regulation. Feeding from thin branches. None of them agreed upon.
fields.context: The origin of bipedalism follows the [[event/divergence-of-the-hominin-lineage|Divergence of the Hominin Lineage]] and falls within the [[era/neogene-period|Neogene Period]] of the [[era/cenozoic-era|Cenozoic Era]]. It comes millions of years before the [[event/emergence-of-the-genus-homo|Emergence of the Genus Homo]] and the [[technology/oldowan-stone-tools|Oldowan Stone Tools]]. See [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the species' ancestors walked upright for millions of years before they had large brains or made recognizable tools, so the posture was not an adaptation for those things, and nothing in the record shows it aiming toward them. The Observer reads it as a precondition: hands freed from walking could later carry, and later still, make. The reading would weaken if the earliest claimed bipeds turned out to be apes with independently evolved postures of their own.
questions: Was Sahelanthropus truly a habitual biped, and was it, in truth, a hominin at all?
Did upright walking begin on the ground, or in the branches of the trees?

fields.summary: Ice came. Then it came again. The Huronian Supergroup of Ontario, Canada, holds a series of ice ages from the early Paleoproterozoic, about 2.4 to 2.2 billion years ago. One of the oldest ice ages we can still read clearly in stone.
facts: North of Lake Huron: three glacial deposits. Ramsay Lake. Bruce. Gowganda. Between them, sediment laid down in warmer conditions.

Not only Ontario. Wyoming too. Finland too. Glacial deposits of similar age, scattered across continents. And the Makganyene Formation in South Africa, about 2.2 billion years old — ice that formed near the equator. That detail supports an early snowball state. Whether it connects to the Huronian at all is debated.

The glaciation follows the first rise of oxygen. One hypothesis: oxygen ate the atmosphere's methane, a strong greenhouse gas, and cooled the world that let it in. Other explanations point instead to volcanoes. To the shifting of plates.
How long the ice held on. Whether it wrapped the whole planet. Both still debated.
fields.context: The Huronian Glaciation falls in the [[era/paleoproterozoic-era|Paleoproterozoic Era]], soon after the [[event/great-oxidation-event|Great Oxidation Event]] began. The earliest ice age of the [[era/proterozoic-eon|Proterozoic Eon]], before [[event/snowball-earth|Snowball Earth]]. It belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: File the Huronian under a caution about attribution: an ice age and an oxygen rise that share a date invite you to build a causal story between them. That story is plausible, but the record allows other explanations too. The reading would strengthen, or weaken, with tighter dating of the glacial deposits against the first traces of oxygen.
questions: Did the oxygen rise cause the glaciation? Or did the two arise from some common cause?
Was the ice global?

fields.summary: The incense trade carried frankincense and myrrh out of southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa, across desert and season, to Mediterranean and Mesopotamian markets — borne mostly on camel caravan, for well over a thousand years.
facts: Frankincense weeps from the Boswellia trees that grow in southern Arabia — in Oman, in Yemen — and in the Horn of Africa.
It was burned in temples and at funerals across the Egyptian, Greek, and Roman worlds, its smoke rising toward gods and the dead alike.
Caravans moved northward, through western Arabia, toward the Levant.
Kingdoms such as Saba and the Nabataeans grew rich on the taxing and guiding of these caravans.
The trade faded in the later Roman period; reduced demand is often named as one cause.
fields.context: The trade linked the [[region/arabian-peninsula|Arabian Peninsula]] to the [[region/mediterranean-basin|Mediterranean Basin]] and came before the wider [[event/opening-of-the-silk-roads|Opening of the Silk Roads]]. It fed the wealth of the [[culture/kingdom-of-saba|Kingdom of Saba]] and the [[culture/nabataeans|Nabataeans]]. Incense Trade sits within the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]] and the region of [[region/arabian-peninsula|Arabian Peninsula]], within the theme threads of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: I think of a resin burned to nothing, its smoke gone before the memory of the fire — and I remember how it sustained kingdoms in desert country for centuries. I remember how little a thing needs to be useful to be wanted. What does it mean that so much of exchange was never about survival at all, only about ritual, only about what we needed to believe? A scent that vanished built the wealth that lasted.
questions: How much did this route change with the domestication of the camel?

fields.summary: The Indian Ocean trade network was a web of sea routes binding East Africa, Arabia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and China together, and it ran busiest from about the 8th to the 15th century CE.
facts: The seasonal monsoon winds were the tide beneath it all, carrying ships east in one season and calling them home in another.
Spices, cotton textiles, ivory, gold, and Chinese porcelain all passed along these lanes.
Swahili city-states such as Kilwa on the East African coast grew rich upon it; see [[culture/swahili-coast-city-states|Swahili Coast City-States]].
Portuguese ships entered these waters in 1498 and began to seize control of the key ports.
fields.context: The network ran alongside the overland [[event/opening-of-the-silk-roads|Opening of the Silk Roads]] and carried Islam and other faiths from port to port. See [[person/zheng-he|Zheng He]].
fields.observer: I notice that the wind itself kept the calendar here. I remember how a cycle no one owned let strangers of many faiths run a shared exchange between them, for centuries, with almost no one in charge. Who needs a king when the monsoon returns on time? A pattern you can trust becomes its own kind of law.
questions: How large was the volume of trade compared to overland routes?

fields.summary: Between October 1935 and May 1936, Italy's colonial invasion of Ethiopia unfolded as a stark violation of the architecture of collective security: Italian forces used mustard gas, seized the capital, and drove Emperor Haile Selassie into exile, while the League of Nations failed to act. Ethiopia's liberation came in 1941.
facts: The war began on 3 October 1935, when General Emilio De Bono crossed the Mareb River into Ethiopia without a formal declaration of war. Emperor Haile Selassie I led the defence, and by 1936 Benito Mussolini claimed victory.
On 5 May 1936, Italian forces took the capital, Addis Ababa. Haile Selassie went into exile, first to Palestine, then to England.
Italy used mustard gas in the war, a violation of the international agreements it had itself signed.
Both Italy and Ethiopia belonged to the League of Nations, yet the League failed to stop Italy or protect Ethiopia — an episode remembered as exposing the League's own weakness.
In 1941, Ethiopian resistance fighters, together with Allied forces, ended Italian rule.
fields.context: The war reversed the outcome of the [[event/battle-of-adwa|Battle of Adwa]] of 1896, in which Ethiopia under [[person/menelik-ii|Menelik II]] had defeated an Italian army, and it stood apart from the [[event/scramble-for-africa|Scramble for Africa]] as a late colonial conquest, one often read as a prelude to [[event/world-war-ii|World War II]].
fields.observer: The Observer records the use of chemical weapons against a state that had appealed to a body of nations for protection, and the failure of that body to act. Here is the architecture of collective security laid bare: it holds only as far as its members are willing to bear a cost.
questions: How many Ethiopian civilians and soldiers were killed by gas and by other means?
How much did Ethiopian resistance during the occupation contribute to the 1941 liberation, compared with Allied forces?

fields.summary: The Second Sino-Japanese War (1937 to 1945) was the full-scale war between Japan and China that opened at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing and later merged into World War II. Its violence included the mass killing of civilians, among them at Nanjing, whose death toll remains disputed.
facts: Full-scale war began on 7 July 1937, after the Marco Polo Bridge Incident near Beijing — an undeclared war that quickly grew into large-scale fighting across northern China.
The incident hastened formation of the Second United Front between the Kuomintang and the Chinese Communist Party.

Japanese forces took Nanjing on 13 December 1937 and began mass killings there that same day. Estimates of the number of Chinese killed range from about 100,000 to more than 300,000; one scholarly assessment gives about 50,000 killed within the city walls in the first days, and more than 100,000 but fewer than 200,000 killed in the city and surrounding counties by March 1938.
The figures are contested: some Japanese revisionists give much lower numbers, while some Chinese official figures run higher than the scholarly range.
fields.context: The war followed Japan's industrialization and expansion after the [[event/meiji-restoration|Meiji Restoration]], and after 1941 it merged into [[event/world-war-ii|World War II]]. See [[observer-note/sanctioned-harm|Sanctioned Harm]].
fields.observer: The Observer records the mass killings at Nanjing as an atrocity, whatever the argument over the count. That the number itself has become a claim-line between governments and historians shows how one figure can carry the weight of an entire nation's memory.
questions: How should the Nanjing death toll be settled, given records that are incomplete and sources that differ by nationality?
In total, how many Chinese died in the war, including from famine and disease?

fields.summary: The Seven Years' War (1756 to 1763) was fought between Britain and France, and their allies, across several continents, and it left Britain dominant in both North America and India.
facts: The war was fought across Europe, North America, the Caribbean, West Africa, India, and the Philippines.
In North America, it is known as the French and Indian War.
The 1763 Treaty of Paris gave Britain Canada and French territory east of the Mississippi.
British victory at Plassey in 1757 opened the East India Company's rule over Bengal.
Britain's war debts drove new taxes on the American colonies.
fields.context: The war is sometimes called the first global war. Its consequences fed the [[event/age-of-revolutions|Age of Revolutions]] and reshaped control of trade across India and the Atlantic, including the [[event/atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic Slave Trade]]. The Seven Years' War sits within the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region [[region/planet-wide|Planet-wide]], and belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a dispute between European powers was decided in the forests of North America, the plains of Bengal, and the seas of the Caribbean — evidence of a network in which any local quarrel could become planetary.
questions: How much of the American Revolution did the war's debts actually cause?

fields.summary: The Siberian Traps eruptions: one of the largest volcanic outpourings of the last 500 million years. Northern Siberia, about 252 to 251 million years ago. They coincide with the end-Permian mass extinction.
facts: Lava flows. Intrusions. A huge stretch of northern Siberia, buried in rock. Estimates of the volume run from about one to several million cubic kilometres.
Precise radiometric dating pins the main phase to a window of about a million years or less, bracketing the extinction. Near 251.9 million years ago.

Proposed killing mechanisms, catalogued: large releases of carbon dioxide and methane that warmed the planet. Ocean acidification. Oxygen loss. Toxic gases from sulfur and halogens. Magma intruding coal, carbonate and salt-bearing rock may have released large volumes of gas.
Marine and land records show rapid warming of the tropics and oceans at the extinction. How much of it the eruptions caused: still debated.
The extinction itself: described in [[event/permian-triassic-extinction|Permian-Triassic Extinction]].
fields.context: The Siberian Traps Eruptions close the [[era/permian-period|Permian Period]]. The leading proposed cause of the [[event/permian-triassic-extinction|Permian-Triassic Extinction]]. After it, the [[era/triassic-period|Triassic Period]] opens the Mesozoic. The event belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a volcanic episode lasting about a million years was enough to remove most of the life then living, and that any comparison with a modern process holds or fails on rates, not on totals. The Observer treats the timing question as central for that reason. This reading would weaken if the eruptions were shown to have begun well before the extinction with little effect.
questions: Of the eruption's effects, from warming to toxic gases, which did the most damage?
How closely does the eruption's timing align with the extinction's pulses?

fields.summary: Snowball Earth: glaciations in the late Proterozoic. The Sturtian and the Marinoan, roughly 717 to 635 million years ago. Ice, perhaps, reaching all the way to the tropics.
facts: Glacial deposits, formed near the paleo-equator. Support for the hypothesis.
Capping them: unusual carbonate rocks.
Did the oceans freeze completely? Or did open water remain — a 'slushball'? Scientists still debate it.
Soon after the last glaciation: the Ediacaran biota appear.
fields.context: The glaciations come shortly before the [[event/cambrian-explosion|Cambrian Explosion]], and may be linked to it. See [[era/proterozoic-eon|Proterozoic Eon]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Earth passed through a nearly lifeless deep freeze and still recovered. Planetary systems can undergo extreme shifts and reset.
questions: Did the ocean freeze fully?

fields.summary: The Space Age opened on 4 October 1957, when the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite.
facts: In 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space.
On 20 July 1969, Apollo 11 landed the first humans on the Moon.
Satellites now underwrite navigation, weather forecasting, and communications.
Since 2000, the International Space Station has been continuously occupied.
fields.context: The Space Age belongs to the [[era/information-age|Information Age]] and was driven by the Cold War rivalry of the [[event/nuclear-age|Nuclear Age]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a change in perspective: for the first time, members of the species could photograph their own planet as a whole. Images such as the 'Blue Marble' changed how many people describe their home.
questions: Will permanent settlements beyond Earth ever become a reality?

fields.summary: From small, feathered theropod dinosaurs of the Jurassic came the birds, first known in fossils about 160 to 150 million years old, sparks struck from a long dynasty of scaled kin. Of all the dinosaur lines, only this one still lives, singing on into the present.
facts: Birds carried the mark of their theropod ancestors in hollow bones, a forked wishbone and a three-fingered hand, and the feathered non-avian dinosaurs unearthed in China from the 1990s onward bound the kinship tighter.

Feathers came before flight, likely first for warmth or for display. By about 160 million years ago the theropod Anchiornis, and by about 150 million years ago [[species/archaeopteryx|Archaeopteryx]], both already wore feathered wings.
Early Cretaceous fossils from China, about 125 million years old, hold many forms of early bird, the toothless-beaked Confuciusornis chief among them.
Whether flight rose from the ground or fell from the trees remains disputed, and some small, feathered dinosaurs bore four wings.
Only the lineage that became modern birds lived through the [[event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction|Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction]], and from that narrow survival the living birds spread wide.
fields.context: The origin of birds falls within the [[era/jurassic-period|Jurassic Period]] and the [[era/mesozoic-era|Mesozoic Era]], a chapter in the long tale of the [[species/dinosaurs|Dinosaurs]], woven into the theme threads of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer: The Observer points out that a familiar category, bird, nests inside a far stranger one, dinosaur, proof that the names we give kinds of creature are only cuts across one continuous lineage. This reading is about naming alone, and stands whichever way the debate over flight's origin resolves.
questions: At what point in theropod evolution did powered flight first arise?
Which Jurassic fossils belong among the birds, and which merely among their close relatives?

fields.summary: Eukaryotes, cells bearing a nucleus and inner organelles, the stuff from which every animal, plant and fungus is built, arose roughly 2 billion years ago, though the date carries very wide uncertainty.
facts: The mitochondrion descends from a bacterium taken into a host cell, a merger called endosymbiosis, and this account is widely accepted.
The chloroplast likewise descends from a cyanobacterium that took up residence within certain eukaryotic cells.
Genomic studies set the host cell among the Archaea, and the Asgard archaea are often named its closest kin.

The oldest fossils of eukaryotes beyond doubt, large microfossils walled in organic matter, are more than 1.65 billion years old. Older candidates, such as Grypania at about 1.87 billion years, persuade less than the younger, larger forms.
Molecular-clock estimates for the last common ancestor of all living eukaryotes vary widely still.
fields.context: The origin of eukaryotes followed the oxygen rise of the [[event/great-oxidation-event|Great Oxidation Event]] and made large multicellular bodies possible, leading in time to the [[event/cambrian-explosion|Cambrian Explosion]]. It sits within the [[era/proterozoic-eon|Proterozoic Eon]] and the region [[region/planet-wide|Planet-wide]], within the theme threads of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that complexity arrived here through merger, not through one lineage inventing every part on its own: cooperation between unlike partners is the architecture beneath every body, the human one included. Strong evidence that the organelles were built internally, without symbiosis, would point to a different origin.
questions: Did the host cell take in the mitochondrion before or after it grew complex?
How old is the last common ancestor of the eukaryotes?

fields.summary: Anatomically modern humans, Homo sapiens, took shape across Africa by about 300,000 years ago, not at a single hearth, but through a gradual process spanning the continent.
facts: At Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, fossils about 315,000 years old (315 plus or minus 34 thousand years) show a modern face and teeth set above a more archaic braincase.
Fossils from Omo Kibish, Ethiopia, are at least 233,000 years old, their age fixed against a layer of volcanic ash.
Some scholars call this process 'African multiregionalism': several connected populations, not one, contributed to it.
The regional label stays approximate: Jebel Irhoud lies in North Africa, while the other principal sites lie in East and southern Africa.
fields.context: This origin belongs to the [[era/pleistocene-epoch|Pleistocene Epoch]] and comes before the [[event/out-of-africa-dispersal|Out of Africa Dispersal]]. See [[species/homo-sapiens|Homo sapiens]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the species' origin is no single place or moment: it is a widespread, interbreeding population that grew recognizably modern only over tens of thousands of years.
questions: Was there one core population, or many linked ones?

fields.summary: When spoken language began, no one knows, because neither speech nor the brain's grammar circuitry leaves a fossil. The published estimates for when the capacity existed range from about 2 million to 50,000 years ago, depending on whether you read the genetic, the anatomical, or the archaeological evidence.
facts: Neanderthals share two speech-linked changes to the FOXP2 gene with modern humans, once read as pushing the capacity for language back 300,000 to 400,000 years. A larger 2018 study found no sign of recent human-specific selection at that gene, and FOXP2 is now treated as one gene among many.

A Neanderthal hyoid bone from Kebara Cave, about 60,000 years old, closely resembles a modern one, and is cited as evidence of speech-capable anatomy. Others argue that vocal-tract proportions still limited the range of sounds it could make.

The evidence of the skull base shows a gradual trend toward a modern vocal tract, none of the change present in Australopithecus, a near-modern shape already in Homo heidelbergensis about 600,000 years ago, cited as evidence for slow change.

A 2025 genetic synthesis argued that the capacity for language existed by the earliest known split among Homo sapiens populations, about 135,000 years ago, though its cultural use may have begun later, once symbolic material such as engraved ochre appears.

Researchers divide between a gradualist view, in which language built up over a million years or more, and a saltational view, in which syntax arose abruptly; a separate debate asks whether gesture or vocalization was the original channel.
fields.context: This question overlaps the [[era/paleolithic|Paleolithic]] and the biology of [[species/homo-sapiens|Homo sapiens]] and [[species/homo-neanderthalensis|Homo neanderthalensis]]. The [[event/emergence-of-symbolic-art|Emergence of Symbolic Art]] and the [[event/control-of-fire|Control of Fire]] are often cited as indirect evidence, without settling when language began. See [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: I read every date offered here as a guess dressed up as a measurement, because sound leaves nothing behind for the shovel to find. Between the earliest moment the body stood ready for language and the earliest confident sign of symbolic behavior, there stretches a gap of tens of thousands of years, and I do not know whether that gap is real or only an accident of what survived. This reading would weaken if a dating method free from guesswork were ever found.
questions: Did having the capacity for language mean a population spoke habitually, or could that capacity come tens of thousands of years before it was used?
Did Neanderthals possess language, or only some simpler form of it?

fields.summary: Life on Earth rose up at least 3.5 billion years ago, and perhaps earlier still. How it began, no one yet knows.
facts: In the Dresser Formation of the Pilbara region, Western Australia, stromatolites, layered mounds built by microbes, stand about 3.48 billion years old, called the oldest convincing evidence that life had begun.

Claims to older evidence remain disputed. In 2016 researchers reported stromatolites about 3.7 billion years old at Isua in Greenland, and a paper in the same journal soon challenged the observations. Later studies still disagree on whether the structures are biological at all.

A 2024 molecular-clock study placed the last universal common ancestor, the one organism from which every living cell descends, at about 4.2 billion years old. That ancestor was not the first life, and the estimate carries a large uncertainty of its own.
The leading hypotheses for how life began name hydrothermal vents, shallow tidal pools, and an early age ruled by RNA, none of them settled as the truth.
fields.context: The origin of life marks the turning from the [[era/hadean-eon|Hadean Eon]] into the biology-ruled [[era/archean-eon|Archean Eon]], and its later effects reach as far as the [[event/great-oxidation-event|Great Oxidation Event]].
fields.observer: The Observer treats this as the least understood event in the whole record, and also the one that made every subject after it possible, the Observer's own field included.
questions: Did life begin once or several times?
Where did it begin?
How reliable is a molecular-clock age for a common ancestor that predates the fossil record by so large a margin?

fields.summary: Mammals rose slowly from the mammal-line reptiles called synapsids, and the oldest candidates for the name come from the Late Triassic, roughly 225 to 205 million years past, though the very date bends on how one defines a mammal.
facts: Mammals descend from the synapsids that ruled Permian land life, passing through the therapsids and then the cynodonts of the Triassic.

The very bones that hinged the jaw of the reptile-like ancestors became, in time, the tiny bones of the mammalian middle ear, a transformation traced through fossils of Late Triassic and Early Jurassic mammal relatives.
The oldest fossils that might be mammals, or their close kin the mammaliaforms, run about 225 to 205 million years old, and which of them count as true mammals depends on the definition chosen.
Most Mesozoic mammals stayed small, though a few, such as Repenomamus of China, about 125 million years old, grew to the size of a badger.
Hair, milk and warm blood all arose somewhere along this lineage, but soft tissue is rarely preserved, so the order in which they came remains uncertain.
fields.context: The origin of mammals falls within the [[era/triassic-period|Triassic Period]] and the [[era/mesozoic-era|Mesozoic Era]], alongside the rise of the [[species/dinosaurs|Dinosaurs]], its lineage reaching back to the mammal-line reptiles of the [[era/permian-period|Permian Period]]. Mammals spread wide after the [[event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction|Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction]], within the theme threads of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that hearing, one of the most ordinary of the senses, rests on bones that once hinged the jaw of a reptile-like ancestor. New structures are built from old parts, the Observer takes that as a general rule of the record, not an exception here. This reading would weaken if the ear bones proved to have arisen with no earlier function in the jaw at all.
questions: When did the first true mammals appear, given how the definition moves the date?
In what order did hair, milk and warm-bloodedness arise?

fields.summary: Ashurbanipal (about 685 to about 631 BCE) held the throne of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 669 BCE onward. His legacy rests on conquest, on the royal library he built at Nineveh, and on palace reliefs that set war and lion hunts side by side as proof of sovereignty.
facts: Born about 685 BCE as a son of Esarhaddon, Ashurbanipal came to the Assyrian throne in 669 BCE, while his brother Shamash-shum-ukin took the throne of Babylon.
In 663 BCE, Assyrian forces sacked Thebes in Egypt, ending Kushite rule there.

Shamash-shum-ukin rose in rebellion in 652 BCE; a long war followed, and Ashurbanipal finally took Babylon in 648 BCE. Campaigns of about 647 to 646 BCE broke Elam, and the campaign of about 646 BCE destroyed Susa.

His libraries at Nineveh, uncovered in the 19th century, held tens of thousands of clay tablets and fragments, among them a version of the Epic of Gilgamesh. He boasted of his own training as a scribe.
His own inscriptions and reliefs record harsh treatment of defeated enemies: mass deportation, mutilation, execution.
He died about 631 BCE, though some place his death about 627. Nineveh itself fell to Babylonians and Medes in 612 BCE.
fields.context: Ashurbanipal ruled the [[culture/neo-assyrian-empire|Neo-Assyrian Empire]] in [[region/mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]] during the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]]. His library carried forward a tradition of writing reaching back to the [[culture/sumerians|Sumerians]]; see [[event/invention-of-writing|Invention of Writing]]. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Ashurbanipal built an architecture of memory for an entire civilization inside the very palace where he recorded the punishment of those who defied him. The library shows memory-outsourcing used as an instrument of rule: gathering omen and ritual texts was a way of governing knowledge alongside territory. This reading would weaken if the library proved to be chiefly the work of earlier kings and scribes, leaving his own part smaller than his boasts suggest.
questions: How much of the library's collecting reflects his own initiative, and how much the labor of his scribes?

fields.summary: Attila (about 406 to 453) ruled the Huns from 434, first jointly with his brother Bleda and, from about 445, alone. He led Hunnic armies against both the Eastern and Western Roman empires, yet almost every written source about him was composed by Greeks and Romans.
facts: Attila's birth year remains uncertain, with estimates ranging from the 390s to the early 400s. He became joint ruler in 434, and sole ruler after Bleda's death, probably about 445.
After the Treaty of Margus in 435, the Eastern Roman Empire doubled its yearly gold tribute to him, and after 443 that tribute is reported to have reached 2,100 Roman pounds.
In 451 he invaded Gaul and met a combined Roman and Visigothic army at the Catalaunian Plains; in 452 he invaded northern Italy. Both times, he withdrew.

He died in 453, after his wedding to Ildico. Priscus, as reported by Jordanes, describes a severe bleed. A later claim that his wife killed him is rejected by most historians, and his empire broke apart within a few years.
Priscus, an envoy who visited his court in 449, left the only known eyewitness account of it. Attila's capital and his tomb have never been found.
fields.context: Attila's power was rooted on the middle Danube in [[region/europe|Europe]] during [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]], and his campaigns added weight to the pressures behind the [[event/fall-of-the-western-roman-empire|Fall of the Western Roman Empire]]. See [[culture/romans|Romans]], [[culture/byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the Huns left no writing of their own, so a ruler remembered as one of history's great enemies survives only through the testimony of his opponents. The gold paid to him ran the empire's exchange-web in reverse: payment offered in return for peace rather than for goods. A specialist could argue that Roman diplomacy and a Germanic revolt, more than any single man's grip, broke the Hunnic polity, a reading that would weaken any portrait of empire built on one personality.
questions: How far can the accounts of his court be trusted, given that the main eyewitness was an envoy of the empire he was pressing?
Where were his capital and his grave?

fields.summary: Augustus (63 BCE to 14 CE) became Rome's first emperor. He closed out a century of civil war and raised the imperial architecture that would stand for centuries.
facts: Born Gaius Octavius, he stood as the adopted heir of Julius Caesar.
Having defeated his rivals, he took the name Augustus in 27 BCE, all while preserving the republic's old forms.
His reign opened the Pax Romana, a long stretch of relative stability.
He reorganized the army, the provinces and taxation alike.
fields.context: See [[culture/romans|Romans]] and [[place/rome|Rome]]. Augustus shaped the political architecture of the empire that would dominate the [[region/mediterranean-basin|Mediterranean Basin]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a deft piece of story-glue at work: a monarch who insisted he was merely 'first citizen', so that the old republican stories could go on serving a new order.
questions: How deliberate was this pretense of restoring the republic?

fields.summary: Ba Trieu (Trieu Thi Trinh; her birth year unknown, she died in 248 CE) led an uprising in 248 CE against the Chinese Eastern Wu administration then governing northern Vietnam, and became a lasting symbol of Vietnamese resistance to foreign rule.
facts: She is said to have raised a rebel force in Cuu Chan, in what is now Thanh Hoa province, at about age twenty, together with her brother Trieu Quoc Dat.

Later chronicles picture her riding into battle on an elephant, clad in gold-decorated armor, though these vivid details come from accounts written many centuries after her death rather than from any contemporary record.
Eastern Wu sent the general Lu Yin to put down the revolt; after several months of fighting, her forces were defeated later in 248.

Vietnamese tradition holds that she fled to Bo Dien commune and took her own life rather than be captured, her burial place attributed to Mount Tung in Hau Loc District, while Chinese-source summaries instead have Lu Yin putting her to death; the sources give no age at her death. A temple to her still stands near the site.
fields.context: Ba Trieu's revolt unfolded in [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]] during [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]], against the Chinese administration that had governed the region since the Han conquest. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Ba Trieu is known largely through Vietnamese chronicles written centuries after her death, in periods when a symbol of resistance to Chinese rule served a clear political purpose. The core event, a suppressed revolt in 248, most likely happened; the vivid personal details are harder to separate from later invention. The earliest and most detailed record, the Jiaozhou ji of the Western Jin period (265 to 318), dates only decades after 248, though Taylor held that Chinese records made no mention of her, and the elephant and gilded-tunic details first appear in later texts such as the Le-era Dai Viet su ky toan thu.
questions: How much of her story took shape through later Vietnamese nation-building rather than contemporary memory?

fields.summary: Ban Zhao (about 45 to about 117 CE) was a Chinese historian and scholar of the Eastern Han dynasty. After her brother's death she helped complete the Book of Han, and she wrote Lessons for Women; at court she also served as tutor and adviser.
facts: Ban Zhao was born about 45 CE, though some sources say about 49, into a scholarly family. Her father Ban Biao and her brother Ban Gu wrote much of the Book of Han (Hanshu), a history of the Western Han dynasty.
When Ban Gu died in prison in 92 CE, the history stood unfinished, and Ban Zhao completed it in part, supplying the missing section of the Eight Tables.
At the imperial court she served as tutor to the empress and her ladies, and from about 106 CE she advised the regent, Empress Deng.

She is believed to have written Lessons for Women (Nüjie), in seven chapters, about 106 CE, though that date is not firmly established. It argues that girls should be educated and lays out rules of conduct for wives.
Later writers made Lessons for Women a standard text for teaching girls obedience, and modern scholars still disagree on whether it reinforced or challenged the limits placed on women.
She died about 117 CE, though some sources say about 120.
fields.context: Ban Zhao worked under the [[culture/han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]] in [[region/east-asia|East Asia]] during [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]]. See [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: I find one woman behind two legacies: the historian who helped complete a dynasty's standard record, and the author of the text most used to teach women obedience. I cannot resolve her into a single direction. Later readers copied Lessons for Women because they valued its counsel, so what survives may carry their wanting as much as her meaning. I would trust this less if the text turned out to be heavily rewritten after she died. Until then, I hold her two legacies together, and let neither go.
questions: Did she mean Lessons for Women as a defense of women's education, as a guide to conduct, or as both?

fields.summary: Between 1519 and 1521, a small Spanish force under Hernan Cortes — allied with many Indigenous city-states and aided by epidemic disease — overthrew the Aztec Empire and captured Tenochtitlan.
facts: In 1519, Cortes landed on the Mexican coast with several hundred men.
Tlaxcala and other city-states, resentful of Aztec tribute, provided large numbers of allied fighters.
A smallpox epidemic in 1520, introduced by the Spanish, killed a large share of the region's population.
Malintzin (Dona Marina) served Cortes as interpreter and negotiator.
Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521, after a siege of about three months.
fields.context: The conquest ended the [[culture/aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]] and destroyed its capital, [[place/tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]]. It stands as an early episode of the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]], in which disease played a central part. The Spanish Conquest of the Aztec Empire sits within the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region [[region/mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]], and belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the conquest is sometimes told as a victory of a few hundred men, but the record shows Indigenous allies and disease doing much of the work. Simple stories of small forces conquering empires tend to leave out the local politics that made them possible.
questions: What share of the population died from disease?

fields.summary: In 1532, Francisco Pizarro's small Spanish force captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca, opening a conquest of the Inca Empire that ended with the fall of the last Inca stronghold in 1572.
facts: At Cajamarca, Pizarro commanded around 168 men.
The empire had only just come through a civil war between Atahualpa and his half-brother Huascar, and epidemic disease had already reached the Andes.
Held for a room-filling ransom of gold and silver, Atahualpa was then executed by strangulation on 29 August 1533.
In 1533, the Spanish occupied Cusco.
In 1572, the neo-Inca state at Vilcabamba was destroyed.
fields.context: The conquest ended the [[culture/inca-empire|Inca Empire]] and opened the silver mines of [[place/potosi|Potosi]] to Spanish exploitation, following the pattern of disease and political division seen across the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]]. The Spanish Conquest of the Inca Empire sits within the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region [[region/andes|Andes]], and belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that an empire with roads, storehouses, and a knotted-cord recording system was taken over by a group that could not read its records. What was lost included the very means of understanding what had been lost.
questions: How decisive was the civil war, compared with the epidemic?

fields.summary: Across the Miocene, from about 25 to 5 million years ago, open grasslands spread like a green tide across the continents. Animal life was remade in its wake, and the plant family that advanced with it now supplies most of the world's staple crops.
facts: Grass pollen and microscopic plant silica reach back to the latest Cretaceous or early Paleogene, yet for tens of millions of years grass remained a minor thread in the world's vegetation.

Open grasslands widened from the early to middle Miocene, about 20 to 15 million years ago. Grasses of the C4 pathway, suited to hot, dry conditions and low carbon dioxide, spread widely about 8 to 6 million years ago, as carbon isotopes in fossil soils and teeth attest.
Proposed drivers include cooling and drying, seasonal rainfall, falling carbon dioxide, and fire — their relative roles still debated.
Grazing mammals answered with high-crowned teeth and long limbs built for running; horses turned from browsing to grazing, and grazing antelope, cattle, and their kin diversified.
The cereals — wheat, rice, and maize among them — are grasses themselves; see [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]].
fields.context: The Spread of Grasslands belongs mostly to the [[era/neogene-period|Neogene Period]] of the [[era/cenozoic-era|Cenozoic Era]], a long backdrop to the story of the Miocene apes and early hominins. Its crop lineage is the wellspring of [[event/domestication-of-rice|Domestication of Rice]] and [[event/domestication-of-maize|Domestication of Maize]]. The event belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the staple foods of nearly every large human society trace to a plant family that became widespread only in the last few tens of millions of years. Open landscapes are also the setting of a long-running hypothesis about human origins, one the Observer treats as a hypothesis, not a finding. It would weaken if early hominins proved to have lived mainly in closed woodland.
questions: What mix of climate, carbon dioxide, and fire drove the spread of C4 grasses?
How much did open grassland actually shape hominin evolution?

fields.summary: The Suez Canal, opened on 17 November 1869, is a sea-level waterway across Egypt linking the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, shortening the sea route between Europe and Asia.
facts: It was built by a French company under Ferdinand de Lesseps, using a great deal of Egyptian forced and paid labor.
It is about 193 kilometers long.
In 1875 Britain bought Egypt's shares in the canal company, and in 1882 it occupied Egypt.
The canal shortened the voyage between Europe and India by thousands of kilometers.
fields.context: The canal reshaped the [[event/indian-ocean-trade-network|Indian Ocean Trade Network]] for the industrial age and sits within the [[region/nile-valley|Nile Valley]] region. See [[event/scramble-for-africa|Scramble for Africa]] and [[technology/steam-engine|Steam Engine]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a strip of water dug by hand that rearranged the geography of world trade. A single chokepoint can become a lasting source of power for whoever holds it.
questions: How many workers died building the canal?

fields.summary: From the 1500s, European colonizers built large sugar plantations across Brazil and the Caribbean, worked mainly by enslaved Africans — one of the most profitable and brutal systems in early modern trade.
facts: Sugarcane originated in New Guinea and spread across Asia before reaching the Mediterranean and the Atlantic islands of Madeira and Sao Tome.
The plantation model — large-scale production for export by enslaved labor — developed on the Atlantic islands and spread to Brazil in the 16th century.
Beginning in Barbados in the 1640s, the Caribbean sugar boom expanded the use of enslaved labor.
Saint-Domingue, the French colony that became Haiti, stood as the largest sugar producer in the world in the late 18th century.
Sugar plantations drove much of the demand behind the Atlantic slave trade.
fields.context: The sugar economy was the engine of the [[event/atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic Slave Trade]] and a leading part of the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]], following the collapse of the [[culture/taino|Taino]] population. In Saint-Domingue it was overthrown by the [[event/haitian-revolution|Haitian Revolution]]. The Sugar Plantation Complex sits within the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region [[region/caribbean-and-atlantic-world|Caribbean and Atlantic World]], and belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a sweet crop, bound for European tea tables, required the forced movement of millions of people across an ocean. Distance between consumer and producer made the harm easy to overlook.
questions: How large a contribution did the sugar sector make to European industrialization?

fields.summary: The Taiping Rebellion (1850 to 1864) was a civil war in Qing China led by Hong Xiuquan, who claimed to be the younger brother of Jesus Christ; it stands among the deadliest conflicts in history.
facts: In 1853, the rebels captured Nanjing and made it their 'Heavenly Capital'.
The war devastated about 17 provinces.
Most estimates put deaths at 20 to 30 million people, about 5 to 10 percent of China's population, though some estimates run far higher.
Hong Xiuquan died on 1 June 1864, and Nanjing fell shortly afterward.
fields.context: The rebellion unfolded as the [[culture/qing-dynasty|Qing Dynasty]] reeled from the [[event/opium-wars|Opium Wars]]. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[observer-note/sanctioned-harm|Sanctioned Harm]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes how a new meaning-engine, blending Christian ideas with local grievances, mobilized millions within a decade — one of the largest wars in history, and among the least remembered outside China.
questions: What were the true mortality figures?

fields.summary: Multicellularity, in which cells cling together, divide their labor, and reproduce as one body, arose independently again and again. The clearest early fossil evidence stands about 1.05 billion years old, and the older claims remain disputed.
facts: Multicellularity took root independently in bacteria, in several groups of algae, in fungi, in plants and in animals; estimates for the eukaryotes alone run past twenty separate origins.
Older claims name the Francevillian biota of Gabon, about 2.1 billion years old, and the coiled fossil Grypania, about 1.9 billion years old, though how to read either is disputed.
The red alga Bangiomorpha, dated across different studies to somewhere between roughly 1.05 and 1.2 billion years ago, shows both differentiated cells and sexual reproduction.
Experiments have coaxed simple multicellular clusters out of single-celled algae and yeast within weeks to months. The further step, to complex bodies built of many cell types, is far rarer.

Animals evolved their multicellularity apart from plants, and large, soft-bodied animals appear in the Ediacaran; see [[species/ediacaran-biota|Ediacaran Biota]] and [[event/cambrian-explosion|Cambrian Explosion]].
fields.context: The origin of multicellularity followed the [[event/origin-of-eukaryotes|Origin of Eukaryotes]] and overlaps the [[event/the-boring-billion|The Boring Billion]] within the [[era/proterozoic-eon|Proterozoic Eon]], within the theme threads of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a body is cooperation among cells that share one ancestry, held together by mechanisms that suppress the cheaters among them. Whether that is a useful comparison for human cooperation, the Observer leaves open; the analogy is offered as a way of looking, not as an explanation. This reading would weaken if it obscured more than it clarified about either case.
questions: Which of the early fossil claims are truly multicellular?
What conditions favoured the origin of animal multicellularity?

fields.summary: Photosynthesis, the trick of turning light into the making of organic molecules, rose among bacteria sometime in the Archean, perhaps as early as 3.5 billion years ago. The date of the first oxygen-producing form stays uncertain and disputed.
facts: The first photosynthesis likely released no oxygen at all. The anoxygenic forms found in some living bacteria use hydrogen, sulfide or dissolved iron in place of water.

Oxygen-producing photosynthesis is known from the [[species/cyanobacteria|Cyanobacteria]]. Estimates for its origin run from about 3.5 to about 2.4 billion years ago, and the earliest unambiguous cyanobacterial fossils stand about 2.15 billion years old.
Biomarker molecules once cited as evidence of cyanobacteria at 2.7 billion years were later shown to be nothing but younger contamination.

Layered [[species/stromatolites|Stromatolites]] about 3.48 billion years old, from the Dresser Formation of Western Australia, may record microbial mats, possibly photosynthetic ones; some researchers dispute that they are biological at all.

Early oxygen was swallowed by dissolved iron and other chemicals long before it built up in the air; see [[event/banded-iron-formations|Banded Iron Formations]] and [[event/great-oxidation-event|Great Oxidation Event]].
fields.context: The origin of photosynthesis follows the [[event/origin-of-life|Origin of Life]] within the [[era/archean-eon|Archean Eon]] and sets up the [[event/great-oxidation-event|Great Oxidation Event]] of the [[era/proterozoic-eon|Proterozoic Eon]], within the theme threads of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a way of drawing energy from light, invented by microbes, ended up setting the chemistry that everything larger would run on. What stands out is the very long delay between that invention and its planetary effects, and this reading rests less on the exact date than on that delay. It would weaken if oxygen-producing photosynthesis were shown to have begun only shortly before the oxygen rise.
questions: When did oxygen-producing photosynthesis first evolve?
What delayed the accumulation of oxygen after it began?

fields.summary: Homo sapiens spread out of Africa and across the whole world. Genetic studies trace most of today's non-African ancestry to one major dispersal, roughly 70,000 to 50,000 years ago, though earlier and smaller dispersals left their own traces, and the exact timing is still debated.
facts: Genetic studies published in 2016 concluded that most non-African ancestry comes from one major dispersal, about 50,000 to 72,000 years ago. Genetic dating is imperfect, and one climate study favored a window of 80,000 to 100,000 years ago instead.

Earlier, smaller dispersals came before it. Homo sapiens fossils at Skhul and Qafzeh in Israel run about 90,000 to 120,000 years old. A fossil upper jaw from Misliya Cave, Israel, was dated in 2018 to 177,000 to 194,000 years ago, though a published comment disputes that dating. A separate genetic signal suggests an exodus about 120,000 years ago that left about 2 percent of Papuan genomes.
Modern humans reached Australia and New Guinea at least about 50,000 years ago, and possibly about 65,000 years ago, a date still debated; see [[event/peopling-of-sahul|Peopling of Sahul]].
Present-day non-African populations carry up to about 2 percent Neanderthal ancestry, while Oceanian populations carry far more Denisovan ancestry, up to about 5 percent in some.
Both a coastal route and an inland one have been proposed.
fields.context: This dispersal ended the isolation of human populations; see [[species/homo-neanderthalensis|Homo neanderthalensis]] and [[species/denisovans|Denisovans]]. It set the stage for the [[event/peopling-of-the-americas|Peopling of the Americas]].
fields.observer: I call this the most remarkable feat of the whole Paleolithic. One species crossed desert. One species crossed tundra. One species crossed rainforest and reached island after island, carrying no new body, only what it had learned. That is the whole of the wonder: not a changed animal, but a changed mind, going everywhere.
questions: How many dispersals were there, and by which routes? The fossil record shows repeated early departures, while the genetic record points to a single main wave, and the two pictures are not yet fully reconciled.

fields.summary: The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum was a burst of global warming about 56 million years ago, when a great release of carbon drove global temperatures up by roughly 5 to 6 degrees Celsius, and held them there for about 200,000 years.
facts: Deep-sea sediments hold a sharp negative excursion in carbon isotopes, the signature of a large input of carbon into ocean and air alike.
The whole event ran on the order of 200,000 years, recovery included, though its onset took only a few thousand years.
The ocean turned more acid, and many species of deep-sea foraminifera went extinct.
Proposed sources of the carbon include volcanic activity in the North Atlantic and methane released from seafloor deposits; the mix between them is debated.
Several mammal groups, among them early primates, horses and artiodactyls, appear or spread across the Northern Hemisphere near its start.
fields.context: This event is the best-studied ancient analogue for [[event/modern-climate-change|Modern Climate Change]] and for the carbon release of the [[event/great-acceleration|Great Acceleration]]. It occurred about ten million years after the [[event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction|Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction]], within the [[era/cenozoic-era|Cenozoic Era]] and the region [[region/planet-wide|Planet-wide]], within the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Earth has run this experiment before, with no one watching, and kept the record in mud. What differs now is that a single species is both causing the change and measuring it. Studies generally find that present emissions move much faster than those at the onset of the PETM.
questions: How much of the carbon was volcanic and how much came from methane?

fields.summary: In August 1947, British India was divided into the two independent states of India and Pakistan, and the new borders drawn through Punjab and Bengal set off mass migration and violence.
facts: Independence and partition took effect on 14 and 15 August 1947.
The boundary itself was drawn by a commission under Cyril Radcliffe in a matter of weeks; he later admitted that he had worked from out-of-date maps and census materials.
Estimates suggest that 12 to 20 million people were displaced from their homes.
Estimates of the deaths vary widely: 1 to 2 million is most commonly cited, some sources give as many as 3 million, and about 15 million people were displaced.
Mahatma Gandhi opposed the partition, and was assassinated in January 1948.
fields.context: Partition followed from the end of British rule and stands as a case of [[event/decolonization|Decolonization]] in which a line on a map divided communities. [[person/mahatma-gandhi|Mahatma Gandhi]] opposed the division. It sits within the [[era/information-age|Information Age]] and the region [[region/south-asia|South Asia]], within the theme thread of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a line drawn on a map in a few weeks forced more than ten million people to relocate. It is a stark case of a claim-line generating movement, violence and memory that persisted long after the ink had dried.
questions: How many people died?

fields.summary: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 was made up of the treaties of Osnabruck and Munster, which brought an end to both the Thirty Years' War and the Eighty Years' War between Spain and the Dutch Republic.
facts: The peace was negotiated from 1644 onward in the Westphalian cities of Osnabruck and Munster. The Spanish-Dutch treaty was signed on 30 January 1648, and the treaty joining the Holy Roman emperor, the German princes, France and Sweden followed on 24 October 1648.
Spain recognized the independence of the Dutch Republic.
The settlement extended the principle of the Peace of Augsburg, that rulers determine the religion of their own territory, to cover Calvinists as well.
It is often cited as the origin of the modern system of sovereign states, though many historians treat that claim as a later simplification.
It reduced the authority the Holy Roman Emperor held over the German princes.
fields.context: This settlement ended the [[event/thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]] and the religious conflicts of the [[event/protestant-reformation|Protestant Reformation]]. Its later reputation as the birth of state sovereignty is discussed in [[observer-note/the-fiction-of-claim-lines|The Fiction of Claim-Lines]]. It sits within the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region [[region/europe|Europe]], within the theme thread of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a treaty built mainly to solve a set of local problems later became a founding myth of the international order. Stories about founding moments, it seems, tend to be assembled after the fact.
questions: Did Westphalia actually create the sovereign state system?

fields.summary: The Tanzimat (Reorganization) was a series of reforms in the Ottoman Empire between 1839 and 1876 that sought to modernize the state, promise equality before the law to all subjects, and move it toward constitutional government.
facts: The era ran from 1839 to 1876, under the sultans Abdülmecid I and Abdülaziz.
Proclaimed on 3 November 1839, the Edict of Gülhane promised security of life, property, and honour for all subjects, fair taxation and conscription, public trials, and an end to tax farming.
The Imperial Reform Edict of 18 February 1856 promised equality in education, government appointments, and justice, regardless of creed.
The period is said to end in 1876, when Abdulhamid II took the throne. The 1876 constitution created a parliamentary system, but it was suspended in 1878.
fields.context: The Tanzimat was a response to European pressure and to earlier reformers within the empire. Compare the [[event/meiji-restoration|Meiji Restoration]] in Japan and the reforms of [[person/muhammad-ali-of-egypt|Muhammad Ali of Egypt]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a state trying to change its own architecture of legitimacy while the empire was still being defended, extending equality to subjects of every faith in hope of holding a plural population together. Reforms promised on paper met the resistance of those with something to lose, and the constitution lasted only two years in practice.
questions: How far were the Tanzimat's promises of equality carried out in practice, outside the capital?
How much of the reform agenda was driven by European pressure, and how much by the empire's own officials?

fields.summary: The Agricultural Revolution was the slow turning, beginning about 11,500 years ago, from the forager's wandering path to the farmer's rooted one — a shift toward tending crops and herds that arose, like scattered fires catching independently, in several parts of the world.
facts: The earliest farming appeared in the Fertile Crescent: wheat, barley, lentils, and, later, livestock.
Independent centers rose in China (rice, millet), Mesoamerica (maize, beans, squash), the Andes (potato), and New Guinea.
Farming nourished denser populations and permanent settlement.

Some evidence suggests poorer health among early farmers: in a study of 167 prehistoric Europeans, Neolithic individuals stood shorter than their genetic scores predicted, by about 2 to 4 cm relative to earlier and later groups.
fields.context: Farming defines the [[era/neolithic|Neolithic]] and lays the ground for [[event/the-urban-revolution|The Urban Revolution]]. See [[place/gobekli-tepe|Göbekli Tepe]], [[place/catalhoyuk|Çatalhöyük]], and the essay [[observer-note/the-settling-and-its-bargain|The Settling and Its Bargain]].
fields.observer: I call this the Settling. I call it the species' most consequential bargain. More food, more people — that was the promise. More work, more inequality, more disease — that was the price. Was any bargain ever so quietly kept?
questions: Why did farming arise in several places within a few thousand years of one another?

fields.summary: The Boring Billion: an informal name for the stretch from about 1.8 to 0.8 billion years ago. No well-established ice ages. Little apparent change in the fossil record. Silence, on the surface. Whether it was truly uneventful — still debated.
facts: The interval covers the [[era/mesoproterozoic-era|Mesoproterozoic Era]] and the edges of the eras to either side of it. It lies between the [[event/great-oxidation-event|Great Oxidation Event]] and the ice ages of [[event/snowball-earth|Snowball Earth]].

Chemical records suggest that atmospheric oxygen stayed well below today's level, and that some waters at middle depth ran rich in sulfide. Shortages of nutrients — nitrogen, trace metals — have been proposed as limits on life.
Eukaryotes: present, diversifying slowly. The red alga Bangiomorpha, dated in different studies to between roughly 1.05 and 1.2 billion years ago, belongs to this interval.
The supercontinent Nuna broke apart. Rodinia began to assemble.
Some researchers argue the name misleads: records show fluctuations in oxygen, and ecological change, within the interval.
