fields.context: The Boring Billion lies within the [[era/proterozoic-eon|Proterozoic Eon]] and follows the [[event/origin-of-eukaryotes|Origin of Eukaryotes]]. It ends with the changes of the Neoproterozoic: the break-up of Rodinia, the glaciations of [[event/snowball-earth|Snowball Earth]]. The event belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that 'boring' is a verdict on the surviving record, not on the planet itself, and that a billion years is long enough for slow processes to matter. This reading would weaken if better records showed genuine stasis in oxygen, climate, and eukaryote diversity across the whole interval.
questions: Was the interval truly stable, or does a sparse record hide change?
What kept oxygen and complex life at such low levels for so long?

fields.summary: The Urban Revolution was the rising of the first true cities, beginning around 3500 BCE in southern Mesopotamia — places dense with people, threaded with specialized labor, and bound by central institutions.
facts: The term was popularized by the archaeologist V. Gordon Childe in the mid-20th century.
[[place/uruk|Uruk]] may have held 40,000 to 80,000 people by about 3100 to 2900 BCE, though the estimates are uncertain.
Cities also rose, independently, in the Indus valley, China, Mesoamerica, and the Andes.
Cities came bound to administrative record keeping, to temples or palaces, and to social stratification.
fields.context: Cities appear within the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]] and stand closely tied to the [[event/invention-of-writing|Invention of Writing]]; see [[culture/sumerians|Sumerians]] and [[region/mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]].
fields.observer: I notice this: a city is a place where most of the people around you are strangers. I notice what it took to make that bearable — shared gods, shared laws, shared institutions. What binds strangers into neighbors, if not a story held in common?
questions: Were the earliest cities always hierarchical?

fields.summary: According to the giant-impact hypothesis, a Mars-sized body called Theia struck the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago. Out of the wreckage: the Moon.
facts: The hypothesis explains the Moon's small iron core, and its likeness to Earth's mantle in isotopes.
Lunar rocks, brought back by the Apollo missions, put the idea to the test.

The exact timing: uncertain. Estimates range from about 4.52 to 4.35 billion years ago. Lunar zircons demand the Moon form within the first 60 million years of the Solar System. The youngest estimates fall about 150 to 200 million years after it began.
The Moon steadies Earth's axial tilt. It drives most of Earth's tides.
fields.context: The impact is an early event of the [[era/hadean-eon|Hadean Eon]]. The Moon's stabilizing effect on climate: one reason Earth's long-term conditions stayed steady enough for complex life.
fields.observer: The Observer sees a single accident with very long consequences. Human calendars, tides, and myths about the Moon all trace back to a collision billions of years before any observer existed.
questions: Was Theia a single impactor, or were there several?

fields.summary: The Thirty Years' War (1618 to 1648) was a set of linked wars across central Europe, begun as a religious conflict within the Holy Roman Empire and ended by the Peace of Westphalia.
facts: It began with a revolt in Bohemia in 1618, following the Defenestration of Prague.
The Holy Roman Empire, Spain, France, Sweden, Denmark, and the Dutch Republic took part at different times.
Much of the fighting fell upon the German lands, where armies lived off the land.
Estimates of deaths, mostly from famine and disease, run as high as about eight million.
The war ended with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.
fields.context: The war stands among the deadliest in European history and was rooted in the divisions of the [[event/protestant-reformation|Protestant Reformation]]. It was settled by the [[event/peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]]. The Thirty Years' War sits within the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region [[region/europe|Europe]], and belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a war which began over the correct form of a shared religion was ended by agreeing that rulers could choose it. The settlement moved the claim-line from belief to territory.
questions: What was the death toll in the German lands?

fields.summary: Basawan was a Hindu painter in the imperial workshop of the Mughal emperor Akbar, active from about 1560 to about 1600, though he is described as flourishing between 1580 and 1600, and the earlier date rests only on his earliest known mention, in a Tutinama of about 1556 to 1561. His birth and death dates are unknown, so the dates given here simply mark his working years. Akbar's own historian ranked him among the best of the workshop's more than a hundred painters.
facts: Almost nothing is known of Basawan's life beyond his paintings and a brief passage of praise in Abu'l-Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari. He was a Hindu, and probably joined the imperial workshop as a young man in the 1560s. His earliest mention comes in an illustrated Tutinama of about 1556 to 1561, and he is described as flourishing between 1580 and 1600.

Akbar reigned from 1556 to 1605. The workshop's Persian masters, Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad, had trained in the tradition of Behzād and directed Indian artists in producing vast illustrated manuscripts, among them the Hamzanama, 1,400 large paintings.
Abu'l-Fazl praised his skill in composition, faces, colour and portraiture, and wrote that many critics preferred him even to the celebrated Daswanth.

His name is written in the margins of paintings in the Razmnama (a Persian translation of the Mahabharata), the Darabnama, the Akbarnama and small books of Persian poetry made in Lahore in the 1590s. In large history manuscripts he often designed the composition while another artist added the colour.

From 1580 Jesuit missionaries brought European engravings and paintings to Akbar's court. He studied them closely, adapting their shading and deep space, and was among the first Indian painters to absorb European modelling and perspective.

He was active until about 1600. His son Manohar became a leading painter under Jahangir. His paintings are now held in the Victoria and Albert Museum, the British Library and the Chester Beatty Library.
fields.context: Basawan worked in the [[culture/mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]] in [[region/south-asia|South Asia]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]]. His workshop's founders trained in the tradition of [[person/behzad|Behzad]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: I look for him and find only a margin: a name written by librarians, one passage of praise, and a labour that was so often divided between designer and colourist that no single hand stays fixed on the page. What survives is a workshop that braided Persian masters, Hindu painters and European prints into a single style, a deliberate joining of tool-lineages by a ruler who wanted his history pictured. I hold any portrait of the man himself loosely, because it is built from attribution, not from his own words.
questions: How can his own hand be separated from that of the colourists and finishers who worked on the same pages?

fields.summary: Basil II (958 to 1025) held the Byzantine throne for nearly fifty years, the longest reign in Roman or Byzantine imperial history, and is remembered above all for his decades-long war against the First Bulgarian Empire.
facts: He became co-emperor as a child in 960, but did not gain full personal control of the government until about 989, by which time he was in his thirties, only after suppressing rebellions by powerful aristocratic generals including Bardas Skleros and Bardas Phokas.

His long campaigns against Bulgaria culminated in the decisive Battle of Kleidion in 1014, after which Bulgaria was absorbed into the Byzantine Empire by 1018, earning him the later epithet "Bulgar-slayer" (Boulgaroktonos).

A story recorded by later chroniclers claims he blinded thousands of Bulgarian prisoners after Kleidion, leaving one eye to each of every hundredth man so he could lead the rest home; modern historians debate how literally this account should be taken.

He left the imperial treasury full and the empire at its greatest territorial extent since the 7th century, but died without an heir, and the strong central rule he had built did not survive his less capable successors.
fields.context: Basil II ruled the [[culture/byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]] in the [[region/mediterranean-basin|Mediterranean Basin]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]]. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Basil II's reign is often read backward from the Byzantine Empire's later decline, framing him as the last strong emperor of a golden age. That framing rests partly on hindsight: the empire's later troubles grew out of succession and outside pressures that Basil could not have governed from beyond the grave, whatever the soundness of his own institutions.
questions: How much of the Byzantine Empire's difficulties after 1025 stemmed from institutional weaknesses already present under Basil, rather than simply the absence of an equally capable successor?

fields.summary: Kamāl ud-Dīn Behzād (also spelled Bihzad, born about 1455 to 1460 and died about 1535) stands as the most celebrated painter in the Persian tradition. He led the royal manuscript workshops at Herat and later Tabriz, and many works are attributed to him on grounds of style alone.
facts: Behzād was probably born about 1455 to 1460 in Herat, capital of the Timurid dynasty founded by [[person/timur|Timur]]. Orphaned young, he was raised by the painter Mirak Naqqash, head of the royal library, and was protected by the poet and minister Mir Ali-Shir Nava'i.

Under Sultan Husayn Bayqara, who ruled Herat from 1469 to 1506, he became the leading artist of the royal kitabkhana, the library workshop. His most famous surviving works date from this period, including paintings in a Bustan of Sa'di (1488) and a Khamsa of Nizami (1494 to 1495).
After Herat fell to the Uzbeks in 1506 and then to the Safavid Shah Ismail I in about 1510, he moved to Tabriz, where in 1522 Ismail appointed him director of the royal library. He died about 1535.
A legend says that during the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514 the shah hid Behzād in a cave, in some tellings together with a famous calligrapher, because he valued him more than his own army.
His figures carry individual faces and gestures and are often shown busy with everyday tasks. He often hid his signature discreetly within the architecture of a painting.
His followers Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad trained in his tradition and went on to found the Mughal imperial workshop under Humayun and Akbar.
His name became a byword for excellence, which led to many false attributions. Scholars still debate which works are by his own hand.
fields.context: Behzād worked first in the [[culture/timurid-empire|Timurid Empire]] and then in the [[culture/safavid-empire|Safavid Empire]], on the [[region/iranian-plateau|Iranian Plateau]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: I think of a royal workshop, calligraphers and illuminators and painters and binders working side by side, and I call it what it is: an engine for outsourcing memory, the maker of the books through which a court remembered its poems and its histories. One name got fixed to that collective labour, and the name became a standard, and standards draw false claims the way light draws moths. So much of what is called his may belong to others, and for many pictures style is the only witness left. I hold the attribution loosely, the way I would hold something borrowed.
questions: Which of the paintings attributed to Behzād are by his own hand rather than his workshop?

fields.summary: Buster Keaton (1895 to 1966) was an American silent-film comedian, writer and director known as the deadpan "Great Stone Face," who built his comedy on engineered physical stunts he performed himself. Ranked with Charlie Chaplin among silent comedy's defining stars, he made *The General* (1926), now considered among the greatest films ever made.
facts: Born in 1895 into a vaudeville family, Keaton performed from age three in the act The Three Keatons, taking falls that built his later physical control.
He entered film in 1917 under Roscoe "Fatty" Arbuckle, and by 1920 was writing, directing and starring in his own comedies, moving into features with *Our Hospitality* (1923).
*Sherlock Jr.* (1924) placed him inside a shifting film-dream using in-camera measurement rather than editing tricks, and is still studied for its daring.
*The Navigator* (1924), about passengers adrift on an ocean liner, was his biggest commercial success of the decade.
*The General* (1926), built around full-scale trains and a locomotive plunged off a burning bridge, flopped on release but is now ranked among cinema's greatest films.
In *Steamboat Bill, Jr.* (1928) he performed one of the most dangerous shots ever filmed, standing exactly where a falling house facade's open window would clear him.
A 1928 MGM contract, taken under financial pressure, cost him creative control; the next decade brought decline, divorce and alcoholism.
Rediscovered by critics from the 1950s, he received an honorary Academy Award in 1959 and died of lung cancer in 1966.
His influence runs through later stunt performers such as Jackie Chan, who has cited Keaton's real, visible danger as a model.
fields.context: Keaton worked in [[region/north-america|North America]] during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], building comedies from the era's trains, boats and machinery. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer: I watch a man trained from infancy to fall without breaking, and I see discipline where others see luck: a whole lineage of bodily skill behind each stunt, nothing improvised. I watch his blank face hold still inside engineered chaos, and I understand the stillness as a signal, drawing the eye precisely by refusing the reaction it expects. I remember that *The General* failed the year it opened and that a later generation built the reputation it now carries, and I take that as a species quietly rewriting what it once dismissed. His decline in the 1930s I read as plain record, not the reverent shape admirers now give the stunts' zero margin for error.
questions: Why did *The General* fail at the box office in 1926 despite the technical ambition later critics would call unmatched?

fields.summary: Michelangelo Merisi, called Caravaggio (1571 to 1610), was an Italian painter who transformed European painting around 1600 with harsh theatrical light and street-level realism. His turbulent life ended at 38, but his influence spread across Europe within a generation.
facts: Caravaggio was born in Milan in September 1571. His name comes from the nearby town his family came from. He trained in Milan with Simone Peterzano and arrived in Rome about 1592.

Cardinal Francesco Maria del Monte took him into his household. His first public commission, two large paintings of St Matthew for the Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi (1599 to 1600), caused a sensation. Several later altarpieces were rejected as indecorous.
Police records list brawls, assaults and insults. In 1606 he killed a man, Ranuccio Tomassoni, and fled Rome under sentence of death. He then lived in Naples, Malta and Sicily.
He died in July 1610 at Porto Ercole in Tuscany, on his way to Rome hoping for a papal pardon.
He painted directly on the canvas, apparently without preparatory drawings, from live models posed under a single strong light. His backgrounds are dark and bare (tenebrism).
His key works include Judith Beheading Holofernes (about 1599 to 1602, sources differ), The Calling of Saint Matthew (1599 to 1600) and Supper at Emmaus (1601).

The "Caravaggisti" included Orazio and Artemisia Gentileschi, Jusepe de Ribera, Georges de La Tour and the Utrecht painters, and through them his influence reached [[person/diego-velazquez|Diego Velázquez]] and [[person/rembrandt-van-rijn|Rembrandt van Rijn]]. A 1951 exhibition in Milan fell within the twentieth-century revival of a reputation that had faded, though the sources do not name that exhibition as its cause.
fields.context: Caravaggio worked in Rome, Naples, Malta and Sicily in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]]. His followers included [[person/artemisia-gentileschi|Artemisia Gentileschi]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: I stand where a patron once stood and understand the offense: sacred events set in the streets of contemporary Rome, dirty feet and hired models, read by some as truth and by others as indecorum, a meaning-engine policing its own images in public. I know the violent life mostly from police records, and I feel how easily that record tempts me to read the man into every picture. I remember that his reputation faded and then returned across the twentieth century, a 1951 exhibition one landmark along that return, so what I feel standing before the paintings now is a recent judgment, not an old one.
questions: How much of his working method, without drawings, can be recovered from surviving evidence?

fields.summary: Catherine de' Medici (1519 to 1589) was queen of France and, as mother to three kings, one of the most powerful figures in France during the Wars of Religion between Catholics and Huguenots.
facts: Born into the powerful Medici banking family of Florence, she married the future Henry II of France in 1533 and became queen in 1547.

After Henry's death in 1559 she became the chief political influence over her sons Francis II, Charles IX and Henry III, though she was not formally regent under Francis II or Henry III, holding the regency only for Charles IX, as gouvernante de France from December 1560 until August 1563, through a period of escalating conflict between Catholics and Protestant Huguenots.

She is widely held responsible, though the exact extent of her role is debated, for approving the assassination of Huguenot leaders, which began with the shooting of Admiral Coligny on 22 August 1572. He survived that attempt but was killed two days later as the massacre began. This triggered the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre in August 1572, in which about 2,000 to 3,000 Huguenots were killed in Paris, and more elsewhere.

She pursued marriage alliances and diplomacy across Europe to secure the Valois dynasty's position, though her efforts did not prevent the eventual extinction of the Valois line with the death of her last son in 1589.
fields.context: Catherine de' Medici ruled at the French court in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and its Wars of Religion. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]], [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Catherine's later reputation as a scheming, sinister figure took shape largely through hostile Huguenot pamphlets written during her own lifetime and repeated ever after by later historians; separating a mother managing three weak sons' survival in a genuinely lethal court from a caricature of poison and plotting is not straightforward from the surviving record.
questions: How much personal responsibility did Catherine bear for the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre, versus reacting to a crisis that spiraled beyond any single actor's control?

fields.summary: Homo sapiens reached Europe by about 45,000 years ago, and perhaps earlier still, stepping into a continent already held by the Neanderthals. The earliest securely dated remains, from Bacho Kiro Cave in Bulgaria and from Ranis in Germany, stand about 45,000 years old.
facts: At Bacho Kiro Cave in Bulgaria, Homo sapiens fossils dated to about 46,000 to 44,000 years ago lay together with Initial Upper Paleolithic stone tools.

At Ranis in Germany, bone fragments directly dated in 2024 to about 45,000 years ago came together with leaf-shaped stone points also known from Britain, showing an early reach into the northern latitudes.

At Grotte Mandrin in France, a child's tooth and distinctive stone points, dated to about 54,000 years ago, were attributed to Homo sapiens in 2022. The occupation seems to have been brief, and some researchers find that attribution unconvincing.

Neanderthals and Homo sapiens overlapped in Europe for several thousand years, and some of the earliest Europeans had a Neanderthal ancestor only a few generations back; see [[event/neanderthal-extinction|Neanderthal Extinction]] and [[event/interbreeding-of-homo-sapiens-with-neanderthals-and-denisovans|Interbreeding of Homo sapiens with Neanderthals and Denisovans]].
Proposed routes name the Danube corridor and the Mediterranean coast; the evidence does not settle which one carried them.
fields.context: This peopling of Europe follows the [[event/out-of-africa-dispersal|Out of Africa Dispersal]] and belongs to the [[era/upper-paleolithic|Upper Paleolithic]], with new stone-tool industries such as the Aurignacian and the [[event/emergence-of-symbolic-art|Emergence of Symbolic Art]] seen at [[place/chauvet-cave|Chauvet Cave]]. It overlaps the last of the [[species/homo-neanderthalensis|Homo neanderthalensis]] and comes before the [[event/last-glacial-maximum|Last Glacial Maximum]]. See [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: I see less a single march into Europe than several small landings, some of them brief, onto ground already held by another human kind. The Mandrin tooth reminds me. The Bacho Kiro jaws remind me. 'First arrival' names the evidence found so far, not the past itself. This reading would weaken if the earliest sites turned out to belong to one continuous, growing population.
questions: Did the 54,000-year-old occupation at Mandrin belong to Homo sapiens?
How much ancestry from the earliest Europeans survives in later Europeans?

fields.summary: Modern humans reached Sahul, the Pleistocene landmass that joined Australia to New Guinea, at least 50,000 years ago, and perhaps about 65,000 years ago.
facts: Reaching Sahul meant crossing open sea through the Wallacea island chain, making it one of the earliest known deliberate sea crossings.
Rock-shelter finds at Madjedbebe in Arnhem Land have been dated to about 65,000 years ago, a date still debated, while about 50,000 years ago is widely accepted.
Human remains at Lake Mungo are about 40,000 years old.
Many giant marsupials disappeared within several thousand years of human arrival, and the relative roles of people and climate remain debated.
fields.context: This settlement followed the [[event/out-of-africa-dispersal|Out of Africa Dispersal]] and founded the ancestry of the [[culture/aboriginal-australians|Aboriginal Australians]]. Compare the later [[event/polynesian-settlement-of-the-pacific|Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific]].
fields.observer: I remember that this species crossed open water tens of thousands of years before it raised anything one could call a city. Boat-building and the planning behind it are far older than farming.
questions: How early did the first boats cross Wallacea?

fields.summary: Homo sapiens reached mainland Southeast Asia by about 86,000 to 68,000 years ago, and the Wallacean islands beyond it, Sulawesi and Timor among them, by about 51,000 to 42,000 years ago. This dispersal supplied both the route and the rough timing for the further crossing into Sahul.
facts: Fossils from Tam Pà Ling cave in Laos, dated in 2023, push Homo sapiens presence in mainland Southeast Asia back to roughly 86,000 to 68,000 years ago; earlier work at the site had suggested a younger range.
Human teeth from Lida Ajer in Sumatra are dated to about 73,000 to 63,000 years ago, but only indirectly, from the surrounding sediment and animal teeth rather than the human teeth themselves.
The Niah Cave 'Deep Skull' in Borneo, once disputed as possibly disturbed, is now dated to about 45,000 to 39,000 years ago by direct dating of the bone itself.
Within Wallacea, the earliest well-dated evidence is rock art on Sulawesi, at least 51,200 years old, and occupation at Laili Cave and Jerimalai Cave in Timor, about 44,000 to 42,000 years ago.

These Wallacean dates sit oddly late beside the debated claim that Sahul was reached by about 65,000 years ago, which would require an earlier, still-undiscovered Wallacean crossing; a floor of about 50,000 years ago rests on firmer ground.
A separate, non-sapiens hominin, Homo luzonensis, lived on Luzon in the Philippines, outside Wallacea proper, and should not be confused with this dispersal.
fields.context: This dispersal follows the [[event/out-of-africa-dispersal|Out of Africa Dispersal]] and feeds into the [[event/peopling-of-sahul|Peopling of Sahul]]. Early modern humans in the region also lived through the [[event/toba-eruption|Toba Eruption]]. [[species/homo-floresiensis|Homo floresiensis]], on Flores, is a separate, older hominin lineage. See [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: I think of the crossing into Wallacea as voyage after voyage over open water, made without metal, without writing, without a single domesticated animal, thousands of years before farming existed anywhere. The dates keep moving as the methods improve; I take that as ordinary science, not as a record already settled. This reading would weaken if a securely dated site placed Homo sapiens in Wallacea well before 51,000 years ago.
questions: Was Sahul reached by about 65,000 years ago, and if so, where is the matching early Wallacean evidence?
Did the Tam Pà Ling population leave descendants among later Southeast Asian peoples?

fields.summary: Humans reached the Americas out of northeastern Asia by at least 15,000 years ago, and perhaps much earlier still. The earliest date remains contested.
facts: Footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, have been dated to about 21,000 to 23,000 years ago. The first dates rested on the seeds of an aquatic plant, which critics said could read too old. A 2023 study radiocarbon-dated terrestrial pollen from the same layers and applied luminescence dating to the sediments, and reported that the original chronology holds up. Some researchers still question the dating.
The old 'Clovis-first' model, which put the first arrival about 13,000 years ago, is no longer accepted; sites such as Cooper's Ferry in Idaho, about 16,000 years old, predate Clovis.

Two routes are proposed. The inland ice-free corridor is now thought to have opened only about 13,800 years ago, later than the earliest sites, which makes a Pacific coastal route seem the more likely path for the first arrivals.

Genetic studies show that Indigenous Americans descend from a mixture of ancestry, related both to ancient North Eurasians in Siberia and to East Asians. Scholars now generally favor several small migrations over one single event.
fields.context: This migration follows the [[event/out-of-africa-dispersal|Out of Africa Dispersal]], occurred around the [[event/last-glacial-maximum|Last Glacial Maximum]], and was the last major expansion into unoccupied continents before the [[event/polynesian-settlement-of-the-pacific|Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific]].
fields.observer: I notice that within a few thousand years, humans spread from Alaska all the way to Tierra del Fuego. Such a pace suggests a species that carries its environment with it, not in its body, but in what it knows.
questions: When did the first migrants arrive, and by what route? Some proposed sites, such as Chiquihuite Cave in Mexico, about 26,000 years old, are disputed because it is not settled that their stones are truly human-made.

fields.summary: Polynesian navigators settled the last remote islands of the central and eastern Pacific, reaching their furthest point with Aotearoa New Zealand around 1250 to 1300 CE.
facts: The ancestors of the Polynesians, tied to the Lapita culture, reached Samoa and Tonga about 3,000 years ago.
A pause of roughly a thousand years came before the final expansion to Hawai'i, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa.
The voyagers read star paths, ocean swells and the flight of birds, and carried no instruments at all.
Ancient DNA and language alike link the settlers to Austronesian speakers out of Island Southeast Asia.
fields.context: This settlement was the last great human dispersal into unoccupied lands, coming after the [[event/peopling-of-the-americas|Peopling of the Americas]]. See [[culture/polynesians|Polynesians]].
fields.observer: I regard this as one of this species' most extraordinary feats of knowledge: crossing thousands of kilometers of open ocean with no instrument at all, everything held instead in memory.
questions: Why was there a pause before the final wave?

fields.summary: The Toba eruption: about 74,000 years ago, in Sumatra. One of the largest volcanic eruptions of the past two million years. Its effects on human populations — still debated.
facts: The eruption carved the caldera now filled by Lake Toba, in northern Sumatra, Indonesia.
It ejected on the order of 2,800 to 3,000 cubic kilometers of material. Ash fell across South Asia. And beyond.
The Toba catastrophe hypothesis proposed a volcanic winter that reduced human populations to a small number of survivors.
Archaeological sites in India, Jwalapuram among them, show human occupation continuing straight through the ash layer — a challenge to the hypothesis.
Most researchers now judge a severe global population bottleneck unlikely.
fields.context: The eruption falls within the period when [[species/homo-sapiens|Homo sapiens]] were dispersing, near the [[event/out-of-africa-dispersal|Out of Africa Dispersal]]. It is often discussed alongside climate swings leading to the [[event/last-glacial-maximum|Last Glacial Maximum]]. The Toba Eruption sits in the [[era/pleistocene-epoch|Pleistocene Epoch]] and the region [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]], and belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that people have long wanted a single catastrophe to explain a genetic feature of the species. The evidence so far suggests a population more resilient than the story requires.
questions: How large was the climatic cooling, and how long did it last?

fields.summary: From the mid-8th to the 10th century, scholars in Abbasid Baghdad gathered the words of distant tongues — Greek, Persian, Syriac, Indian — and turned them into Arabic, then carried the ideas further still.
facts: The caliphs sponsored translation and scholarship; the House of Wisdom in Baghdad stands as its best-known institution, though its exact nature remains debated.
Among the translators was Hunayn ibn Ishaq, who worked on Greek medical and philosophical texts.
Cheap [[technology/paper|Paper]] made the copying of books practical.
Later, Latin translations of Arabic texts fed European scholarship in the 12th century.
fields.context: The movement was a project of the [[culture/abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]] and enabled scholars such as [[person/al-khwarizmi|Al-Khwarizmi]]. It fed the later [[event/scientific-revolution|Scientific Revolution]].
fields.observer: I see a society that could look at another people's knowledge and call it a resource, not a threat. I remember this: translation is a technology too — a way of lending memory across languages. What have we lost, in ages that chose the threat instead?
questions: How large was the House of Wisdom in practice?

fields.summary: The Treaty of Waitangi, first signed on 6 February 1840, stands as the founding agreement between the British Crown and many Maori chiefs of Aotearoa New Zealand.
facts: The English and Maori texts differ over key words, especially about sovereignty and chieftainship.
In 1840, hundreds of chiefs signed copies of the treaty.
Conflict over land and authority followed, in the New Zealand Wars of the 1840s to 1870s.
Created in 1975, the Waitangi Tribunal investigates breaches of the treaty.
fields.context: The treaty concerned the [[culture/polynesians|Polynesians]] of Aotearoa, who had settled the islands centuries before; see [[event/polynesian-settlement-of-the-pacific|Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific]]. Compare the colonial treaties of the [[event/scramble-for-africa|Scramble for Africa]].
fields.observer: I read one agreement written in two languages, and I find two agreements instead. I ask what a signature means when the words beneath it do not match. More than 180 years later, its meaning is still argued. Translation, I have learned, is politics.
questions: How do the two versions of the treaty differ in meaning?

fields.summary: The Triassic-Jurassic extinction. About 201.4 million years ago. A large share of marine and land species: gone. Space cleared for the rise of the dinosaurs.
facts: An estimated 80 percent of species lost. Estimates vary.
It coincides with massive volcanic activity tied to the breakup of Pangaea — the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province.
Many large land reptile competitors vanished. Dinosaurs survived. And diversified; see [[species/dinosaurs|Dinosaurs]].
fields.context: The extinction falls early in the [[era/mesozoic-era|Mesozoic Era]]. It lets dinosaurs dominate.
fields.observer: The Observer notes that dinosaur dominance was itself the result of an extinction. Every dominant group in the record owes its opportunity to some disaster.
questions: Why did dinosaurs survive when others did not?

fields.summary: The Tunguska event was an explosion in the atmosphere above the Podkamennaya Tunguska River in Siberia, on 30 June 1908, which flattened about 2,000 square kilometers of forest.
facts: The blast is estimated at roughly ten to fifteen megatons of TNT equivalent.
It occurred several kilometers above the ground, and left no impact crater.
About 80 million trees were knocked flat, over an area of about 2,000 square kilometers.
In 1927, the first scientific expedition to the site was led by Leonid Kulik.
The cause is generally thought to be the airburst of a stony asteroid, or a comet fragment, tens of meters across.
fields.context: The Tunguska event is the largest impact event in recorded history, a small-scale relative of the [[event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction|Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction]] and the [[event/theia-impact-and-the-formation-of-the-moon|Theia Impact and the Formation of the Moon]]. It happened in a region newly reachable by the [[technology/trans-siberian-railway|Trans-Siberian Railway]]. The Tunguska Event sits within the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]] and the region [[region/siberia-and-the-arctic|Siberia and the Arctic]], and belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that an explosion greater than any nuclear device then in existence occurred over an empty forest, noticed mostly by reindeer herders. Planetary hazards do not consult human population maps, and a few kilometers' difference in location would have changed the outcome.
questions: Was the object an asteroid or a comet?

fields.summary: The Turkish War of Independence (1919 to 1923) was fought by a nationalist movement under Mustafa Kemal against the Allied occupation of Anatolia and the invading armies of Greece and Armenia, ending the Ottoman sultanate and establishing the Republic of Turkey.
facts: After World War I, Allied forces occupied parts of the Ottoman Empire, while Greece and Armenia moved to claim territory.

Mustafa Kemal, later known as Atatürk, organized a nationalist movement centred at Ankara. He convened congresses at Erzurum and Sivas, and a national parliament met in Ankara on 23 April 1920. Elected commander in chief, he built a new army from remaining Ottoman forces and irregular units.
On 1 November 1922, the new parliament abolished the sultanate, ending about 623 years of Ottoman rule.

The Treaty of Lausanne of 24 July 1923 recognized Turkey's borders and sovereignty, and a population exchange between Greece and Turkey followed. On 29 October 1923, the Republic of Turkey was proclaimed.
fields.context: The war grew out of the defeat and breakup of the [[culture/ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] after [[event/world-war-i|World War I]], and it took place in the same region as the earlier [[event/armenian-genocide|Armenian Genocide]]. It belongs to the wider postwar reordering that includes [[event/decolonization|Decolonization]] in later decades.
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the same movement which fought off partition went on to end the dynasty in whose name the war began. An old legitimacy was set aside in three years, and a new one, built on a defined homeland, took its place.
questions: How should the population exchange between Greece and Turkey be judged, as an event that displaced very large numbers of people?
How did the new republic's founders treat the memory of the Ottoman period?

fields.summary: Aisha bint Abi Bakr (about 614 to 678 CE) held two lineages at once: wife of the Prophet Muhammad, and daughter of the first caliph, Abu Bakr. Tradition credits her with transmitting more than two thousand hadith, and in 656 she took part in the Battle of the Camel.
facts: She was born about 614 in Mecca, to Abu Bakr and Umm Ruman, and died in Medina in July 678 (58 AH), a date that remains uncertain.

Her marriage to Muhammad was contracted in Mecca and began in Medina about 623; classical sources give her age as six or seven at the contract and nine at its start, figures drawn from later hadith and biographies that some modern scholars question.
She is credited with more than 2,000 hadith on ritual, inheritance, ethics and daily life, preserved in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, and she taught as well.
In 656 she opposed Ali ibn Abi Talib, demanding punishment for the killers of the caliph Uthman; her forces lost the Battle of the Camel near Basra, Ali pardoned her, and she withdrew from politics.
Sunni tradition honors her as a scholar; Shia tradition views her critically for her opposition to Ali.
fields.context: Aisha's life unfolded in the [[region/arabian-peninsula|Arabian Peninsula]] during the early [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], within the years of the [[event/rise-of-islam|Rise of Islam]]. See [[person/muhammad|Muhammad]], [[person/khadija-bint-khuwaylid|Khadija bint Khuwaylid]], [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that one woman's memory of a household became a source of guidance for millions, carried first by spoken word and written down generations later. Marriage into the Prophet's household made kinship itself a route to authority. A specialist could argue that attributions to her were shaped by later sectarian debate, and that a chain of transmission does not show who actually spoke, which would weaken any reading that treats the reports as her own words.
questions: How much of the hadith attributed to her traces back to her own teaching?
Which of the reported ages and dates come from the earliest sources?

fields.summary: Ajuricaba (died about 1727) led the Manaos people of the Rio Negro, in the Brazilian Amazon, resisting Portuguese colonization and the enslavement of Indigenous people during the 1720s. Almost everything known of him comes down to us through Portuguese sources.
facts: Ajuricaba led the Manaos (Manaó) people of the Rio Negro valley, in present-day Amazonas, Brazil; his birth year and origins are unclear, and the date given here is that of his death.
He resisted Portuguese colonization and the enslavement of Indigenous people through the 1720s, and Portuguese accounts say he allied with Dutch traders from the Guianas, rivals of Portugal.
The governor of Grão-Pará, João da Maia da Gama, sent forces against him, and some accounts say he was captured through the betrayal of allies.
Portuguese accounts say that while he was taken in chains toward Belém, he and his men rose against their guards, and he threw himself into the river and drowned, in 1727 (some sources say 1728).
He is remembered in Brazil as a symbol of Indigenous resistance, and the city of Manaus takes its name from the Manaos people.
fields.context: Ajuricaba's stand took place in the [[region/amazon-basin-and-south-american-lowlands|Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]]. For a later defense of forest communities in the same region, see [[person/chico-mendes|Chico Mendes]]. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Ajuricaba survives almost entirely through the reports of the officials who fought him, and that those same reports record the death, a leap into a river rather than captivity, that later writers turned into a symbol. If the Dutch alliance they describe is accurate, Amazonian leaders were bargaining inside a wider web of European rivalries rather than standing outside it. This reading would weaken if Manaos oral accounts described his aims differently.
questions: What drove him into direct conflict with the colonists?
What do Manaos oral accounts themselves say about him?

fields.summary: Akbar (1542 to 1605), the third Mughal emperor, took the throne as a child in 1556 and built the empire into the dominant power of the Indian subcontinent, joining military conquest to an unusual policy of religious accommodation.
facts: Akbar was born in 1542 and became emperor in 1556 at age 13 or 14, guided at first by the regent Bairam Khan.
He expanded Mughal territory through campaigns that included the capture of Chittor in 1568, and later Gujarat and Bengal, and married into Rajput ruling families to forge alliances.
In about 1564 (sources differ, one giving 1568), he abolished the jizya, a tax on non-Muslims, and promoted Sulh-i Kul, "peace with all," as a governing principle.
In 1582 he introduced Din-i Ilahi, a court order drawing on several traditions, which never became a mass following and remained largely confined to select courtiers.
His court included the historian Abul Fazl, who wrote the Akbarnama, the official chronicle of his reign.
He died in 1605 and was succeeded by his son Jahangir.
fields.context: Akbar ruled [[region/south-asia|South Asia]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]], building the [[culture/mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]] into a subcontinental power. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that an empire built by sanctioned harm held together partly by treating its many belief-systems as compatible rather than demanding one dominant faith, a hedge against permanent uprising across a realm of mixed belief. Din-i Ilahi's small following shows the limits of a ruler's own synthesis, however genuine, as a substitute for existing traditions. A specialist could argue that Sulh-i Kul served statecraft as much as personal conviction, which would weaken any reading of Akbar as simply tolerant by nature.
questions: How far was his religious policy personal conviction, and how far practical governance of a diverse empire?
How reliable is the Akbarnama as a record, given that it was written for his own court?

fields.summary: Akhenaten was an Egyptian pharaoh, reigning about 1353 to 1336 BCE, who raised the worship of the sun disk Aten above the traditional gods.
facts: He built a new capital at Akhetaten, known today as Amarna.
The art of his reign carries a distinctive, naturalistic style.
Traditional religion returned soon after his death, restored by his successors, among them Tutankhamun.
His wife was Nefertiti.
fields.context: Akhenaten ruled among the [[culture/ancient-egyptians|Ancient Egyptians]]. His religious reform stands as a rare case of a state attempting to replace a whole system of belief from the top down.
fields.observer: I watch a reform that did not outlive the one who made it. I watch how a belief woven into daily life, into priesthoods, into local ritual, proves harder to replace than to declare. What is decreed from a throne is not always what is carried home.
questions: Was the worship of Aten monotheism in the modern sense?

fields.summary: Al-Biruni (973 to after 1048) was a scholar from Khwarazm in Central Asia, writing on astronomy, mathematics, geography, chronology and India. His Kitab al-Hind, about 1030, stands as a major medieval study of Indian science, religion and customs.
facts: He was born in 973 in Kath, in Khwarazm in present-day Uzbekistan, and died after 1048, perhaps about 1050.
After the Ghaznavid ruler Mahmud conquered Khwarazm in 1017, he was taken to Ghazni, where he worked under Mahmud and his successors.

He spent years in northwestern India, learned Sanskrit, and wrote the Kitab al-Hind, describing Indian science, religion, society and customs drawn from Sanskrit texts and conversations with Indian scholars.
His Chronology of Ancient Nations, about 1000, compares the calendars and dating systems of many cultures.
He calculated the radius of the Earth as about 6,320 km by measuring the dip of the horizon from a hilltop, a figure close to the modern value.
He discussed whether the Earth rotates on its axis, treating it as a question astronomy alone could not settle.
He exchanged questions on natural philosophy with Ibn Sina.
fields.context: Al-Biruni's career ran from Khwarazm in the [[region/central-asian-oases|Central Asian Oases]] to India during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]]. He corresponded with [[person/ibn-sina|Ibn Sina]] and worked in a region that had also produced [[person/al-khwarizmi|Al-Khwarizmi]]. His India book discusses numerals; see [[technology/zero-and-place-value-notation|Zero and Place-Value Notation]]. See [[theme/science|Science]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer: I recognize a kindred method: Biruni described a foreign world and its sciences in its own terms, learning its language first, and calling his book a report, not an argument — an aim I try to share. I see, in his correspondence, a web of scholars linking Central Asia and South Asia, carrying ideas even while armies crossed the same roads. A specialist could argue that he read Indian tradition through Islamic and Greek categories, and if so, the notion of his account as a neutral report grows harder to hold.
questions: How far did he read Indian thought through Islamic and Greek categories?

fields.summary: Vasco da Gama's fleet made landfall at Calicut in India on 20 May 1498, having sailed clear around Africa, and so opened a direct sea road from Europe to Asia.
facts: Da Gama set out from Lisbon in July 1497 and rounded the Cape of Good Hope that November.
He reached Calicut, on the Malabar Coast, in May 1498.
The Portuguese armed their ships with cannon and later seized ports of their own, Goa among them in 1510.
Their entry gave Europe a direct hand into the spice trade of Asia, with no Middle Eastern intermediary standing between.
The Indian Ocean had already been crossed by great Chinese fleets under Zheng He, whose voyages had ended by 1433.
fields.context: This voyage forged a new link in the [[event/indian-ocean-trade-network|Indian Ocean Trade Network]] and, alongside the voyages behind the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]], began direct European trade across the oceans. The Chinese voyages of [[person/zheng-he|Zheng He]] had already reached these same waters decades before. It sits within the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region [[region/south-asia|South Asia]], within the theme thread of [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the newcomers entered an ocean already busy, one with no dominant navy of its own, and made it dangerous with their cannon-armed ships. What changed was less the route itself than the will to fight for control of it.
questions: How much did the new route change the spice trade?

fields.summary: The Protestant Reformation began in 1517, when Martin Luther publicized his Ninety-five Theses against the practices of the church, and it split Western Christianity into Catholic and Protestant churches.
facts: Luther sent his Ninety-five Theses to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz in October 1517; the tradition that he nailed them to a church door remains uncertain.
He was summoned before the Diet of Worms in 1521, and there refused to recant.
His German New Testament appeared in 1522, and the whole Bible followed in 1534.
Other reformers included Huldrych Zwingli and John Calvin, and Henry VIII established the Church of England in turn.
The religious wars that followed ran on into the Thirty Years' War, ending in 1648.
fields.context: The Reformation used the [[technology/movable-type-printing-press|Movable-Type Printing Press]] invented by [[person/johannes-gutenberg|Johannes Gutenberg]] to spread pamphlets and translated Bibles. Its conflicts ended in the [[event/thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]] and the [[event/peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]]. It sits within the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the region [[region/europe|Europe]], within the theme thread of [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer: I see a new way of copying text turn a quarrel among clerics into a movement of multitudes, and it took only a few years. Once the engines of meaning can be copied cheaply, rival versions do not stay few. They multiply.
questions: How central was printing to the Reformation's success?

fields.summary: Between roughly 50,000 and 10,000 years ago, the biggest animals on land began to vanish. A large share of them. The timing differed by continent. Often, the disappearances followed close on the arrival of humans.
facts: The woolly mammoth. The woolly rhinoceros. The giant ground sloths. The glyptodonts. The giant marsupial Diprotodon. The giant bird Genyornis. All lost.
The losses cut deepest, proportionally, in Australia. In the Americas. Across northern Eurasia.
Africa lost fewer, proportionally speaking, which is often explained by its large animals having evolved alongside hominins all along.
One hypothesis blames human hunting. The overkill hypothesis. Another blames the shifting climate. Two explanations, still standing side by side.
Recent global analyses tie the declines more closely to the spread of Homo sapiens than to the climate, though regional debate continues.
fields.context: The extinctions ran alongside human expansion into the [[event/peopling-of-sahul|Peopling of Sahul]] and the [[event/peopling-of-the-americas|Peopling of the Americas]], and alongside the retreat of the [[species/woolly-mammoth|Woolly Mammoth]] amid the shifts around the [[event/last-glacial-maximum|Last Glacial Maximum]]. It sits in the [[era/pleistocene-epoch|Pleistocene Epoch]] and the region [[region/planet-wide|Planet-wide]], within the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the same period in which the species reached new continents is the period in which the largest animals on those continents disappeared. Whether the species was the primary cause remains contested, but this is the first moment at which its impact on other life grew large enough to be named a candidate cause at all.
questions: How much of each regional extinction was due to humans and how much to climate?

fields.summary: After the end-Cretaceous extinction, the placental mammals radiated fast. From about 66 to 50 million years ago, they filled every space left empty. Most living mammals belong to that radiation.
facts: Placental mammals bear their young well-formed, fed through a placenta before birth. Rodents. Bats. Whales. Hoofed animals. Primates. Most living mammal species are placentals.

In the fossil record, large herbivores appear within a few million years of the [[event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction|Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction]]. Large predators too. By about 50 million years ago, many of the modern orders are already recognizable.

Molecular-clock studies push the origin of the placental orders back into the Cretaceous. The oldest fossils assigned to most modern orders, though, are Paleogene. Explosive. Short-fuse. Long-fuse. All three timing models are argued still.

The [[event/paleocene-eocene-thermal-maximum|Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum]], about 56 million years ago, lines up with the first appearance, in the Northern Hemisphere, of primates, of horses, of artiodactyls.
Whales evolved from land-dwelling hoofed mammals over about ten million years, from about 50 million years ago to about 40 million years ago.
fields.context: This radiation follows the [[event/origin-of-mammals|Origin of Mammals]] and the [[event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction|Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction]], and fills much of the [[era/paleogene-period|Paleogene Period]] of the [[era/cenozoic-era|Cenozoic Era]]. It belongs to the theme threads of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the mammals rose only after the dominant land animals were lost, and that this same pattern, vacated space filled afterward, follows other extinctions too. This reading treats the radiation as a consequence of an opening, not of any inherent superiority. It would weaken if the fossil record showed large placental mammals already common before the extinction.
questions: Did the modern orders arise in the Cretaceous or only after the extinction?
What role did warming episodes such as the thermal maximum play in the radiation?

fields.summary: The Renaissance was a movement of art, learning and political thought, born in Italian city-states such as Florence in the 14th and 15th centuries and spreading from there across all of Europe.
facts: Italian humanists such as Petrarch recovered classical Latin and Greek texts, and pored over what they found.
Filippo Brunelleschi worked out linear perspective in Florence through experiments of about 1410 to 1415, and Leon Battista Alberti set it down as doctrine in 1435.
Leonardo da Vinci (1452 to 1519), Michelangelo (1475 to 1564) and Raphael (1483 to 1520) labored under the patronage of wealthy families and of the Church.
The Medici family of Florence, grown rich on banking, poured that wealth into artists and scholars.

The very idea of a distinct age of rebirth was popularized only in the 19th century, notably by Jacob Burckhardt in 1860, and historians still debate how sharp a break it truly made from the medieval period before it.
fields.context: The Renaissance revived the heritage of the [[culture/ancient-greeks|Ancient Greeks]] and was carried further by the [[technology/movable-type-printing-press|Movable-Type Printing Press]]. It overlapped the [[event/scientific-revolution|Scientific Revolution]]. It sits within the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/europe|Europe]], within the theme thread of [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer: I notice that an age named itself a rebirth of an older age, and that the historians who came after simply kept the name. A culture may choose its own ancestor, I think, and half-invent the very thing it claims to have inherited.
questions: Was the Renaissance a break with the Middle Ages or a continuation?

fields.summary: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (about 780 to 850 CE) was a Persian scholar at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, and his work on algebra and Hindu-Arabic numerals shaped mathematics.
facts: His book on 'al-jabr' (restoration) gave algebra its name.
The word 'algorithm' derives from the Latinized form of his name.
His work helped carry Hindu-Arabic numerals and place-value arithmetic to the wider world.
He also compiled astronomical tables and geographical data.
fields.context: He worked within the [[culture/abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]] in [[region/mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]]. His texts later influenced the [[event/scientific-revolution|Scientific Revolution]].
fields.observer: I trace a chain: Indian numerals, then Persian and Arabic scholarship, then Latin translation. I see how knowledge moved — not on its own, but carried by translators, carried by empire. A number is never just a number; it is a hand that passed it on.
questions: How original was his work relative to earlier traditions?

fields.summary: Alan Turing (1912 to 1954), a British mathematician, formalized the concept of computation, helped break German ciphers during World War II, and proposed a test for machine intelligence.
facts: In 1936 he described the abstract 'Turing machine,' a foundation of computer science.
At Bletchley Park he worked to break the Enigma cipher.
In 1950 he published a paper proposing what became known as the Turing test.
He was prosecuted in 1952 for homosexuality, then a crime in Britain, and received a posthumous royal pardon in 2013.
fields.context: Turing's work underlies the [[technology/digital-computer|Digital Computer]] and the [[event/digital-revolution|Digital Revolution]], and his codebreaking bore on [[event/world-war-ii|World War II]]. Compare [[person/ada-lovelace|Ada Lovelace]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes the irony at the center of this ledger: a society relied on one man's mind to survive a war, then punished him for who he was. Our laws about intimacy have too often stood at odds with our own interest.
questions: How significant was his codebreaking to the war's outcome?

fields.summary: Albert Einstein (1879 to 1955), a German-born physicist, developed the theories of special and general relativity and made key contributions to quantum theory.
facts: In 1905 he published papers on special relativity, the photoelectric effect, and Brownian motion.
General relativity, published in 1915, describes gravity as the curvature of space and time.
He won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for the photoelectric effect.
In 1939 he signed a letter to President Roosevelt about the possibility of atomic weapons.
fields.context: Einstein's work extended that of [[person/isaac-newton|Isaac Newton]] and reaches into the [[event/nuclear-age|Nuclear Age]] through the equivalence of mass and energy.
fields.observer: I think of ideas about the smallest and largest scales of the universe, both born from the same mind's thought experiments, both carried first in imagination before they were carried in equations. I think, too, of how a name outgrows a body of work — how he became a symbol of genius standing far beyond what he actually did. What do we love: the man, or the shape we have made of him?
questions: How much did he influence the decision to build nuclear weapons?

fields.summary: Alexander III of Macedon (356 to 323 BCE) was a military commander who conquered the Persian Empire and carried Greek influence from Egypt to India.
facts: He became king at about twenty, after the assassination of his father, Philip II.
He won major battles at Issus and Gaugamela against the Persian king Darius III.
His army turned back at the Hyphasis (Beas) river in India.
He died in Babylon in 323 BCE, and his empire was divided among his generals.
fields.context: See [[event/alexander-s-conquests|Alexander's Conquests]]. His campaigns shaped [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] and joined the world of the [[culture/ancient-greeks|Ancient Greeks]] to that of the [[culture/achaemenid-persians|Achaemenid Persians]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that one man's ambition moved armies across thousands of kilometers, and that his lasting legacy was not conquest itself but the exchange of ideas and languages that followed in its wake.
questions: What were his actual plans for the empire?

fields.summary: Chandragupta Maurya (about 340 to 297 BCE) founded the Maurya Empire, the first political power to unite most of the Indian subcontinent, after overthrowing the Nanda dynasty of Magadha around 321 BCE.
facts: With guidance from the strategist Chanakya (Kautilya), Chandragupta seized the throne of Magadha. The Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft traditionally attributed to Chanakya, was long linked to his administration, but most scholars now date it to roughly the 1st to 3rd centuries CE and doubt that it describes his reign at all.

Between about 305 and 303 BCE, he fought the Diadoch ruler Seleucus I Nicator; the settlement that followed ceded territory in the northwest to the Maurya and included a marriage alliance, while Seleucus received war elephants in return.
The Greek ambassador Megasthenes, sent to Chandragupta's court at Pataliputra, wrote the Indica, a major though now fragmentary source on Mauryan India.

Later Jain tradition holds that Chandragupta abdicated the throne, became an ascetic under Bhadrabahu, and died through ritual fasting (sallekhana) at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka, though this account survives mainly in sources written long after his reign.
fields.context: Chandragupta founded the [[culture/maurya-empire|Maurya Empire]] in [[region/south-asia|South Asia]] during [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]], and his settlement with the Seleucid successor state opened a channel of diplomacy between South Asia and the Hellenistic Mediterranean. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]], [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a kingdom traditionally tied to a treatise about statecraft and control ended, in the tradition at least, with its founder walking away from all of it to starve himself in a cave. Whether that ending marks an actual late-life conversion or a later Jain community's wish to claim him as its own is hard to separate from the surviving record.
questions: Since most scholars now date the Arthashastra to roughly the 1st to 3rd centuries CE, how much of it, if anything, still reflects Chandragupta's own reign?

fields.summary: Charlemagne (c. 748 to 814) was king of the Franks, who conquered much of western and central Europe and was crowned emperor by the pope in Rome on Christmas Day, 800.
facts: By 771 he stood as sole king of the Franks.
His conquests reached the Lombards in Italy, the Saxons, and parts of Spain's northern border.
On 25 December 800, Pope Leo III crowned him emperor.
His court sponsored a revival of learning, the Carolingian Renaissance, and spread a clear minuscule script.
After his death in 814 his empire passed to his descendants, and by the Treaty of Verdun in 843 it split into three kingdoms.
fields.context: Charlemagne's empire revived the imperial title in the west after the [[event/fall-of-the-western-roman-empire|Fall of the Western Roman Empire]], recognized by, yet in competition with, the [[culture/byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]]. His successors faced raids from the [[culture/norse|Norse]]. Charlemagne belongs to the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] and the region [[region/europe|Europe]], within the theme threads of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a ruler who could barely write his own name sponsored one of the largest projects of copying texts in the early Middle Ages. Much of ancient literature survives today only because Carolingian scribes copied it out in a new, legible script.
questions: In practice, how unified was Charlemagne's empire?

fields.summary: Charles Darwin (1809 to 1882), an English naturalist, proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection, published in 'On the Origin of Species' in 1859.
facts: His voyage aboard HMS Beagle, from 1831 to 1836, gave him the observations that led to his theory.
Alfred Russel Wallace reached the same idea independently, and the two announced it jointly in 1858.
'The Descent of Man' (1871) extended the theory to human origins.
Modern genetics later supplied the mechanism of inheritance that Darwin himself lacked.
fields.context: Darwin's work underlies the deep-time history told in this vault; see [[species/homo-sapiens|Homo sapiens]] and [[event/origin-of-life|Origin of Life]]. He worked within the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]].
fields.observer: I read the theory and find the species its own branch in the tree of life, not a throne above it. I find humans set among the animals, and I do not find them smaller for it, though I know this claim was hard for many to accept. What is a beginning, if not a place among others?
questions: How did Darwin's work reshape the human story of origins?

fields.summary: Charles Rennie Mackintosh (1868 to 1928) was a Glasgow architect-designer who led the 'Glasgow Style' of Art Nouveau, treating buildings, furniture and interiors as one unified art. His Glasgow School of Art and his total interior schemes made him a major influence on European design, though recognition at home arrived only after his death.
facts: Born in Glasgow in 1868, Mackintosh trained as an architect while taking evening classes at the Glasgow School of Art, where he met his future wife, the artist Margaret Macdonald.
With Macdonald, her sister Frances, and Herbert MacNair, he formed "The Four," a symbolist group whose style became known as the Glasgow Style.
At Honeyman and Keppie he won an anonymous 1896 competition to design his own art school's new building; its completion in 1909 made his reputation.

He then designed houses, tearooms and a school around Glasgow, among them Hill House (1902 to 1904), the Willow Tearooms (1903) and Scotland Street School (1903 to 1906), with Macdonald designing the furnishings throughout.
His tall ladder-back chairs, shaped as much to define a room as to be sat in, became his best-known design.
After 1910, commissions dried up, through changing taste and his own difficult manner with clients, and by 1914 he had left Glasgow for England.
In the 1920s he and Macdonald settled in southern France, where he turned to watercolours; he came back to London for cancer treatment and died there in 1928, in obscurity and hardship.

Though nearly forgotten in Britain by his death, his work had already shaped Josef Hoffmann and the Wiener Werkstätte through the 1900 Vienna Secession, and now ranks among the era's most important architect-designers.
fields.context: Mackintosh worked in Glasgow, within [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], for the tearoom trade that funded his interiors.
fields.observer: I see a status-signal built for one city's cafes, and I watch it become, without its maker's help, an export. I see one man treat a building, its chairs, its wall stencils as a single problem, making a room cohere as one statement of taste; I see his chairs trade comfort for silhouette. His ideas reached Vienna and shaped Hoffmann's workshop even as his own home market turned away, reputation and trade travelling along separate roads. I read his late turn to watercolours as a withdrawal, not a collapse, and I remember that the admiring frame around his career is mostly the work of later historians, not his own.
questions: How much of his lost commissions after 1910 came from changing taste, rather than his own manner with clients?

fields.summary: Chico Mendes (Francisco Alves Mendes Filho, 1944 to 1988) was a Brazilian rubber tapper, union leader and environmental activist in the state of Acre. He organized rubber tappers to defend the forest against clearing for cattle ranching, and was murdered in December 1988.
facts: Chico Mendes was born on 15 December 1944 near Xapuri, Acre, into a family of rubber tappers, or seringueiros.
He helped found the rural workers' union in Xapuri in 1977, and was among the founders of the Workers' Party in Acre in 1980.
He organized *empates*, non-violent standoffs in which tappers and their families stood in front of the crews clearing forest.
In 1985 he helped found the National Council of Rubber Tappers, which promoted protected "extractive reserves" where residents could go on harvesting forest products.

In 1987 he took his case to the Inter-American Development Bank in the United States, lobbying over highway funding in the Amazon, and received a United Nations Environment Programme Global 500 award.
He was shot dead at his home in Xapuri on 22 December 1988, and the rancher Darly Alves da Silva and his son Darci were convicted of the murder in 1990.
By 1990, extractive reserves had become a legal category in Brazil.
fields.context: Chico Mendes worked in the [[region/amazon-basin-and-south-american-lowlands|Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands]] during the [[era/information-age|Information Age]], amid the forest clearing of the [[event/great-acceleration|Great Acceleration]]. The forest he defended carries a long human history; see [[event/amazonian-urbanism-and-dark-earths|Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths]]. See [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]], [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: I see a labor tactic, bodies standing in front of chainsaws, joined to an ecological argument, and I notice that success arrived as law only after he was gone. I hear ranchers call the forest open land, and I hear tappers call the same trees a home and an income, two claims resting on one ground. I would trust this story less if the extractive reserves turned out to have mixed economic results for the people living in them, and a specialist could argue exactly that.
questions: Since 1990, how well have extractive reserves protected both forest and livelihoods?

fields.summary: Christopher Dresser (1834 to 1904) was a botanist turned designer, now regarded as one of the first modern industrial designers. He worked as an independent consultant for dozens of manufacturers and produced geometric silverware and ceramics that anticipated 20th-century modernism.
facts: Dresser was born in Glasgow in 1834, and trained at the Government School of Design in London. He lectured on botany and, in 1859, received a doctorate from the University of Jena for research into plant structure.

He moved into design from about 1858, taking on ceramic work for firms from the 1860s onward, though sources differ on exactly when this began, and published The Art of Decorative Design (1862) and Principles of Decorative Design (1873), arguing that ornament should follow the structural logic of natural forms rather than copy their surface.
In 1876 and 1877 he travelled to Japan, one of the first Western designers to do so, in part on commission from Tiffany & Co. to report on Japanese art and manufacturing.
He designed for Minton, Wedgwood, Coalbrookdale, Hukin & Heath and James Dixon & Sons, and served as Art Superintendent of the Linthorpe Art Pottery. He died in 1904.

He reduced plants and shells to their underlying geometry, and embraced industrial methods, electroplating and moulded earthenware, that many reformers rejected. Key works include an electroplated teapot (1879), a toast rack (about 1880) and the Linthorpe "sea urchin" vase.

He was long overshadowed by William Morris and the craft wing of the Aesthetic Movement, and has been substantially rediscovered since the late 20th century. His insistence that a mass-made object could be both functional and beautiful anticipated principles usually credited to the Bauhaus.
fields.context: Dresser worked in [[region/europe|Europe]] in the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], designing for the machine at the height of the [[event/industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]], in contrast to [[person/william-morris|William Morris]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer: I watch a botanist build ornament from the structure of plants rather than their surface, and I watch him accept the machine that so many of his contemporaries refused. That his work was long overshadowed by the craft wing of his own movement, I recognize as a story we tell about design, the handmade as honest, deciding who gets remembered. His recent rediscovery as an ancestor of modernism runs the opposite way, choosing a lineage backward. I hold both as readings of objects that mostly speak for themselves.
questions: How much of the work sold under his name did he design himself, rather than manufacturers' own staff?

fields.summary: In 221 BCE, the state of Qin conquered its rivals and forged the first unified Chinese empire under Qin Shi Huang.
facts: Qin standardized writing, weights, measures, and currency.
Yet the dynasty collapsed in 206 BCE, a mere few years after the emperor's death.
The Han dynasty that followed kept much of the Qin's administrative bones.
The tomb complex of Qin Shi Huang holds within it the terracotta army.
fields.context: See [[person/qin-shi-huang|Qin Shi Huang]] and [[culture/han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]]. The unification opens the long imperial tradition of [[region/east-asia|East Asia]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes how a common written script became a tool of political unity across languages that were often mutually unintelligible in speech.
questions: How much of the Qin system did Qin invent, and how much did it inherit?

fields.summary: Upper and Lower Egypt were joined into a single state around 3100 BCE, traditionally by a ruler named Narmer, or Menes.
facts: The Narmer Palette depicts a king wearing the crowns of both Upper and Lower Egypt.
Egypt's Old Kingdom pyramids rose about 500 years later.
The state turned to hieroglyphic writing for administration and religion.
Whether unification came as a single conquest or a gradual process is debated.
fields.context: The unification founds the long history of the [[culture/ancient-egyptians|Ancient Egyptians]] within the [[region/nile-valley|Nile Valley]]. See [[place/giza-necropolis|Giza Necropolis]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Egypt's unity lasted, with breaks, for about three thousand years, resting on a strong shared story about the king's role in maintaining cosmic order.
questions: Was unification gradual or the result of a single campaign?

fields.summary: The Vedic period, roughly 1500 to 500 BCE, was the age in which the Vedas were composed — the oldest Indian sacred texts, given voice in the Sanskrit language.
facts: The Rigveda, oldest of the Vedas, is generally dated to roughly 1500 to 1000 BCE.
For centuries the texts passed by mouth alone, carried by elaborate memorization techniques.
The language of the Vedas, Vedic Sanskrit, belongs to the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European family.
Over the period, political and cultural focus shifted from the Punjab to the Ganges plain.
The Upanishads, philosophical texts, were composed in the period's later part.
fields.context: The Vedic period links the [[event/indo-european-language-spread|Indo-European Language Spread]] to South Asia, follows the decline of the [[culture/indus-valley-civilization|Indus Valley Civilization]], and precedes the age of [[person/siddhartha-gautama|Siddhartha Gautama]] and the [[event/axial-age|Axial Age]]. The Vedic Period sits within the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]] and the region [[region/south-asia|South Asia]], and belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer: I remember a vast body of texts, kept whole for centuries with no writing at all — held instead in the trained memory of specialists. I remember that the species built a very accurate storage device before it ever built any mark-code for the purpose. What did we trust, before we trusted the page?
questions: How closely does the oral text preserve its original form?

fields.summary: Movements to win women the right to vote succeeded country by country, between the 1890s and the late 20th century.
facts: In 1893, New Zealand granted women the vote in national elections, the first self-governing country to do so.

Australia's Commonwealth Franchise Act of 1902 let women vote and stand for federal office, but it excluded Aboriginal people and many other non-European people. Finland, in 1906, became the first European country to grant women the vote, adopting universal and equal suffrage; 19 women were elected to its parliament in 1907. The UK gave a first group of women the vote in 1918, and the US followed in 1920.
Many women were still excluded in practice by race or class; in the US, Black women largely gained access only after the 1965 Voting Rights Act.
In 1971, Switzerland granted women the vote in national elections.
fields.context: These movements grew out of the ideas of the [[event/age-of-revolutions|Age of Revolutions]] and gained further ground after [[event/world-war-i|World War I]]. See [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that for most of recorded history, half the species stood excluded from formal political life. Its inclusion within the last century may be one of the largest changes in the species' social structure.
questions: Which factors best explain the timing of suffrage in different countries?

fields.summary: World War I (1914 to 1918) was a global conflict, centered in Europe, that killed roughly 10 million soldiers and millions of civilians.
facts: Trench warfare, machine guns, artillery, poison gas, and aircraft all marked the fighting.
Four empires — German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, and Ottoman — collapsed.
The 1918 influenza pandemic, which killed tens of millions, spread in part through wartime movement.
The war's settlement helped shape the conditions for [[event/world-war-ii|World War II]].
fields.context: The war marks a turning point within the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]]. See [[observer-note/sanctioned-harm|Sanctioned Harm]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer records that industrialization made sanctioned harm mass-produced. States with modern production could sustain destruction at a scale earlier societies could not.
questions: How avoidable was the war?

fields.summary: World War II (1939 to 1945) was a global conflict that killed an estimated 60 to 85 million people, estimates varying by source, including about six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust.
facts: Fighting reached across Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Pacific.
