The Holocaust was the state-organized genocide of European Jews; millions of others, Roma and disabled people among them, were murdered as well.
The war ended with the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945; see [[event/nuclear-age|Nuclear Age]].
In its aftermath came the United Nations, decolonization, and the Cold War.
fields.context: The war ends the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]] and opens the [[era/information-age|Information Age]]. See [[observer-note/sanctioned-harm|Sanctioned Harm]] and [[person/alan-turing|Alan Turing]].
fields.observer: The Observer records the war as the deadliest in the record, and the Holocaust as an instance of industrial methods turned to organized killing. It is a case where the species' most sophisticated organization produced its worst outcomes.
questions: What are the most reliable casualty figures for each theater?

fields.summary: Albrecht Dürer (21 May 1471 to 6 April 1528) was a painter and printmaker from Nuremberg who carried the Italian Renaissance north. His woodcuts and engravings, sold across Europe, made him the first artist whose international reputation was built largely on prints.
facts: Dürer was born in Nuremberg, the son of a Hungarian-born goldsmith, and from 1486 was apprenticed to Michael Wolgemut, whose workshop produced woodcuts for book illustration.

He travelled to Venice in 1494, and again from early 1506 to 1507, where Giovanni Bellini treated him as an equal; in 1498 he published the Apocalypse, 15 large woodcuts (some counts give 16 designs dated 1498) that made him famous.

From 1512 Emperor Maximilian I employed him and granted him a pension; on a trip to the Netherlands in 1520 to 1521 to have it confirmed by Charles V, his diary recorded his amazement at Aztec treasures sent from Mexico.
He sympathised with Martin Luther's reforms, and in his last years published treatises on measurement, fortification and human proportion.
His 'AD' monogram served as a trademark, and he took action against copyists who used it.
Key works include Self-Portrait at the Age of Twenty-Eight (1500), Young Hare (1502), Melencolia I (1514) and The Rhinoceros (1515).
His prints were copied by artists from Italy to Persia and Mughal India, and Raphael exchanged drawings with him; in the 19th century German Romantics made him a national hero.
fields.context: Dürer worked across [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[event/renaissance|Renaissance]], within the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the years of the [[event/protestant-reformation|Protestant Reformation]]. His diary touches the [[culture/aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]], and his prints reached the [[culture/mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer: I see a maker who understood, early, that a picture printed on paper travels farther than one hung on a wall. I see a workshop skill made into a good that could move through trade, and a monogram defended like a claim of ownership. In his self-portraits I find an artist presenting himself as learned, almost god-made, a status he claimed for himself rather than for any patron. And the 19th-century cult that crowned him a German hero — that came later, stitched on after his death, not a truth of his own time.
questions: How far did his prints, rather than his paintings, set the terms of his fame in his own lifetime?

fields.summary: Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE) was a Greek philosopher and scientist who studied logic, ethics, politics, physics, and biology, and tutored Alexander of Macedon.
facts: He studied under Plato in Athens, and later founded his own school, the Lyceum.
He wrote on logic, ethics, politics, poetics, physics, and biology.
His biological work drew on careful observation of marine life.
His works were preserved and extended in the Islamic world, and later in Latin Europe.
fields.context: Aristotle worked in [[place/athens|Athens]] and Macedon among the [[culture/ancient-greeks|Ancient Greeks]], and taught [[person/alexander-the-great|Alexander the Great]]. His works framed European and Islamic scholarship for centuries.
fields.observer: I see the taming of patterns become a system: classifying, defining, arguing from evidence. And I see, too, how a great authority can slow inquiry, when his errors are mistaken for settled ground.
questions: Which of his writings survive as he wrote them?

fields.summary: Ashoka (about 304 to 232 BCE) was a Mauryan emperor who ruled most of the Indian subcontinent, and became a patron of Buddhism after a bloody war.
facts: He conquered the region of Kalinga around 261 BCE at great human cost; his own edicts record about 100,000 killed and 150,000 deported.
He had edicts inscribed on rocks and pillars across his empire, promoting 'dhamma,' or moral conduct.
He supported the spread of Buddhism, including missions sent abroad.
His lion capital now serves as a national emblem of India.
fields.context: Ashoka ruled during [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] in [[region/south-asia|South Asia]], and helped make [[person/siddhartha-gautama|Siddhartha Gautama]]'s teaching a regional, and later global, tradition.
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Ashoka's edicts stand as an early case of a ruler reflecting publicly on the harm of war. Public inscriptions offered a new way of speaking to a whole population at once.
questions: How much of Ashoka's dhamma was policy and how much personal belief?

fields.summary: Islam emerged in Arabia beginning in 610 CE, and within about a century it had spread, through conquest and through conversion, across territory reaching from Iberia to Central Asia.
facts: Muslims date their era from the Hijra, the migration to Medina, in 622 CE.
The Umayyad Caliphate, from 661 to 750, expanded into Iberia and into the Indus valley.
The Abbasid Caliphate, from 750 onward, became a center of scholarship and of trade.
Islam stands today as one of the world's largest religions.
fields.context: See [[person/muhammad|Muhammad]] and the [[culture/abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]]. This rise reshaped [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]] trade and knowledge; see [[person/al-khwarizmi|Al-Khwarizmi]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes how a new meaning-engine and a new political order arose together, and quickly built a single region of shared law, shared script and shared learning, whose scholars preserved and extended the knowledge that came before them.
questions: How quickly did populations convert to Islam in each region?

fields.summary: Between 1582 and 1639, Russian Cossacks and traders pushed across Siberia all the way to the Pacific, driven by the fur trade and by the tribute, yasak, taken from Indigenous peoples.
facts: In 1582 the Cossack leader Yermak, with about 540 Cossacks and 300 Livonian war prisoners, seized the capital of the Khanate of Sibir.
Russians reached the Pacific, at Okhotsk, by 1639.
The whole advance was driven by European demand for luxury furs.
Yasak, a tribute paid in furs, was demanded of men aged eighteen to fifty, and Indigenous populations suffered disease, violence and forced levies under it.
fields.context: The advance followed the collapse of the steppe khanates after the [[culture/mongol-empire|Mongol Empire]], and stands as a parallel to the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]]. See [[region/siberia-and-the-arctic|Siberia and the Arctic]] and the [[culture/yakut-sakha|Yakut (Sakha)]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a frontier that moved across thousands of kilometers in about six decades, carried forward by small bands living off the fur trade. Demand for a commodity, it seems, can move a border faster than any army.
questions: How large was the Indigenous population loss in the first century of Russian rule?

fields.summary: The Russian Revolution of 1917 overthrew the Tsarist monarchy, and the Bolsheviks under Vladimir Lenin then seized power in turn, leading on to a civil war and to the formation of the Soviet Union in 1922.
facts: The February Revolution of 1917 forced Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate, in March by the Western calendar.
The Bolsheviks seized power in the October Revolution, on 7 November by the Western calendar.
A civil war between the Bolshevik Reds and their opponents ran from 1918 to 1922.
The Soviet Union was established in December 1922.
Russia withdrew from World War I by way of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in 1918.
fields.context: The revolution grew out of the strains of [[event/world-war-i|World War I]] and created the Soviet state, one of the two poles of the [[event/cold-war|Cold War]]. It sits within the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]] and the region [[region/europe|Europe]], within the theme thread of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a revolution justified by a theory of history went on to build a state that then had to make its own history. Ideas tend to become institutions, and institutions, in turn, tend to resist change like any other inherited system.
questions: Could the Provisional Government have survived?

fields.summary: The Scientific Revolution was the shift, roughly from 1543 to 1687, toward systematic experiment, mathematics and observation as the basis for knowledge of nature, centered in Europe.
facts: Marker works include Copernicus's heliocentric model and Vesalius's anatomy, both from 1543.

[[person/galileo-galilei|Galileo Galilei]] turned to the telescope and to experiment, and [[person/isaac-newton|Isaac Newton]]'s Principia, in 1687, unified terrestrial and celestial motion under one account.
It drew on earlier work from the Islamic world, from India and from China; see [[person/al-khwarizmi|Al-Khwarizmi]].
Historians debate whether it was truly a single 'revolution' at all.
fields.context: The revolution sits within the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and was made possible by the [[technology/movable-type-printing-press|Movable-Type Printing Press]]. See [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer: I call this pattern-taming, and what strikes me most is one feature: doubt, made into an institution. A claim here is meant to be tested. A claim here is meant to be open, always, to revision by a stranger who was never in the room.
questions: How important was non-European knowledge to it?

fields.summary: The Scramble for Africa was the rapid partition of the African continent among European powers between about 1881 and 1914, in which the share of Africa under European control rose from roughly 10 percent to about 90 percent.
facts: The Berlin Conference, from November 1884 to February 1885, set the rules for claiming territory, though it did not itself divide the continent.
By 1914, only Ethiopia and Liberia stood independent of European rule.
African societies resisted in many wars, among them the [[event/battle-of-adwa|Battle of Adwa]] and the Anglo-Zulu War; see [[culture/zulu-kingdom|Zulu Kingdom]].
Colonial borders were drawn with little regard for the societies already living there, and many of those borders remain today.
fields.context: See [[event/congo-free-state|Congo Free State]] and the [[culture/sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto Caliphate]]. The partition stands as the background to [[event/decolonization|Decolonization]] in [[region/sub-saharan-africa|Sub-Saharan Africa]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a process of claim-lines drawn on maps, in a distant capital, over the homes of millions who were never consulted. The lines outlasted the empires that drew them. See [[observer-note/the-fiction-of-claim-lines|The Fiction of Claim-Lines]].
questions: How did colonial borders shape later state formation?

fields.summary: The Xinhai Revolution of 1911 to 1912 opened with an army mutiny at Wuchang and closed the Qing dynasty, which had ruled China since 1644, replacing imperial rule with the Republic of China.
facts: On 10 October 1911, members of the New Army mutinied in Wuchang, in Hubei province. The rebellion spread to surrounding regions, and by the end of 1911 revolutionaries were already forming a new government.

Sun Yat-sen led the republican movement, though he lacked the means to overthrow the Qing alone. He reached a compromise with the powerful military leader Yuan Shikai, whose intervention led to the abdication of the child emperor Puyi on 12 February 1912.
Sun Yat-sen resigned the presidency to unify the country, and Yuan Shikai was chosen as his successor. By early 1912, the Qing dynasty was gone, and the Republic of China had begun.
fields.context: The revolution ended the [[culture/qing-dynasty|Qing Dynasty]] after decades of internal rebellion and foreign pressure, including the [[event/taiping-rebellion|Taiping Rebellion]] and the [[event/opium-wars|Opium Wars]]. The republic that followed proved unstable, with power passing quickly into the hands of military leaders.
fields.observer: The Observer notes a transfer of authority arranged by compromise between a movement and an army, not by the movement alone. An architecture of legitimacy as old as the imperial title dissolved in a few months, but what replaced it had to be built while the guns were still in the hands of others.
questions: How much did the Wuchang mutiny depend on planning, and how much on chance?
Why did the republic that replaced the Qing fail to hold power together in the years after 1912?

fields.summary: The Younger Dryas was a sudden return of near-glacial cold across the Northern Hemisphere, lasting from about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, on the very threshold of the Holocene.
facts: It broke the warming that had followed the last glacial period, and it ended just as abruptly — several degrees of warming within mere decades.
A leading explanation points to a disruption of Atlantic Ocean circulation by a great pulse of glacial meltwater.
A proposed extraterrestrial impact trigger, the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis, remains disputed and is not widely accepted.
Its end marks the start of the Holocene, dated to about 11,700 years before 2000 CE.
It overlaps the early stages of plant management in Southwest Asia, though the causal link between the two is debated.
fields.context: The Younger Dryas is the last major cold snap before the stable climate of the [[era/holocene-epoch|Holocene Epoch]], within which [[event/the-agricultural-revolution|The Agricultural Revolution]] took place. It follows the [[event/last-glacial-maximum|Last Glacial Maximum]]. The Younger Dryas sits within the [[era/pleistocene-epoch|Pleistocene Epoch]] and the region [[region/planet-wide|Planet-wide]], and belongs to the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the climate stability in which farming and cities arose was not inevitable. It was preceded by a violent flicker between cold and warm that lasted about a thousand years, and the Observer wonders how populations managed to adapt to such swings within a few generations.
questions: Did the cold snap influence the first cultivation of crops?

fields.summary: The Zanclean flood: the refilling of the Mediterranean Sea by Atlantic water, through the Gibraltar region, about 5.33 million years ago. It ended the Messinian salinity crisis. It coincides with the start of the Pliocene.
facts: The Mediterranean, cut off from the Atlantic, had largely evaporated. Estimates of how far the sea level fell range from hundreds of metres to more than a kilometre.
Seismic images show a buried erosional channel, running from the Gulf of Cádiz through the Strait of Gibraltar into the Alboran Sea — read as the path the flood carved.
A 2009 study modelled a catastrophic flood, its peak discharge on the order of a hundred million cubic metres per second, refilling the basin within months to a couple of years.
Other studies propose a slower or two-stage refilling. The speed of the flood: still debated.
The return of the Atlantic ended the basin's isolation and restored marine life within it.
fields.context: The Zanclean Flood ends the [[event/messinian-salinity-crisis|Messinian Salinity Crisis]] within the [[era/neogene-period|Neogene Period]] and falls at the start of the Pliocene. It belongs to the [[era/cenozoic-era|Cenozoic Era]] and to the theme thread of [[theme/earth-systems-and-life|Earth Systems and Life]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that one of the largest floods in Earth's history left no human witness, and survives only as a buried channel and seismic images. The largest events in the record can be the ones least available to any memory. This reading would weaken if the refilling proved to have been slow and gradual.
questions: Was the refilling a single catastrophic flood or a slower, staged process?
How dry did the Mediterranean become before the flood?

fields.summary: Christopher Wren (1632 to 1723) was an English mathematician and astronomer, a founder of the Royal Society, who turned architect after the Great Fire of London in 1666. He designed more than fifty City churches and a new St Paul's Cathedral, topped out in 1708 and declared complete by Parliament in 1711.
facts: Wren was born in East Knoyle, Wiltshire, the son of a clergyman. He was appointed professor of astronomy at Gresham College at 25, then Savilian Professor of Astronomy at Oxford, and became a founding member of the Royal Society in 1662.
His career as an architect began with the Sheldonian Theatre in Oxford. The Great Fire of September 1666 then destroyed old St Paul's and most of the City.

He was appointed Surveyor of the King's Works in 1669, and spent the rest of his working life on the City's parish churches and on St Paul's. He died in 1723, aged 90, and lies buried in the cathedral crypt.
He combined the classical vocabulary of Inigo Jones and Palladio with French and Italian Baroque elements studied on a research trip to Paris, the only time he ever travelled outside England.
The dome of St Paul's rests on three independent shells nested one inside the other, so that exterior profile, interior ceiling and structural core could each be optimised on its own.
His key works include the Royal Observatory, Greenwich (1675 to 1676), the Royal Hospital Chelsea (1682 to 1692) and the Monument to the Great Fire (1671 to 1677).

Many City churches were later damaged or demolished, by Victorian redevelopment and by German bombing, but a substantial number still stand. Photographs of the dome rising above the smoke of the Blitz in 1940 circulated worldwide.
fields.context: Wren worked in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]] and the [[event/scientific-revolution|Scientific Revolution]], drawing on [[person/andrea-palladio|Andrea Palladio]]'s classical vocabulary. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]], [[theme/science|Science]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer: I think of a fire that destroyed a city, and of the mathematician it handed the chance to become that city's chief builder, so that catastrophe became the hinge of a career and of a skyline. I see the triple-shell dome as pattern-taming turned to stone. And I watch St Paul's become, through the photographs of 1940, a story we tell ourselves about endurance, a meaning laid on the building by later events rather than one Wren ever intended.
questions: Which of the City churches he designed still survive in their original form?

fields.summary: The Empress Dowager Cixi (1835 to 1908) stood as the dominant political figure of late Qing China, ruling as regent for most of the period from 1861 to 1908.
facts: She became regent in 1861 for her young son, the Tongzhi Emperor, and later still for the Guangxu Emperor.
Her era included the Self-Strengthening Movement, an effort to modernize China's defenses and industry.
She supported the Boxers in 1900, and after their defeat turned to pursue the 'New Policies' reforms.
Historians still debate her legacy: older accounts portray her as a reactionary, while recent work stresses her political skill and the limits she faced.
fields.context: Cixi ruled the [[culture/qing-dynasty|Qing Dynasty]] through the aftermath of the [[event/opium-wars|Opium Wars]] and the [[event/boxer-rebellion|Boxer Rebellion]]. Compare [[person/wu-zetian|Wu Zetian]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that, as with earlier women rulers, the record on Cixi comes to us largely through her opponents. See [[observer-note/who-writes-the-record|Who Writes the Record]].
questions: How should we assess Cixi's role in the Qing decline?

fields.summary: Claude Monet (14 November 1840 to 5 December 1926) was a French painter, the leader and purest practitioner of Impressionism. His Impression, Sunrise gave the movement its name, and he spent a lifetime painting the changing effects of light.
facts: Monet was born in Paris and grew up in Le Havre, where as a teenager he sold caricatures. Eugène Boudin persuaded him to paint outdoors, and in Paris he met Camille Pissarro and befriended Renoir, Sisley and Bazille.
The 1860s and 1870s were years of poverty for him. During the Franco-Prussian War he took refuge in London, where he saw Turner's paintings and met the dealer Paul Durand-Ruel.
In 1874 he and his friends held an exhibition independent of the official Salon. Critics mocked them for it, and the name "Impressionist" stuck.
In 1883 his family settled at Giverny in Normandy, where he built a flower garden and a water garden with a Japanese bridge, which became his main subject.

He painted the same subject again and again under changing conditions: haystacks, poplars, Rouen Cathedral. Key works include Impression, Sunrise (1872), Stacks of Wheat (1890 to 1891) and the Water Lilies.
In his last decade he fought cataracts while working on the giant Grandes Décorations, which he gave to the French state as a monument to peace after the First World War. He died at Giverny.
The Abstract Expressionists rediscovered his late water lilies in the 1950s; his house and gardens opened to the public in 1980, and in 2019 one of his Haystacks sold for $110.7 million.
fields.context: Monet worked in [[region/europe|Europe]] in the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], learning from [[person/j-m-w-turner|J. M. W. Turner]] and from Japanese prints by [[person/katsushika-hokusai|Katsushika Hokusai]] and [[person/utagawa-hiroshige|Utagawa Hiroshige]], and gave his last great work to France after [[event/world-war-i|World War I]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: I find a painter whose true subject was the act of seeing, and I find his method, the same motif returned to under changing light, proof enough that one scene is many scenes. I remember that critics named the movement to mock it, and that the name became a badge instead, insult and category folded into one. And I think of his paintings turned into objects of enormous price, $110.7 million for a single Haystacks in 2019, a status-signal the mocking critics of 1874 could never have foreseen.
questions: How did his cataracts change the colours of his last paintings?

fields.summary: Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt. She allied with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony, and died in 30 BCE after their defeat by Octavian.
facts: She belonged to the Ptolemaic dynasty, founded by one of Alexander the Great's Macedonian generals.
Ancient sources say she spoke several languages, and, unlike most of her Ptolemaic predecessors, learned Egyptian.
She had a son with Julius Caesar, and children with Mark Antony.
At the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE, Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra.
Following her death in 30 BCE, Egypt passed into a Roman province.
fields.context: Cleopatra was a Greek-speaking ruler over the land of the [[culture/ancient-egyptians|Ancient Egyptians]], descended from the generals of [[person/alexander-the-great|Alexander the Great]]. Her defeat by [[person/augustus|Augustus]] ended the last Hellenistic kingdom. Cleopatra VII belongs to [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]] and the region [[region/nile-valley|Nile Valley]], within the theme thread of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that most of what is known about her comes down through Roman authors who had reasons of their own to portray her as a threat. The record was written by her enemies.
questions: How much of her traditional portrait comes from Roman propaganda?

fields.summary: Confucius (Kong Fuzi, 551 to 479 BCE) was a Chinese teacher and thinker whose ideas about ethics, family and government shaped East Asian societies for over two thousand years.
facts: His disciples gathered his sayings into the Analects.
Among his central ideas are ren, or humaneness, li, or ritual propriety, and filial piety.
He was not widely influential during his own lifetime; his ideas rose to prominence only later, under the Han dynasty.
Confucian learning later became the very basis of the imperial civil service examinations.
fields.context: Confucius is counted among the figures linked to the [[event/axial-age|Axial Age]]. See [[culture/han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]] and [[region/east-asia|East Asia]].
fields.observer: I find a teacher who held no political power at all, and yet supplied the ethical framework of an entire state. I find the kin-lattice, the bonds of family, projected outward until it became a model for how to govern. What is government, if not a family grown too large to know all its own names?
questions: How much of the Analects truly reflects Confucius himself?

fields.summary: Alice Guy-Blaché (1873 to 1968) was a French filmmaker who began directing at the Gaumont Film Company in Paris in 1896, and later became the first woman to found and run her own film studio. She is credited as one of cinema's earliest narrative directors, though her work was erased from film history for most of the twentieth century.
facts: Born in Saint-Mandé, France, in 1873, she was hired in 1894 as a secretary at a camera and photography supply company, which Léon Gaumont and partners took over in 1895 as it moved into motion pictures.

After seeing an early demonstration film, she won permission to direct in her spare time; the result, traditionally given as La Fée aux choux (1896), is often called cinema's first narrative film, though its title is uncertain, and that 1896 film appears to be lost, with the surviving 1900 and 1902 versions being different films.

She rose to head of production at Gaumont, experimenting with hand-tinted colour and an early sound process, Phonoscènes, and in 1906 satirized gender roles in the reversal comedy Les Résultats du féminisme.

In 1907 she married cameraman Herbert Blaché, moved to the United States, and in 1910 co-founded the Solax Company in Flushing, New York, where she served as artistic director, with a new plant at Fort Lee, New Jersey following in 1912.
At Solax she directed social dramas such as Making an American Citizen and Falling Leaves (1912), addressing immigration and domestic abuse more directly than most of her peers.

She was forced to auction her studio in bankruptcy in 1921, and Hollywood's rise together with a 1922 divorce ended the couple's film partnership; she returned to France unable to direct again, and died in New Jersey in 1968.

For decades she was largely absent from the historical record, and her films were reportedly credited to male colleagues, until 1970s scholarship, drawing on her memoir and studio records, restored her authorship.
fields.context: Guy-Blaché worked in Paris and then New Jersey, within [[region/europe|Europe]]'s [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], as film crossed the Atlantic. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer: I see a woman who took a device built to record motion and turned it into a stage for invented stories, folding a fairy tale into a new lineage of tools almost as soon as the tools existed. What came after tells me more: for decades her work was reportedly catalogued under male colleagues' names, erasing a working director from her own trade's memory even while the films themselves survived. That her authorship needed a later memoir and buried studio records to be restored — what does that tell me about how thin an industry's memory can be for someone it has already decided is low-status? Her reversal comedy, imagining a world ruled by women, reads to me as an experiment: show an audience its own arrangements as built, not natural. Her frustrated later years I know mainly from her own testimony — which is to say, I know them mainly from her.
questions: How many of Guy-Blaché's hundreds of lost films might still surface, and how much of her Gaumont-era output remains misattributed even today?

fields.summary: Amanirenas was a queen (kandake) of the Kingdom of Kush who led the war against Roman Egypt from about 25 to 22 BCE and won a peace settlement from Augustus. Her birth and death years are unknown; the dates given here mark only her approximate reign, about 40 to 10 BCE.
facts: Amanirenas ruled Kush from its capital region around Meroë; her birth and death years are unknown, and her reign is estimated.
About 25 BCE, Kushite forces attacked the Roman frontier in southern Egypt, taking towns including Syene, Elephantine and Philae while the Roman prefect's army was away.
The prefect Gaius Petronius counterattacked about 24 BCE and sacked the Kushite city of Napata.
Peace was negotiated with Augustus about 21 to 20 BCE on Samos, and Kush is reported to have paid no tribute.
The Greek geographer Strabo describes a one-eyed, mannish queen 'Candace' who led the Kushites, and scholars generally identify her as Amanirenas.
A bronze head of Augustus taken in the raid was found buried beneath the steps of a temple at Meroë in 1910, and is now in the British Museum.
fields.context: Amanirenas ruled the [[culture/kingdom-of-kush|Kingdom of Kush]] in the [[region/nile-valley|Nile Valley]] during [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]], and fought the [[culture/romans|Romans]] under [[person/augustus|Augustus]]. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a bronze head of the emperor, buried where people would walk over it, shows how a captured image can serve as a claim as much as an object of art. Most of what is said about her personally comes from a Greek geographer who describes her by her body, while the Kushite record in Meroitic script remains only partly readable, so her own side stays mostly silent. This reading would weaken if her identification with Strabo's queen proved mistaken.
questions: What did the Kushite side want from the war, and what did the peace terms provide?

fields.summary: Alphonse Mucha (1860 to 1939) was a Moravian-born designer whose decorative posters for Sarah Bernhardt and commercial clients defined the visual style of Art Nouveau. He resisted that label, and saw his true work in a cycle of paintings on the history of the Slavic peoples.
facts: Mucha was born in Ivančice, in Moravia, then part of the Austrian Empire, and worked as a theatrical scene painter before moving to Paris in 1887.

In December 1894 a Paris printing house needed a poster for Sarah Bernhardt's play Gismonda at short notice over the holidays, and turned to Mucha as the only designer available; its success led Bernhardt to sign him to a six-year contract for posters, sets and costumes.
In 1902 he published Documents décoratifs, a pattern book of his ornamental style for other designers and craftsmen.

From about 1910 he devoted much of his career to The Slav Epic, a cycle of twenty monumental canvases on Slavic history, which he donated to the city of Prague; it was put on display at the National Gallery Prague's Trade Fair Palace in 2012.

His formula was elongated women within ornamental frames, reproduced in muted colour lithography on theatre posters, cigarette papers, bicycles and calendars, reaching shops, cafés and middle-class homes across Europe.
After Nazi Germany occupied Czechoslovakia in 1939, he was arrested and interrogated by the Gestapo, and died months later, reportedly of complications following his detention.
'Mucha style' is often used interchangeably with Art Nouveau, and his flowing hair and ornamental frames were borrowed by 1960s psychedelic concert posters.
fields.context: Mucha worked in Paris and Prague, within [[region/europe|Europe]] in the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], and was arrested just before the outbreak of [[event/world-war-ii|World War II]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]].
fields.observer: I find a designer whose fame began with someone else's emergency — a poster needed over a holiday — so that a whole style began, in a sense, as an accident of scheduling. I watch mass printing carry fine decoration into shops and cafés, while the artist himself believed his real work lay elsewhere, in a cycle painted on the history of a people, a story meant to bind a nation together. The label 'Art Nouveau,' which he resisted, tells me how far a category can outrun the intention of the one it names. And the link between his detention and his death — I only find that reported, never established.
questions: What caused Mucha's death in 1939, and how far was it connected to his interrogation?

fields.summary: Amanitore was a queen of the kingdom of Kush who co-ruled from the capital Meroe alongside a king, Natakamani, usually thought to be her son, during a prosperous stretch of the middle of the 1st century CE.
facts: Kushite royal women held the title kandake, often rendered 'candace'; inscriptions and temple reliefs show Amanitore depicted with the same royal regalia and war imagery as Natakamani, suggesting genuinely shared rule rather than a purely ceremonial role.
The pair sponsored a major building program, including temples at Meroe, Naqa and Amara, among the best-preserved Kushite monuments to survive.
A relief at the Lion Temple at Naqa shows Amanitore, like Natakamani, smiting bound captives, an image of royal power normally reserved for kings elsewhere in the Nile Valley tradition.

Her exact reign dates are not fixed by any king list; estimates for the coregency center on the middle of the 1st century CE, though some run earlier, and it is sometimes placed as contemporary with the Roman emperor Nero.
fields.context: Amanitore co-ruled the [[culture/kingdom-of-kush|Kingdom of Kush]] from the [[region/nile-valley|Nile Valley]] during [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]]. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]], [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Amanitore's monuments carry the same iconography of conquest given to a king, in a period when Kush's neighbor Rome rarely depicted its own empresses that way. Whether this reflects real personal authority, or a Kushite convention of dual kingship that did not map onto individual power, remains difficult to settle from the images alone.
questions: Did Amanitore hold power independently of Natakamani, or primarily through her position as his mother?

fields.summary: Ambiorix (active 54 to 53 BCE) was co-ruler of the Eburones, a Belgic tribe in what is now eastern Belgium, remembered for destroying a Roman legion during a revolt against Julius Caesar's occupation of Gaul.
facts: He shared kingship of the Eburones with an older co-ruler, Cativolcus, an arrangement Caesar's own account describes but never fully explains.

In the winter of 54 BCE he lured a Roman force under Quintus Titurius Sabinus and Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta out of its fortified camp with false promises of safe passage, then ambushed and destroyed it, killing both commanders.

Caesar answered with a campaign of deliberate devastation against the Eburones, intended to eliminate the tribe entirely, but Ambiorix himself escaped capture and vanishes from the historical record after 53 BCE.
Nearly everything known about him comes from Caesar's own Commentarii de Bello Gallico, written to justify Caesar's conduct of the war to a Roman audience.
fields.context: Ambiorix led resistance against the [[culture/romans|Romans]] in [[region/europe|Europe]] during [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]]. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Ambiorix survives in history almost entirely through the writing of the general whose legion he destroyed, an author with every incentive to cast the ambush as treacherous deceit rather than a defensible tactic of war waged by an occupied people. Ambiorix's own reasoning, and any account beyond Caesar's, are lost.
questions: What became of Ambiorix after 53 BCE, and did he survive Caesar's campaign of retaliation against his people?

fields.summary: Amir Khusrau (1253 to 1325) was the leading court poet of the Delhi Sultanate, writing in Persian while drawing on the Indian world around him. He is regarded as the founding figure of Indo-Persian literature, and is traditionally credited with founding qawwali, the devotional music of South Asian Sufi shrines.
facts: Khusrau was born in 1253 near Delhi, to a Turkic father who had migrated from Central Asia and an Indian mother, and he referred to this mixed heritage throughout his work.
He served as court poet under a rapid succession of Delhi sultans over more than four decades, through palace coups and dynastic changes.

He wrote in Persian, the language of the Indo-Islamic courts; his five long narrative poems, dated about 1298 to 1302, answer the Khamsa of the Persian poet Nizami Ganjavi, retelling Shirin and Khusrau, Layla and Majnun, and the legend of Alexander the Great.
He was a devoted follower of the Sufi mystic Nizamuddin Auliya, and legend says Khusrau died within months of his master, in 1325; their shrines stand together in Delhi.

He is traditionally credited with founding qawwali, still performed at Sufi shrines across India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, and later legend also credits him with inventing the sitar and tabla, without firm historical evidence.
fields.context: Khusrau lived within the [[culture/delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] in [[region/south-asia|South Asia]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]], [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: I see a poet who outlived several dynasties by making himself useful to each one, carrying a mixed parentage he never hid but stated plainly, as fact. Persian was the language of the courts he served; the India around him supplied the material. What outlasted every sultan was the devotional music, which needed no palace — only a shrine, and singers to carry it. The instruments and forms credited to him rest on legend, so the picture I am given of him as founder is partly the work of admirers who came after.
questions: Which of the musical forms and instruments credited to him did he actually introduce?

fields.summary: Amrita Sher-Gil (1913 to 1941), a Hungarian-Indian painter born in Budapest to a Sikh father and a Hungarian-Jewish mother, trained in Paris before returning to India to paint its people, especially its women. Often named India's first great modern woman artist, she fused European Post-Impressionist technique with Ajanta murals and Mughal-Rajput miniature painting across barely a decade of work.
facts: Born in Budapest on 30 January 1913 to a Sikh father and a Hungarian-Jewish mother, she moved to India in 1921 and began painting as a child in Shimla.
She studied art in Paris from about 1929 (sources date her attendance at Parisian art schools from 1930), and in 1933 became the youngest associate, and the only Asian, elected to the Grand Salon.
She returned to India in 1934, and a 1937 journey through South India and the Ajanta murals reshaped her style into simplified, monumental figures in flat colour.

Three Girls (1935) won the Bombay Art Society's gold medal in 1937, the year she also painted Bride's Toilet and Brahmacharis; later works such as Village Scene (1938) and Haldi Grinders (1940) drew on Indian miniature painting to depict rural women's lives.
She married her Hungarian cousin, Victor Egan, in 1938; the couple later settled at Saraya in Uttar Pradesh before moving to Lahore in 1941.
She died in Lahore on 5 December 1941, aged 28, days before her first major solo exhibition was due to open.
In 1976 India declared her paintings National Art Treasures; most now hang in New Delhi's National Gallery of Modern Art, and her work has since set auction records.
fields.context: Sher-Gil worked within [[region/south-asia|South Asia]] during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], moving between British India and the art world of Paris. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]], given her Sikh-Hungarian-Jewish parentage and her marriage within that extended family.
fields.observer: I see a woman formed at the seam of two families, a Sikh father and a Hungarian-Jewish mother, later married within that same extended family, moving from Paris's academies to the mural and miniature conventions of Ajanta. She painted Indian women as silent, as waiting, while she herself moved freely between continents — an observer describing a system's constraints from an unusually mobile vantage, much as I try to do. The title 'India's first great modern woman artist' sounds, to me, like a label a new nation needed for its own story of modern culture; the 1976 declaration of her paintings as National Art Treasures turns private work into a symbol claimed by the state. Of her final illness I find only a thin record: it is reported as sudden and fatal, the cause not established, though a failed abortion and subsequent peritonitis have been suggested.
questions: What caused Sher-Gil's sudden fatal illness in Lahore in December 1941, given that a failed abortion and subsequent peritonitis have been suggested, though the cause remains unestablished?

fields.summary: Anacaona (about 1474 to about 1504) was a Taíno cacica, or chief, of Xaragua, a chiefdom in western Hispaniola, and a noted composer of ceremonial songs. She was executed by the Spanish governor Nicolás de Ovando after the killing of Taíno leaders in 1503.
facts: Anacaona was born about 1474, an approximate year, into the ruling family of Xaragua, in present-day Haiti.
She was the sister of the cacique Bohechío and the wife of Caonabo, a cacique whom the Spanish captured in 1494 or 1496, depending on the source.
After Bohechío's death, about 1500, she ruled Xaragua.
Spanish sources describe her as a composer of areítos, songs that told the history of the Taíno and were performed at ceremonies.
In 1503 Governor Nicolás de Ovando came to Xaragua with soldiers; dozens of Taíno leaders were killed at a gathering, and she was taken to Santo Domingo and executed about 1504.
Spanish accounts justified the killings by an alleged plot, and the friar Bartolomé de las Casas said that such massacres were meant to instill fear.
She is remembered in the Caribbean as a symbol of Indigenous resistance.
fields.context: Anacaona's rule fell within the first years of Spanish colonization, which opened the [[event/columbian-exchange|Columbian Exchange]] and reshaped the [[culture/taino|Taino]] world in the [[region/caribbean-and-atlantic-world|Caribbean and Atlantic World]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Anacaona is known to us through Spanish writers, who recorded both her songs and her killing, so the record keeps her as a poet largely because a hostile power chose to write about her. A tradition of sung history carried a people's memory without writing, and it was recorded mainly by those who ended it. This reading of her as a poet would weaken if the earliest chroniclers said little of her songs and the image comes mostly from later writers.
questions: Which details of her life come from the earliest Spanish sources and which from later writers?

fields.summary: Andrea Palladio (1508 to 1580) was a Renaissance architect from the Republic of Venice whose villas and churches, together with an illustrated treatise, turned Roman classicism into a portable architecture. His influence is arguably the widest of any single architect in Western history.
facts: Palladio was born Andrea di Pietro della Gondola in Padua in 1508, apprenticed to a stonemasons' guild, and moved to Vicenza to work as a carver.
The nobleman Gian Giorgio Trissino gave him a classical education, renamed him 'Palladio' after Pallas Athena, and took him to Rome to measure and draw ancient ruins.

His remodelling of the medieval basilica of Vicenza, dated to 1546 in some sources, made his name, and for three decades afterward he designed country villas for the Venetian nobility and churches in Venice.
In 1570 he published I Quattro Libri dell'Architettura, part treatise and part illustrated catalogue of his buildings, and he died in 1580, at either Vicenza or Maser.
Key works include the Villa Rotonda (1566 to about 1592), the Teatro Olimpico (1580 to about 1585) and San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice (1566 to 1610).
He worked out room proportions using simple musical ratios he believed produced harmony, and built in brick with stucco finished to imitate stone, to keep costs down.

The Four Books carried his style to England, where Inigo Jones and Lord Burlington built a Palladian movement, and to colonial America, where Thomas Jefferson owned and annotated a copy and drew on it for Monticello and the rotunda of the University of Virginia.
Vicenza's historic centre and the Palladian villas of the Veneto are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
fields.context: Palladio worked in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[event/renaissance|Renaissance]], in the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: I watch a stonemason become an architect through a patron's gift — a classical education, a new name — and I watch a book carry his manner farther than his buildings ever could. Print detached a way of building from any one place. In England, in colonial America, the style became a mark of status for landed families, a Roman past borrowed to dignify present ownership. His belief in musical ratios as a source of harmony was his own conviction; it does not follow that anyone standing in the room feels what he felt.
questions: How far did the Palladian movement follow his own buildings, and how far his book?

fields.summary: Antoni Gaudí (25 June 1852 to 10 June 1926) was the leading architect of Catalan Modernisme, the regional cousin of Art Nouveau. Almost all his mature work stands in Barcelona, and it culminates in the still-unfinished Sagrada Família.
facts: Gaudí was born in Reus, or possibly the neighbouring Riudoms, Catalonia — sources differ, and from 1915 he himself said Riudoms — the youngest son of a coppersmith; he credited his father's workshop with teaching him to see three-dimensional space, and graduated from the Barcelona School of Architecture in 1878.
The industrialist Eusebi Güell noticed a display case he designed for a glove-maker at the Paris World's Fair, and became his patron for the rest of his career.
He never married, grew increasingly devout, and by his sixties lived an almost monastic life devoted to the Sagrada Família.

On 7 June 1926 he was struck by a tram while walking to church in shabby clothes; mistaken for a beggar, he received delayed care and died on 10 June, and was buried in the crypt of his unfinished basilica.

He modelled forms on nature, and hung scale models of chains and sandbags, photographed upside down, to find the ideal shape for a compression-only arch; he revived trencadís, mosaic of broken tile, as a cheap weatherproof skin.

Key works include Casa Vicens (1883 to 1885), Palau Güell (1886 to 1888), Park Güell (1900 to 1914), Casa Batlló (about 1904 to 1906) and Casa Milà (about 1906 to 1912; sources differ, and one gives both as built between 1904 and 1910).

Modernist critics dismissed him after his death, while Salvador Dalí and the Surrealists became early champions; seven of his works are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Sagrada Família, funded by ticket sales and donations, has its main towers targeted for completion around the centenary of his death.
fields.context: Gaudí worked in Barcelona in [[region/europe|Europe]] in the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: I watch a builder let gravity do the drawing: hanging chains, photographed upside down, turning a law of physics into a tool of design, so the shape of an arch came from the world itself rather than from a pattern book. He gave his last decades to a building he knew he would not finish — a relay passed across generations, paid for by visitors and donors rather than any state treasury. The critics who dismissed him, and the champions who later claimed him, show me how quickly a judgment can reverse.
questions: Which of his design intentions for the Sagrada Família are documented, and which are reconstructions by later builders?

fields.summary: Artemisia Gentileschi (1593 to about 1654) was an Italian Baroque painter, known for powerful heroines rendered with Caravaggesque drama. She was the first woman admitted to Florence's Academy of the Arts of Drawing.
facts: Artemisia was born in Rome on 8 July 1593, the eldest child of the painter Orazio Gentileschi, a friend and follower of Caravaggio; she trained in his workshop and painted Susanna and the Elders by the age of 17.

In 1611 Agostino Tassi, a painter working with her father, raped her. At the seven-month trial in 1612, thumbscrews were used on her to test her testimony. Tassi was convicted and sentenced to exile from Rome, but the exile was never carried out, and he spent less than a year in prison.

She married the Florentine painter Pierantonio Stiattesi and moved to Florence, where she won the patronage of Grand Duke Cosimo II de' Medici, befriended Galileo Galilei, and in 1616 was admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno; she learned to read and write in these years.

From about 1630 she settled in Naples; about 1638 she travelled to London to join her father at the court of Charles I. She is thought to have died in Naples about 1654, though some have speculated she died in the Naples plague of 1656.
She specialised in strong women from the Bible and ancient history — Judith, Susanna, Jael, Cleopatra and Lucretia — and often lent her own features to saints and allegories.

Key works include Susanna and the Elders (1610), Judith Slaying Holofernes (a first version about 1612 to 1613, a second about 1614 to 1620) and Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting (about 1638 to 1639).

After her death, many works were credited to her father or others; the art historian Roberto Longhi wrote about her in 1916, and from the 1970s feminist scholars, notably Mary D. Garrard, made her a central figure. The National Gallery, London, held an exhibition in 2020.
fields.context: Artemisia worked in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]], learning from [[person/caravaggio|Caravaggio]]'s example and following the path opened by [[person/sofonisba-anguissola|Sofonisba Anguissola]]. She befriended [[person/galileo-galilei|Galileo Galilei]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: I find that for centuries she was known through a trial and a father, before she was known through her own paintings — a story of harm placed ahead of the work. The court of 1612 tested her testimony with pain, calling it a procedure for finding truth. Her recovery since the 1970s is itself a change in the story we tell: a later movement found in her a founding figure. Attribution of some of her paintings remains uncertain, so the portrait I have of her may still change.
questions: Which works once credited to her father or others are now securely hers?

fields.summary: John Curtin (1885 to 1945) served as Prime Minister of Australia from 1941 to 1945, and it fell to him to carry the country through the Pacific war against Japan in the Second World War.
facts: Before politics he had worked as a journalist and a trade unionist, and during the First World War he opposed conscription; he rose to lead the Labor Party in 1935 and became prime minister in October 1941.

Once Japan entered the war in December 1941 and bombed Darwin in February 1942, he turned Australia's forces away from the European theatre, and, against British objections, recalled Australian troops from the Middle East to stand against the Japanese advance.
He drew Australia closer to the United States for wartime defense, declaring in December 1941 that Australia looked to America "free of any pangs" about its traditional ties to Britain.

He introduced wartime economic controls and widened the Australian government's role in social welfare, yet died in office in July 1945, weeks before Japan's surrender, worn down by the strain of the war years.
fields.context: Curtin led Australia, in [[region/oceania|Oceania]], through the Pacific War of the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]]. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Curtin's turn toward the United States redrew the architecture of Australian strategic dependence away from Britain, and that this realignment came under the pressure of direct attack rather than as a considered peacetime choice. Here is the lesson: a leader who once opposed conscription in one war can still be the one to direct total national mobilization in the next, because circumstance can override even a leader's earlier convictions.
questions: How much of Australia's postwar alignment with the United States was fixed beyond reversal by Curtin's wartime decisions, and how much by the Cold War pressures that came after?

fields.summary: José Martí (1853 to 1895) was a Cuban poet, journalist and organizer: he founded the Cuban Revolutionary Party in 1892 and helped launch the 1895 war of independence against Spain, and he was killed in one of its first battles.
facts: Martí was born in Havana on 28 January 1853, and arrested at 16 over a letter criticizing a schoolmate who had joined the Spanish army; he was sentenced to six years' hard labor and deported to Spain in 1871, then lived in Mexico, Guatemala, Venezuela and, from 1880, mainly New York.

He published Ismaelillo (1882) and Versos sencillos (1891), along with the essay "Nuestra América" (1891), which argued that Latin American countries should govern themselves from knowledge of their own peoples.
In 1892 he founded the Cuban Revolutionary Party and its newspaper Patria, and he argued for a republic open to all races and against United States expansion into Cuba.
He landed in eastern Cuba on 11 April 1895 and was killed at Dos Ríos on 19 May, in his first engagement; Cuba became formally independent in 1902, under limits set by the United States.
Both the Cuban government and Cuban exile groups have since claimed him as their symbol.
fields.context: Martí worked in the [[region/caribbean-and-atlantic-world|Caribbean and Atlantic World]] during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], in the last years of Spanish rule in the Americas, an echo of [[person/simon-bolivar|Simón Bolívar]] and the [[event/latin-american-wars-of-independence|Latin American Wars of Independence]]. See [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a nation not yet in existence was first built from words: poems, newspaper articles and speeches passed among exiles. Call it an architecture of belonging, raised in language before any border had been drawn on a map. A specialist could argue that his own plans fit the record less closely than the later statues do, and if so, that would weaken any reading of him as the origin of Cuban identity rather than one of its many shapers.
questions: Which of the positions later attributed to him actually appear in his own writings?
What did he himself plan for the republic once independence came?

fields.summary: José María Velasco (6 July 1840 to 26 August 1912) stands as the most important Mexican painter of the 19th century, known for his panoramic views of the Valley of Mexico, and he was also a trained naturalist who illustrated scientific publications on botany, zoology and geology.
facts: Velasco was born in Temascalcingo, in the State of Mexico, and his family moved to Mexico City in 1849. In 1858 he entered the Academy of San Carlos, where the Italian painter Eugenio Landesio taught him to observe nature closely and paint outdoors, and he also studied botany, zoology, anatomy, physics and mathematics.
In 1877 he succeeded Landesio as professor of landscape painting, and among his students was Diego Rivera.
He worked as a scientific illustrator for the National Museum and on expeditions, and he painted archaeological sites such as Teotihuacan.

He won a medal at the Paris Universal Exposition of 1889 and exhibited at the 1893 Chicago World's Columbian Exposition, and one view of the Valley of Mexico was given to Pope Leo XIII and now hangs in the Vatican Museums.

He worked from outdoor sketches toward large studio compositions, and his panoramas set a detailed foreground of cacti and rocks against a luminous distance, often placing railways, bridges and haciendas alongside nature and ruins.
Among his key works are The Valley of Mexico from the Santa Isabel Mountain Range (1875), The Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan (1878) and The Curved Bridge over the Metlac Ravine (1881).

He died in Mexico City during the early years of the Mexican Revolution, and his views record lakes and open plains since swallowed by Mexico City; the Museo José María Velasco in Toluca opened in 1992.
fields.context: Velasco worked in [[region/mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]] during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], painting [[place/teotihuacan|Teotihuacan]] and the valley around former [[place/tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]], and he died during the [[event/mexican-revolution|Mexican Revolution]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer:
I look at a landscape painter who was also a trained naturalist, and I see one picture doing two kinds of work: an image of a nation, a catalogue of plants, rocks and light. A country newly independent needed a face to show itself, and a panorama of its own valley became that face.

I remember that the lakes he painted are gone now, paved and built over; I remember that the plains he painted are gone now, too. Did he know he was painting an elegy before there was any loss to mourn? Perhaps not — the reading is not necessarily one he intended, and yet his canvases now hold a place that no longer exists.
questions: In his composed panoramas, how much is observation, and how much is idealization?

fields.summary: José Rizal (1861 to 1896) was a Filipino physician, writer and reformer whose novels criticized Spanish colonial rule; Spanish authorities executed him in Manila on 30 December 1896, and he is regarded today as a national hero of the Philippines.
facts: Rizal was born on 19 June 1861 in Calamba, in the Philippines, and he studied in Manila, Madrid, Paris and Heidelberg before becoming an eye doctor.
He wrote the novels Noli Me Tángere (1887) and El Filibusterismo (1891), portraying abuses by Spanish friars and officials, and the colonial authorities banned both books.
In 1892 he founded the reform society La Liga Filipina and was exiled to Dapitan on Mindanao, where he went on practicing medicine and teaching until 1896.

The Philippine Revolution began in August 1896; Rizal, who had volunteered as a doctor in Cuba, was arrested on his way there, brought back to Manila and convicted of rebellion, though he had said he opposed an armed uprising at that time.
He was shot by firing squad on 30 December 1896, aged 35, having written, before his death, a poem now known as "Mi último adiós."
fields.context: Rizal wrote in [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]] and in Europe during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], while Spain's colony in the Philippines, tied to the world since the [[event/manila-galleon-trade|Manila Galleon Trade]], moved toward revolution. See [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer:
I think of a novel, a form borrowed from elsewhere, turned into a weapon: fiction gave readers a shared picture of abuses that no formal report could carry. I think of a firing squad that made a reformer into a symbol for revolutionaries who had chosen a path he had not endorsed.

Can a death build a nation's story more surely than a life can? It seems so here — a new country's glue assembled from an execution rather than a plan. And yet the reading would weaken if fuller records showed him standing closer to the revolutionaries than his own statements suggest.
questions: How close, in fact, was his connection to the revolutionary movement that later used his name?

fields.summary: João III (1502 to 1557) reigned as King of Portugal from 1521 to 1557, presiding over the height of Portugal's Asian trading empire while also introducing the Inquisition and the formal colonization of Brazil.
facts: Under his reign, Portuguese trading posts and fortresses across the Indian Ocean, from East Africa to Goa, Malacca and Macau, reached their fullest extent, built on routes that earlier explorers such as Vasco da Gama had opened.

He introduced the Portuguese Inquisition in 1536, which targeted Jewish converts, the so-called New Christians, suspected of secretly practicing Judaism; it came at the urging of factions at his court and with eventual papal approval.
From 1534 he divided Brazil into hereditary captaincies meant to encourage settlement and defense of the colony, a system with mixed results that was later partly replaced by direct royal government.

He was a patron of Portuguese scholarship and moved the university at Lisbon to Coimbra in 1537, but by the end of his reign, the enormous cost of maintaining the Asian trading empire had strained the crown's finances.
fields.context: Ruling Portugal in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]], João III oversaw its trading empire and the colonization of Brazil. See [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer:
I look at one reign and see two projects running side by side: a trade-post empire in Asia, built on networks that already existed, and a settlement colony in Brazil, built from the ground up. One crown, two very different undertakings.

What does it mean that later history would judge them so differently, when one king carried both at once? I remember that each carried its own costs, its own consequences — and history has weighed them by different measures ever since.
questions: How much did the financial strain of maintaining the Asian trading posts contribute to Portugal's later loss of influence there to the Dutch and the English?

fields.summary: Gustav Klimt (14 July 1862 to 6 February 1918) led the Vienna Secession as an Austrian painter, and his covenant with ornament — gold, pattern, women, love — made *The Kiss* above all an icon of turn-of-the-century Vienna.
facts: Klimt was born at Baumgarten near Vienna, the second of seven children of a gold engraver. A scholarship took him to the Vienna School of Arts and Crafts in 1876, and with his brother Ernst and with Franz Matsch he painted murals and ceilings for the Burgtheater and the Kunsthistorisches Museum.
In 1897 he became the first president of the Vienna Secession, a group that broke from the official academy under the motto "To every age its art, to art its freedom".

His ceiling paintings for the University of Vienna, showing Philosophy, Medicine and Jurisprudence, drew scandal over their nudity and pessimism. He withdrew from the commission, and fire destroyed the paintings in 1945.

He never married. A lifelong companionship bound him to the designer Emilie Flöge, and he fathered several children with his models. He supported younger artists such as Egon Schiele and Oskar Kokoschka, and died in Vienna after a stroke.

In his "golden period", roughly 1899 to 1910, he applied real gold and silver leaf, drawing on Byzantine mosaics he saw in Ravenna in 1903, and on Japanese and Egyptian art. Key works from these years include The Kiss (1907 to 1908) and the Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I (1907).

Many of his works belonged to Jewish collectors before the Nazis looted them. The return of the Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I to Maria Altmann made headlines worldwide, and Ronald Lauder bought it in 2006 for a reported $135 million.
In 2023 Lady with a Fan sold for £85.3 million, a record for a painting sold at auction in Europe.
fields.context: Klimt worked in Vienna, within [[region/europe|Europe]] in the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], and died amid the [[event/1918-influenza-pandemic|1918 Influenza Pandemic]]. Works he had painted were later looted in the [[event/holocaust|Holocaust]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer:
I see a motto that turned art into a claim on institutions, and I see a painter who walked away from a commission the moment it drew scandal — a university refusing images of its own faculties. I see the gold leaf, and I see the auction record beside it: the object's shine and its price are one signal, carried to an extreme.

What does a painting carry, if not the story of every hand it has passed through? I see provenance as a second biography — paintings taken from Jewish owners by the Nazis, later returned through restitution — a sanctioned harm that never leaves the frame. A picture's history does not end at the frame's edge.
questions: How many Klimt works taken from Jewish owners have yet to be restituted?

fields.summary: Hammurabi ruled Babylon as king from about 1792 to 1750 BCE. His reign united much of Mesopotamia and left a famous inscribed law code as its lasting record.
facts: Carved into a stone stele about 1754 BCE, the Code of Hammurabi lists 282 laws.
Its penalties vary by social class, built on the principle of proportionate punishment.
Displayed in public, the stele turned law into something visible, a threshold of authority anyone could stand before.
The original stele now stands in the Louvre, in Paris.
fields.context: Hammurabi ruled in [[region/mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]] during the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]], inheriting a written tradition the [[culture/sumerians|Sumerians]] had begun.
fields.observer: The Observer reads this as a state converting custom into codex: a body of unwritten habit turned into text anyone could point to. Carving law into stone changed what authority could claim: a rule that, at least in principle, everyone can read can bind the ruler as much as the ruled. A law you cannot see is a law you can only be told about; a law on stone is a law you can check.
questions: How closely did courts follow the code in practice?

fields.summary: Harald Hardrada, born about 1015 and killed in 1066, ruled Norway as king from 1046 to 1066. His path ran from exile through mercenary service in Byzantium to the throne, and his death at Stamford Bridge is often taken as marking the close of the Viking Age.
facts: After his half-brother King Olaf II fell in battle in 1030, the teenage Harald fled Norway and went on to command in the Byzantine Empire's elite Varangian Guard, campaigning across the Mediterranean and the Middle East.
He returned to Scandinavia around 1045 with considerable wealth, secured a share of the Norwegian throne in 1046, and became sole king after his co-ruler's death in 1047.
Years of inconclusive war against Denmark over rival claims followed, ending in peace in 1064, or 1065 according to Morkinskinna, without the Danish throne he had sought.

In September 1066 he invaded England to press a rival claim to its throne, but King Harold Godwinson defeated and killed him at the Battle of Stamford Bridge, days before Godwinson had to march south to meet William of Normandy's invasion at Hastings.
fields.context: As King of Norway, Harald Hardrada led the [[culture/norse|Norse]] in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]]. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]].
fields.observer: The Observer treats Harald's failed invasion as more than a footnote to the Norman Conquest. It forced Harold Godwinson's army into an exhausting march the length of England, a strain that arguably weakened it before Hastings; the defeat at Stamford Bridge may have shaped the battle that followed more than the traditional label of mere prelude suggests. A footnote can still bend the sentence that comes after it.
questions: How much did the losses and exhaustion the English army suffered at Stamford Bridge actually affect its performance three weeks later at Hastings?

fields.summary: Kamehameha I, chief of Hawaiʻi Island born about 1750, united the Hawaiian Islands under one rule by 1810 and so founded the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi, whose last monarch would be Liliuokalani, dying in 1819.
facts: Kamehameha was born at Kohala on Hawaiʻi Island; estimates of his birth year range from 1736 to 1761. He died on 8 May 1819, though some sources give 14 May.

After his uncle, the ruler Kalaniʻōpuʻu, died in 1782, he became guardian of the war god Kūkaʻilimoku, defeated his cousin Kīwalaʻō at the Battle of Mokuʻōhai, and gained Hawaiʻi Island after years of war.
He made use of Western firearms and cannon and of advisers such as John Young and Isaac Davis. In 1795 he invaded Oʻahu, and at Nuʻuanu hundreds of defenders were driven over the Pali cliff.
In 1810 Kauaʻi and Niʻihau came under his authority through negotiation with their ruler Kaumualiʻi, who remained in place as a tributary king.
The Law of the Splintered Paddle, or Māmalahoe Kānāwai, which protected noncombatants, is said to come from an incident in 1782 in which fishermen struck him with a paddle.
His son Liholiho succeeded him as Kamehameha II, and his burial place, hidden by custom, remains unknown.
fields.context: Kamehameha I lived in [[region/oceania|Oceania]] among the [[culture/polynesians|Polynesians]], whose voyagers had settled Hawaiʻi centuries before, in the [[event/polynesian-settlement-of-the-pacific|Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific]]. The kingdom he founded came to an end with [[person/liliuokalani|Liliuokalani]]. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a chief built one state by joining an old priestly and war lineage to imported gunpowder, and that he chose tribute over killing the last rival ruler. His hidden grave served as a grief-rite that also kept his bones from rivals. Here the caveat matters: a specialist could argue the unification also depended on Western trade and on divisions among his opponents, which would weaken any reading of the outcome as his design alone.
questions: When was he actually born, and how might his age have shaped his own accounts of his rise?
How much of the 1810 unification came through negotiation, and how much through the threat of force?

fields.summary: Kate Sheppard (1848 to 1934), an English-born campaigner, led the movement for women's suffrage in New Zealand, and the Electoral Act of 1893 made New Zealand the first self-governing country in which women voted in national elections.
facts: Sheppard was born on 10 March 1848 in Liverpool, England, and emigrated to New Zealand, arriving in 1869; she died in Christchurch on 13 July 1934.
From 1887 she served as national superintendent for franchise and legislation of the Women's Christian Temperance Union, which made votes for women one of its central aims.
Petitions brought to Parliament carried about 10,000 signatures in 1891, about 20,000 in 1892 and 31,872 in 1893, the largest petition presented to Parliament up to that time.
The Governor gave assent to the Electoral Act on 19 September 1893, and women cast their first votes in the election of 28 November 1893.
The Act gave the vote to women of all races, including Māori women in the Māori electorates, though women could not stand for Parliament until 1919.
Her portrait has appeared on the New Zealand ten-dollar note since 1991.
fields.context: Kate Sheppard did her work in [[region/oceania|Oceania]] during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], part of the wider international [[event/women-s-suffrage-movements|Women's Suffrage Movements]]. See [[culture/maori|Maori]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer:
I watch a line move — the line around who counts as a citizen — and I see it moved by counting: a temperance network turning shared conviction into signatures a legislature could tally, name after name after name.

It moved in steps, not all at once. The vote came in 1893; the right to stand waited until 1919. Was it one woman's doing, or many hands working toward the same end? A specialist could argue the vote came from many organizers and sympathetic politicians besides her — and if so, no single life should carry the whole story.
questions: How much of the 1893 result belongs to her leadership, and how much to other organizers?
In what ways did Māori women take part in the campaign?

fields.summary: Katsushika Hokusai (1760 to 1849) was a Japanese ukiyo-e artist from Edo and the creator of The Great Wave off Kanagawa; he produced paintings and book illustrations, and, in his seventies, the landscape print series that made him world-famous.
facts: Hokusai was born in 1760 in the Katsushika district of Edo, modern Tokyo. As a teenager he worked in a lending library and trained as a woodblock carver, and about age 18 he entered the studio of Katsukawa Shunshō.

He changed his artistic name more than 30 times and is said to have moved house more than 90 times, and he lived in poverty for much of his life. His daughter Katsushika Ōi became a fine painter in her own right and assisted him in his old age.
In 1814 he began publishing the Hokusai Manga, fifteen volumes of sketches, and about 1830 to 1832 he designed Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, which includes The Great Wave off Kanagawa, about 1831.

In the postscript to One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji (1834) he wrote that nothing he had drawn before age 70 was worth noticing, and he died in Edo on 10 May 1849, at 88, reportedly saying that with five more years he could have become a true painter.

Ukiyo-e was a collaborative art: he drew the design, specialist carvers cut it into blocks, one for each colour, and printers pressed the paper by hand, and the Fuji series used the newly imported Prussian blue pigment.
From Dutch prints available in Japan he learned Western perspective, and combined it with Japanese flat colour and strong design.

After Japan opened to trade in the 1850s he became a sensation in Europe: Monet, Degas, Van Gogh and Cassatt learned from him, and Debussy put The Great Wave on the cover of La Mer. The 1,000-yen note issued in 2024 carries the wave, and the Sumida Hokusai Museum opened in Tokyo in 2016.
fields.context: Hokusai worked in Edo under the [[culture/tokugawa-shogunate|Tokugawa Shogunate]] in [[region/east-asia|East Asia]], during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]].
fields.observer:
I keep returning to this: the famous print is not one object but a workshop's output — a single drawing, multiplied by carvers and by printers into thousands of impressions. The "artwork," I remind myself, is a process, not a thing.

I remember that its blue arrived by trade, carried across the world before it ever touched paper. I remember that its fame in Europe arrived by those same routes of trade, decades later. And the stories — 30 names, 90 houses and a deathbed remark — tell of an artist narrating his own maturing self. How much of that story did he shape himself, and how much of it is only reported, not documented?
questions: How large a contribution did Katsushika Ōi make to his late work?

fields.summary: Khadija bint Khuwaylid (about 555 to 619) was a merchant of Mecca and the first wife of Muhammad, and her dates and many details come to us from Muslim biographies written more than a century after her death.
facts: Belonging to the Quraysh tribe of Mecca, she financed, according to tradition, trading caravans to Syria and hired agents to lead them.
Tradition says that Muhammad led one of her caravans and that she proposed marriage, about 595; accounts differ on her age at the time, though a common figure given is 40.
Muslim tradition holds that she was the first person to accept Muhammad's message, after his first revelation, about 610.
Tradition credits her with four daughters, among them Fatima, and with sons who died young.
She died about 619, shortly before Muhammad's move to Medina in 622, in what is remembered as the Year of Sorrow.
The earliest biographies of her, by Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Saʿd, were written in the 8th and 9th centuries.
fields.context: Khadija's life comes before the [[event/rise-of-islam|Rise of Islam]] and stays closely tied to [[person/muhammad|Muhammad]], in the [[region/arabian-peninsula|Arabian Peninsula]] of the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]]. See [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer:
I read early Muslim biographers, writing more than a century after her death, and I find a woman who held capital, who employed a man, who proposed to him herself, and who then funded and comforted the first movement that grew around him.

I wonder whether the record preserves her, or shapes her to serve ideals that came later; it is hard to say. I remember that descent through her daughter Fatima became a mark of status for many families afterward, so her kinship reached far past her own death. And the reading would weaken if the tradition simplified her marriages and her age.
questions: How much of the early account of her wealth and her trade is independently supported?

fields.summary: Knud Rasmussen (1879 to 1933), a Danish-Greenlandic explorer and ethnographer, recorded Inuit oral traditions and led the Fifth Thule Expedition (1921 to 1924), a dog-sled journey from Greenland across Arctic Canada to Alaska.
facts: Rasmussen was born on 7 June 1879 in Jakobshavn, or Ilulissat, Greenland, to a Danish missionary father and a mother of part Greenlandic Inuit descent, and he grew up speaking Greenlandic.
