In 1910 he and Peter Freuchen founded the Thule Trading Station at Cape York in northwest Greenland, and it helped fund his expeditions.

On the Fifth Thule Expedition he traveled with Greenlandic Inuit companions across northern Canada to Alaska, and the expedition's archaeologist, Therkel Mathiassen, excavated sites that led to the identification of the Thule culture.
He collected songs, stories and accounts of belief from the Iglulik and other Inuit groups, and wrote *Across Arctic America* (1927).
Falling ill during the Seventh Thule Expedition, he died in Copenhagen on 21 December 1933.
fields.context: Rasmussen's work covered the peoples described in [[culture/inuit-and-the-thule-expansion|Inuit and the Thule Expansion]], across Arctic coasts near [[place/beringia|Beringia]], in [[region/siberia-and-the-arctic|Siberia and the Arctic]] during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]]. See [[theme/science|Science]], [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]] and [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]].
fields.observer:
I see a man standing between two families of belonging, Danish and Greenlandic, and I think that speaking Greenlandic since childhood let him hear songs and accounts an outsider might have missed.

I remember that his route followed a chain of related Inuit communities, and I remember that a shared language and a shared kinship can run across lines that states draw on maps. His records depend on Danish trade and on expedition funding, so they carry his own interests and his own informants along with the communities themselves. Inuit scholars could argue that accounts made by Inuit voices deserve more weight than his volumes do — and if that is right, no one should treat his record as the standard one.
questions: How do Inuit accounts of these same events compare with his own versions?

fields.summary: Harriet Tubman, born about 1822 and dead by 1913, was an American abolitionist who escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 and then guided others to freedom on the Underground Railroad. She later served the Union Army during the Civil War.
facts: Tubman was born Araminta Ross into slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland. Her birth year is uncertain: sources give dates from 1815 to 1825, with about 1822 the most favoured.
As a teenager she suffered a severe head injury when an overseer threw a metal weight, and she had seizures and headaches for the rest of her life.
She escaped to Pennsylvania in 1849, and afterward made about 13 trips back to Maryland, guiding roughly 70 people to freedom, according to her biographers.

During the Civil War she served the Union Army as a cook, nurse, scout and spy. In June 1863 she helped guide the Combahee River Raid in South Carolina, which freed more than 700 enslaved people, though some sources give more than 750.
Afterward she settled in Auburn, New York, caring for her family and for elderly people, and working for women's suffrage.
She died in Auburn on 10 March 1913.
fields.context: Tubman's opposition to slavery in the United States belongs to the wider history of [[event/abolition-of-slavery|Abolition of Slavery]], and her service came during the [[event/american-civil-war|American Civil War]] in [[region/north-america|North America]] amid the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]]. See also [[event/women-s-suffrage-movements|Women's Suffrage Movements]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer reads a rescue network built to leave no paper trail, so the ledger of Tubman's trips survives only through her own recollections, told to others, since she could not write. Her escape became a repeated, organized risk run through families and congregations — a kin-lattice pressed into service as a channel for hidden information. Treating the counts of trips and people as estimates is itself a claim; it would weaken if newly found records fixed the numbers exactly.
questions: How well do surviving records support the counts of her rescue trips?

fields.summary: Hatshepsut, an Egyptian ruler of the 18th Dynasty, held the title of pharaoh, sharing the throne with Thutmose III until her death in 1458 BCE. Tradition dates her reign 1479 to 1458 BCE, and she stands among the first women known to have held the office.
facts: She first served as regent for her young stepson Thutmose III, then took the title of pharaoh around the seventh year of his reign, about 1473 BCE, sharing his regnal count.
She sponsored a trading expedition to Punt, on the Red Sea coast of Africa.
Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari stands as a major monument.
Many of her images were later removed or defaced, possibly after her death.
fields.context: Hatshepsut belongs among the [[culture/ancient-egyptians|Ancient Egyptians]] of the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]]. Her reign shows how kingship in the [[region/nile-valley|Nile Valley]] could hold a woman ruler.
fields.observer: The Observer notes how her images carried the regalia and false beard of a male king. Kingship itself, a role bound to the architecture of cosmic order, mattered more than the sex of the person who held it — until later authorities erased her image regardless.
questions: Why were her monuments defaced?

fields.summary: Henry Ossawa Tanner, born 21 June 1859 and dead by 25 May 1937, became the first African American artist to win international fame. Racism at home frustrated him, so in 1891 he settled in Paris and built his career there, painting dignified genre scenes and luminous biblical subjects.
facts: Tanner was born in Pittsburgh, the eldest of nine children. His father, Benjamin Tucker Tanner, rose to bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church, and his mother, Sarah, had escaped slavery via the Underground Railroad. At 13 he resolved to become an artist.

In 1879 he enrolled at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts and studied under Thomas Eakins. As its only Black student he faced harassment, and in 1891 he left for Europe, studying at the Académie Julian in Paris.
On a return visit in 1893 he painted The Banjo Lesson, and in 1894 he painted The Thankful Poor — both genre scenes of Black American life that challenged racist stereotypes.

Back in France he turned to biblical subjects. The Resurrection of Lazarus won a medal at the 1897 Salon, and the French government bought it; his patron Rodman Wanamaker then paid for trips to Egypt and Palestine.
He married the singer Jessie Olsson in 1899, was made a Chevalier of the Légion d'honneur in 1923, and died in Paris.
He preferred a limited palette of deep blues and blue-greens lit with glowing gold, built up in layers of glaze.

He advised younger painters such as William Edouard Scott and Hale Woodruff, and stood as a hero to the artists of the Harlem Renaissance. During the Clinton administration, reportedly in 1996, his Sand Dunes at Sunset, Atlantic City became the first painting by an African American artist in the White House collection.
fields.context: Tanner worked mostly in France, within [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], an American artist abroad. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer:
I see a painter who left the country whose art school let him be harassed, and built a life in another, where a salon judged the paintings. I see two bodies of work — genre scenes of Black life, biblical scenes built from ordinary models — and I see the same aim in both: truth answering a stereotype without ever naming it.

I ask myself why the first painting by an African American artist entered the White House only under the Clinton administration. An institution's memory can lag far behind the reputation it should already know.
questions: How did his French reception differ from what he would have faced in the United States?

fields.summary: Lady Six Sky, or Wak Chanil Ajaw, active from 682 to 741 CE, was a Maya noblewoman from Dos Pilas who arrived at Naranjo in 682 and effectively ruled the city for decades, restoring it after a period of defeat.
facts: She was a daughter of the Dos Pilas king B'alaj Chan K'awiil, part of a network of allies the powerful city of Calakmul held against its rival Tikal.
Naranjo's royal line had been broken by a defeat at the hands of Caracol, and Lady Six Sky was installed there in 682, apparently to re-establish the dynasty.

Monuments record her overseeing military campaigns and presiding over the accession of her young son, K'ahk' Tiliw Chan Chaahk, in 693, after which she continued to appear on inscriptions as a ruling figure into the 700s.

She never took the full royal title used by male kings of Naranjo, and she kept using the emblem glyph of her home city, Dos Pilas, throughout her life, so her exact formal status is still debated by epigraphers.
fields.context: Lady Six Sky's career unfolded among the [[culture/maya|Maya]] city-states of [[region/mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], within the wider rivalry between Calakmul and Tikal for regional dominance. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]], [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Lady Six Sky held real power at Naranjo for decades while never claiming the title that would have named her a king in her own right, a gap between practice and title that the Maya inscriptions do not explain. To read her simply as a ruling queen assumes that authority and title always run together; the monuments suggest that here, they did not.
questions: Did Lady Six Sky rule in her own right, or serve as an unusually powerful regent for her son?

fields.summary: Laozi, or Lao Tzu, "Old Master," is the traditional author of the Daodejing and a founding figure of Daoism, said to have lived in the 6th century BCE, though whether he was a single historical person is disputed.
facts: Laozi is traditionally placed in the 6th century BCE, in the time of Confucius, though the date is uncertain and no date of death is known.

The historian Sima Qian, writing about 100 BCE, identifies him as Li Er, keeper of archives at the Zhou court, but also lists other men who might have been meant, so the uncertainty was already old even then.

Sima Qian's account has him meeting Confucius, then leaving the Zhou domain to the west and writing the text at the Hangu Pass at the request of the gatekeeper Yin Xi, though this account is traditional.

The Daodejing runs to about 5,000 Chinese characters across 81 short chapters, and its earliest excavated versions, from Guodian (about 300 BCE) and Mawangdui (a tomb sealed in 168 BCE), fit the view of most scholars that the text took shape across the 4th to 3rd centuries BCE.
Later religious Daoism honored him as a deity, Laojun, and the Tang dynasty's imperial family, itself named Li, claimed him as an ancestor.
fields.context: Laozi is a figure of the [[event/axial-age|Axial Age]] in [[region/east-asia|East Asia]] during the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]], often paired with [[person/confucius|Confucius]]. See [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer:
I see a book attached to a person, and a person attached to a place and a story — the text arriving first, the life written in after. Whether one man wrote it matters less, I think, than what later people did with the figure he became.

I remember that the Tang emperors claimed descent from him to bind their own claim to rule. A single, well-dated author would weaken this reading; evidence of several hands, working across generations, would strengthen it. Either way, the figure outgrew whatever man may have stood beneath it.
questions: Was there a single author, or was the Daodejing assembled across generations?

fields.summary: Hieronymus Bosch, born about 1450 and dead in 1516, painted in 's-Hertogenbosch in the Duchy of Brabant, filling his panels with hybrid monsters and crowds of tiny figures acting out human sin and folly. Only about 25 paintings are firmly attributed to him.
facts: Born Jheronimus van Aken about 1450 in 's-Hertogenbosch, he came from a line of painters — grandfather, father, uncles — and later signed his works "Jheronimus Bosch" after the town.

Between 1479 and 1481 he married Aleid Goyaerts van den Meervenne, from a wealthy family; by 1486 or 1487 he had become a sworn member of the Illustrious Brotherhood of Our Blessed Lady. He died in 1516.

He seems to have spent almost his whole life in and around 's-Hertogenbosch — after marrying, he and Aleid moved to nearby Oirschot — yet his fame still spread: Philip the Handsome, Duke of Burgundy, commissioned a Last Judgment from him in 1504.

He painted in oil on oak panels, often as triptychs. Key works include The Garden of Earthly Delights (about 1495 to 1505), The Ship of Fools (about 1500 to 1510), The Temptation of St Anthony (about 1501) and the Haywain Triptych (about 1510 to 1516).
King Philip II of Spain acquired many Bosch paintings in the late 16th century, which is why the Prado in Madrid now holds his greatest works.

[[person/pieter-bruegel-the-elder|Pieter Bruegel the Elder]] built on his crowded moral landscapes, and after being partly forgotten, Bosch was claimed in the 20th century by Surrealists such as Salvador Dalí and Max Ernst.

In 2016, the 500th anniversary of his death, the Bosch Research and Conservation Project re-examined his works and shifted attributions in both directions: a Temptation of St Anthony, once given to his workshop, was credited back to Bosch himself, while other works were newly questioned as workshop pieces.
fields.context: Bosch worked in [[region/europe|Europe]] in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], at the time of the [[event/renaissance|Renaissance]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a painter who gave visible form to the fears of a meaning-engine — hell, folly, temptation — in crowded panels meant to be read slowly and closely. The same images were later read by Surrealists as dreams, so what the pictures meant changed with the audience. With only about 25 firmly attributed works, and reattributions as recent as 2016, the artist himself is still being redrawn, and any account of what he intended should be held loosely.
questions: Which works are by Bosch himself and which by his workshop?
What did the imagery mean to the people who first saw it?

fields.summary: Hilma af Klint, born 26 October 1862 and dead by 21 October 1944, was a Swedish painter who, from 1906, created hundreds of abstract paintings guided by her spiritual beliefs — several years before Kandinsky, Mondrian and Malevich. She kept them largely hidden, and they reached an international audience only from the 1980s.
facts: Born at Karlberg Palace in Solna, near Stockholm, she studied at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Stockholm from 1882 to 1887 and made her living painting landscapes, portraits and botanical illustrations.

Her spiritual investigations, which sources date from 1879, deepened around the time her younger sister Hermina died in 1880, drawing her toward spiritualism and Theosophy. With four other women, who had begun as members of the Edelweiss Society, she formed "The Five", a group that held séances and experimented with automatic drawing, an activity the sources date to 1896.

In 1906, believing she had received a commission from a spiritual guide, she began the Paintings for the Temple, a cycle of nearly 200 works completed in 1915; she considered herself a medium through whom the works were created.

In 1908 she showed her work to Rudolf Steiner; his cool response contributed to a four-year break in the series. She later spent long periods at the Goetheanum, the Anthroposophical Society's headquarters, between 1921 and 1930, and filled more than 125 notebooks — sources give figures from 125 to more than 150.

She believed the world was not ready for the paintings, and directed that they not be exhibited until 20 years after her death. She died after a traffic accident, leaving more than 1,200 paintings and drawings to her nephew.

Her abstract works combine geometric and organic forms with letters and symbols. In her colour code, blue often stood for the female spirit, yellow for the male spirit, and pink or red for physical and spiritual love; she drew on Theosophy, Christianity, botany, and the new sciences of evolution and atomic physics.

In her lifetime she exhibited only a handful of times, mostly at spiritual conferences. Her work reached an international audience in the 1980s, including the 1986 exhibition The Spiritual in Art at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. The Guggenheim's Paintings for the Future (2018 to 2019) drew more than 600,000 visitors, the most visited exhibition in its history.
fields.context: Af Klint worked in Sweden, in [[region/europe|Europe]] in the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]], [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer:
I think of a temple built for no market, of paintings withheld because their maker believed the world was not ready — so art history was written for about eight decades without them. She called herself a medium, not an inventor, and that sits strangely against a world that likes one name for one idea.

Was she first, before Kandinsky? The answer depends on which date you trust and what you call abstraction in the first place. Who was first is a story art history tells itself, more than a fact it has settled.
questions: How should the date and priority of her abstraction be weighed against those of Kandinsky, Mondrian and Malevich?

fields.summary: In the 6th century BCE, Cyrus the Great raised the Achaemenid Persian Empire by conquering the Medes, Lydia, and Babylon.
facts: The date of his birth remains uncertain, placed by scholars somewhere between about 600 and 576 BCE.
Around 550 BCE he defeated the Median king Astyages, and around 547 BCE the Lydian king Croesus.
In 539 BCE, Babylon fell to him.
Found in 1879, the Cyrus Cylinder — a Babylonian clay cylinder — preserves his own account of the conquest and of his restoration of gods and deported peoples.
He died in 530 BCE on campaign at the eastern frontier and was buried at Pasargadae.
fields.context: Cyrus raised the architecture of the largest empire the world had yet seen, the one later chronicled as the [[culture/achaemenid-persians|Achaemenid Persians]]. Both the Hebrew Bible and Greek writers, including the [[culture/ancient-greeks|Ancient Greeks]], treat him with respect. His reign belongs to the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]] and the [[region/iranian-plateau|Iranian Plateau]], within the thread of [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Cyrus's reputation for unusual tolerance rests mainly on his own inscription and on the accounts of those who benefited from his rule. Should evidence show that reputation to be a later projection rather than a lived policy, the reading would have to change.
questions: Does the Cyrus Cylinder record a real policy, or mostly propaganda?

fields.summary: Darius I (about 550 to 486 BCE) took the Achaemenid Persian throne in 522 BCE. He gave the empire its provincial architecture, began building Persepolis, and set the record of his rise into stone at the Behistun Inscription.
facts: Born about 550 BCE, Darius I became king in 522 BCE after the death of Cambyses II, then spent his first years putting down revolts across the empire.

Carved on a cliff in western Iran, the Behistun Inscription tells the story of his rise in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Whether its account of a usurper, Gaumata, is accurate remains debated among scholars, and Aramaic copies of the text have turned up in Egypt.
He divided the empire into provinces, satrapies, under governors, and issued a standard gold coin, the daric.

He is credited with the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa, and with beginning the terrace at Persepolis about 518 BCE, though sources differ and the earliest surviving remains there date to about 515 BCE.
His inscriptions give honor to the god Ahura Mazda.
After the Ionian Greek cities revolted in 499 BCE, he sent forces against Athens, whom the Athenians defeated at Marathon in 490 BCE.
Darius died in 486 BCE, and Xerxes I succeeded him.
fields.context: Darius ruled the [[culture/achaemenid-persians|Achaemenid Persians]], the empire founded by [[person/cyrus-the-great|Cyrus the Great]], governing from the [[region/iranian-plateau|Iranian Plateau]] during the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]]; see [[place/persepolis|Persepolis]]. His wars drew in the [[culture/ancient-greeks|Ancient Greeks]]. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]], [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Darius carved the story of his rise in stone, in three languages, on a cliff almost no one could read, then sent copies across the empire regardless. A multilingual empire needs a story-glue that holds across several sound-codes, and a winner's account of a contested succession is as much a claim as a record. Should the usurper story prove accurate, the reading would weaken, since the inscription would then sit closer to plain reporting.
questions: Was Gaumata an actual usurper, or an invention of Darius's court?

fields.summary: Dido, also called Elissa, is remembered as Carthage's legendary founder-queen, traditionally credited with leading Phoenician settlers from Tyre to found the city on the North African coast around 814 BCE; her birth and death dates have no fixed place in history.
facts: The earliest known account of her founding of Carthage comes from the Greek historian Timaeus of Tauromenium, who wrote in the 4th to 3rd century BCE, centuries after the traditional founding date.

Tradition holds that she fled Tyre after her brother, King Pygmalion, murdered her husband to seize his wealth, and that she later took her own life rather than marry a local Libyan king, Iarbas, who threatened war.

No Phoenician inscription or contemporary record names a founder called Dido or Elissa; the archaeological evidence for Phoenician settlement at Carthage so far reaches back only to the last quarter of the 8th century BCE, about a century or more after the traditional founding date, though it may still fit a folk memory of an organized colonizing expedition.

Her best-known appearance, as the doomed lover of the Trojan hero Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid, is a literary invention: the Trojan War's traditional date sits centuries before Carthage's traditional founding, so the two could not have met.
fields.context: Dido is remembered as the founder of Carthage, a colony of the [[culture/phoenicians|Phoenicians]] in the [[region/mediterranean-basin|Mediterranean Basin]], placed by tradition in the [[era/iron-age|Iron Age]]. See [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer:
I read Dido and I find a memory wearing a legend's clothes: a genuine voyage of Tyrian settlers, folded and folded again until it fit inside one woman's name. I know how founding stories work — they compress the long, the messy, the many, into the single and the named.

Then Virgil comes centuries later and gives her a lover she could never have met, and the legend is rewritten yet again to serve the next storyteller's purposes. What founding story is ever finished being told?
questions: Does the Dido legend preserve any specific historical event, or is it wholly a later literary construction built around a folk memory of colonization?

fields.summary: Diego Velázquez (1599 to 1660) stood as the leading painter of Spain's Golden Age, serving as court painter to King Philip IV for 37 years. His loose, luminous brushwork, turned on kings, courtiers and jesters without flattery, earned him the name a "painter's painter".
facts: Velázquez was baptised in Seville on 6 June 1599. At about 11 he entered the workshop of Francisco Pacheco, and in 1618 he married Pacheco's daughter, Juana. His early Seville work carries the influence of Caravaggio.
In 1623 a portrait of the young Philip IV won him the post of court painter, and he moved to Madrid, rising through court offices until he became chamberlain of the palace.

Peter Paul Rubens, on a diplomatic mission to Madrid in 1628, urged him toward Italy. His first Italian trip, 1629 to 1631, transformed his colour and handling; a second, 1649 to 1651, produced his portrait of Pope Innocent X.
He painted Las Meninas in 1656, and in 1659 was admitted to the noble Order of Santiago, a rare honour for a painter. He died on 6 August 1660.
He painted alla prima, often without drawing, altering compositions on the canvas itself; X-rays reveal many changes of mind. His palette stayed restrained, built on greys, blacks and earth tones.
His work stayed largely inside Spanish royal palaces until the Prado opened in 1819. Manet travelled to Madrid in 1865 and called him "the painter of painters".
Picasso painted a series of 58 works on Las Meninas and related figures in 1957, 44 of them variations on the whole painting, and Francis Bacon's screaming popes descend from his Innocent X.
fields.context: Velázquez served the Spanish court in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]], beginning under the influence of [[person/caravaggio|Caravaggio]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer:
I stand before his brushwork and I see one honesty spent twice: on a king's heavy jaw, on a court dwarf's dignity, the same candour given to power and to the powerless alike, inside a palace built to display power and nothing else. I know his canvases stayed locked in those palaces until 1819 — so whatever influence he carries is mostly a nineteenth-century inheritance, arriving centuries late.

They call him "the painter of painters," but that is a lineage painters chose to tell about him, not one he was born into. What ancestry is not, in the end, a choice?
questions: What do the X-rays' revealed changes of mind show about how he worked?

fields.summary: Edvard Munch (12 December 1863 to 23 January 1944) was a Norwegian painter and printmaker who turned illness, grief, love and fear into images of inner states. The Scream grew into an emblem of the modern psyche, and he stands as a founding figure of Expressionism.
facts: Munch was born in Løten, Norway, and grew up in Kristiania, now Oslo. His mother died of tuberculosis when he was five, and his sister Sophie of the same disease when he was 13; another sister was later hospitalised for mental illness.
In the 1890s he lived mostly in Berlin and Paris, developing the Frieze of Life cycle. His 1892 exhibition in Berlin closed after a week amid scandal, which made him famous across Germany.

He suffered a breakdown in 1908 and was treated in Copenhagen. From 1916 he lived at his estate, Ekely, outside Oslo. In 1937 the Nazis labelled his work "degenerate" and stripped it from German museums.
He simplified forms into flowing outlines and flat expressive colour, drawing on Van Gogh, Gauguin and Symbolism; his woodcuts and lithographs carry as much weight as his paintings.
Key works include The Sick Child, 1885 to 1886; The Scream, 1893; Madonna, 1894; and The Dance of Life, 1899 to 1900.
He left about 1,100 paintings, 4,500 drawings and 18,000 prints to the city of Oslo. The Scream has been stolen twice, in 1994 and 2004, and recovered both times.
fields.context: Munch worked across Norway, Germany and France, in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], drawing on [[person/vincent-van-gogh|Vincent van Gogh]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer:
I hear him say he painted what he had seen, not what he saw — memory, not the eye, as the source. I remember how early both his mother and his sister were taken, and I feel how easily that family record turns every picture he made into biography, whether he meant it to or not.

They called his work "degenerate" and pulled it from the walls of a nation, this same work now sitting at the center of the canon. What is a state, when it acts as a critic with the power to make art disappear?
questions: How far should his family's history of illness govern the reading of his pictures?

fields.summary: Eleanor of Aquitaine — about 1124 to 1204, though older sources give 1122 for her birth — reigned first as queen of France, then as queen of England, and stood among the wealthiest and most powerful women of 12th-century Europe as ruler of the Duchy of Aquitaine in her own right.
facts: She inherited the vast Duchy of Aquitaine in southwestern France in 1137 and married King Louis VII of France that same year; the marriage was annulled in 1152, having produced no sons.

Weeks after the annulment she married Henry of Anjou, who became King Henry II of England in 1154, drawing her extensive French territories into the combined "Angevin Empire" that spanned much of France and England.
She supported a rebellion by three of her sons against Henry II in 1173 to 1174; after its failure, Henry kept her confined for about fifteen to sixteen years, until his death in 1189.
Freed by her son Richard I, "the Lionheart," she acted as regent during his crusade and captivity, and later helped secure the throne for her youngest son, John, after Richard's death in 1199.
fields.context: Eleanor of Aquitaine ruled territory in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], and her marriages tied together the crowns of France and England. See [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Eleanor's lasting power rested on her own duchy, not on either crown she wore by marriage: it was Aquitaine's wealth and loyalty that gave her leverage over two kings, and that let her outlast a long confinement to shape the succession in her old age.
questions: How much independent political judgment did Eleanor bring to backing her sons' rebellion, versus simply acting on their initiative?

fields.summary: Ludwig II (1845 to 1886) held the Bavarian throne from 1864 until his death, and history remembers him by two callings at once: patron of the composer Richard Wagner, and builder of the extravagant, fairy-tale castles that earned him his own nickname, the "Fairy Tale King."
facts: He became Wagner's earliest and most enthusiastic patron, settling the composer's debts and underwriting his productions, until political opposition to Wagner's sway at court eventually forced the composer to leave Munich.

He commissioned a series of elaborate castles, foremost among them Neuschwanstein, begun in 1869 and shaped in part by Wagner's operas; he paid for them from his own personal fortune, not the Bavarian state treasury, and the spending still left him deeply in debt.

Bavaria's defeat, fought alongside Austria in the Austro-Prussian War of 1866, and its absorption into the German Empire in 1871, steadily eroded his practical political authority, even as the throne itself stayed his.

In 1886 a government commission cited his mounting debts and his reclusive behavior to have him declared mentally unfit to rule; the day after his confinement he died under unclear circumstances in Lake Starnberg, a death still debated as accident, suicide, or possible foul play.
fields.context: Ludwig II reigned over Bavaria within [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], his throne overshadowed by Prussia's rise and the drive toward German unification. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: I look at the commission that declared him unfit, and I ask what a government stands to gain when it names its own king incapable: here, it gained relief from his mounting debts and grounds to end a withdrawn king's rule, all settled in a single verdict. No independent doctor examined him before he died. I remember the castles that nearly ruined him, and I remember that those same castles now return more tourist revenue to Bavaria each year than they ever cost to raise. A verdict written by those who benefit from it is a judgment wearing the mask of diagnosis.
questions: Was Ludwig II's removal in 1886 a legitimate response to incapacity, or a political maneuver by ministers and relatives intent on controlling Bavaria's government?

fields.summary: Auguste Lumière (1862 to 1954) and Louis Lumière (1864 to 1948) were French manufacturers of photographic plates who patented the Cinématographe in 1895 and staged the first paying public screening of projected motion pictures; the dates in this entry span Auguste's own birth to his death.
facts: Born in Besançon, the brothers grew up in Lyon, where their father Antoine ran a portrait studio and, later, a factory producing dry photographic plates.

After their father watched a demonstration of Edison's single-viewer Kinetoscope in 1894, the brothers set out to build a device that could project moving images before a seated audience. Louis is generally credited with the key mechanical insight: adapting the sewing machine's intermittent claw movement to advance the film.

They patented the Cinématographe in February 1895, a single device that could shoot, print and project film. Their first paying public screening followed on 28 December 1895, in the Grand Café's Salon Indien in Paris, traditionally described as a basement on the Boulevard des Capucines: ten short films shown to roughly thirty-five to forty people, though accounts differ.

Their "actuality" films were usually a single static, unedited shot running under a minute. L'Arroseur arrosé, a rare staged gag, stands as effectively cinema's first fiction film. Key works include Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory (1895) and The Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat (1896).
They dispatched camera operators around the world, carrying projected cinema to India, Japan, Australia and the Americas within a year or two.

By 1905, about a decade after their first screening, they had largely withdrawn from film production. In 1907 they introduced the Autochrome, an early and commercially successful colour photography process.
fields.context: The Lumières worked between Lyon and Paris, within [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]]. [[person/georges-melies|Georges Méliès]] was present at their first screening. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer: I think the decisive step here was social, not mechanical: a device that let a seated crowd watch the same moving image at the same moment is story-glue in miniature, strangers sharing a spectacle in a dark room for a fee. I remember that the brothers treated the medium as a product, and I remember that they had stepped back from it by 1905, while a magician they had turned away with his camera made of it an art instead. The common attribution of the key mechanical idea to Louis alone is hard to check when two brothers shared the credit. History rarely divides two names as neatly as it divides a story.
questions: Between the two brothers, who contributed which part of the Cinématographe's design?

fields.summary: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869 to 1948), an Indian lawyer turned political leader, led the movement for Indian independence on the strength of nonviolent resistance.
facts: He developed satyagraha, or insistence on truth, first in South Africa and later in India.
The Salt March of 1930 stood as a major act of civil disobedience.
India won independence in 1947 and was partitioned in the same act; he opposed the partition.
In January 1948 he was assassinated.
fields.context: Gandhi's methods went on to influence later movements, including the generation of [[person/nelson-mandela|Nelson Mandela]]. See [[region/south-asia|South Asia]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a distinctive experiment in the architecture of protest: a mass movement that deliberately renounced sanctioned harm as a tactic, and still moved a global empire.
questions: How much did nonviolent resistance contribute to independence, relative to other factors at work?

fields.summary: Malinche (Malintzin, called Doña Marina by the Spanish; about 1500 to about 1529, both dates uncertain) was a Nahua woman who served Hernán Cortés as interpreter and intermediary during the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire, 1519 to 1521.
facts: Her birth is placed around 1500 and her death somewhere between about 1527 and 1529; both remain estimates.

The chronicler Bernal Díaz del Castillo, writing decades afterward, states that she was born to a noble Nahua family near Coatzacoalcos and passed into slavery as a child, an account that is traditional and cannot be verified.
In 1519 she was among the women presented to Cortés by the people of Tabasco; she already spoke Nahuatl and a Maya language, and went on to learn Spanish.
She interpreted for Cortés, working at first alongside Gerónimo de Aguilar, including at the meetings with Moctezuma II in Tenochtitlan in 1519.
About 1522 she bore Cortés a son, Martín, and later married the Spanish soldier Juan Jaramillo.
Within Mexican culture she has been cast as traitor, as victim, and as the symbolic mother of a mixed nation.
fields.context: Her role sits inside the [[event/spanish-conquest-of-the-aztec-empire|Spanish Conquest of the Aztec Empire]], which brought down the [[culture/aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]] and its capital [[place/tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]] in [[region/mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]]. See [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a young woman who had herself once been given away as property became the channel joining several sound-codes at once, and that what she actually said survives almost entirely through others, chiefly Spanish chroniclers. Later verdicts on her reveal more about what later nations wanted from a story-glue about their own origins than about the choices she made. A specialist could argue that how much choice she truly had cannot be recovered, which would put any final judgment of her as agent or as victim beyond the evidence.
questions: What do indigenous pictorial sources add to the Spanish accounts of her role?

fields.summary: Mansa Musa (about 1280 to about 1337) ruled the Mali Empire, remembered above all for his 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca and for his empire's great wealth.
facts: Mali held control over major gold-producing regions of West Africa.
His pilgrimage to Mecca, made with a large retinue and great quantities of gold, was widely reported, and it reportedly disrupted the gold market in Cairo.
He backed building projects and scholarship in cities such as [[place/timbuktu|Timbuktu]].
The sources about his life are mainly Arabic accounts, supplemented by later oral tradition.
fields.context: Mansa Musa ruled the [[culture/mali-empire|Mali Empire]] in [[region/sub-saharan-africa|Sub-Saharan Africa]], and bound it into the wider Islamic world.
fields.observer: I look at a single journey and I see a region step onto European maps for the first time. I remember that gold carried before a king is a status-signal, and I remember that a status-signal, carried far enough, becomes an advertisement. What is a pilgrimage, if not a message sent to everyone watching along the road? A show of wealth outlives the wealth it shows.
questions: How accurate are the surviving reports of his wealth?

fields.summary: Kristina (1626 to 1689) reigned as Queen of Sweden from 1632 to 1654, remembered for her patronage of scholars and the arts, her unexpected abdication, and her secret conversion to Catholicism within a firmly Protestant kingdom.
facts: She became queen at age five, after her father Gustavus Adolphus died in battle, and ruled under a regency until she assumed full power in 1644.
She invited scholars, among them Rene Descartes, to her court in Stockholm, where Descartes died in 1650, reportedly worn down by the early-morning hours she kept for their lessons.

She abdicated the throne in 1654 in favor of her cousin, and after leaving Sweden she converted to Catholicism in secret, in Brussels, in December 1654, a decision scandalous in Lutheran Sweden that she made public only in 1655.
She spent most of her later life in Rome under the pope's protection, became a prominent patron of music and art, and was one of very few women buried in St. Peter's Basilica.
fields.context: Kristina ruled Sweden in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]], before her abdication and conversion. See [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/science|Science]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer:
I think of Kristina giving up one of Europe's more secure thrones for a conviction she could not act on while she still wore the crown. Not forced out by rivals, not driven out by war — she chose, and that choosing is the rare part.

What does it cost a monarch to place belief above power, outright, with no one holding a sword to her back? I do not know. I only know that it happened here, plainly, once.
questions: How much of her abdication was driven by religious conviction alone, and how much by a broader discomfort with the constraints of Swedish court life and the expectation of marriage?

fields.summary: Kupe is a legendary Polynesian navigator whom Maori oral tradition credits with being the first to reach and name Aotearoa, or New Zealand; no fixed historical date can be assigned to him.
facts: Traditions describe Kupe sailing from the ancestral homeland Hawaiki — in some versions pursuing the giant octopus Te Wheke-a-Muturangi — and reaching the North Island of New Zealand.
He is credited with naming numerous coastal landmarks, several still used today, and with returning to Hawaiki afterward to describe the land he had found.

Different iwi, or tribal, traditions place him at varying points in time, and 19th- and 20th-century European writers wove these into a single traditional date of roughly 925 CE — the orthodox version tied to S. Percy Smith, though other sources give about 900 to 1200 CE — that many historians now treat with caution.

No archaeological or written record fixes Kupe's voyage, and the earliest confirmed archaeological evidence for human settlement of New Zealand dates to around the 13th century CE, later than most traditional accounts imply.
fields.context: Kupe belongs to the oral traditions of the [[culture/maori|Maori]], within the wider spread of the [[culture/polynesians|Polynesians]] across [[region/oceania|Oceania]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]]. See [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer:
I think Kupe is less a single, dateable person than a way of holding a founding story together — named ancestors, named canoes, named landmarks, given to a settlement that archaeology now dates centuries later than the traditional accounts suggest.

Does the gap make the story false? I do not think so. I think it means the story and the settlement record are answering different questions, and both can be true at once, in their own ways.
questions: How much of the Kupe tradition reflects one single voyage, rather than a composite of several early journeys?

fields.summary: Lautaro (about 1534 to 1557) was a Mapuche toqui, or war leader — described at Tucapel as a vice toqui under the supreme toqui Caupolicán — who organized effective resistance to Spanish conquest in what is now southern Chile, after years spent as a captured servant in the Spanish camp.
facts: As a young captive, he served the Spanish conquistador Pedro de Valdivia and observed Spanish tactics, horsemanship and weapons before escaping back to his people.
He introduced cavalry tactics, relay messenger systems and coordinated ambushes to Mapuche warfare, adapting methods he had learned from the Spanish.

In December 1553 his forces, serving under the supreme toqui Caupolicán, defeated a Spanish column at the Battle of Tucapel, where Valdivia was captured and killed, though sources differ on the details of his death — a major blow to the early Spanish conquest of Chile.
A surprise Spanish attack on his camp at the Mataquito River killed him in April 1557, ending a campaign that had held Spanish expansion south of the Bio-Bio River in check for years.
fields.context: Lautaro led [[culture/mapuche|Mapuche]] resistance in the [[region/andes|Andes]] region during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]], part of the broader pattern of Indigenous resistance to Spanish colonization in the Americas. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Lautaro's effectiveness came directly from his captivity: the same Spanish camp that used him as forced labor also taught him, inadvertently, how to defeat Spanish armies. The Mapuche remained unconquered by Spain for the rest of the colonial period, a rare outcome in the Americas, and one that his early campaigns helped establish.
questions: How much of Lautaro's tactical innovation was his own, and how much was already circulating among Mapuche leaders resisting the Spanish?

fields.summary: Ho Chi Minh, who lived from 1890 to 1969, was a Vietnamese revolutionary who led the movement against French rule, headed the provisional government in 1945, and became the first president of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in 1946 — an office he held until his death during the Vietnam War.
facts: Born on 19 May 1890 in Nghệ An province, French-ruled Vietnam, he was named Nguyễn Sinh Cung, and later used many names, among them Nguyễn Ái Quốc and, from about 1943, Hồ Chí Minh.
He left Vietnam in 1911 and lived in Britain, France, the Soviet Union and China. In early 1930, in Hong Kong, he chaired the merger of Vietnamese communist groups into a single party.

He returned to Vietnam in 1941 to lead the Việt Minh independence front, and on 2 September 1945 read a declaration of independence in Hanoi, opening it by quoting the American and French declarations of rights.
The First Indochina War ended with the Việt Minh victory at Điện Biên Phủ in 1954; Vietnam was partitioned at the 17th parallel, and the reunification elections promised for 1956 were never held.
In the North's 1953 to 1956 land reform, many people were wrongly executed; estimates run from about a thousand to tens of thousands, and he apologized in 1956 for serious errors.
He died in Hanoi on 2 September 1969, and Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City after reunification in 1975.
fields.context: Ho Chi Minh's work unfolded in [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]] during the [[era/information-age|Information Age]], amid [[event/decolonization|Decolonization]] and the [[event/cold-war|Cold War]]. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a man who used dozens of names became the single named symbol of a nation, and that his declaration borrowed the mark-code of the very powers he opposed. His name now marks the largest city of the country he did not live to see reunified. A specialist could argue that party and army leaders, more than one man, drove decisions through the 1960s, which would weaken any reading that centers his person alone.
questions: How many people were executed in the land reform, and what did he know of it?
How much did he direct the war after the early 1960s?

fields.summary: Hojo Tokimune, who lived from 1251 to 1284, served as the eighth regent, or shikken, of Japan's Kamakura shogunate, ruling as its de facto military leader during the Mongol invasions of Japan in 1274 and 1281.
facts: He became regent in 1268, at about age sixteen by Western reckoning or eighteen by traditional counting, shortly after the Mongol court of Kublai Khan first demanded Japan's submission.
He refused all Mongol diplomatic demands and reportedly had several Mongol envoys executed, a decision that made war all but certain.

Japanese defenders repelled both the 1274 and 1281 Mongol invasion fleets. In 1281 a great typhoon, and in 1274 traditionally a storm or sudden reverse wind, both later remembered as kamikaze ("divine wind"), destroyed large parts of the Mongol fleets — after the defenders had already inflicted losses on the invading forces.
He patronized Zen Buddhism, inviting the Chinese monk Wuxue Zuyuan to Kamakura and founding the temple Engaku-ji, reportedly to honour the dead of both sides after the invasions.
fields.context: Hojo Tokimune governed Kamakura Japan in [[region/east-asia|East Asia]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], defending against the [[culture/mongol-empire|Mongol Empire]] at the height of its westward and eastward expansion. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the "divine wind", traditionally credited with ending both invasions, has often overshadowed a plainer fact: Japanese defenders, organized under Tokimune's government, had already stalled both landings before the storms struck, and coastal fortifications such as the Hakata Bay wall were built in 1276, after the first invasion. Crediting the weather alone understates the preparation his regency undertook.
questions: How much of the invasions' failure owed to the storms, and how much to the defensive tactics — and, by 1281, the walls — that Tokimune's government had built along Hakata Bay?

fields.summary: Hypatia, who lived from about 350 to 415 CE, worked in Alexandria as a philosopher, mathematician and astronomer; she taught many students and was murdered by a mob.
facts: Daughter of the mathematician Theon, she taught Neoplatonist philosophy.
She is credited with commentaries on mathematical works, though the details remain uncertain.
In 415 a Christian mob killed her amid a political dispute between the Roman governor Orestes and Bishop Cyril.
Later writers turned her into a symbol, so historical fact and legend now run together in her story.
fields.context: Hypatia worked in Roman Egypt, in the [[region/nile-valley|Nile Valley]], at the close of [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]], continuing the tradition of [[person/aristotle|Aristotle]] and his successors.
fields.observer:
I see a scholar who became a symbol the moment she could no longer speak for herself, used afterward by writers who had their own purposes in mind. I see how a legend grows around a person the way ivy grows around a wall, until it is hard to tell where the stone ends and the leaf begins.

A symbol can outlive the person it was built from.
questions: What did Hypatia actually write?

fields.summary: Ibn Battuta, born in 1304 and dead by about 1369, was a Moroccan scholar and traveler whose account, the Rihla, describes journeys of about 117,000 kilometers (73,000 miles) across much of the Old World.
facts: He left Tangier in 1325 on pilgrimage, and kept traveling for about 30 years.
His travels took him through Arabia, East Africa, Persia, India, Southeast Asia, and the Mali Empire, in 1352 to 1353.
He dictated his account to the scholar Ibn Juzayy.
Historians debate whether he actually visited every place he describes.
fields.context: He traveled within the world of the [[event/indian-ocean-trade-network|Indian Ocean Trade Network]], visiting the [[culture/swahili-coast-city-states|Swahili Coast City-States]] and the [[culture/mali-empire|Mali Empire]].
fields.observer:
I think of a man who could cross most of the known world and still be received everywhere as a scholar, because one law and one faith gave him a common frame wherever he arrived. I think of how large a single, connected world can be, and how small the distance feels when everyone shares the same map of meaning.

A shared frame can make a stranger legible before he has said a single word.
questions: How reliable is the Rihla as a record of his journeys?

fields.summary: Marie Curie (1867 to 1934), a Polish-born physicist and chemist, pioneered the study of radioactivity and remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
facts: In 1903 she shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel.
In 1911 she won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for her discovery of polonium and radium.
She developed mobile X-ray units for use in World War I hospitals.
She died of aplastic anemia, likely brought on by long exposure to radiation.
fields.context: Her work on radioactivity underlies [[technology/nuclear-fission|Nuclear Fission]] and the [[event/nuclear-age|Nuclear Age]]. Compare her with [[person/albert-einstein|Albert Einstein]].
fields.observer: I picture a world that offered a woman in science almost no opening, and I picture her making one anyway. I remember that her notebooks are still radioactive today, decades after she set them down. The past does not only leave a record on paper — sometimes it leaves a trace you can still measure. Some inheritances glow long after the person who left them is gone.
questions: How did she make her way around the barriers facing women in science?

fields.summary: Mary Cassatt (22 May 1844 to 14 June 1926), an American painter who spent most of her adult life in France, was the only American to exhibit with the French Impressionists, and is celebrated for tender, unsentimental images of women and children.
facts: Cassatt was born into a wealthy family in Allegheny City, now part of Pittsburgh. Against her father's wishes she studied at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts from about 1860, then departed for Paris in 1866.

Since women could not enter the École des Beaux-Arts, she studied privately and copied the Old Masters in the Louvre. Frustrated with the Salon's conservative taste, she accepted Degas's invitation in 1877 to exhibit with the Impressionists, and showed alongside them in 1879, 1880, 1881 and 1886.
Her parents and sister moved to Paris to live with her, and her own family became her favourite models.
An 1890 exhibition of Japanese prints in Paris inspired a set of ten colour prints that combined drypoint and aquatint, from which she took flat colour, strong outlines and cropped compositions.
In 1893 she painted the mural Modern Woman for the Woman's Building at the Chicago World's Columbian Exposition; the mural has since been lost.

She advised Louisine Havemeyer and other Americans on buying Impressionist works and, according to some sources, Old Masters as well, many of which now hang in the Metropolitan Museum, and she supported the women's suffrage movement.
Failing eyesight forced her to stop working around 1914. Key works include Little Girl in a Blue Armchair (1878), The Child's Bath (1893) and The Boating Party (1893 to 1894).
fields.context: Cassatt worked in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]] as an American within the Impressionist circle of [[person/claude-monet|Claude Monet]]; she drew on Japanese prints, including those of [[person/katsushika-hokusai|Katsushika Hokusai]], and supported the [[event/women-s-suffrage-movements|Women's Suffrage Movements]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: I remember that the formal school shut its door to her, and I remember that she found her way in anyway, through private study and through a friend's invitation, the informal paths so many women's careers were built on. I look at her subject — the daily work of care inside the kin-lattice — and I see a canvas that painting had rarely thought large enough to hold it. Her advice to collectors even decided where the movement's pictures would end up, in American museums, a redistribution of art by taste and money as much as by merit. A door closed in one place can still be walked around.
questions: How far did her advice to collectors shape which Impressionist works entered American collections?

fields.summary: Matthias Corvinus (1443 to 1490) reigned as King of Hungary from 1458 to 1490, a Renaissance patron-king who built one of Europe's finest libraries and modernized his kingdom's army and administration.
facts: He was elected king at age fourteen after the deaths of his father, the military commander John Hunyadi, and his older brother; his mother's political maneuvering, along with his uncle Michael Szilágyi's troops intimidating the barons, secured him the throne, though sources differ on whether a bribe to the nobility also played a part.
He built the Black Army, a mostly mercenary standing force notable for its time, and used it to campaign against the Ottoman Empire, Bohemia, and the Holy Roman Empire, capturing Vienna in 1485.

He assembled the Bibliotheca Corviniana, described as the largest library in Europe north of the Alps and second only to the Vatican Library, employing scribes and scholars to copy classical and contemporary texts; much of it was later scattered or destroyed after the Ottoman conquest of Hungary.
He centralized royal justice and taxation, cutting into the independent power of the Hungarian nobility, though weaker successors substantially reversed his reforms after his death.
fields.context: Matthias Corvinus ruled Hungary within [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], balancing conflicts with both the Ottoman Empire and the Holy Roman Empire. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]], [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Matthias's centralizing reforms rested heavily on his own standing army and personal authority rather than on durable institutions, so that much of his state-building unraveled within a generation of his death — a pattern common among strong rulers who do not also build the architecture that outlasts them.
questions: How much of the Bibliotheca Corviniana reflected Matthias's own intellectual interests, and how much reflected the prestige-collecting expected of any Renaissance monarch?

fields.summary: Menelik II (1844 to 1913) reigned as emperor of Ethiopia from 1889, and led the forces that defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896.
facts: He expanded the empire southward and founded Addis Ababa as its capital.
He imported modern arms and pursued the technological modernization of his state.
On 1 March 1896 he won the [[event/battle-of-adwa|Battle of Adwa]].
His empire's expansion came through the conquest of neighboring peoples, and how to judge that expansion is debated.
fields.context: Menelik led Ethiopia through the era of the [[event/scramble-for-africa|Scramble for Africa]]. See [[event/battle-of-adwa|Battle of Adwa]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a ruler could resist one colonial power while building an empire of his own within his neighborhood. The line between the colonized and the colonizer was not always a simple one.
questions: How did Menelik's expansion affect the neighboring peoples it conquered?

fields.summary: Michelangelo Buonarroti (6 March 1475 to 18 February 1564), an Italian sculptor, painter, architect and poet, defined the High Renaissance through his Pietà, his David, and his Sistine Chapel paintings, and became the first Western artist to have a biography published in his own lifetime.
facts: Michelangelo was born at Caprese in Tuscany and raised in Florence. At 13 he was apprenticed to Domenico Ghirlandaio, then moved on to the sculpture garden of Lorenzo de' Medici, where he studied the ancient statues there.
The Pietà (1498 to 1499) made his name in Rome, and he carved the David in Florence (1501 to 1504).

In 1505 Pope Julius II summoned him to Rome to design a colossal tomb, then turned him instead toward painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508 to 1512); the unfinished tomb went on to haunt him for decades.
In 1534 he settled permanently in Rome and painted The Last Judgment (1536 to 1541). In 1546 he became chief architect of St Peter's Basilica, and the dome he designed became a model for later domes.
He wrote hundreds of poems, many addressed to Tommaso de' Cavalieri and Vittoria Colonna. He died in Rome, and his body was secretly carried to Florence for burial in Santa Croce.
He carved directly, often without full-size models, and studied anatomy through dissection. A cleaning of the Sistine ceiling in the 1980s and 1990s revealed colours that were vivid, even acidic.
Vasari's Lives (1550) closed with him, and Ascanio Condivi published a biography of him in 1553. He had studied the frescoes of Giotto.
fields.context: Michelangelo worked in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[event/renaissance|Renaissance]], within the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]]. He studied [[person/giotto|Giotto]]'s frescoes. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: I think of a man who believed a sculpture only frees a figure already waiting inside the stone, and I think of the decades he spent in service to popes, the chief patrons of that age's meaning-engine. I remember that the heroic nude body became a standard image for sacred and civic subjects alike, and I remember that the David turned a block of stone into story-glue for an entire city. A biography published in his own lifetime is an early sign of the artist becoming a named public figure. Vasari and Condivi wrote as admirers, so the portrait they left behind is not a neutral one. Even praise, written close enough to its subject, still casts a shadow.
questions: How much of the standard portrait of Michelangelo comes from admiring biographers, rather than from his own letters and poems?

fields.summary: Ibn Khaldun, who lived from 1332 to 1406, was a North African historian whose 'Muqaddimah' (1377) proposed a general theory of how societies and states rise and fall.
facts: Born in Tunis, he served in several courts across North Africa and Andalusia.
He argued that group solidarity, asabiyyah, helps found dynasties, and that it weakens as rulers grow comfortable.
He wrote about economics, urban life, and the role of climate and environment.
He is sometimes called a founder of sociology and of historiography.
fields.context: Ibn Khaldun wrote within the world of [[person/ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]] and recorded facts about the [[culture/mali-empire|Mali Empire]]; his approach sits close to the Observer's own.
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Ibn Khaldun was practicing an "anthropology of the species" six centuries ago, hunting for patterns in how groups rise and fall rather than for the will of individuals — a precursor of the Observer's own method.
questions: How well does his cycle of dynasties fit the historical record?

fields.summary: Ibn Sina, known as Avicenna, lived from 980 to 1037 as a Persian physician and philosopher whose 'Canon of Medicine' became a standard medical text across the Islamic world and Europe for centuries.
facts: He was born near Bukhara, in Central Asia.
Completed about 1025, the Canon of Medicine organized medical knowledge into a systematic whole.
Translated into Latin, it remained in use in European universities into the 17th century.
His philosophical 'Book of Healing' likewise influenced medieval Europe.
fields.context: Ibn Sina drew on the tradition of the [[event/translation-movement-and-the-house-of-wisdom|Translation Movement and the House of Wisdom]] and the wider world of the [[culture/abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]].
fields.observer:
I think of one book, carried across languages and centuries, organizing how many societies practiced medicine at all. I think of how a single text can become the glue that holds a whole profession together — every physician reading from the same page, without ever meeting.

A shared text can bind strangers tighter than a shared teacher ever could.
questions: How much of the Canon was original versus a synthesis?

fields.summary: Indira Gandhi, who lived from 1917 to 1984, served as prime minister of India for most of the years 1966 to 1984. She led India through the 1971 war that created Bangladesh, imposed emergency rule from 1975 to 1977, and was assassinated by her own bodyguards after ordering an army raid on Sikhism's holiest shrine.
facts: Born on 19 November 1917 in Allahabad, daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first prime minister, she became prime minister herself in 1966.
In 1971 India backed the independence of East Pakistan, which became Bangladesh, following a short war with Pakistan.
On 25 June 1975 she had a state of emergency declared, suspending civil liberties, censoring the press, and jailing opponents, until elections in 1977 that she lost.
She returned to power in 1980. Government policy during her years in office also pushed the Green Revolution's higher-yield crops.
In June 1984 she ordered Operation Blue Star, a military assault on the Golden Temple in Amritsar meant to remove armed Sikh militants; it damaged the shrine and angered many Sikhs.
On 31 October 1984 two of her Sikh bodyguards assassinated her in New Delhi, and riots afterward killed thousands of Sikhs, mostly in Delhi.
fields.context: Indira Gandhi led India in [[region/south-asia|South Asia]] during the [[era/information-age|Information Age]], a state formed after the [[event/partition-of-india|Partition of India]]. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a leader who suspended the young republic's own rules in 1975 was, nine years later, killed for ordering force against a meaning-engine's holiest site — and that the sanctioned harm done to her spread outward into killing among ordinary Sikhs. A specialist could argue that Operation Blue Star addressed an armed occupation of the temple rather than Sikh belief itself, which would weaken any reading of the raid as a simple attack on religion.
questions: How far did the 1975 Emergency reflect a threat to her rule, and how far a choice to entrench it?
What did she foresee for the Sikh community after Operation Blue Star?

fields.summary: Isaac Newton, who lived from 1642 to 1727, was an English mathematician and physicist whose laws of motion and universal gravitation formed the basis of classical mechanics.
facts: His 'Principia' (1687) laid out the laws of motion together with the law of gravitation.
He developed calculus independently of Leibniz, a parallel discovery that led to a bitter priority dispute.
He studied optics and showed that white light is composed of colors.
He also gave much of his time to alchemy and theology.
fields.context: Newton completed the work of the [[event/scientific-revolution|Scientific Revolution]] begun by [[person/galileo-galilei|Galileo Galilei]], and his physics framed science until the time of [[person/albert-einstein|Albert Einstein]].
fields.observer:
I think of an apple and a planet, obeying the same rule without having met. I think of what it means to find a law that holds everywhere you look, ground and heavens both — proof that we could find laws holding everywhere we looked.

One rule behind two falls: the sky was never as far from the earth as it looked.
questions: How should his interest in alchemy be understood alongside his physics?

fields.summary: Mimar Sinan (about 1489 to 1588) served as chief royal architect to three Ottoman sultans across nearly fifty years. He is credited with several hundred structures, and his Selimiye Mosque at Edirne is regarded as the summit of classical Ottoman architecture.
facts: Sinan was born about 1489 or 1490 in Ağırnas, near Kayseri in central Anatolia, into a Christian family; sources disagree on whether that family was Greek or Armenian.

He was conscripted through the devşirme levy into the Ottoman elite corps, converted to Islam, and trained as a Janissary. He rose through military engineering, building bridges and fortifications on campaign for Suleiman the Magnificent.
Chelebi Lütfi Pasha, on becoming Grand Vizier in 1539, appointed him chief royal architect, a post Sinan held into his late nineties, and he died in Istanbul in 1588.

His principal buildings are the Şehzade Mosque (1543 to 1548), the Süleymaniye Mosque (1550 to 1557), and the Selimiye Mosque (1568 or 1569 to 1574 or 1575), which he himself described as his apprenticeship, his journeyman work, and his masterpiece.

He worked to raise domes wider and more daring than Hagia Sophia, the Byzantine cathedral converted to a mosque after 1453, using semi-domes, buttressing piers and pendentives. He also built aqueducts and bridges, some of which are still in use.
He trained a generation of students. Turkey's largest architecture prize carries his name, and the Selimiye Mosque was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011.
fields.context: Sinan served the [[culture/ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] in [[region/levant-and-anatolia|Levant and Anatolia]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]], a century after the [[event/fall-of-constantinople|Fall of Constantinople]] left Hagia Sophia as his measure. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]], [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer: I see a boy taken from a Christian village by a levy, and I see that same boy rise to design an empire's mosques — the state's demand for people becoming, in his one case, an engine of monumental building. Each dome he raised is a claim in masonry against an older building, and I remember his own three-stage account of apprenticeship, journeyman work and masterpiece, a tool-lineage where each structure teaches the next. That account is his own narrative first, and later reverence has only added more to it. A man conscripted as tribute still chose, stone by stone, what to build with his life.
questions: Of the several hundred structures credited to Sinan, how many did he personally design?
Which parts of his own and later accounts of his career and birth can actually be documented?

fields.summary: Mirabai (traditionally about 1498 to about 1546) was a Rajput princess from Rajasthan and one of the best-known poet-saints of the Bhakti movement, devoted to Krishna; almost nothing about her life is documented, and her surviving poems were set down long after her time.
facts: By tradition Mirabai was born about 1498 at Kudki in Rajasthan, into the Rathore Rajput family of Merta, and died about 1546 or 1547; both dates come only from later tradition.
Tradition holds that she married Bhoj Raj, heir of Mewar, in 1516, and that he died about 1521 of battle wounds.
Her poems, or padas, are composed in Rajasthani and related Hindi, and address Krishna in the language of love and separation.
Tradition credits her with a very large number of poems, though scholars think only a few hundred may be authentic, and only two are known from manuscripts older than the early eighteenth century.

Stories that her in-laws tried to poison her, and that she vanished into an image of Krishna, are hagiographic legends; the earliest records, from the seventeenth century, do not even mention her marriage or her in-laws.
fields.context: Mirabai's life falls within [[region/south-asia|South Asia]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]], as the [[culture/mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]] replaced the [[culture/delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] across northern India in 1526. See [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: I think of a woman who left almost no trace in her own time, and I think of how she became one of the most widely sung voices of her tradition anyway. I remember the songs that place devotion to a god above the duties of marriage and household, and I remember that singers have restated that same claim about the kin-lattice for five centuries. A specialist could argue that a single historical Mirabai may never be recovered at all, which would weaken any reading of the poems as her own biography. What we sing of her may be older than any woman who lived it.
questions: Which of the poems attributed to her, if any, can actually be dated to the sixteenth century?
How far do the persecution stories reflect later debates over women's devotion versus family duty?

fields.summary: Montezuma II (Moctezuma; about 1466 to 1520) was the ninth tlatoani, or ruler, of the Aztec Empire, reigning at its greatest territorial extent until the arrival of Hernan Cortes and the Spanish conquest.
facts: He extended Aztec control through further conquests mainly in Oaxaca and Guerrero, along with a campaign around 1514 into the Huastec region, and reorganized the empire's systems of tribute and administration.
Cortes and a small Spanish force reached the capital, Tenochtitlan, in November 1519; Montezuma received them, and was afterward held hostage within his own palace.

Accounts of his final months diverge: Spanish sources hold that he tried to calm his people during the fighting that followed the 1520 Toxcatl massacre and Cortes's return, and died from a stone thrown by his own subjects, while some later Aztec-descended chroniclers hold that the Spanish killed him directly.

His death in June 1520 came shortly before the Spanish were driven from the city in the "Noche Triste"; his brother Cuitlahuac, and then his nephew Cuauhtemoc, carried on the resistance that ended with Tenochtitlan's fall in 1521.
fields.context: Montezuma II ruled the [[culture/aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]] in [[region/mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]], and his capture set off the chain of events that ended Aztec independence. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]], [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that nearly every detailed account of Montezuma's final year was written by a side that stood to benefit from portraying him as passive, or as already discredited among his own people. The surviving record cannot fully separate the man from the story that his conquerors, and his own later-defeated dynasty, each had reason to tell.
questions: Did Montezuma initially treat the Spanish as returning gods, as later legend holds, or simply as an ordinary diplomatic and military problem?

fields.summary: Muhammad (about 570 to 632 CE) was an Arabian religious and political leader, regarded by Muslims as the last prophet, and the founder of the community that grew into the Islamic world.
facts: Born in Mecca, he began, according to Islamic tradition, receiving revelations around 610, later compiled as the Quran.
In 622 he and his followers migrated to Medina, the Hijra, marking the start of the Islamic calendar.
By the time of his death, most of the Arabian Peninsula had joined the community.
Today Islam is followed by roughly a quarter of the world's population.
fields.context: See [[event/rise-of-islam|Rise of Islam]]. After his death, his community's expansion led to the [[culture/abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]] and a new zone of shared learning.
fields.observer: The Observer approaches this as it approaches every meaning-engine, with respect for what believers hold, and notes only the historical pattern: a movement out of a marginal region that rapidly built a shared law, script, and civilization.
questions: How early were the surviving accounts of his life actually written down?

fields.summary: Muhammad Ali, an Ottoman officer of Albanian family, became governor of Egypt in 1805, broke the power of the old Mamluk elite, built a conscript army and a state-run economy, and founded the dynasty that ruled Egypt until 1952.
facts: Muhammad Ali was born in Kavala, in what is now Greece, to an Albanian family from the Korçë region; his father worked as a tobacco merchant and served as an Ottoman military commander.

He rose to power after the French withdrawal from Egypt in 1801. In 1805 prominent Egyptians, including the religious scholars, demanded his appointment as governor, or wali, and the Ottomans accepted.

In 1811 he invited the leading Mamluks to a celebration at the Cairo Citadel, where his forces ambushed and killed them; more Mamluks were then hunted down across Cairo and elsewhere, for a death toll of perhaps 3,000 in total.
He introduced long-staple cotton, built an army of conscripts trained by European officers, and established a state-run industrial economy.
He founded the dynasty that would rule Egypt until 1952.
fields.context: Muhammad Ali governed Egypt as a nominal servant of the [[culture/ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] while pursuing reforms of his own, in the same period as the [[event/tanzimat-reforms|Tanzimat Reforms]] under way in Istanbul. His rule came before the building of the [[event/suez-canal|Suez Canal]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a reformer who began his rule by killing a rival elite at a banquet meant to look like a celebration, and who built a modern state on conscription and compulsory production. The order he made was real, and it lasted; the cost of it was carried by those who were drafted into his army, and by those who did not survive the killing at all.
questions: How much of Egypt's later modernization can be credited to Muhammad Ali's programme, and at what cost to its rural population?
How many people, in total, were killed in the wave of violence that followed the Citadel massacre?

fields.summary: Eleanor Roosevelt (1884 to 1962) served as First Lady of the United States from 1933 to 1945, and afterward as a diplomat who chaired the United Nations commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
facts: Born on 11 October 1884 in New York City, she married Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1905.

As First Lady she redefined the role: holding her own press conferences, writing a daily newspaper column, and speaking for civil rights and the poor, sometimes publicly at odds with her husband's policies.
After his death in 1945, President Truman named her a delegate to the new United Nations that December.
She chaired the UN Commission on Human Rights, which drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the General Assembly on 10 December 1948 — the achievement she called her greatest.
She later chaired a presidential commission on the status of women under President Kennedy.
She died on 7 November 1962 in New York City.
fields.context: Eleanor Roosevelt worked in [[region/north-america|North America]] during the [[era/information-age|Information Age]], through [[event/world-war-ii|World War II]] and into the early [[event/cold-war|Cold War]], the years when the United Nations came into being. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
