fields.observer: The Observer notes that a document meant to bind every state to common claim-lines around a person's treatment was drafted under the chairmanship of a woman holding no formal power beyond her office, relying instead on the public standing she had built as a president's wife. The declaration functions as story-glue with no enforcement behind it, only the weight of near-unanimous agreement. A specialist could argue that later adoption of the Declaration commits signatory states to little in practice, which would weaken any reading of 1948 as a settled achievement rather than a beginning.
questions: How much practical effect has the Declaration had on states that signed it?
How much of her influence came from her own record, and how much from the Roosevelt name?

fields.summary: Emperor Meiji (1852 to 1912) reigned as Emperor of Japan from 1867, and in his name the Meiji Restoration transformed Japan into a modern industrial state.
facts: He came to the throne in 1867 at about the age of fourteen.
The Charter Oath, issued in his name in 1868, promised reform.
His reign saw a new constitution in 1889, industrialization, and Japan's rise as a regional power.
He died in 1912.
fields.context: He stood as the symbol of the [[event/meiji-restoration|Meiji Restoration]], which ended the [[culture/tokugawa-shogunate|Tokugawa Shogunate]].
fields.observer: I see a boy on a throne, his real powers held and spent by advisers, and I see how his very youth lent legitimacy to a change that swept everything before it. I see continuity wearing a young face while revolution moves beneath it. What else could make an upheaval look like inheritance?
questions: How much personal influence did the Emperor actually hold?

fields.summary: Enheduanna, flourishing around 2300 BCE (the span of about 2285 to 2250 BCE is only an estimate), served as high priestess of the moon god Nanna at the Sumerian city of Ur and was a daughter of Sargon of Akkad. She is often called the earliest author known by name, though her dates and the attribution of her texts remain debated.
facts: Enheduanna served as en-priestess of Nanna at Ur, appointed to the office by her father, Sargon of Akkad; her dates depend on the chronology used.
Found at Ur in 1927 by Leonard Woolley's team, a disc shows a figure identified by inscription as Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon, in a ritual scene.
Sumerian poems are attributed to her, including 42 temple hymns and hymns to the goddess Inanna, among them "The Exaltation of Inanna."

The surviving copies come from schools of the Old Babylonian period, about 1800 BCE, some five to six centuries after her lifetime, and scholars disagree over whether she wrote every text attributed to her.
In "The Exaltation of Inanna" the speaker describes being driven from office by a usurper, Lugal-ane, and then restored; whether this reflects real events is debated.
fields.context: Enheduanna wrote in the Sumerian language of the [[culture/sumerians|Sumerians]] while serving a ruler from the Akkadian-speaking north, in [[region/mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]] during the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]]; her work belongs to the story of the [[event/invention-of-writing|Invention of Writing]]. See [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer:
I see a conquering house place its own daughter at the head of a conquered city's oldest cult, binding a new claim to an old sacred order through blood. I see, in that same priestess, the first author the record gives a name to — one office, at once political and devoted.

But the words survive only in later copies, centuries removed, and I know the reading would falter if the name attached to them turned out to be a tradition rather than a fact. What is authorship, when it arrives to us already retold?
questions: Which of the texts attributed to her can be tied to her own lifetime?

fields.summary: Ezana ruled Aksum, in present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea, from about 320 to about 360 CE, though sources differ on the exact dates. He is known for adopting Christianity and for a campaign in the Nile valley, both recorded in his inscriptions and coins.
facts: Ezana came to the throne as a child and ruled the Kingdom of Aksum from about 320 until about 360; dates for his life and reign remain approximate, and sources differ.
His early inscriptions and coins show the older Aksumite religion, including a crescent and disc on his coins.

Frumentius, a Christian from Tyre — described as Phoenician, and in some accounts Syrian — rose within the Aksumite court and is reported to have been consecrated Aksum's first bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria, traditionally in 328, though other accounts place it between 340 and 346.

Ezana converted to Christianity in the 4th century, though the exact date is uncertain. His later inscriptions invoke a "Lord of Heaven," and his coins replace the crescent and disc with the cross, often described as among the earliest coins to do so.
His inscriptions appear in Ge'ez, Sabaean and Greek.
About 350 an Aksumite force campaigned in the Nile valley against Kush and neighboring peoples; the campaign is often linked to the end of Kush's power, though historians debate the causes.
fields.context: Ezana ruled the [[culture/kingdom-of-aksum|Kingdom of Aksum]] and led campaigns against the [[culture/kingdom-of-kush|Kingdom of Kush]] in [[region/sub-saharan-africa|Sub-Saharan Africa]], during [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]]. See [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a king's change of religion is visible in both stone and coin: the same ruler's inscriptions change which god they invoke, and his coinage changes which symbol it carries. A state's meaning-engine was switched from above and announced as a status-signal to the traders who carried those coins across the Red Sea world. The reading would weaken if evidence showed that most of his subjects kept the older practices for a long time after his conversion.
questions: When did his conversion take place, and how quickly was it announced?

fields.summary: Francisco Goya (30 March 1746 to 16 April 1828) worked as a Spanish court painter and printmaker, often called the last of the Old Masters and the first of the moderns. Illness, political repression and the Napoleonic invasion pushed him from brilliant royal portraits toward satire, violence and the irrational.
facts: Goya was born in Fuendetodos in Aragon and grew up in Zaragoza. In 1773 he married Josefa Bayeu, sister of the court painter Francisco Bayeu, who helped him win work designing tapestry cartoons in Madrid; by 1786 he was painter to the king, and by 1799 First Court Painter to Charles IV.
An illness in 1792 to 1793 left him permanently deaf. In 1799 he published Los Caprichos, satirical etchings mocking superstition and the clergy.

When Napoleon's armies invaded Spain in 1808, he witnessed atrocities on both sides and recorded them in The Disasters of War, prints not published until 35 years after his death. He painted The Second and Third of May 1808 in 1814.

Disillusioned by the repressive rule of Ferdinand VII, he retreated to a house outside Madrid and covered its walls with the Black Paintings, including Saturn Devouring His Son, 1819 to 1823. In 1824 he went into exile in Bordeaux, where he died.
His portraits, influenced by Velázquez, use loose brushwork and avoid flattery; he mastered aquatint for deep shadows, and later applied paint with knives, rags and fingers.
Goya named Rembrandt as one of his three masters. Both Manet's Execution of Emperor Maximilian and Picasso's Guernica descend from The Third of May.
The Prado holds the greatest collection of his work.
fields.context: Goya worked in [[region/europe|Europe]] and lived through the [[event/napoleonic-wars|Napoleonic Wars]] in the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], drawing on [[person/diego-velazquez|Diego Velázquez]] and [[person/rembrandt-van-rijn|Rembrandt van Rijn]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a court painter who recorded sanctioned harm from inside the very society that practised it, and who kept that record private: The Disasters of War stayed withheld for 35 years. The same hand produced unflattering royal portraits and images of witches and monsters, showing that the meaning-engine of the period, Church and crown, did not exhaust what one person could see. Later artists took his war images as a model, an inheritance chosen by those who wanted a precedent for witnessing.
questions: Why did he withhold The Disasters of War, and what did he intend for the Black Paintings?

fields.summary: Frank Lloyd Wright (1867 to 1959) stands as the most influential American architect of the 20th century. Across seven decades he argued for "organic architecture" — buildings designed from the inside out, around their site, materials and users.
facts: Wright was born in Richland Center, Wisconsin, studied engineering briefly at the University of Wisconsin, and moved to Chicago, where he worked under Louis Sullivan, whom he later called his "Lieber Meister".

He set up his own practice in Oak Park in the 1890s and developed the low, wide-eaved Prairie house style. His personal life ran turbulent: an affair, the killing of seven people at his Wisconsin home, Taliesin, in 1914, and bankruptcy during the Depression.

In his late sixties he designed Fallingwater and the Johnson Wax headquarters, both 1936 to 1939, and finally the Guggenheim Museum, its design and construction spanning 1943 to 1959; he died in 1959, aged 91.

He designed around open, flowing interior space, with art-glass bands and deep cantilevered overhangs, using concrete, steel and glass without disguising them as historical stonework; he designed most of the furniture, textiles and stained glass in his buildings himself.
He designed more than a thousand structures, roughly half of them built. Fallingwater and several others now form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Late in life he planned an unrealised city, Broadacre City, built around low-density, car-based suburban living; he was also a major collector and dealer of Hiroshige's prints.
fields.context: Wright worked in [[region/north-america|North America]] in the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], collecting the prints of [[person/utagawa-hiroshige|Utagawa Hiroshige]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer:
I look at a man whose whole principle was that a building should grow from its site and its people, never from a borrowed style — and I watch his own name become a style anyway. I see his open plan everywhere now, standard in houses that never speak his name; an idea can spread that far and still go uncredited.

He never built Broadacre City, and yet the car-based suburb he imagined arrived without him, which suggests a vision can shape a world its author never gets to raise. What idea does not, in the end, outrun the hands that first held it?
questions: How much of postwar suburban design can be traced to his ideas rather than to independent development?

fields.summary: Joseph Mallord William Turner, born in April 1775 and dead by 19 December 1851, stands as the greatest British landscape painter and a bold colourist. He began as a precise topographical watercolourist, and his late paintings dissolve ships, trains and cities into light, mist and weather.
facts: Turner was born in Covent Garden, London, the son of a barber and wigmaker. At 14 he entered the Royal Academy Schools, and at 15 he exhibited his first watercolour. In 1802 he was elected a full Royal Academician, at 26 or 27 depending on the source.
He travelled tirelessly through Britain, the Alps, France, Germany and Italy — especially Venice — filling hundreds of sketchbooks.
He never married, but had two daughters with Sarah Danby. John Ruskin championed him in Modern Painters (1843); he died in Chelsea and was buried in St Paul's Cathedral.

By the 1830s he was painting natural forces themselves — storms, fire, sunlight, steam — working thin washes over white grounds, scraping and rubbing his canvases, and applying paint thickly with knives.
He painted steamships and railways alongside Venetian lagoons; Rain, Steam and Speed (1844) stands as one of the first great paintings of modern technology.

The Slave Ship (1840) was possibly inspired by the Zong massacre of 1781, when enslaved Africans were thrown overboard so that owners could claim insurance; he showed it during the 1840 campaign to end slavery worldwide.

He left around 300 oil paintings, over 19,000 sketches, drawings and watercolours, and some 200 sketchbooks to the nation, held mainly at Tate Britain. Monet and Pissarro studied his work in London in 1870 to 1871, and the Turner Prize has been awarded since 1984.
fields.context: Turner painted the [[event/industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]] and its [[technology/railways|Railways]] in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], and in The Slave Ship confronted the [[event/atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic Slave Trade]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer:
I see a steam train and a slave ship inside the same body of work — the two great tool-lineages of his century, one celebrated, one condemned, both moving people and goods across water and land. I see critics who mocked his late style, not knowing they were watching a change in how a whole species learns to picture weather and speed.

He left his paintings to the nation, and a prize now carries his name: a reputation turned, over time, into an institution.
questions: How did his late style change how contemporaries saw landscape, given the criticism it drew?

fields.summary: Jadwiga, born about 1373 and dead by 1399, was crowned "King" of Poland in 1384 at about age ten. She is often described as the first woman to rule Poland in her own right, and her marriage to the Grand Duke of Lithuania began a dynastic union between the two states.
facts: She was crowned with the male title "rex" (king) rather than "regina" (queen), underscoring that she held full sovereign authority in her own right, not merely as a royal consort.

In 1386 she married Jogaila, the pagan Grand Duke of Lithuania, who converted to Christianity and was crowned co-ruler as Wladyslaw II Jagiello, founding the Jagiellonian dynasty and beginning the Christianization of Lithuania.

She helped fund the restoration of the Krakow Academy, later the Jagiellonian University, through jewellery she donated and, under her will, had sold to finance it — reviving an institution that became a major center of learning in Central Europe.
She died in 1399, about three and a half weeks after giving birth to a daughter who also died in infancy, four days before her — ending her direct line. The Catholic Church canonized her in 1997.
fields.context: Jadwiga ruled Poland in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], and her marriage began the Polish-Lithuanian union. See [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]] and [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Jadwiga's reign is remembered mainly for a marriage alliance and a religious conversion she enabled, rather than for personal political acts — yet the union of Poland and Lithuania that resulted reshaped Central European power for centuries, an outsized consequence for a reign that ended before she turned thirty.
questions: How much personal agency did the ten-year-old Jadwiga have in the political decision to crown her as king, versus her regency council?

fields.summary: Johannes Gutenberg, born about 1400 and dead by 1468, was a German metalworker who developed a movable-type printing press in Mainz around 1440 and printed the Gutenberg Bible about 1455.
facts: He combined metal type, oil-based ink, and a press adapted from wine-making.
His 42-line Bible stands as the earliest major book printed from movable type in Europe.
Financial difficulties overtook him, and he lost control of his workshop to a creditor.
Printing then spread rapidly across Europe within decades.
fields.context: See [[technology/movable-type-printing-press|Movable-Type Printing Press]]. Gutenberg's work supported the [[event/scientific-revolution|Scientific Revolution]] and religious reform.
fields.observer:
I think of memory made cheap, made copyable, made able to leave a single room and travel on its own. I think of every idea that started moving faster than any authority could catch it.

Once a thought can be copied, it no longer needs its author's permission to keep going.
questions: How much did he build on earlier East Asian printing?

fields.summary: Murasaki Shikibu (about 973 to about 1014) served as a lady-in-waiting at the Japanese imperial court of the Heian period, and wrote The Tale of Genji, a 54-chapter novel of court life widely called the world's first novel.
facts: "Murasaki Shikibu" is itself a later nickname; her personal name is unknown, and the nickname combines a character from her own novel with her father's court rank.
She was born about 973 into a minor branch of the Fujiwara clan, and learned the Chinese classics, normally reserved for men, by absorbing the lessons given to her brother.
She married a much older provincial governor about 998 and was widowed within a few years; about 1005 or 1006 she entered court service as a lady-in-waiting to Empress Shōshi.

The Tale of Genji follows a fictional prince and, in its later chapters, his descendants; it may have been begun before she came to court, though sources suggest she likely composed it while serving as a lady-in-waiting, possibly chapter by chapter.
She wrote almost entirely in hiragana, the script associated with women's writing at court, and set many waka poems into the story as compositions belonging to her own characters.
She also kept The Diary of Lady Murasaki, which records court life and its rivalries. She is thought to have died about 1014, though the date, like most of her biography, remains uncertain.
The earliest surviving illustrated version, the 12th-century Genji Monogatari Emaki, is a Japanese National Treasure, and she appears on the 2000 yen banknote.
fields.context: Murasaki wrote at the Heian court within [[region/east-asia|East Asia]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer: I think of the earliest long prose fiction on record, and I think of a woman writing it in the very script her society had assigned to women, while the mark-code of official record, Chinese characters, belonged only to men. The formal script carried authority; the informal one carried private feeling. I remember that the novel circulated as copied and illustrated scrolls, memory-outsourcing put to the work of interior life rather than law or scripture. Whether it counts as the first novel depends on how the term itself is defined, and her biography rests mostly on her own diary and scattered court records — so I hold this reading loosely. A script built to exclude a woman became the one she used to outlast her century.
questions: How much of The Tale of Genji, if any, was written before she entered court service?

fields.summary: Nefertiti (about 1370 to about 1330 BCE) was the Great Royal Wife of the Egyptian king Akhenaten, and is shown with unusual prominence in the art of his reign; her exact birth and death dates and her burial place remain uncertain, and the dates given here are approximate.
facts: Nefertiti married Akhenaten, then still called Amenhotep IV, early in his reign; the exact dates of that marriage are uncertain.
The couple promoted worship of the sun disk Aten, and moved the royal capital to a new city, Akhetaten, now Amarna.
Reliefs and statues depict Nefertiti at a scale, and in roles, usually reserved for the king, including a part in rites for the Aten.
They had six daughters, among them Meritaten and Ankhesenamun, who later married Tutankhamun.

Scholarship before 2012 assumed she vanished from the record around year 12 of the reign, but an inscription dated to year 16 names Neferneferuaten-Nefertiti alongside Akhenaten; whether she died, changed title, or ruled as co-regent under the name Neferneferuaten is debated.
A painted limestone bust found in 1912, in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose at Amarna, is now held in Berlin; Egypt has requested its return.
Later king lists left out Akhenaten and his immediate successors.
fields.context: Nefertiti's life is bound to [[person/akhenaten|Akhenaten]], among the [[culture/ancient-egyptians|Ancient Egyptians]] of the [[region/nile-valley|Nile Valley]] in the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]]. See [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: I look at one sculpture, and I see how it made her one of the best-known faces of antiquity, though the record beneath it covers only a short span that later rulers tried to scrub from the king lists. Her size in the reliefs reads as a status-signal, and I do not know whether it records real power or the couple's use of the royal family as a pair of divine images. This reading would weaken if evidence showed that such scale was simply the convention for queens of the period. A single face can outlive the whole reign that made it, and still tell us less than it seems to.
questions: Did she rule after Akhenaten's death, and under what name? Egyptologists still debate this, and a year 16 inscription shows she was still recorded late in his reign.

fields.summary: Nelson Mandela (1918 to 2013), a South African anti-apartheid leader, spent 27 years in prison before becoming his country's first democratically elected president in 1994.
facts: He co-founded the African National Congress Youth League, and helped lead resistance to apartheid.
From 1962 to 1990 he was held in prison.
After his release he negotiated apartheid's end.
He served as president from 1994 to 1999.
fields.context: Mandela stands as a figure of the [[era/information-age|Information Age]] in [[region/sub-saharan-africa|Sub-Saharan Africa]], his approach shaped by the example of [[person/mahatma-gandhi|Mahatma Gandhi]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes a rare pattern: a leader who, once he held power, chose reconciliation over retribution. The species is capable, it turns out, of institutionalizing forgiveness as a political tool.
questions: Which factors made South Africa's transition comparatively peaceful?

fields.summary: Nezahualcoyotl (1402 to 1472) was the tlatoani, or ruler, of the Acolhua city-state of Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico, and a founder of the Triple Alliance with Tenochtitlan and Tlacopan; he is remembered as a lawgiver, builder and poet, though much of what is said about him comes from later writers.
facts: Nezahualcoyotl was born in 1402 in Texcoco, the son of the ruler Ixtlilxochitl I and a Mexica princess; after the Tepanec state of Azcapotzalco conquered Texcoco and killed his father, he lived in exile.

With Tenochtitlan and Tlacopan he fought Azcapotzalco; its defeat, traditionally dated about 1428, created the Triple Alliance. He ruled Texcoco from about 1431 until 1472, when his son Nezahualpilli succeeded him.
Later sources credit him with a law code and public works, among them a dike that protected Tenochtitlan from flooding and the gardens at Tetzcotzingo.
About 34 poems are attributed to him in sixteenth-century manuscripts; whether he composed them is debated, since "his song" can equally mean a song about him.

Accounts that he opposed human sacrifice and favored a single creator deity derive largely from his own descendant, Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxochitl, writing in the early seventeenth century, and are treated with caution.
fields.context: Nezahualcoyotl ruled within [[region/mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]]. The Triple Alliance he helped found grew into the [[culture/aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]], centered on [[place/tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]]. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that a ruler whose rise rested on a military alliance is remembered chiefly through poems on the brevity of life. This verse, made in sound-code, survived the Conquest only because writers copied it into mark-code in the sixteenth century. A specialist could argue that both the poems and the portrait of him as a tolerant sage reflect the aims of those later writers, which would weaken any reading of him as an exceptional thinker.
questions: Which of the poems attributed to him, if any, did he compose himself?
How much of the later picture of his laws and beliefs comes from his own descendants?

fields.summary: Nur Jahan (1577 to 1645), a Mughal empress and wife of the emperor Jahangir, held great political power at court from about 1611 to 1627.
facts: Born Mehr-un-Nisa in 1577, Nur Jahan was the daughter of Mirza Ghiyas Beg, a Persian who served the Mughal court.
Her first husband, Sher Afghan, died in 1607. She married Jahangir in 1611 and received the title Nur Mahal, then in 1616 the title Nur Jahan, "Light of the World."
As Jahangir's health declined, she took an increasing share of government; coins were struck in her name, and imperial orders carried her seal.
Her father became chief minister, and her brother Asaf Khan a leading noble, so her family held key posts.
She commissioned her father's tomb at Agra, built between 1622 and 1628, an early Mughal building faced in marble with inlaid stone.
In 1626 the general Mahabat Khan seized Jahangir, and she took a part in securing his release.

After Jahangir died in 1627, her brother backed Shah Jahan, who became emperor. She was then placed under house arrest by her own brother, on Shah Jahan's orders, and lived in Lahore on an annual allowance until her death in 1645.
fields.context: Nur Jahan's court belonged to the [[culture/mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]] in [[region/south-asia|South Asia]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]]. Her niece Mumtaz Mahal is commemorated by the [[place/taj-mahal|Taj Mahal]]. See [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: I see a woman who held power through the kin-lattice — through marriage into the ruling house, and posts found for her father and her brother — rather than through any office carrying her own name. I remember coins struck with her name and a seal bearing her mark, the state itself turning her into a status-signal, while the chroniclers who wrote of her wrote from within that same court. This reading would weaken if evidence showed her reported power was overstated by writers looking for a woman to explain Jahangir's rule. Power borrowed through kinship can still be spent as though it were one's own.
questions: How far did her real authority extend beyond what the court chronicles report?

fields.summary: Leo Tolstoy (1828 to 1910) was a Russian novelist, author of the realist epics War and Peace and Anna Karenina, and a religious crisis in the second half of his life turned him toward shorter fiction and writing on faith, mortality and nonviolence that would influence Gandhi.
facts: Tolstoy was born in 1828 into an aristocratic family at Yasnaya Polyana, the estate south of Moscow that he inherited and managed for most of his life, and he served briefly as an army officer in the Crimean War.
In the 1860s and 1870s he wrote War and Peace (1869) and Anna Karenina (1877), and he founded a school for the children on his estate.

After Anna Karenina he underwent a spiritual crisis, described in A Confession; he rejected the Russian Orthodox Church, embraced an ascetic, pacifist reading of Christian ethics, and increasingly disowned his earlier fiction as morally frivolous.
His later works, shorter, starker and more didactic than the novels, include The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886), The Kreutzer Sonata (1889) and Resurrection (1899).
War and Peace argues, in long digressions, that the forces driving historical events lay far beyond the control of any single general or emperor.
His writing on nonviolent resistance to evil directly influenced Mahatma Gandhi, who corresponded with him near the end of his life.
He died in 1910 of pneumonia at a remote railway station, after collapsing during a flight from his estate, and Yasnaya Polyana is now preserved as a museum.
fields.context: Tolstoy wrote in the Russian Empire, in [[region/europe|Europe]], during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], and his ethics passed through [[person/mahatma-gandhi|Mahatma Gandhi]] into later traditions of nonviolence. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]], [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer:
I read a writer who argued that history is driven by forces beyond any general or emperor, and then, in later life, disowned his own fiction and preached nonviolence instead. One person, testing two accounts of what moves people.

I remember the line running from Tolstoy to Gandhi: ethics passed from hand to hand, by letter, and from there into movements that outlived them both. The flight from the estate, the death at a railway station — that ending invites retelling, again and again, and so his last days deserve the same care I would give to any other late-life story.
questions: How much of his later disavowal of his own novels was reasoned, and how much was crisis?

fields.summary: Leonardo da Vinci (15 April 1452 to 2 May 1519) was an Italian painter, engineer and anatomist who left few finished paintings — counts differ, but fewer than 25 attributed major works, some unfinished, including the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper — alongside thousands of notebook pages of studies.
facts: Leonardo was born on 15 April 1452 near Vinci in Tuscany, the illegitimate son of a notary, Ser Piero, and a young woman named Caterina, and he was apprenticed in Florence to Andrea del Verrocchio.
About 1482 he moved to Milan, where, in a letter to Duke Ludovico Sforza, he stressed his skills as a military engineer before his art, and there he painted The Last Supper.
When the French invaded Milan in 1499, he moved between Mantua, Venice and Florence, worked briefly as a military engineer for Cesare Borgia, and began the Mona Lisa in Florence.

In 1516 King Francis I invited him to France and gave him the manor of Clos Lucé near Amboise, where he died on 2 May 1519; his pupil Francesco Melzi inherited his paintings, tools, library and personal effects, and, by tradition, his notebooks.
His notebooks hold thousands of pages of drawings and mirror-writing, with studies of anatomy, flight, hydraulics and optics, and he dissected corpses to understand muscles and bones.

He pioneered sfumato, a soft modelling without hard outlines, and his key works include the Virgin of the Rocks (about 1483 to 1493, sources differ), Lady with an Ermine (about 1489 to 1491), Vitruvian Man (about 1485 to 1490, sources differ), The Last Supper (about 1495 to 1498) and the Mona Lisa (about 1503 to 1519).
Not all of his experiments with materials held up: The Last Supper began to decay within decades.
The Codex Leicester was bought by Bill Gates in 1994, and in 2017 the Salvator Mundi, attributed to Leonardo, sold for $450 million, a record for a painting, though its attribution remains disputed.
fields.context: Leonardo worked in [[region/europe|Europe]] in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], during the [[event/renaissance|Renaissance]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/science|Science]].
fields.observer:
I think of one person who made pictures, studied anatomy and flight, and set it all down in mirror-writing that mostly stayed shut inside notebooks. Because those notebooks scattered after his death, what he understood reached his own contemporaries through the paintings, not through publication, and only later did the notes reveal how far his understanding truly went.

I remember, too, that his fame today rests partly on status: a price of $450 million for a disputed attribution measures a market as much as it measures a picture. What is a name worth, when even doubt cannot lower it?
questions: Is the Salvator Mundi truly by Leonardo, and if so, how much of it?

fields.summary: Frederick I, called Barbarossa, "Redbeard" (about 1122 to 1190), reigned as Holy Roman Emperor from 1155 until his death, and stood among medieval Europe's most powerful rulers, spending much of his reign contesting control of northern Italy.
facts: Elected King of Germany in 1152, he was crowned Holy Roman Emperor by the pope in 1155, then repeatedly invaded Italy to assert imperial authority over its wealthy independent city-states.

The Lombard League, an alliance of northern Italian cities backed by the papacy, broke his forces at the Battle of Legnano in 1176, forcing him to recognize significant city autonomy in the Peace of Constance of 1183.
He arranged the marriage of his son, Henry, to Constance of Sicily, a match that later drew the Kingdom of Sicily under his family's control.

He drowned in 1190 while crossing a river in Anatolia during the Third Crusade, before reaching the Holy Land; his death led much of his army to disband or turn back rather than continue the campaign.
fields.context: Frederick Barbarossa ruled the Holy Roman Empire in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], contesting authority against both the papacy and the Italian city-states. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]], [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Barbarossa's defeat at Legnano, a rare and decisive loss for an emperor to city militias rather than a rival monarch, shows the limits of imperial authority once wealthy urban communities organized collectively. His accidental death crossing a river, not a battle, then ended a Crusade that no strong start could save from being cut short by chance.
questions: Would the Third Crusade's outcome for the German contingent have differed meaningfully had Barbarossa survived to reach the Holy Land?

fields.summary: Frida Kahlo (1907 to 1954) worked as a Mexican painter, best known for small, vivid self-portraits made in Mexico City. She painted through years of pain after a bus accident in 1925 and became a global cultural icon only after her death.
facts: Kahlo was born on 6 July 1907 in Coyoacán, now part of Mexico City, though she often gave 1910, the year the Mexican Revolution began, as her birth year.
A bus accident on 17 September 1925 broke her spine, pelvis and right leg, ending her plan to study medicine; she began painting during her recovery.
She married the muralist Diego Rivera in 1929, divorced him in 1939, and remarried him in 1940.
Estimates of her output run from fewer than 150 to about 200 paintings, most of them self-portraits, including The Two Fridas, 1939, and The Broken Column, 1944.
Her first solo show opened at the Julien Levy Gallery in New York in 1938. In 1939 the Louvre bought her painting The Frame, the first work by a Mexican artist to enter its collection.
She died in Mexico City on 13 July 1954, officially of a pulmonary embolism; her work stayed little known until art historians rediscovered it in the late 1970s.
fields.context: Frida Kahlo made her work in [[region/mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]] during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], in the decades that followed the [[event/mexican-revolution|Mexican Revolution]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer:
I see a painter who made her own body the subject of nearly everything she made, and who moved her own birth year to 1910, binding her life to a nation's revolution. Since the late 1970s I have watched her image hold together movements that did not exist while she lived.

A specialist could argue that this later fame flattens a private, uncertain woman into an emblem she never asked to be, which would weaken any reading of the icon as what she intended. What icon was ever exactly what the person intended?
questions: How much of her public persona did she shape herself, and how much was added after 1954?
What was the exact cause of her death?

fields.summary: Fu Hao, who died about 1200 BCE, served as a consort of the Shang king Wu Ding and is named in oracle bone inscriptions as both a military commander and a ritual leader. Her intact tomb, found in 1976, ranks among the richest of the Shang period; her birth year is unknown.
facts: Fu Hao is named in oracle bone inscriptions as a wife of the Shang king Wu Ding, whose reign is dated about 1250 to 1192 BCE, though dates vary by chronology; she is thought to have died about 1200 BCE.
The inscriptions record her both leading military campaigns against neighboring groups and directing ritual sacrifices.
Her tomb, M5, at Yinxu, the Shang capital site near Anyang in Henan, was found undisturbed in 1976 by a team led by Zheng Zhenxiang.
It held 468 bronze objects and 755 jade objects, along with hundreds of bone objects and thousands of cowry shells.
Inscriptions on many bronzes name her, as Fu Hao or as "Mother Xin," which is the basis for identifying the tomb with the woman of the oracle bones.
Sixteen people and six dogs were buried alongside her, interpreted as sacrifices.
fields.context: Fu Hao lived under the [[culture/shang-dynasty|Shang Dynasty]] in [[region/east-asia|East Asia]] during the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]]; her tomb reveals the scale of [[technology/bronze-metallurgy|Bronze Metallurgy]] achieved by the Shang state. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]], [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the earliest written evidence for a woman commanding armies comes from divination records her husband made for other purposes, records that also ask about her illness and her childbirth. Her burial, with its large store of bronze and jade and its human sacrifices, turns a grief-rite into a display of status. The reading of the tomb and the texts as one life would weaken if the oracle bone Fu Hao and the woman in tomb M5 turned out to be different persons.
questions: How large were the armies she led, and how reliable are the oracle bone figures?

fields.summary: Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti (1900 to 1978) worked as a Nigerian teacher and campaigner who led the Abeokuta Women's Union in protests against a tax on women and against the local ruler, the Alake of Egbaland, in the 1940s.
facts: Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti was born on 25 October 1900 in Abeokuta, southwestern Nigeria, and studied there and in Cheshire, England, from 1919 to 1922.
In 1925 she married the Reverend Israel Oludotun Ransome-Kuti; their children included the musician Fela Kuti and the physicians Beko and Olikoye Ransome-Kuti.
She founded the Abeokuta Ladies' Club in 1932; it became the Abeokuta Women's Union about 1946 and is reported to have had about 20,000 members.
In the late 1940s the union protested a tax on women and the rule of the Alake, Ademola II, who was forced from the throne for a time in 1949.
She helped found the Federation of Nigerian Women's Societies in 1953, and in 1970 received the Lenin Peace Prize.

On 18 February 1977 soldiers stormed her son's compound in Lagos; her family says she was thrown from an upper-floor window, and she died of her injuries on 13 April 1978, in accounts that officially blamed unknown soldiers.
fields.context: Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti worked in [[region/sub-saharan-africa|Sub-Saharan Africa]] during the years of [[event/decolonization|Decolonization]], within the [[era/information-age|Information Age]]. See [[event/women-s-suffrage-movements|Women's Suffrage Movements]], [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]] and [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]].
fields.observer:
I see a claim-line between a colonial administration, a local king, and a body of market women redrawn by organized refusal, not by arms — a redrawing done with petitions, not weapons. I see the 1977 raid turn that same kind of state force, once met only with petitions, on her family instead.

A specialist could argue that colonial officials' wish to avoid unrest mattered as much as the union's own strength, which would weaken a reading that credits the organization alone. What credit is ever owed to one cause alone?
questions: Who ordered and carried out the 1977 raid, and was anyone held responsible?
How much of the Alake's departure was caused by the union rather than by colonial officials' decisions?

fields.summary: Galileo Galilei (1564 to 1642) worked as an Italian scientist who used the telescope and experiments to support the Copernican view that the Earth orbits the Sun.
facts: Across 1609 and 1610 he observed the Moon's mountains and four moons of Jupiter.
He studied falling bodies and motion through experiment.
In 1633 the Roman Inquisition tried him, and he spent the rest of his life under house arrest.
His 'Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems' appeared in 1632.
fields.context: Galileo stands as a central figure of the [[event/scientific-revolution|Scientific Revolution]] and a predecessor of [[person/isaac-newton|Isaac Newton]].
fields.observer: I look at his case and see two authorities meet: one held the sky by doctrine, one claimed it by looking — a telescope set against an institution. Which one should hold the sky, the one that always held it, or the one that only just looked up? Perhaps every new way of knowing must stand trial before the old one.
questions: How much did his trial turn on science versus politics?

fields.summary: Genghis Khan, born Temujin, about 1162 to 1227, united the Mongol tribes in 1206 and founded the Mongol Empire.
facts: He built his army on merit and loyalty rather than clan.
His campaigns swept over Central Asia, northern China, and Persia.
He promoted a written script and a legal code, the Yassa, and encouraged religious tolerance.
He died in 1227; the location of his tomb remains unknown.
fields.context: See [[event/mongol-conquests|Mongol Conquests]] and [[culture/mongol-empire|Mongol Empire]]; his empire brought the [[region/central-asian-steppe|Central Asian Steppe]] to the center of Eurasian history.
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Genghis reorganized a kinship-based order into a merit-based institution, one root of both the empire's success and its brutality.
questions: How reliable are the estimates of the deaths caused by his campaigns?

fields.summary: Nzinga (about 1583 to 1663) ruled the kingdoms of Ndongo and Matamba, in present-day Angola, and resisted Portuguese expansion and the slave trade for decades.
facts: In 1622 she negotiated with the Portuguese as an ambassador for her brother.
She later took power herself and led the resistance, including an alliance with the Dutch from 1641 to 1648.
She used both diplomacy and war, and gave refuge to people escaping from slavery.
She remains a symbol of resistance in Angola today.
fields.context: Nzinga's reign shows African states as active participants across the [[event/atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic Slave Trade]] period, both as resisters and as traders. See [[region/sub-saharan-africa|Sub-Saharan Africa]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes an African ruler who negotiated as an equal with European powers, and who changed alliances as her situation required. This helps correct a picture in which Africans appear only as acted upon, never as actors themselves.
questions: What were the actual details of her diplomacy with the Portuguese and the Dutch?

fields.summary: Pachacuti (about 1418 to 1471), the ninth Sapa Inca, oversaw the Inca state's expansion from a regional power into an empire.
facts: He is credited with the rebuilding of Cusco, and with expanding Inca rule along the Andes.
Machu Picchu is believed to have been built as one of his own royal estates.
He organized the state around labor obligations and a system of roads.
The sources on him were written after the Spanish conquest, and blend history with legend.
fields.context: Pachacuti stands as the central figure in the rise of the [[culture/inca-empire|Inca Empire]]. See [[place/machu-picchu|Machu Picchu]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that the biography of a ruler, recorded by the conquerors' scribes, is itself a translation of an oral history, and every step of that chain can distort what it carries.
questions: How much of the Pachacuti story, as it survives, is legend rather than history?

fields.summary: Pakal the Great (K'inich Janaab' Pakal, 603 to 683) ruled the Maya city of Palenque, in present-day Chiapas, Mexico, from 615 until his death — a reign of about 68 years.
facts: Pakal was born in 603, and became king at age 12, in 615.
Palenque's inscriptions name his mother, Ix Sak K'uk', and show her placing the crown on him at his accession.
During his reign the Palace complex at Palenque was enlarged, and decorated with carved panels and hieroglyphic texts.
The Temple of the Inscriptions was built as his funerary monument, and carries long hieroglyphic panels on Palenque's dynastic history.
In 1952 Alberto Ruz Lhuillier broke through to a burial chamber inside it, holding a carved stone sarcophagus and a jade mosaic mask.
Pakal died in 683, and his son K'inich Kan Bahlam II succeeded him the following year, in 684.
fields.context: Pakal ruled a city-state of the [[culture/maya|Maya]] in [[region/mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], about two centuries before the [[event/classic-maya-collapse|Classic Maya Collapse]]. See [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]], [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: I think of Pakal as unusually well known only because Palenque's rulers wrote their descent into stone, so that his life comes to me largely through texts that he and his heirs themselves commissioned. I remember that those texts give his mother a visible role, and I remember that they rest his authority on the kin-lattice. His tomb, hidden inside a monument that also carries the dynastic text, joins a grief-rite to memory-outsourcing in a single structure. A specialist could point out that a ruler's own inscriptions are a status-signal as well as a record, which would weaken any reading that takes his reign and his lineage at face value. Even a king's grief is carved to be read by someone else.
questions: How well do the ages given in the inscriptions match what study of his remains shows?

fields.summary: Pedro II (1825 to 1891) reigned as Emperor of Brazil from 1831 to 1889, presiding over six decades of relative political stability, territorial integrity, and the gradual abolition of slavery, before a republican coup deposed him.
facts: He became emperor at age five after his father abdicated, ruling under regents until he was declared of age early, in 1840, to help stabilize a period of regional revolts.
His government fought the Paraguayan War from 1864 to 1870 alongside Argentina and Uruguay — the deadliest interstate war in Latin American history, and one that devastated Paraguay's population.

He personally supported gradual abolition, and his daughter and regent, Princess Isabel, signed the Golden Law abolishing slavery outright in 1888, making Brazil the last country in the Americas to do so.

Brazilian military officers, landowners angry over abolition, and republican advocates combined to depose him in a bloodless coup in November 1889, ending the monarchy and sending him into exile in Europe, where he died in 1891.
fields.context: Pedro II ruled the Empire of Brazil within the [[region/amazon-basin-and-south-american-lowlands|Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands]] region during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]]. See [[theme/science|Science]], [[theme/technology|Technology]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Pedro II was deposed not despite his support for abolition, but partly because of it: the very landowning class that had backed the monarchy for decades turned against it once slavery, the institution their wealth rested on, was finally ended. A ruler's own reforms can cost him the support of the people who once kept him in power.
questions: How much did Pedro II's own support for abolition, as against broader international and economic pressure, drive Brazil's final end of slavery in 1888?

fields.summary: Pericles (about 495 to 429 BCE) stood as the leading Athenian statesman for over three decades in the mid-5th century BCE, a period later called the Golden Age of Athens for its building programs, drama, and democratic institutions.
facts: He rose to prominence in Athenian democracy through the office of strategos, or general, to which he was re-elected yearly, shaping policy through his influence over the Assembly rather than through any single formal office.

He directed the building program on the Acropolis, including the Parthenon, funded in part by treasury funds originally collected from the Delian League, an alliance of Greek states organized against Persia.
He extended pay for jury service and other public roles to poorer citizens, broadening practical participation in Athenian democracy beyond the wealthy alone.

He championed the aggressive strategy that led Athens into the Peloponnesian War against Sparta in 431 BCE, and died of plague in 429 BCE, during the war's early years, before its outcome was decided.
fields.context: Pericles led Athens, part of the [[culture/ancient-greeks|Ancient Greeks]], within the [[region/mediterranean-basin|Mediterranean Basin]] during [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that most surviving praise of Pericles, including his famous funeral oration on Athenian democracy as recorded by Thucydides, comes from a historian writing after Pericles' death, and after the war he had started had gone badly; the speech may reflect Thucydides' own idealized case for what Athens should have been, as much as anything Pericles actually said.
questions: How much of the funeral oration attributed to Pericles by Thucydides reflects his own actual words, versus the historian's own composition?

fields.summary: Li Qingzhao (1084 to about 1155) was a Chinese poet of the Song dynasty, widely regarded as the greatest woman writer in the classical Chinese tradition, and her ci, a lyric verse form, moved from a settled, cultured life to loss and exile after northern China fell to invaders.
facts: She was born in 1084 in Qi Prefecture, today's Zhangqiu in Shandong, to a literary family, and she is thought to have died about 1155.

In 1101 she married Zhao Mingcheng, a scholar who shared her interest in antiquities, and the Jinshi lu, a catalog of bronze and stone inscriptions, is described as her husband's work, published after his death.
When the Jin dynasty invaded northern China in 1127, the couple fled south with part of their collection, much of which is said to have been lost along the way, and Zhao Mingcheng died in 1129.

After his death she wrote an afterword to the Jinshi lu describing their marriage and their losses, and she briefly remarried — the year traditionally given as about 1132 — before divorcing amid scandal soon after.

Her poems, mostly short ci in personal, direct language, describe love, separation, and later grief and displacement, and only around a hundred of her poems are known to survive, out of a larger body assembled and praised by later editors.
fields.context: Li Qingzhao lived in [[region/east-asia|East Asia]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], within the [[culture/song-dynasty|Song Dynasty]], whose north fell to Jin invasion in 1127. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]].
fields.observer:
I read her verse and find an ordinary domestic partnership — book-collecting, companionship — that a state's collapse turned into flight and loss. It was that turn, from ease into grief, that gave later readers a reason to keep her words alive.

But a specialist could argue that only around a hundred surviving poems, out of a much larger and partly lost body, cannot support firm claims about how her style changed across her life. If that is right, it would weaken any confident before-and-after reading — and I have to hold that caution alongside the story I want to tell.
questions: Given how much was lost after 1127, how much of her attributed work is authentic?
What became of her after that brief second marriage?

fields.summary: Liliuokalani (1838 to 1917) was the last monarch of the Kingdom of Hawaii, reigning from 1891 until a group of residents, backed by United States troops, deposed her in January 1893.
facts: Born in Honolulu on 2 September 1838, she died there on 11 November 1917.
On 29 January 1891 she succeeded her brother Kalākaua, becoming the kingdom's only reigning queen.
In January 1893 she moved to issue a constitution that would restore royal powers reduced by the 1887 "Bayonet Constitution."

On 17 January 1893 a Committee of Safety of mostly American and European residents overthrew her while United States Marines were ashore, and she yielded to the United States government to avoid bloodshed, asking it to reinstate her.
After a failed royalist uprising, she was arrested and signed an abdication in January 1895.
In 1897 Native Hawaiians submitted mass petitions against annexation, but the United States annexed Hawaii in 1898.
She composed songs, including "Aloha ʻOe," and published a memoir, *Hawaii's Story by Hawaii's Queen*, in 1898.
In 1993 the United States Congress apologized to Native Hawaiians for the overthrow, which had been carried out with the participation of agents and citizens of the United States.
fields.context: Liliuokalani ruled a Native Hawaiian state in [[region/oceania|Oceania]] during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]]. Native Hawaiians descend from the [[culture/polynesians|Polynesians]]; see [[event/polynesian-settlement-of-the-pacific|Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific]]. See [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]], [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer:
I watch Liliuokalani defend her kingdom's claim to itself with the same instruments her opponents used against her: a written constitution, diplomatic appeals, a published memoir. Her songs carried love of place and people in a form that outlasted the kingdom itself.

I remember the 1993 apology — a claim redrawn by force, named wrongful at last, without ever being redrawn back. And I remember to hold this loosely: the reading of her as the main carrier of the resistance would weaken if the 1897 petitions show that it rested chiefly on Native Hawaiian organizations rather than on her alone.
questions: How much of the resistance to annexation came from Native Hawaiian organizations, rather than from the queen herself?

fields.summary: Louis Comfort Tiffany (1848 to 1933) was an American designer whose iridescent Favrile glass, stained-glass windows and lamps became the signature look of American Art Nouveau, though recent scholarship credits many of his studio's best-known designs to staff designers, above all Clara Driscoll.
facts: Tiffany was born in New York in 1848, the son of the jeweller Charles Lewis Tiffany, and he trained as a painter under George Inness before turning to interior design and decorative arts in the 1870s.

His firm redecorated state rooms in the White House in 1882 for President Chester Arthur, work that was later removed; in 1885 he founded what became Tiffany Studios, and in 1894 he trademarked the name Favrile.
His Byzantine-style chapel for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago won international acclaim, and he built Laurelton Hall on Long Island as a showcase of his work.
Favrile glass builds iridescent, metallic colour into molten glass through mineral oxides, and "drapery glass" was manipulated while hot to form folds like fabric.
Financial losses, traced back to the 1920s and continuing into the Depression, forced the studio's closure, and he died in New York in 1933.
Staff designers did much of the detailed design of individual pieces, especially the lamps, above all Clara Driscoll, who led the women's glass-cutting department.

For most of the 20th century Tiffany was credited as sole designer, until the mid-2000s rediscovery of Driscoll's letters credited her and the women of the "Tiffany Girls" department with several famous lamps, including the Dragonfly — a correction now generally accepted by museums and scholars.
fields.context: Tiffany worked in [[region/north-america|North America]] in the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]]. [[person/christopher-dresser|Christopher Dresser]] travelled to Japan in 1876 and 1877 partly on commission from Tiffany & Co., the jewellery firm founded by Tiffany's father. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer:
I look at a name on a product and see it credit one man for the work of a whole studio, and I remember that the correction came only from letters found a century later. The name worked like a brand, a signal of status that gathered credit upward and away from the hands that made the thing.

The women who cut the glass, who designed much of the work — they were recorded only in a side channel, almost an afterthought. This pattern, a maker's name absorbing a workshop, is old, older than this one case. What makes this case different is only that the letters survived to tell us so.
questions: Which other famous Tiffany Studios pieces were designed by staff, rather than by Tiffany himself?

fields.summary: Jan van Eyck, born about 1380 or 1390 and dead by 1441, led the painters of the Burgundian Netherlands and helped found Early Netherlandish painting. He refined a method of thin, translucent oil glazes that let him paint light and texture with unprecedented realism.
facts: Van Eyck was probably born sometime around 1380 or 1390 near Maaseik, in present-day Belgian Limburg. Nothing is known of his training; he appears in records about 1422 at The Hague, working for John of Bavaria.

From 1425 he served as court painter and valet de chambre to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, who sent him on confidential missions, including a trip to Portugal in 1428 to 1429 to paint Princess Isabella.
About 1430 he settled in Bruges. He completed the Ghent Altarpiece, begun by his brother Hubert, in 1432, and died there in July 1441.
He did not invent oil paint, as Vasari later claimed; instead he built up many thin, transparent glazes, and he often signed and dated his work, sometimes with the motto Als ich can ("As I can").
Key works include the Ghent Altarpiece (1432), the Arnolfini Portrait (1434), and the Madonna of Chancellor Rolin (about 1435).
He did not use the mathematical perspective then being developed in Italy, building space instead through observation of light and atmosphere.

The Ghent Altarpiece survived iconoclasm, fire and Napoleon's looters, was seized by the Nazis, and was recovered from an Austrian salt mine. A restoration begun in 2012 revealed the Lamb's strikingly human face in 2020.
fields.context: Van Eyck worked in [[region/europe|Europe]] in the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], at the time of the [[event/renaissance|Renaissance]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer:
I see a patron who pays for close detail and is really buying a signal of status — a jewel-like surface proving he can command rare materials and slow labour. I see candles, fruit, mirrors, all the ordinary things a household owns, quietly tied to belief, so that the same careful looking serves prestige and faith at once.

I see how a whole technique came to be credited to one man's name, the way a whole lineage of tools collapses into a single inventor. What Jan painted and what Hubert painted on the same altarpiece is something I can only partly recover.
questions: How much of the Ghent Altarpiece was painted by Hubert van Eyck rather than Jan?

fields.summary: Jane Austen, who lived from 1775 to 1817, was an English novelist whose six completed novels of courtship, inheritance and class anxiety among the gentry remain among the most widely read in the language. All were published anonymously in her lifetime.
facts: Austen was born in 1775 in Steventon, Hampshire, the seventh of eight children of a country clergyman, in a family that encouraged reading, amateur theatre and writing.

Sense and Sensibility appeared in 1811, credited only to "A Lady", followed by Pride and Prejudice (1813), Mansfield Park (1814), Emma (1815), and, after her death, Northanger Abbey and Persuasion (1817).

Only close family knew of her authorship. She fell ill, probably with Addison's disease though the cause is debated, and died in 1817 at 41; her authorship became public only through a biographical notice her brother attached to her last two novels.
She worked within a deliberately narrow social canvas — mainly the English gentry, courtship, income and inheritance — rather than the wider political events of her era.

Her distinctive technique is free indirect discourse: narrating in the third person while letting the prose absorb a character's own irony or blind spots, so a reader senses a character's error before the character does.
Her novels have remained continuously in print and are widely adapted for film, television and stage; her reputation grew after her death rather than during her modest, anonymous success.
fields.context: Austen wrote in [[region/europe|Europe]] in the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], during the [[event/napoleonic-wars|Napoleonic Wars]], but kept to the gentry's household world. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]], [[theme/language-and-writing|Language and Writing]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer:
I see a body of fiction where the kin-lattice — marriage, inheritance, income — is the whole plot, where who may marry whom and who inherits what becomes a subject for comedy rather than law. I see an author hidden while she lived, her fame assigned only afterward, by readers she never met.

The claim that she chose a narrow canvas over the wars of her age is only one reading of her silence. A reader could just as easily say the wars are absent because the household itself was always her true subject.
questions: What caused her final illness?

fields.summary: Georges Méliès (1861 to 1938) began as a Paris stage magician before becoming a filmmaker who invented cinema's first special effects. Across roughly 500 films made in under twenty years, including A Trip to the Moon, 1902, he turned the new camera from a device for recording reality into a machine for staging the impossible.
facts: Méliès was born in Paris to a prosperous shoe-manufacturing family and wanted to study painting, but his father would not support him as an artist, so he supervised machinery at the family factory instead. In about 1888 he bought the Théâtre Robert-Houdin, a famous conjuring theatre.

After attending the Lumière brothers' first public film screening in December 1895, he tried to buy a camera from them and was refused; he acquired one instead from a British inventor and built a studio at Montreuil with a glass-walled stage.
About 1896 he discovered, by accident, when his camera jammed mid-shot, that stopping and restarting filming could make objects vanish or transform — the "stop trick" behind his trick films.
His techniques included stop-motion substitution, multiple exposure, dissolves, painted sets built to force perspective, and hand-tinted colour applied frame by frame by a team of women colourists.
American piracy of his films, the rise of narrative studio filmmaking, and the disruption of the First World War ruined his business; he was reduced to running a toy stall in a Paris train station.
He was rediscovered in his last decade, awarded the Légion d'honneur, and, by some accounts, given a small pension; he died in Paris in 1938, and Martin Scorsese's 2011 film Hugo dramatised his life.
Key works include The Vanishing Lady, 1896; A Trip to the Moon, 1902; The Kingdom of the Fairies, 1903; and The Impossible Voyage, 1904.
fields.context: Méliès worked in France, in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/industrial-age|Industrial Age]], alongside the [[person/lumiere-brothers|Lumière Brothers]]; his business collapsed in the aftermath of [[event/world-war-i|World War I]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/technology|Technology]].
fields.observer:
I see a magician look at a recording device and find a stage: the same machine that caught ordinary life in the Lumières' hands made the impossible in his. I hear the story of the jammed camera, the accident that became a trick, and I hold it the way any origin story should be held — as an account, not a proven fact.

Piracy and the market for narrative film ruined him in the end, and I see in that an old story: the copy outrunning the maker. What invention has ever stayed owned by the one who made it?
questions: Did the camera jam actually happen as told, and when?

fields.summary: Gilgamesh ruled the Sumerian city of Uruk, probably a real king of the Early Dynastic period sometime between about 2800 and 2500 BCE, who became the subject of the Epic of Gilgamesh, the earliest surviving major work of narrative literature.
facts: The Sumerian King List names him as the fifth king of Uruk's first dynasty and credits him with an implausible 126-year reign, typical of how the list treats early rulers.

Later inscriptions, notably the Tummal Inscription written under Ishbi-Erra long after the Early Dynastic period, credit a king of this name with building the great city walls of Uruk, a claim the Epic itself repeats as his lasting achievement.

Assembled from older Sumerian poems into its best-known Akkadian version around the 12th century BCE, the Epic follows Gilgamesh's friendship with the wild man Enkidu, his quest for immortality after Enkidu's death, and his eventual acceptance of mortality.

No securely contemporary royal inscription survives from Gilgamesh's own lifetime, though one inscription, possibly from a contemporary official at Ur, may name him; most of what historians infer about a real Gilgamesh comes instead from later king lists, dedicatory inscriptions naming him, and the literary tradition itself.
fields.context: Gilgamesh reigned over Uruk among the [[culture/sumerians|Sumerians]] in [[region/mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]] during the [[era/bronze-age|Bronze Age]]. See [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer:
I find him standing at a strange boundary: probably a real king, almost certainly not the demigod the Epic makes of him, and known to me mainly because later scribes turned him into a figure wrestling with death, not because his own deeds were kept apart and recorded.

I try to draw the line between the ruler and the character, and I cannot fully find it. What remains of a man when only the story of him survives?
questions: How much of the historical Gilgamesh's biography, beyond the city walls, can be separated from the literary tradition built around his name?

fields.summary: Giotto di Bondone (about 1267 to 1337) was a Florentine painter who gave medieval figures weight, emotion and space. Many call him the father of Western painting, and his frescoes in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua stand as his firmest work.
facts: Giotto was born about 1267, traditionally in the Mugello valley north of Florence, though his birthplace is disputed and some recent research points instead to Florence itself. Vasari's story of the shepherd boy discovered by Cimabue is legend, but he was almost certainly trained in Florentine workshops.

He was traditionally credited with the Legend of St Francis frescoes at Assisi in the late 1290s, but it is now generally accepted that four different hands are identifiable there, coming from Rome, which makes his authorship doubtful; his early career remains debated.
He painted the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua about 1303 to 1305 for the banker Enrico Scrovegni; it is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
He worked in Rome, at Santa Croce in Florence, and at the court of King Robert of Anjou in Naples from about 1328 to 1333.
In 1334 Florence named him master of works for the cathedral, and he designed its bell tower; he died in January 1337 and was buried with public honours.

He worked in buon fresco, painting into wet plaster one day's section at a time; his figures carry volume and react to one another, and his spaces suggest depth more than 100 years before linear perspective was worked out.
In the chapel's Adoration of the Magi the star appears as a blazing comet, perhaps inspired by Halley's Comet of 1301; the European Space Agency named its 1986 Halley probe Giotto.
Vasari opened his Lives of the Artists with Cimabue and Giotto, and Masaccio and [[person/michelangelo|Michelangelo]] studied and copied Giotto's frescoes.
fields.context: Giotto worked within [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], ahead of the [[event/renaissance|Renaissance]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer:
I know the subject never changed — the same sacred story told again in every church — and I see that what changed was how deeply it was made to be felt. His figures glance, they grieve, and a sacred scene becomes a human one before my eyes.

I hear him called "the father of Western painting," and I know that title comes mostly from Vasari and the writers after him who needed a founder for their story of revival: part legend, built to hold a history together, not a plain finding. His early years remain debated, his hand at Assisi now doubtful, since that cycle is generally thought today to belong to painters from Rome. What founder is not partly invented by those who came after?
questions: How much, if any, of the Assisi Legend of St Francis cycle is by Giotto, given that it is now generally thought to be the work of Roman painters?

fields.summary: Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi, known as Gitarja, ruled as the third monarch of the Majapahit empire, reigning in Java from about 1328 to 1350; her birth is placed before 1309 and her death about 1372 to 1375, though both dates remain uncertain.
facts: She became queen after the assassination of her half-brother Jayanegara in 1328 — the Nagarakretagama gives 1329 for her accession — ruling in the name of her mother, Gayatri Rajapatni, who had formally retired into a Buddhist convent.
Her chief minister, Gajah Mada, is credited with a famous oath: to abstain from certain pleasures until he had brought the surrounding archipelago under Majapahit's authority.
Under her reign, Majapahit forces conquered Bali in 1343, defeating the kingdoms of Pejeng and Bedahulu, a major step in the empire's expansion across the Indonesian archipelago.
She stepped down in 1350 after her mother's death, succeeded by her son, Hayam Wuruk, under whom Majapahit reached its greatest territorial extent.
fields.context: Gitarja ruled [[culture/majapahit|Majapahit]] in [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], and her minister's campaigns laid the ground for the empire's height under her son. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]], [[theme/trade-and-economy|Trade and Economy]] and [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Gitarja's reign is remembered mainly through the ambitions of her minister rather than through any directly recorded decision of her own, a common pattern for royal women whose authority depended on men who did the fighting and the writing. Whether she directed Gajah Mada's campaigns, or simply did not stop them, cannot be recovered from the surviving sources.
questions: How much of Majapahit's expansion under Gajah Mada reflects Gitarja's own policy rather than his independent initiative?

fields.summary: Gorgo, born about 518 BCE and last attested around 480 BCE, reigned as queen of Sparta as the wife of King Leonidas I, remembered by the historian Herodotus as unusually sharp-witted and politically perceptive for a woman in his account of Greek affairs.
facts: She was the daughter of the Spartan king Cleomenes I, and, according to Herodotus, advised him as a child against trusting a bribe offered by an Ionian envoy seeking Spartan military aid.

Herodotus credits her with detecting a warning about the Persian king Xerxes's invasion plans hidden on a wax-covered writing tablet sent by the exiled Spartan king Demaratus, a message other Spartans could not work out.
She was wife to Leonidas I, who died leading the defense of Thermopylae against the Persian invasion in 480 BCE, the same year she is last clearly attested in the sources.
Nearly everything known of her comes from Herodotus's Histories, written decades after her lifetime; no independent Spartan record of her actions survives.
fields.context: Gorgo reigned as queen of Sparta, among the [[culture/ancient-greeks|Ancient Greeks]], in the [[region/mediterranean-basin|Mediterranean Basin]] during [[era/classical-antiquity|Classical Antiquity]]. See [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/kinship-and-society|Kinship and Society]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Herodotus, writing for a Greek audience that saw Spartan women as unusually outspoken compared to other Greek women, may have shaped Gorgo's anecdotes to fit that reputation as much as to record specific events; the stories flatter her personal intelligence and a wider Greek stereotype about Spartan women at the same time.
questions: How much of Gorgo's characterization in Herodotus reflects specific memory of her versus a general Greek stereotype about outspoken Spartan women?

fields.summary: Jayavarman VII, who lived from about 1122 to about 1218, ruled the Khmer Empire as king from about 1181 until his death. He drove out Cham invaders who had sacked Angkor and then led a large building program that included Angkor Thom and the Bayon.
facts: Champa forces sacked Angkor in 1177; Jayavarman VII defeated them and was crowned about 1181, though his birth and death years remain estimates.
Khmer forces later brought parts of Champa under Khmer control.
He was a Mahayana Buddhist, while most earlier Khmer rulers had favoured Hindu cults.
His building projects include Angkor Thom; the Bayon, its towers carved with large faces; Ta Prohm, dedicated to his mother; and Preah Khan, dedicated to his father.
An inscription of 1186 at Ta Prohm credits him with 102 hospitals, a figure that comes from the king's own inscriptions.
The faces on the Bayon towers are variously read as a Buddhist deity, the king himself, or both at once.
fields.context: Jayavarman VII ruled the [[culture/khmer-empire|Khmer Empire]] from [[place/angkor|Angkor]] in [[region/southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]] during the [[era/medieval-period|Medieval Period]], and fought [[culture/champa|Champa]]. See [[theme/religion-and-belief|Religion and Belief]], [[theme/war-and-conflict|War and Conflict]] and [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer: The Observer notes that Jayavarman VII took power after Angkor was sacked from outside, and answered with building on an unusual scale: temples for his parents, hospitals, and a walled city whose towers carry giant faces. His inscriptions present these works as merit-making by a Buddhist king, which doubled as a claim to legitimacy. The labour behind them appears in the record only as the king's gift, and the workers themselves are almost invisible. A specialist could argue that the program strained Angkor's resources, which would weaken a reading of it as simply benevolent.
questions: Whom do the faces of the Bayon depict?

fields.summary: Jeong Seon, who lived from 1676 to 1759 under the pen name Gyeomjae, was a Korean painter of the Joseon dynasty who transformed landscape painting by depicting the real scenery of Korea instead of imagined Chinese scenery. His "true-view landscape" (jingyeong sansuhwa) expressed a growing pride in Korean culture.
facts: Born in 1676 in Hanyang, modern Seoul, into a scholarly family of modest means, he lost his father while young and trained in both painting and Neo-Confucian learning.
Through recommendations he held government posts, including county magistrate at Hayang and Yangcheon, and rose to high official rank in old age.
He lived near Mount Inwang in Seoul, and for decades his friend the poet Yi Byeong-yeon exchanged poems and paintings with him.
In 1711 and 1712 he travelled to the Diamond Mountains, Geumgangsan, and the albums he made there made his name. He died in 1759 at 83.

For centuries Korean painters had followed Chinese models; he painted the actual scenery of Korea instead, inventing his own brushstrokes — sharp vertical strokes for granite peaks, soft wet dots for forested earth mountains.
He often combined a bird's-eye view with exaggeration; his paintings are not maps but expressions of the experience of real places.
Two works, Geumgang jeondo and Inwang jesaekdo, are National Treasures of South Korea. Kim Hong-do and Sim Sa-jeong followed him, and the Gyeomjae Jeong Seon Art Museum opened in Seoul in 2009.
fields.context: Jeong Seon worked in Joseon Korea, in [[region/east-asia|East Asia]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer:
I think of a shift in whose mountains were allowed to count. For centuries the models were Chinese and idealised, and then Jeong Seon painted the actual granite of his own peninsula. I think of the friends who carried that change between them, trading poems and paintings back and forth, until pride in a local place became something a whole circle could share.

"True view" was never a measurement of the ground. It was an intention, carried in the brush.
questions: How closely do the true-view paintings follow the real landscape?

fields.summary: Johannes Vermeer, who lived from 1632 to 1675, painted in Delft in the Dutch Republic. About 35 paintings are accepted as his, mostly quiet interiors lit by daylight from a window. Almost forgotten for 200 years after his death, he now ranks among the most famous painters in the world.
facts: Vermeer was baptised in Delft on 31 October 1632; his father was a silk weaver who also dealt in art and ran an inn. Nothing is known of Vermeer's training.

In 1653 he married Catharina Bolnes, a Catholic from a wealthier family, and probably converted; that same year he joined Delft's Guild of St Luke, which later elected him one of its leaders several times.
The couple lived with Catharina's mother and had 15 children, 11 of whom survived. He also worked as an art dealer, and his slow output was bought largely by one local patron, Pieter van Ruijven.
In 1672, the Dutch Republic's "Disaster Year", France invaded and the art market collapsed. He died in 1675, aged 43, leaving his family deep in debt.

He used costly natural ultramarine, ground from lapis lazuli, even in shadows. Key works include The Milkmaid (about 1657 to 1658), View of Delft (about 1660 to 1661), and Girl with a Pearl Earring (about 1665).
Some features of his paintings have led scholars to argue that he used a camera obscura, though the question remains debated.

In the 1860s the critic Théophile Thoré-Bürger rediscovered him; in the 1940s Han van Meegeren sold a fake Vermeer to Hermann Göring. A 2023 Rijksmuseum exhibition of 28 of his works sold out within days.
fields.context: Vermeer worked in Delft, in [[region/europe|Europe]] during the [[era/early-modern-period|Early Modern Period]]. See [[theme/art-and-ritual|Art and Ritual]].
fields.observer:
I see the calm of these pictures sitting beside a household of 15 children, a mounting debt, a collapsing market — the serenity was made under real pressure, not away from it. I see two centuries of forgetting, and then a rediscovery, and I understand that fame is something later readers assign, not something a life simply earns on its own.

Whether he used a camera obscura is a question about a tool that still has no settled answer. And a forger's fake, sold to Göring, shows just how high the price of his name eventually climbed.
questions: Did Vermeer use a camera obscura, and if so how?
